The ancients ascribed unto foreign words a supernatural power [^203]. Language is no accidental production of a people, but the creation of its genius, the bearer of its ideas. That which was experienced by the early Christians was, evidently, higher even than so great a collective creation as the language of each nation, and needed the ideational wealth of all languages. It stood even above this latter. Bl. Theodoret by the tongues in which glossolalists spoke understands "certain noetic languages wherewith angels chant praises and hymns unto God" [^204]. For this reason the gift of tongues need not necessarily be understood as continuous discourse in foreign languages; the glossolalist could borrow therefrom the most expressive words; unto this, apparently, the expression of the Apostle Paul points: **"Ye have received *(Orig. p. 39)* the Spirit of adoption, whereby we cry, Abba, Father"** [^205]. That elevation in which the glossolalist found himself could impart unto his speech even in his native tongue an obscurity that required interpretation. His speech issued from those depths of the soul that are not illumined by the light of consciousness—from the spirit, and not the intellect. It is possible that this speech was supplemented by other expressions of feeling, for example by sighs, unto which, perhaps, the words of the Apostle point:

Paul: **"The Spirit Itself [Himself] maketh intercession for us with groanings which cannot be uttered"** [^206]. Intense spiritual animation could summon to the aid of the word also the sounds of singing, inasmuch as music in general expresses our feelings more powerfully than the word. (If so, we might comfort ourselves with the thought that not only the content of Christian prayers and hymns, but also their very melody was inspired by the Spirit of God and, of course, has preserved His seal down to our own time).

### Significance and Dignity of the Gift of Tongues

One thing can be stated with certainty concerning the gift of tongues: that from the internal side, as regards the state of the soul, speaking with tongues was a state of special spiritual, profound prayer. In this state man spoke directly unto God, with God, and penetrated into mysteries. This was a state of religious ecstasy [^207], for the accessibility of which unto himself the Apostle Paul warmly thanketh God [^208]. From the external side it was so sublime a phenomenon, entirely worthy of the Spirit of God, that for unbelievers themselves it was a sign demonstrating visually the presence of the Godhead Himself in Christian assemblies [^209]. This was a state of the highest spiritual elevation. Especially sublime in this phenomenon was the fact that, notwithstanding all the force of the feeling that then seized man, he did not lose mastery over himself; he could restrain and regulate the external manifestations of this state—remaining silent while another spoke, awaiting his own turn. **"And the spirits of the prophets are subject to the prophets"** [^210], testifieth the Apostle Paul. To such a degree did this state stand above any neuropathic-physiological ground.

And yet the Apostle Paul places the gift of tongues below prophecy. In the gift of tongues there was something, as it were, elemental, answering to that stage of development at which mankind then stood. In this gift there was something in common with those primitive forms of prophesying which it assumed, for example, under Saul [^211], and which in turn in its external forms recalled the mantic frenzy of paganism. The Apostle Paul, by his contrast of speaking with tongues unto prophecy, deprives of ground the inclination toward enthusiastic *(Orig. p. 40)* excesses and the darkening of clear Christian consciousness, as these had begun to assert themselves in Corinth. He closes before the Church the road upon which the Gnostics subsequently entered—the road toward the degeneration of this gift into orgiasm and magic [^212]. Through the conjunction of interpretation, speaking with tongues, like prophecy, received edifying power for all. In the time of St. Irenaeus († 202) speaking with tongues, although preserved, visibly transitions into prophecy. At least, the function of a prophet distinctive in the Apostle Paul—"to reveal secrets"—St. Irenaeus ascribes unto the glossolalist: "We have heard many brethren in the Church who possessed prophetic gifts, and through the Spirit spake with diverse tongues, and for the common profit brought forth the secrets of men, and expounded the mysteries of God" [^213].

### Traces of Glossolalia in Ancient and Present Divine Worship

Nonetheless, as the expression of a profound, awe-inspiring religious feeling, the gift of tongues could not fail to exert a great and lasting influence upon Christian divine worship. It created that gracious breath which was preserved in this divine worship, and, when this gift ceased, was preserved by being cast into other forms. In later and even contemporary divine worship one can point out certain particulars that constitute traces of ancient speaking with tongues in divine services. From speaking with tongues one may derive, for example, the ancient liturgical exclamation **"Maranatha,"** appointed at the Eucharist in the *Teaching of the Twelve Apostles* [^214] and cited, presumably from liturgical practice, by the Apostle Paul [^215]. This exclamation is a Syriac phrase signifying "Our Lord hath come" (prophetic past) or "Come!": *Mar*—Lord, *an* or *ana*—our, *atha*—hath come, or *tha*—come. Thus the exclamation expresses the intense expectation of the near advent of Christ among the early Christians. Exegetes strive in vain to explain the Syriac language of this exclamation [^216]; yet on the supposition that it issued from the mouth of a glossolalist during divine worship, this oddity is explained naturally. Even St. John Chrysostom seeks only traces of glossolalia in the divine worship of his own time: "And now we have only signs of the gifts of that time. Even now we speak two or three and in turn, and when one falls silent, another begins; yet all these are only signs and monuments of the former things. For this reason, when we begin to speak, the people answer: **'And to thy *(Orig. p. 41)* spirit,'** expressing thereby that from antiquity they spoke thus not by their own wisdom, but by the inspiration of the Spirit" [^217].

Traces of speaking with tongues must also be such fragmentary words in the ancient sung office (*asmatike akolouthia*) as "Unto the universe, Alleluia," as well as in contemporary divine worship a certain disconnectedness and abruptness (and the mystery bound up therewith) of the exclamations at the most important part of the Liturgy (its Anaphora / "canon") and at the conclusion of Vespers and Matins. Of the same character is the exclamation **"Wisdom!"** (*Sophia*), indicating the solemnity not of those prayers and hymns before which it is proclaimed, but of the very moment of the church service itself (for example, the Entrance).

It is possible that a centuries-old echo of glossolalia in the former Graeco-Slavonic divine service was the so-called vocalized refrains (*popevki* / *terirems*), or the addition unto the text of a hymn, at especially solemn places, of extraneous syllables—a custom preserved down to the sixteenth century. In the oldest of Russian typikons, that of the Moscow Synodal (Typography) Library of the 11th–12th centuries, at the Gradual Psalms (*anabathmoi* / *stepenny*) of Sunday Matins, which then replaced the present Polyeleos, there is appointed **"Alleluia"** with such vocal refrains: *"aleneluia aleneve enevene luia aleneve eneve neveneve eneve eneluia"* [^218]. In the Horologion of the Krakow edition of 1491, at the refrains of the Introductory Psalm of Vespers, **"Glory to Thee, O Lord,"** there are appointed such refrains: *"Glory to Thee, O Lord, anene naana neanene naaa inane, Who hast created all things"* [^219]. A trace of glossolalia is likewise the use during divine worship, and that too at its most solemn moments, of Hebrew and Greek words: **"Alleluia,"** **"Amen"** [^220], **"Kyrie, eleison"** [^221]. In glossolalia also has its foundation the aspiration toward creating a distinct liturgical language: in Roman Catholicism this legitimate aspiration, proceeding from the conviction that one must converse with God in a special, angelic language, is carried to an extreme, yet it is not alien unto all the Orthodox Churches: the Greek liturgical language (itacistic) was scarcely ever colloquial (as its etacistic form in the oldest Latin transcriptions demonstrates), nor was liturgical Slavonic [^222].

*(Orig. p. 42)*  

### Freedom and Norm in Apostolic Worship

With the abundance of spiritual gifts in the apostolic Church and their extensive employment during divine worship, the latter could not fail at that time to differ from our own by considerable freedom and diversity. The content of divine worship was determined by which of the charismatic persons participated in it, and what revelations or what inspiration each received during divine services. But since a distinctive property of Christian inspiration is that the spirits of the prophets are subject to the prophets—that is, the preservation during inspiration of full consciousness and self-mastery—such freedom and diversity of the divine worship of that time permitted a certain restriction through correct order and ritual (*ordo* / *taxis*), through free submission unto which it only gained in its grandeur and beauty. Thus already in this enthusiastic period of Christianity the foundation was laid for a strictly defined order (*chin*) of divine services. The entire indicated section of the First Epistle to the Corinthians has precisely the aim of introducing more order into liturgical assemblies, and in particular of determining the order of the employment during divine worship of spiritual gifts. The Apostle Paul desires that prophetic revelations, as providing edification not only unto the heart, but also unto the intellect, should prevail during divine worship over speaking with tongues, which yields unto prophecy by its indeterminacy and subjectivity: **"Desire spiritual gifts, but rather that ye may prophesy"** [^223]—in other words, the Apostle desires that the didactic *(Orig. p. 43)* element in divine worship should prevail over lyrical [^224];—in order that there should be no overloading of the liturgical material with homogenous content: **"And if any man speak in an unknown tongue, let it be by two, or at the most by three, and that by course; and let one interpret... Let the prophets speak two or three, and let the other judge"** [^225], in order that there should not be simultaneous speaking [^226] of several persons (and "that by course" is a requirement not very insistent). In all these requirements the Apostle refers to the fact that **"so it is in all churches of the saints"** [^227]. Consequently, throughout the various churches a more or less uniform order of divine worship was already beginning to be established. It took place decently (*euschemōn*, elegantly, aesthetically) and in order (*kata taxin*, in well-ordered sequence) [^228]: the former depended upon the latter.

It is possible that the order in which the ministrations of the charismatics alternated during divine worship is indicated by the following words of the Apostle: **"When ye come together, every one of you hath a psalm, hath a doctrine, hath a tongue, hath a revelation, hath an interpretation. Let all things be done unto edifying"** [^229]. The tongue and revelation (prophecy), as the most intense degrees of inspiration, are set in the middle: they are prepared for by inspired chanting ("a psalm") and by the teaching of the instructor (*didaskalos*) and conclude with the equally calm speech of the "interpreter" (interpretations for speaking with tongues and, presumably, prophecy). All this "charismatic" worship could be prefaced and prepared for by the ordinary service, consisting of the reading of Holy Scripture, hymns, and prayers. This same passage from the Apostle Paul, apparently, speaks in favor of the fact that in the divine worship of that time there predominated the performance of liturgical material by individual persons, and not by the entire assembly [^230]. In favor of this also speaks the remark of the Apostle Paul: **"Else when thou shalt bless with the spirit, how shall he that occupieth the room of the unlearned say Amen at thy giving of thanks, seeing he understandeth not what thou sayest?"** [^231]. The participation of the entire congregation in divine worship *(Orig. p. 44)* is represented here under the form of listening to that which is chanted and spoken by the charismatics, with the expression of this participation by the word "Amen."

### Divine Worship according to the Apocalypse

How well-ordered and firm a structure had developed in divine worship toward the close of the apostolic era, and what beauty this imparted unto worship, is clearly seen from the Apocalypse, a book which in many places is a reflection of the liturgical practice of that time. The Apocalypse first of all allows us to ascertain a decisive break, so far as this was possible, between Christian worship and that of the synagogue. The synagogue is directly termed therein "of Satan" (*synagōgē tou satana*, assembly of Satan) [^232]. It is rightly thought that at the foundation of the principal apocalyptic vision (ch. 4) of God sitting upon the throne and the Lamb with the twenty-four elders lies the picture of the contemporary Liturgy celebrated by a bishop with a college of presbyters falling prostrate before the throne of God and the Lamb in the midst thereof; beneath the altar are the souls of them that were slain for the word of God—the tombs of the martyrs, upon which the early Christians celebrated the Eucharist. It is characteristic that the elders worship God and the Lamb when the Cherubim sing: **"Holy, holy, holy, Lord..."** and that unto their singing they add: **"Thou art worthy, O Lord, to receive glory and honour and power: for Thou hast created all things, and for Thy pleasure they are and were created"** [^233]. All this recalls liturgical hymns and prayers. Throughout the entire Apocalypse there is scattered also an array of other unmistakably liturgical formulae. Such, for example, is the doxological formula, frequently varied: **"To Him be glory and dominion unto ages of ages. Amen"** [^234] or: **"Blessing, and honour, and glory, and power, be unto Him that sitteth upon the throne, and unto the Lamb unto ages of ages"** [^235]. Sometimes unto these and similar formulae there is added beforehand or behind *Alleluia* and *Amen*, *even so, Amen* [^236]. In various places the Apocalypse gives up to ten hymns in honor of the Lamb [^237] and mentions the song of Moses the servant of God [^238]. In the words: **"Blessed is he that reads, and they that hear the words *(Orig. p. 45)* of this prophecy"** [^239], the Apocalypse is directly designated for liturgical use, wherein by him who reads, *ho anagignōskōn* in the singular (*anagnōstēs*), is meant the church reader (*lector*), who read the Scripture unto the assembly of listeners (*hoi akouontes*) [^240].

### Feasts in the Apostolic Century

Alongside the development of the daily cycle of divine services, the apostolic century laid the foundations also of the Christian church year. Initially the Apostles and believers observed Jewish feasts, presumably with the same zeal with which they visited the Temple daily. Even the Apostle Paul, that preacher of complete freedom from the Jewish and legal yoke, strives not to spend outside Jerusalem any of the great Jewish feasts, interrupting for them his missionary journeys and hastening unto them from Asia Minor and Greece into Palestine [^241]. This close connection of apostolic Christianity with the Jewish calendar, however, was bound to become weaker and weaker. If for pagan converts circumcision was not considered necessary, then still less were Jewish feasts. Nevertheless, Paul had even in this regard to protect his neophytes from Judaizing Christians: **"Let no man therefore judge you in meat, or in drink, or in respect of an holyday, or of the new moon, or of the sabbath days"** [^242]—a passage demonstrating that the Jewish ecclesiastical year was considered non-obligatory for all Christians without exception.

### The Day of the Lord (Sunday)

Yet the celebration of Sunday laid the beginning of the Christian church year, which began gradually to eclipse the Jewish [^243].

The first definite indication of the celebration of Sunday during the time of the Apostles is found in the First Epistle to the Corinthians, written presumably around A.D. 58 at the close of the Apostle Paul's two-year stay in Ephesus during his third missionary journey. The Apostle counsels the Corinthian Christians to make the charitable collection for the benefit of the Palestinian brethren on the first day of the week, as he had previously appointed in the churches of Galatia. On this day each believer is to lay by him in store, as God hath prospered him, for the poor and keep it until the arrival of the Apostle to hand over unto him [^244]. Here, consequently, is an indication of the sanctification of Sunday solely by charity. Yet from the very same year we have an indication in Acts of the sanctification of Sunday by a liturgical assembly as well. When the Apostle Paul from that same *(Orig. p. 46)* missionary journey was returning to Jerusalem and made a halt in Troas, then **"upon the first day of the week, when the disciples came together to break bread, Paul, ready to depart on the morrow, preached unto them, and continued his speech until midnight"** [^245]. The assembly was not on account of the impending departure of the Apostle Paul, but for the sake of Sunday; otherwise the writer of Acts would have said not "upon the first day of the week," but "on the eve of departure." Sunday is sanctified in this case by the Eucharist (*breaking of bread*), which is celebrated in the evening; in the upper chamber where the believers were gathered, the writer of Acts remarks, **"there were many lights"** (*hikanai lampades*): it was not merely illuminated on account of the evening hour, but brightly illuminated, evidently on occasion of the feast and, perhaps, following the example of the Jewish Sabbath: divine worship is prolonged from evening until dawn.

There is reason to think that the veneration of Sunday by the Apostles began long before the indicated time. It is remarkable that on the first Pentecost after the Ascension of the Lord, the Apostles and believers go neither to the Temple for the solemn morning sacrifice, nor to the synagogue, but arrange their prayer assembly in a private house. And Pentecost in that year fell upon the first day of the week [^246]. Nevertheless, at least initially, the new Christian feast could hardly have completely displaced the Sabbath from the liturgical practice of believers. Eusebius says of the Ebionites that they, "calling the Apostles apostates from the law, observed the Sabbath and in general led a manner of life similar to the Jews; yet, even as we, celebrated also Sundays, for the commemoration of the resurrection of the Lord" [^247]; in this practice of the Ebionites one may see a trace of the primitive practice of Jewish Christians [^248]. In the Apocalypse Sunday, which the Gospels and Epistles still call one of the sabbaths (*hē mia* or *prōtē tōn sabbatōn*) [^249], already receives the distinct name of the Lord's Day, *hē kyriakē hēmera* [^250].

### Pascha and Fasting

With Sunday, it seems, the cycle of feasts of the young Church was exhausted. Hardly in the words of the Apostle Paul: **"For even Christ our Passover is sacrificed for us: therefore let us keep the feast, not with old leaven..."** [^251] can one see an indication of *(Orig. p. 47)* Christian Pascha in contradistinction unto the Jewish. Rather can such an indication be seen in the thoroughness with which the Evangelist John notes the coincidence of Christ's death with the Jewish Passover [^252]. The insistence with which Christian tradition has always attributed to the Apostles themselves the institution of Great Lent allows us to seek at least its rudiments in this period. It is possible that the words of the Savior: **"When the bridegroom shall be taken away from them, then shall they fast,"** cited by so ancient a writer as Tertullian as the foundation for the Paschal fast, were understood in this sense by the Apostles themselves and prompted them to sanctify by fasting, which they in general loved [^253], the annual anniversary of the Lord's death. Since this day fell upon the Jewish Passover, when the observance of Jewish feasts ceased among Christians, the latter could easily come to the thought of sanctifying by fasting precisely the day of the Jewish Passover in commemoration of Christ's death. Under the form of such a fast Pascha initially existed, as we shall see from the primitive testimony concerning it in the second century in St. Irenaeus. Even in the third century Pascha was reduced to a fast, was a Pascha of the Cross (*Pascha staurosimon*), alongside which even then there scarcely began to emerge as an independent feast the Pascha of the Resurrection (*Pascha anastasimon*)—under the guise of the solemn conclusion of the Paschal fast. This fast under the Apostles was probably broken by some on the very day of the Jewish Passover, and by others on the Sunday following it. According to the testimony of Socrates (5th c.), those who celebrated the feast of Pascha on the fourteenth day of Nisan, that is, on the same day as the Jews, asserted that this had been handed down unto them from the Apostle John, while those who celebrated Pascha on the Sunday following the Jewish Passover said that they had received their custom from the Apostles Peter and Paul. Yet neither the one nor the other, the historian remarks, can produce written testimony for this [^254].

*(Orig. p. 48)*

## The Second Century

However much in common the second century of church history has with the third in the external life of Christianity (persecutions), and in its internal life (in the state of enlightenment, for example), nevertheless it (the 2nd c.) bears upon itself, especially in its first half, in the era of the Apostolic Fathers, a distinct impress bringing it somewhat closer unto the apostolic age. Nor could the divine worship of this century fail to have a distinct character. For divine worship this was a transition from apostolic freedom and primitive formation to those firm norms and stable rites (*chinov*) which the third century already presents unto us in abundance, especially in its canonical monuments. Therefore the second century fully merits independent examination by the historian of divine worship.

### Sources

Indications concerning the divine worship of the second century can be found first of all among the writers of that era, that is, in the writings of the Apostolic Fathers and Apologists. Such are the Epistle of the Apostle Barnabas (A.D. 70–100), the First Epistle of St. Clement, Bishop of Rome (c. A.D. 96), the *Shepherd* of Hermas (A.D. 100–150), the Epistles of St. Ignatius the God-Bearer († 107 or 115), the Epistle of St. Polycarp of Smyrna († 167), the *First Apology* of St. Justin Martyr (A.D. 139), the *Epistle to Diognetus* by an unknown author, and the writings of St. Irenaeus of Lyon († 202). Important information concerning divine worship has also been preserved in the writings of pagan authors of that time—especially in the letter of Pliny to Emperor Trajan and in the satire of Lucian of Samosata (in the second half of the 2nd c.), *On the Death of Peregrinus*. Yet almost the most important liturgical monument of this epoch is the *Teaching of the Twelve Apostles* (*Didachē tōn dōdeka apostolōn*). The discovery of this monument by Metropolitan Philotheos Bryennios of Nicomedia in 1875 in the library of the Jerusalem Metochion in Constantinople and its publication by him in 1883 created an epoch in the study of the earliest history of Christianity. Traces of familiarity with this monument exist in Clement of Alexandria († 217) [^255]. Eusebius of Caesarea assigns it to the number of disputed and spurious books of the New Testament [^256], while Athanasius the Great assigns it to the non-canonical, but readable books—alongside the Wisdom books, Esther, Judith, and Tobit [^257]. Diverse scholars assign the date of composition of the monument to various years, ranging from A.D. 70 to the 5th–6th centuries; the majority and the most authoritative scholars date it to A.D. 100–135 (Funk, Harnack) [^258]. In favor of the great antiquity of the monument speaks the existence in its era of the ministries of apostles, prophets, and teachers, and *(Orig. p. 49)* the extraordinary simplicity of the monument. This monument lies at the foundation of Book VII of the *Apostolic Constitutions*.

### Divine Worship according to Pliny's Letter

As regards the cycle and composition of the divine worship of that time, the most circumstantial and valuable account concerning this we have in the well-known letter of the Bithynian proconsul Pliny Secundus (the Younger) to Emperor Trajan from A.D. 111–115 [^259]. Having conducted by order of the emperor an inquiry concerning the Christians, their teaching, and their conduct, Pliny reports [^260]:

"They (the Christians) affirmed that the whole of their guilt, or their error, was that they were accustomed on a stated day to meet before dawn (*stato die ante lucem convenire*) and to sing alternately among themselves a hymn to Christ, as to a god (*carmenque Christo quasi Deo dicere secum invicem*), and to bind themselves by an oath (*sacramento se obstringere*) not to any crime, but that they would not commit theft, robbery, or adultery, nor break their pledged faith, nor refuse a deposit when called upon. When this was done, it was their custom to depart, and to meet together again to partake of food, which was, however, ordinary and innocent (*promiscuum tamen et innoxium*). But even this they ceased to do after the issuance of my edict, by which, according to your commands, I had forbidden secret societies (*hetairias*)."

The letter is cited in Tertullian, wherein the passage concerning liturgical assemblies is rendered: "a pre-dawn meeting for singing (*ad canendum*) unto Christ and God and for a joint commitment to discipline (*ad confoederandam disciplinam*)" [^261], and in Eusebius, where this same passage is rendered thus: "the Christians arise very early and sing praise to Christ as God" [^262]. Pliny's testimony shows that among the Christians of that time there were, at least on feast days, two liturgical assemblies—one at early morning, the other by day or in the evening.

### Matins according to Pliny's Letter

The first assembly described by Pliny represents the most ancient type of morning divine service, Matins (*orthros* / *utrenya*). The assembly begins while it is still night, but evidently not long before dawn. By such an assembly the Christians partly violated the prohibition of nocturnal *(Orig. p. 50)* assemblies that was already contained in the Laws of the Twelve Tables. Yet it is possible that they were also forced into nocturnal gatherings by persecutions for the faith. However, Christians had also other, stronger motives for nocturnal prayer. Night by its mysteriousness in general disposed unto prayer and was chosen for worship both by paganism [^263] and by Judaism [^264]. On the basis of certain evangelical sayings Christians could expect the Second Coming of Christ at midnight—a motive very strong for nocturnal assemblies, if one bears in mind the then intense expectation of this Coming. Of this motive Lactantius (4th c.) directly speaks: "We keep vigils at night on account of (*propter*) the coming of our King and God" [^265]. But, it seems, the strongest motive for nocturnal worship was the circumstance that the Resurrection of Christ took place at night, before dawn, and was discovered in the deep morning while darkness yet was. Every Matins in general was regarded by the ancients, as other monuments of the 2nd–3rd centuries testify (as we shall see below), as a service in honor of the Resurrection of Christ; especially was Sunday Matins bound to have such a meaning.

The composition of the morning service in the account of the pagan, unto whom, of course, Christian liturgical terminology was alien and completely incomprehensible, and who translated it into ordinary language, presents itself under the form of two parts: *carmen* and a certain oath, *sacramentum*.

***Carmen***—ordinarily means *verse*; by this word was designated everything written in verses: inscriptions, oracle pronouncements, laws, prayers, songs. Therefore here also this word could encompass both prayers and hymns in honor of Christ; it indicates that both were brief and possessed metrical form. The subject of these verses is Christ and the glorification of His divinity—which may indicate the predominance in the hymns of a purely Christian element and the insignificance of the Old Testament element (a conclusion in agreement with Ephesians 5:19 and the 3rd-century monument *Testamentum Domini Nostri Jesu Christi*, concerning which see below). The mode of execution of the "verses" is designated by the word *dicere*, which, although it can signify singing (it is so rendered by Tertullian), points rather to chanting alternating with reading or resembling it, recitative (an indication of the simplicity of primitive Christian singing). More particularly the manner of this reading or singing of the verse in honor of Christ is defined as mutual in the assembly—*secum invicem*. This expression is understood in the sense that the believers alternately sang each his own hymn—a practice unto which the Apostle Paul points in 1 Corinthians 14:26 (**"every one of you hath a psalm"**) and which still existed in the time of the Council of Laodicea (which by its 59th canon prohibited this improvisation by laymen of their own hymns) [^266]. But the addition to *invicem* of *secum* also rather indicates a joint reciprocal singing—antiphonal, hypophonic (with the humming / chanting of the final words by the entire *(Orig. p. 51)* assembly), or epiphonic (with the accession unto the singing on the part of the whole congregation of a special refrain [^267]). The testimonies of other monuments concerning the existence at that time of these genres of singing render such a sense most probable for this expression. The circumstance that in a brief and official report this feature of Christian chanting is noted testifies that in divine worship antiphonal chanting was already beginning to win for itself that prominent place which it received later (in the 4th–6th centuries) in the so-called Sung Office (*asmatike akolouthia*) with its three-antiphon structure.

As regards the other part of the Christian morning service, for Pliny's enigmatic expression concerning it: "they bind themselves by an oath..." there has not to this day been found in scholarship a satisfactory explanation. To understand this literally of an oath is precluded by the general view of Christianity concerning oaths and the absence of any reports concerning the use of a common oath during divine worship. For baptismal vows [^268] this expression is too strong, and baptism could not be administered at every morning service. Rather artificial also is the explanation that here is meant the reading of the Word of God, in particular the Decalogue, containing precisely the prohibition of all the sins enumerated here and in the same order, a reading unto which was joined an exhortation to keep these commandments, unto which exhortation (sermon) the assembly responded "Amen," and this was a kind of oath; to designate the reading of Holy Scripture and preaching by such a term Christians could because they loved to call themselves the "host / warfare of Christ," *militia Christi*, and *sacramento se obstringere* ordinarily signified the military oath of allegiance. Perhaps here is meant some rite that subsequently fell out of use, yet a rite, apparently, exceedingly profound and awe-inspiring. Furthermore, this expression stands in connection with the accusation against Christians of forming secret societies (*hetairiai*), whose members bound themselves by an oath for solidarity in the execution of their partisan enterprises.

### The Agape according to Pliny

As regards the second assembly of Christians "on a stated day" (Sunday), Pliny's expression "to partake of food" leaves no doubt that here the Eucharist or the Agape is meant. The time of day at which the second assembly took place is not indicated; but its contrast unto the morning service and the practice of the apostolic era and the third century compel us to assign it to the evening, earlier or later. In the morning in antiquity they generally took no food, with the exception of the aged and young children; still less could there be a common banquet in the morning [^269]. A certain difficulty is presented by the closer definition given by Pliny of the food that Christians partook of at *(Orig. p. 52)* this assembly, that it was "ordinary and innocent." Hitherto this expression was understood as a counterweight unto the accusation against Christians of slaughtering children for the agapes [^270]. But such accusations against Christians began much later than Pliny: they are not mentioned by the earliest apologies: the *Epistle to Diognetus*, or the *Apology* of Aristides, written unto Trajan's successor [^271].

The first to mention such an accusation is St. Justin Martyr, wherein the invention and propagation of this accusation he attributes unto the Jews [^272]. The expression "ordinary food (*promiscuum*—public and common, *epikoinos* and *koinos*) and innocent" points unto the simplest and most modest food and is intended to show that Christians by their repasts do not violate the entire series of Roman laws issued not long before this time against luxurious banquets (*leges sumptuariae*), that is, those very *hetairiai* (or *sodalitates*) mentioned by Pliny [^273]. In particular, "innocent (*innoxius*) food" is frequently applied by writers of that time to fasting food without meat [^274]. Unto a special inclination of Christians toward such food point the Apostle Paul [^275] and Clement of Alexandria. Thus Pliny's testimony in such an understanding sheds curious light for us both upon the very food of Christian agapes and upon the first rudiments of Christian fasting diet; the agapes were modest and fasting repasts, perhaps with fish [^276]. According to the 2nd-century apocryphon *Acts of Paul and Thecla*, at the tomb there was "great joy" (*agapē pollē*, *gaudium magnum*): the youth brought "five loaves of bread with salt, and besides herbs and water" [^277]. Such food was more worthy of partaking with the Eucharist than flesh-meat.

### The Agape according to the *Teaching of the Twelve Apostles* and Other Monuments

Pliny's report leaves no doubt that at this time the Eucharist was celebrated jointly with the agapes. Unto the same practice points another monument of the same era, the *Teaching of the Twelve Apostles*. Here is found the *(Orig. p. 53)* prayer before the Eucharist over the cup and the broken bread, and the prayer after being filled (chs. 9 and 10). Both the very content of these prayers and the title of the second clearly demonstrate that the Eucharist was united with an ordinary repast. It is remarkable that in the *Apostolic Constitutions* (a 4th-century monument) these same prayers are cited in an altered form adapted to the Eucharist alone without a repast, wherein the superscription "after being filled" is replaced by "after communion" [^278]. The indicated prayers in the *Teaching of the Twelve Apostles* are accompanied by the observation that the prophets may "give thanks" (that is, pronounce prayers at the Eucharist) "as much as they will" [^279]. Consequently, since the monument had only local significance, the models of Eucharistic prayers given in the monument can be viewed as an individual attempt to replace prayer improvisation with a uniform formula [^280]. If such an attempt was being made regarding the Eucharist, then for other church services there was long bound to exist the former freedom in prayers and psalmody.

The celebration of the Eucharist jointly with the agapes in this era is confirmed also by St. Ignatius the God-Bearer: "It is not lawful without the bishop either to baptize or to celebrate a love-feast," he writes unto the Smyrnaeans [^281]; with baptism could be correlated only a sacrament.

Of other writers of that time, the author of the *Epistle to Diognetus* mentions the agapes, but too briefly for one to be able to extract new data on this subject: Christians "have a table in common, yet not an ordinary one" [^282]. The expression may speak for the inseparability of the Eucharist from the agape.

### The Liturgy and the Agape according to St. Justin Martyr

St. Justin Martyr in his *First Apology* makes it perceptible that in the mutual relation of the Eucharist and the agape there occurred by his time an essential change. The Eucharist had become so segregated into an independent service that in describing it St. Justin makes no mention whatever of any repast. Yet in connection with the Eucharist he mentions aid on the part of the wealthy unto the poor, which is ordinarily understood as an indication of the agape, which had already assumed a purely charitable character.

Here are the passages from St. Justin relating hereto. The newly baptized
"we bring unto those who are called brethren, into the common assembly, in order with all earnestness to offer common prayers both for ourselves and for the illuminated [newly baptized] and for all others everywhere, that we may be accounted worthy, having learned the truth, to be found by our works also good citizens and keepers of the commandments, so that we may obtain eternal salvation. Having ended the prayers, we greet *(Orig. p. 54)* one another with a kiss. Then there is brought unto the president of the brethren bread and a cup of water and wine." There follows a description of the Eucharist and an elucidation of its significance and institution, after which the Apologist continues: "And those of us who are well-to-do help the poor, and we always hold together with one another. For all things wherewith we are supplied, we bless the Maker of all through His Son Jesus Christ and the Holy Spirit. And on the day called Sunday [day of the Sun] there is an assembly in one place of all who live in cities or in the country, and the memoirs (*apomnēmoneumata*) of the Apostles or the writings (*syngrammata*) of the Prophets are read, as long as time permits (*mechri enchorei*). Then, when the reader (*ho anagignōskōn*) has ceased, the president verbally instructs and exhorts to the imitation of these good things. Then we all rise together and offer up prayers. And, as we said before, when our prayer is ended, bread and wine and water are brought, and the president in like manner offers prayers and thanksgivings, according to his ability."

There is given a briefer description of the Eucharist than previously:
**"And they who are well to do, and willing, give what each thinks fit; and what is collected is deposited with the president, and he takes care of orphans and widows... And on the day called Sunday [day of the Sun] all who live in cities or in the country gather together to one place, for it is the first day on which God, having wrought a change in the darkness and matter, made the world; and Jesus Christ our Savior on the same day rose from the dead"** [^283].

St. Justin says nothing of the time of day for this liturgical assembly, but the fact that this assembly was preceded by baptism does not allow us to assign it unto the morning and consequently to identify it with the pre-dawn assembly of Pliny, as older church historians did, naively trusting Pliny's bureaucratically boastful assertion that he had compelled Christians to discontinue their evening repasts, and supposing that from Trajan onward they were forced to transfer the Eucharist unto the morning. Thus the practice described in Justin, presumably, differs in nothing from that of Pliny.

Yet Justin's testimony is important because it already indicates a fully established ritual of the Eucharist, which has a preparatory part rather noticeably separated from it, consisting of reading and prayer. This is the part that subsequently formed what came to be called *ta typika* of the Liturgy (or the Liturgy of the Catechumens) in distinction from its canon [anaphora], and what served as the prototype of Vespers. Furthermore, in Justin the partaking of the Eucharist is clearly posited before the charitable repast (the agape). Of such a practice speaks also the apocryphal *Acts of John*, according to which the Apostle with a certain Andronicus performs a commemoration upon the tomb of the latter's wife on the third day after her death: after the Eucharist, for which the deceased woman also arose, the faithful partook of food [^284]. At the same time, St. Justin ascertains the transition of the agapes into a purely charitable institution [^285]. In another place St. Justin supplements the information communicated here concerning the evening divine service, noting that at it **"solemn rites and hymns (*pompas kai *(Orig. p. 55)* hymnous*) are offered through the word for our creation, for all means unto our well-being, for various kinds of produce, for the changes of the seasons, and petitions are sent up that we may rise again in incorruption"** [^286]. (The content of these prayers is close unto the prayers of the *Teaching of the Twelve Apostles*.) Remarkable here is the mention of solemn rites during divine worship, something new in comparison with other monuments (perhaps litiya processions, entrances for prayers).

### The Agape according to Lucian

The satirist Lucian of Samosata (second half of the 2nd cent.) attributes unto the founder of Christianity the institution of "new mysteries"—calling Christian worship evidently by this term—and recounts that when Peregrinus, the hero of the satire, who had by deceit achieved among Christians the most prominent position, having become among them a prophet, *thiasarchēs*, *synagōgeus*, and president, was cast into prison, "from the very earliest dawn there stood at the prison gates a crowd of old women, widows, and orphans." "And among them the leaders of the sect, bribing the guards, spent the entire night with him; partaking of elaborate suppers (*deipna poikila*), they read their sacred books... By virtue of his imprisonment, large sums of money were brought unto Peregrinus" [^287]. Here again Christian worship is reduced to evening suppers, wherein, as in Justin, a prominent place is occupied at this sacred supper by the reading of Holy Scripture, which Pliny, apparently, does not mention. One may think that this element of divine service now came forward for the first time, occupying a distinct and prominent position alongside hymns and prayers, thanks unto the final formation of the New Testament canon.

Thus, however fragmentary and few the reports of the 2nd century concerning the church services of that era may be, these reports authorize the conclusion that there existed two divine services during the course of the day—one morning, the other evening. The first consisted of hymns and prayers and, perhaps, of the reading of Holy Scripture; at the second, in addition to all of this, the Eucharist and the agape were celebrated. The second service was the more essential, behind which the first remained, as it were, in the shadow, which is why a number of the enumerated monuments make no mention whatever of the first, morning service without the Eucharist and agape. Nor is it mentioned by the *Teaching of the Twelve Apostles*, which speaks of the Eucharist and the agape repeatedly [^288]. One cannot fail to observe during the course of the 2nd century a gradual process of the separation of the Eucharist from the agape as its independent and most sacred part, whereas in the apostolic century they, apparently, merged into one single sacred whole (moreover, in the Apostle Paul also one discerns a desire for such separation in his instructions unto the Corinthians concerning the reverent reception of the Eucharistic Gifts). Already the *Teaching of the Twelve Apostles* speaks of the Eucharist without mentioning agapes. In Justin, moreover, the agape is completely lost beside the Eucharist, being neither described nor named. In any case, the Eucharist at the agapes now began to precede the partaking of other food.
*(Orig. p. 56)*

### Days of Divine Worship

Remarkable also is the fact that the majority of monuments of the 2nd century speak of divine worship only on the day of the Lord / Sunday (besides Pliny and Justin, also the *Teaching of the Twelve Apostles*: **"On the Lord's Day, gathering together, break bread and give thanks, having first confessed your sins, that your sacrifice may be pure"** [that your sacrifice may be pure] [^289]. Yet in view of the fact that both from the apostolic century and from the 3rd century we possess testimonies concerning the daily celebration of the Eucharist, we must think that such a practice existed now as well. Presumably on Sundays there were general assemblies of the Christians of an entire city, of the whole episcopate and eparchy, and on weekdays private assemblies in houses [^290]. Eparchies at that time were often no larger than present-day parishes [^291], so that general assemblies took place for the most part at the bishop's: **"Take heed to have but one Eucharist,"** writes St. Ignatius unto the Philadelphians, **"for there is one flesh of our Lord Jesus Christ, and one cup unto the unity of His blood, one altar, as there is one bishop with the presbytery and deacons; where the shepherd is, thither do ye follow as sheep"** [^292]. Still, the exhortation to have one Eucharist with the bishop shows that it was not always solitary for the Christians of a given city. In another place St. Ignatius exhorts not to hold prayer assemblies without the bishop, or at least without the presbyters [^293].

### Hours of Prayer

There was not abandoned in the 2nd century the custom, adopted by the first Christians from the Old Testament Church, of sanctifying with prayer three most important times of the day—morning, midday, and evening. **"Neither pray ye as the hypocrites"** (that is, the Jews, as the context shows), says the *Teaching of the Twelve Apostles*, **"but as the Lord commanded in His Gospel, after this manner pray ye: Our Father..."**—the Lord's Prayer is cited, and there is added: **"Thrice a day pray ye thus"** [^294]. Here one may see an indication of the continued use here and there among Christians even of this time of Jewish prayers (the *Shema* and *Shemoneh Esreh*) for the three hours of prayer, and a decisive demand to replace these prayers with a purely Christian one. As these hours of prayer, monuments of the apostolic era and the 3rd century designate the 3rd, 6th, and 9th. Consequently, they were honored with prayer in the 2nd century as well. Thus *(Orig. p. 57)* we have here the first germ of the present-day Order of the Hours: it consists as yet of the Lord's Prayer alone, which even now occupies in the Hours a central and primary place. The Hours do not yet possess a Christian symbolic meaning, but are sanctified by prayer simply as the most important divisions of the day.

### Order of Service

As regards the composition of the services of that time, the reports already cited outline it in general terms. A series of other reports allows us to say even more upon this question. First of all, it is beyond doubt that in divine worship there already existed a rather firmly and definitely established *ordo*, an order, departure from which was forbidden. Clement, Bishop of Rome, writes unto the Corinthians (ca. 100): **"We ought to do all things in order, whatsoever the Master hath commanded us to perform at appointed seasons. He hath commanded the oblations and divine services (*prosphoras kai leitourgias*—presumably the Eucharist and other services) to be celebrated not carelessly nor without order, but at fixed times and hours. Where also and through whom He willeth them to be performed, He Himself hath determined by His own supreme will. They therefore that make their offerings at the appointed seasons are acceptable and blessed"** [^295].

### Constituent Parts of Divine Worship

#### Prayer

The first and most important constituent part of every divine service, *prayer*, is regarded by St. Ignatius as the best instrument of church communion, upon condition of close union therein: **"In the common assembly let there be one prayer, one supplication, one mind, one hope."** Thus, unto prayer and union therein there was now principally reduced that *koinōnia* (communion) which in the apostolic era was a constant co-presence or common life of the faithful, entirely possible given their small numbers at that time [^296]. The principal subject of prayers was brethren of the same faith: **"Pray for all the saints,"** exhorts St. Polycarp [^297]; yet according to the commandment of the Apostle, prayer extended also unto all men: **"And pray ye without ceasing for other men also; for there is in them a hope of repentance, that they may attain unto God,"** writes St. Ignatius [^298]. **"Pray also for kings, and for powers, and for princes, even for them that persecute you, and for enemies of the Cross,"** exhorts St. Polycarp [^299]. As we have seen, the *Teaching of the Twelve Apostles* furnishes, presumably, the most ancient written formula of Eucharistic prayer; it also points unto the use of the Lord's Prayer. Unto the existence of a series of definite prayers and unto the central position among them of the Lord's Prayer, apparently, points the expression of St. Polycarp: **"Let us be watchful in prayer and perse*(Orig. p. 58)*vere in fasting; in supplications beseeching the all-seeing God not to lead us into temptation"** [^300].

#### Psalmody and Hymns

Further than prayer advanced the development of another constituent part of divine worship—*chanting / hymnody*. We have seen how Pliny reduces to it the entire morning service. In St. Ignatius's farewell epistles church hymns sound forth, as it were, unceasingly, revealing in him a great lover of singing: **"Form a choir in love and sing praises unto the Father in Christ Jesus"** [^301]; **"Join into a choir, every one of you, that being harmonious in love and taking up the song of God in unison, ye may sing with one voice unto the Father through Jesus Christ"** [^302]. Therefore one cannot suspect of historical unreliability the report of Socrates' *Ecclesiastical History* that it was precisely Ignatius who introduced antiphonal chanting into the Church of Antioch [^303]. If so, then the antiphonal manner of singing became thus already from the 2nd century predominant and characteristic in the Eastern Church (the three-antiphon system) in contrast unto the Western, where hypophonic and epiphonic chanting (responsories) was more accepted. What a profound impression was produced at first by the antiphonal manner of singing, alien unto primitive antiquity (in Old Testament worship, as we have seen, its existence is doubtful), is shown by the tradition which the historian Socrates appends unto his report concerning the introduction of antiphonal chanting by St. Ignatius—namely, that the thought of this singing was inspired in Ignatius by a vision of angels who thus precisely glorified God. And how new antiphonal singing was for the Christian Church of that era is shown by the slowness and difficulty with which it spread. In that very Antioch in which the origin of this chanting is linked with the name of Ignatius, there labored in the 4th century upon its establishment, according to the testimony of Bl. Theodoret, the presbyters Diodore and Flavian [^304]. When St. Basil the Great introduced this singing into the Church of Neocaesarea, its clergy resisted, appealing unto the ancient practice of congregational singing received from the founder of the Church, St. Gregory of Neocaesarea, unto which Basil the Great replies unto the Neocaesareans that antiphonal singing had already been accepted in Egypt, Libya, Palestine, Arabia, Phoenicia, and Syria. In the West this singing was first introduced by St. Ambrose (4th cent.) *(Orig. p. 59)* into the Church of Milan [^305], whence it was transferred unto North Africa by St. Augustine (5th cent.), and in the Roman Church it was adopted under Pope Celestine I (422–432) [^306].

The innovation of St. Ignatius by its mere fact demonstrates how greatly the chant material of divine worship had increased by that time. The cause of this growth was presumably the hymnographic activity of the Gnostics, which impelled pastors to fight against them with the same weapon, that is, by composing their own hymns. Thus Valentinus and other Gnostics composed psalms for the propagation of their false teaching [^307]. The hymns of Bardesanes survived down to the time of St. Ephrem the Syrian (4th cent.) [^308]. Yet of Orthodox hymnographers of the 2nd century there has reached us only the name of the Martyr Athenogenes († 159), of whom St. Basil the Great says that before his death he composed a hymn that became exceedingly famous and was long preserved (this hymn, as we shall see, is considered to be **"O Gladsome Light"** [*Phōs Hilaron* / *Svete Tikhiy*]). Unto St. Justin Martyr is attributed [^309] the composition of a lost book, *Psaltēs* (The Singer / Psalmist), which presumably constituted a collection of songs (termed psalms, perhaps because paganism had made the designation "hymns" odious unto Christians) [^310]. Eusebius cites a 3rd-century treatise against the heresy of Artemon, wherein it is stated among other things: **"How many psalms and songs (*ōdai*) were written from the beginning by faithful brethren, praising (*hymnousi*"** [*theologountes*] **Christ as the Word of God"** [^311]. In the martyrdom acts of St. Ignatius it is related that the venerators of the saint chanted hymns at his tomb for several days [^312].

### Reading of Holy Scripture: Formation of the New Testament Canon

The initial history of the *liturgical use of Holy Scripture* is closely bound up with the history of the New Testament canon. The first definite testimony concerning the reading of Holy Scripture during Christian divine worship is the above-cited passage from St. Justin Martyr concerning the reading in the "assembly of the brethren" of the "memoirs of the Apostles and the writings of the Prophets," a passage speaking of the practice ca. 140. That by this time the New Testament scriptures, and that in almost the entire scope of their present canon, had received in *(Orig. p. 60)* the eyes of Christians an authority equal unto the Old Testament is proved by the constant references unto them in contemporary works and by the striving to establish harmony between the two testaments (with this latter, one might say almost exclusively, the *Epistle of Barnabas*, appearing at the end of the 1st century, is already occupied). Of course, such reverence toward themselves and the honorary place in divine worship connected with this reverence the New Testament writings acquired not at once and not without a struggle. In this regard great importance must have belonged unto the idea of the New Testament in general expressed by the Apostle Paul and developed by him in detail, which assigned unto the entire Old Testament, and consequently unto its scriptures, an apparently not very elevated place. Carried unto an extreme by Marcion, this idea led in the latter's case even unto the complete rejection of the Old Testament and the striving to replace all its books with the Pauline epistles. Marcion's teaching upon this point was undoubtedly a continuation of those disputes regarding both testaments which began already under the Apostles between Jewish Christians and Gentile Christians, and an echo of which even in the 4th century is the recognition of the Catholic Epistles and the Apocalypse, belonging unto Apostles of Hebrew stock, as "disputed" (*antilegomena*). Only gradually could Jewish Christians be inclined toward recognizing the New Testament in that corpus wherein there entered into it not only the writings of the Apostles of the circumcision, but also of authors who declared themselves apostles of the Gentiles, that is, Paul and his assistants (among the latter could be numbered also the Evangelist Mark, who stood as a mediator, as it were, between both tendencies, and was therefore placed between Matthew and Luke [^313]). On the other hand, Gentile Christians also, only with the final clarification in the ecclesiastical consciousness of the degree of obligatoriness which the Old Testament law could still possess, were able to call the Old Testament their own and set the Apostle Peter on a par with the Apostle Paul. As the heresies of the Ebionites, and especially of the Gnostics and Manichaeans demonstrate, the 2nd century is still a witness of this struggle between two tendencies in Christianity, and it serves as the greatest honor for the Church of Christ that, having initially been formed in an overwhelming majority from Gentiles, and in the 2nd century having broken completely with Judaism, she resisted on the question of the inspired canon and its use in divine worship a current so natural under these circumstances as Marcionism, and declared not only the writings of all the Apostles to be of equal value, but also the Old Testament as equal in divine inspiration unto the New. Yet the fact that according to St. Justin the reading of the "memoirs of the Apostles" preceded the "writings of the Prophets" clearly shows at what stage in the 2nd century the question concerning the significance of the Old Testament still stood: in the 3rd century Old Testament readings already precede New Testament ones. Traces of this struggle between the two tendencies of theological thought—still so fierce in the 2nd century—concerning the comparative significance of the writings of the Apostles of the circumcision and the Apostle Paul have been preserved also by our present order of liturgical readings from the New Testament: the Catholic Epistles are not read at all on Sun*(Orig. p. 61)*days, and in the church year they follow after the Pauline epistles; the Gospel of Mark is read in Great Lent and occupies in the annual cycle of readings the same place as the Catholic Epistles; an exception is made for the Evangelist Matthew, as the most ancient and most revered in the primitive Church.

### The Gospel and the Apostle

In the New Testament canon already in the 2nd century there are clearly segregated as two parts thereof—the Gospels, on the one hand, and the other apostolic writings, on the other. **"Let us have recourse unto the Gospel as unto the flesh of Jesus,"** says St. Ignatius already, **"and unto the Apostles as unto the presbytery of the Church"** [^314]. St. Irenaeus already proves the impossibility of any other number of Gospels than four:

> "For since there are four zones of the world in which we live, and four principal winds, and since the Church is scattered throughout all the earth, and the pillar and ground of the Church is the Gospel and the Spirit of life, it is fitting that she should have four pillars, breathing out incorruption from every side, and vivifying men. And the Cherubim, too, have four faces, and their countenances are images of the dispensation of the Son of God... The living creatures are quadriform, and quadriform is the Gospel and the working of the Lord. And for this reason four principal covenants were given unto the human race: one under Adam before the Flood, another after the Flood under Noah, the third the giving of the Law under Moses, and the fourth that which reneweth man and recapitulateth all things in itself through the Gospel... Seeing that God made all things harmonious and well-ordered, it was fitting that the Gospel also should possess an aspect well-arranged and harmonious. Having examined the opinion of those who handed down the Gospel unto us upon the basis of their own principles, let us now pass on unto the remaining Apostles" [^315].

Yet St. Irenaeus lived at the close of the 2nd century. St. Justin's expression concerning the liturgical reading of the New Testament does not yet draw so sharp a line between the Gospels and the remaining apostolic writings. Characteristic in this expression is the designation of the apostolic writings as *memoirs*, when the majority of them bear the superscription of epistles and possess the character of the latter, and when it would have been most exact to designate their totality as *writings*, as the Old Testament books are called in St. Justin. Does not such a designation point unto the preferential use during the divine service of that time of apostolic writings of a narrative character, that is, the Gospels and Acts? In our present divine worship also the Gospel possesses a broader use than the Apostle; while in Coptic worship, which has preserved traces of a profoundly ancient practice, a Gospel is appointed at every service of the daily cycle. At the same time, Justin's expression may indicate that the Gospels in his time were not sharply segregated from Acts, which was so natural given the common authorship of the latter with the Third Gospel. Even in 3rd-century monuments, as we shall see, the New Testament is divided into three parts: Gospel, Acts, and Epistles, and not into two (Gospel and Apostle). *(Orig. p. 62)* A trace of such an exalted ancient view of the Acts in our present divine worship is their use during the Pentecostarion period [Paschal season]. Unto granting the Gospels an honorary place in the New Testament canon there could easily and early contribute their analogy with the 'Law' (Torah) of the Old Testament canon, which in antiquity was divided into two main parts—the Law and the Prophets. It seems that the Gospels themselves also have in view their analogy with the Pentateuch, when, for example, the Gospel of Matthew titles its first section **"The book of the generation"** (*biblos geneseōs*, Slav. *kniga rodstva*), while the Gospel of John begins with the opening words of the Book of Genesis [^316].

### The Manner of Reading Holy Scripture

As regards the *manner of reading* Holy Scripture in divine worship in the 2nd century, the sole above-cited 2nd-century testimony concerning this reading (that of St. Justin) allows us to say that it was performed by a reader (*ho anagignōskōn*), and not by the president of the assembly (bishop or presbyter), who came forward after the reading with the homily. An echo of such a division of reading and preaching in divine worship in our present services is the obligatory reading of the Gospel at the Liturgy by the deacon, and not by the priest. Concerning the selection of readings nothing is known.

### Preaching / The Homily

With the reading of Holy Scripture *preaching* stood in intimate connection. How essential a place it occupied at every liturgical assembly is demonstrated by the exhortation of the Apostle Barnabas: **"Ye ought not to separate yourselves from others, but coming together into one place, inquire what is fitting and profitable for all the beloved in common"** [^317]. Initially in the 2nd century, given the incomplete universal familiarity with the apostolic writings, the vacillations regarding their authenticity provoked by the appearance of apocrypha, and the ripening opposition unto Judaism which was unfavorable unto the widespread use of Old Testament scriptures in divine worship, preaching during divine service was able, if not to replace the reading of Scripture—resting constantly and wholly upon it—at least to occupy a more prominent position therein. Unto this there also contributed the continuing operation in the Church of spiritual gifts—apostleship, prophecy, and teaching—which imparted unto ecclesiastical preaching almost the same stamp of inspiration as that possessed by the writings of the Apostles themselves. *(Orig. p. 63)* At least the writings of such apostles, prophets, and teachers as Barnabas and Hermas were long set on a par with apostolic writings. Yet Hermas also sends out and publishes his prophecies through the mediation of presbyters headed by Clement, remarking: "for unto him (Clement) this is committed," just as he reads them in the city together with the "presbyters, presidents of the Church" [^318]. Thus the right of preaching is increasingly confirmed as belonging unto the ecclesiastical hierarchy. In Justin's testimony, consequently around the middle of the 2nd century, in the Church only the president preaches, although spiritual prophetic gifts exist even in the time of Irenaeus [^319]. The further on, however, the more preaching in divine worship was bound to yield its former place unto the reading of Holy Scripture. Our present Typikon, in appointing for the morning service the reading of patristic homilies, seeks to preserve the memory of the most ancient type of divine worship.

### The Church Year in the II Century: Sunday

The church year in the 2nd century develops just as much through the multiplication of feasts and commemorations as through the strengthening and deepening of those inherited from the preceding period. Thus Sunday completely supplants the Sabbath. It alone is mentioned as a weekly festal day in the Apostle Barnabas, in Pliny, Justin, and in the *Teaching of the Twelve Apostles*. Of the Sabbath not only does no monument make mention, but its abrogation for the New Testament is proved alongside circumcision and sacrifices, as an institution called forth by the hardness of heart of the Jews [^320]. **"Behold how He saith,"** writes Barnabas: **"Your present sabbaths are not acceptable unto Me, but those which I have appointed, which shall dawn"** **"when, having set an end unto all things, I shall make the beginning of the eighth day, that is, the beginning of another world." Therefore also we keep the eighth day with joyfulness, on which also Jesus rose again from the dead** [^321]. Here is ascertained the complete replacement of the Jewish Sabbath by Sunday, wherein this replacement is justified from the Old Testament itself, and unto Sunday there is attributed, besides the commemoration of Christ's resurrection, a symbolic meaning analogous with the Sabbath. (This day is called the eighth as following upon the seventh, the Sabbath; cf. its symbolic meaning in Justin [^322]). In St. Ignatius the God-Bearer Sunday is called *Kyriakē* [^323]—a term representing an abbreviation of the apocalyptic *Kyriakē hēmera* [the Lord's Day].

### Pascha

In this same century there is undoubtedly already honored in a special manner the annual day of the death and resurrection of Christ, that is, the feast of *Pascha* (its existence in the apostolic century, as we have seen, is only probable).
*(Orig. p. 64)*
A fragment of the utmost value in this regard from the letter of St. Irenaeus, Bishop of Lyons, unto Victor, Bishop of Rome, preserved by Eusebius, sheds light upon the primitive character of the feast of Pascha. The epistle was written concerning the disputes over the time of the celebration of Pascha, which began already under St. Polycarp, Bishop of Smyrna († 167), provoked a series of councils, and continued with still greater intensity, apparently, under St. Irenaeus, Bishop of Lyons († 202). The disputes concerned whether Pascha should be celebrated together with the Jewish Passover on the 14th–15th day of the first spring lunar month, or on the first Sunday after that day.

### St. Irenaeus on Pascha

One need only read attentively the aforementioned fragment, paying heed unto every word thereof, in order to make it clear that the dispute itself concerning the time of Pascha arose because by this time the character of the feast itself, the view of it, was beginning gradually to change; namely, whereas previously Pascha was viewed as a fast in honor of the death of the Savior, Who died precisely on the day of the Jewish Passover, now they wished to unite with it also the joyful commemoration of Christ's resurrection, which did not accord with fasting and was more fitting not for any single day of the week upon which the Jewish Passover might fall, but for Sunday. In Rome Pascha had already begun to acquire a second keynote, so to speak; while in Asia Minor, where life did not move with such rapidity, there was preserved, presumably, the original, most ancient view of Pascha. Therefore in the dispute the bishops simply failed to understand one another. Still less could comprehend the cause of the dispute and all stages of its development Eusebius, for whom Pascha was already as bright a feast as it is for us. Yet he did very well in that he presented St. Irenaeus's epistle in his own paraphrase not in its entirety, but merely its beginning, while citing the most essential portion in the original text. Thereby Eusebius preserved from inevitable distortion the most ancient witness concerning our greatest feast:

**"For the dispute is not only concerning the day, but also concerning the very manner of the fast"** (a clear indication that the "day," that is, of Pascha, was honored and celebrated precisely by fasting); **"for some think that they ought to fast only one day, others two, others still more; while some reckon their day as forty hours day and night"** (*hoi de tessarakonta hōras te kai nykterinas symmetrousi tēn hēmeran autōn* [οἱ δὲ τεσσαράκοντα ὥρας τε καὶ νυκτερινὰς συμμετροῦσι τὴν ἡμέραν αὐτῶν]). **"And such variety in observance"** [^324] **"did not originate in our time, but long before in the days of our ancestors, who, in all probability, did not observe strict accuracy, and transmitted unto posterity a simple and individual custom. Yet nonetheless they all maintained peace, and we live in peace with one another, and the disagreement regarding the fast"** (again, not the "feast") **"confirms the agree-** *(Orig. p. 65)* **-ment of faith"** [^325].

Unto this extract from St. Irenaeus, Eusebius subjoins his narrative concerning the dispute regarding Pascha in the time of St. Polycarp: when, during the latter's visit unto Bishop Anicetus of Rome, there became evident their disagreement both upon this question and upon others, **"they contended little with each other concerning other matters, but immediately came unto agreement, while regarding this question they were unwilling even to dispute, because neither could Anicetus persuade Polycarp not to observe what he had always observed, living in companionship with John, the disciple of our Lord; nor did Polycarp persuade Anicetus to observe it, for Anicetus declared that he was obligated to maintain the customs of the presbyters who had preceded him."**

### The Paschal Fast

This testimony of St. Irenaeus allows us to behold also the first seed of our present Holy Quadragesima (Forty Days' Fast / Great Lent), which at that time, being restricted unto one or two days, was regarded not as a pre-Paschal fast, but as a Paschal fast—as Pascha itself. The Paschal fast, according to this testimony, lasted in some places a single day, in others two, in others still longer; while in yet others it embraced an interval of forty hours. Three of these four specifications are clear. Only the last is expressed in such a manner that it admits—or at least once admitted—a different interpretation. Namely, Rufinus († 410), the first and most ancient translator of Eusebius's *History* into Latin, a younger contemporary of its author, renders the concluding phrase of Irenaeus thus: *"quidam vero quadraginta, ita ut diurnas ac nocturnas horas connumerent diei"* [some indeed forty, so measuring their day by counting diurnal and nocturnal hours]. Consequently, Rufinus discerned in Irenaeus here an indication of a forty-day duration of the pre-Paschal fast, achieving this simply by placing a punctuation mark after the word *tessarakonta* [τεσσαράκοντα; "forty"] and seeing in the remaining words the thought that they fasted not only during the daylight hours, but also during the night. Yet for such a thought the concluding words of Irenaeus would provide an exceedingly strange and indeed downright impossible expression. If the Holy Father had desired to express the idea that Christians fasted not merely until evening, as the Jews did on the Day of Atonement, but continued the fast until late at night, he ought to have stated that Christians fasted throughout the day and part of the night. Why should there be mention here of "hours" if their quantity is not indicated? Why the unusual term "reckon" (literally, "commensurate," *symmetrousi*)? What meaning attaches unto the addition of "their" unto "day"? And indeed, was it possible for ordinary mortals to fast throughout forty days around the entire clock without food? In the lives of the holy ascetics such prolonged fasting is recounted as an exceptionally rare phenomenon even among them, for which there was truly required a fortitude of spirit akin unto that of Moses, Elijah, and Christ.

All these peculiarities in St. Irenaeus's expression fall away if one perceives in this passage a reference unto the custom of certain Christians to fast before Pascha neither one day nor two, but precisely forty hours. While some—indeed the majority—measured (*symmetrousi*) their fast by days, others measured it by hours, fasting in return not for one or several such units of time, but for the symbolic number forty, sanctified *(Orig. p. 66)* by so many lofty examples of fasting, and substituting, by reason of their infirmity, hours for days. The words "hours" and "measure," which are so difficult under Rufinus's interpretation, receive under this true understanding their most natural sense, as does also the expression "their day": a forty-hour fast may be called a single day of fasting, only a day of a peculiar sort ("their own"). Furthermore, under such an understanding there will not be between the fasting practice of different Christians (probably Christians of different local Churches) that impassable disparity which would exist if in one place they fasted one, two, or "more" days, while in others an entire forty. The very word "more" (*pleionas*) in juxtaposition with one and two cannot signify more than three, four, and the like [^326]. Nevertheless, at this time, so to speak, the idea of a forty-day fast in imitation of Christ's fast was already in the air among Christians.

It is characteristic that the Asiatics ended the Paschal fast on that (*kata tautēn*) day [^327] whereon other Christians, according to Irenaeus, began it, that is, on the day of the Jewish Passover. In the time of St. Epiphanius of Cyprus there existed a branch of the Quartodecimans (as were called the partisans of celebrating Pascha together with the Jews on the 14th of Nisan, who separated themselves from the Church on this account; in Latin, *quartodecimani*), which restricted unto a single day—the 14th of Nisan—both the pre-Paschal fast and the feast of Pascha itself [^328]. If the Quartodecimans of the 2nd century were correct in their dispute with the Roman Church of that era regarding the antiquity of their practice, it is possible that the branch of Quartodecimans mentioned by St. Epiphanius preserved the most ancient practice of the Paschal fast. Against such a supposition nothing can be argued from the circumstance that the Church condemned the Quartodecimans as heretics (more accurately, as schismatics): she condemned them not for fidelity unto antiquity, but for rupturing ecclesiastical unity on its account. (They met with the fate of our Old Believers). Yet it is also possible that the one-day fast at Pascha on the 14th of Nisan was not an ancient practice preserved by sectarians, but a practice created by them: it was the same one-day Pascha-fast known unto other Christians, only among the sectarians fixed not unto the Friday preceding Sunday, but unto the 14th of Nisan.

Yet however that may be, it is beyond doubt that the pre-Paschal fast developed not out of Christ's forty-day fast in the wilderness, as older liturgical scholars long believed, but out of a one- or two-day fast in honor of the Savior's death on the day of the Jewish Passover [^329]. This fast among certain Churches or Christians was gradually extended unto forty hours (corresponding unto the number of hours Christ remained in the tomb), then unto a week (Passion Week), then unto several weeks, and finally unto forty days.

*(Orig. p. 67)*

### Disputes concerning the Time of Pascha

Given such a character of Pascha in the 2nd century, those vehement controversies which were then waged over it become entirely intelligible. The dispute concerned whether to unite with the commemoration of the Savior's death (by fasting) the commemoration of His resurrection (with joy), or not to unite them; and if they were to be united, unto which of these two commemorations preference should be accorded: whether unto the commemoration of the Savior's death, which fell on the 14th of Nisan (on whatever day of the week this date might occur), or unto the commemoration of His resurrection, which necessarily fell on the day of the week whereon it occurred, that is, on Sunday (whatever numerical day of the month this Sunday might have, provided only that it followed upon the 14th of Nisan). The former was maintained by the Churches of Asia Minor; the latter, by the Roman Church and the majority of other Churches. The chief literary champion of the Asia Minor practice regarding the time of Pascha was Melito, Bishop of Sardis, who composed *Two Books on the Pascha* (c. 170). Its literary opponents were Apollinaris, Bishop of Hierapolis, Clement of Alexandria, and St. Hippolytus, Bishop of Rome. In Palestine, Rome, Pontus, Gaul, and Greece councils convened and pronounced in favor of the Roman practice. Pope Victor (c. 196) threatened the Asiatics with excommunication. The aforementioned epistle of St. Irenaeus had as its very purpose to reconcile the contending parties. Apparently the dispute continued down unto the Council of Nicaea, which adopted the Roman practice as universal. The Council of Antioch (341 [cited in the original text as 333]) excommunicates from the Church those **"who celebrate Pascha together with the Jews"** [^330]. The custom of fasting [misprinted in Russian text as *prostit'sya*, "to take leave," for *postit'sya*, "to fast"] at Pascha is rebuked even by St. John Chrysostom [^331].

### Wednesday and Friday

In the *Teaching of the Twelve Apostles* (*Didache*) we find an injunction regarding the fast of Wednesday and Friday: **"Let not your fasts be with the hypocrites"** (that is, the Jews, specifically the Pharisees), **"for they fast on the second and fifth days of the week; but fast ye on the fourth and the preparation day [Wednesday and Friday]"** [^332]. *The Shepherd* of Hermas mentions a fast bearing the designation of "station" (*statio*) [^333]. Since later writers designate by this name perhaps Wednesday and Friday [^334], this passage of Hermas is regarded as the most ancient witness unto these weekly fasts.
