"If in the same commentary (the Acts) of Luke there is indicated the third hour of prayer, at which those filled with the Holy Spirit were taken to be drunken, and the sixth, at which Peter went up into the upper chamber, and the 9th, at which they went into the temple, why do we not understand this not in such wise that one must pray indiscriminately always and everywhere and at every time, but in such wise that these were hours both more significant (*insigniores*) in human affairs, dividing the day, distributing labor, and having their effect in civic life, and more solemn in divine prayers, which is proved also by the example of Daniel, who prayed thrice a day, of course with the setting apart (for prayer) of certain hours, and none other than those which became thence significant also for the apostles, that is, the 3rd, 6th, and 9th?" [^446]

There is in Tertullian mention also of nocturnal prayers: in demonstrating unto a Christian woman the inconvenience for her of a pagan marriage, Tertullian speaketh of a pagan husband: "will he willingly let thee go unto nocturnal assemblies (*convocationibus*), if that should be required?" [^447]

Origen holdeth a loftier view concerning the hours of prayer than his teacher Clement of Alexandria: "The entire life of a holy man ought to be one great, unceasing prayer, a part whereof shall be prayer in the proper sense, which ought to be performed not less than three times a day"; having referred unto Daniel, the Apostle Peter, and David in proof of the necessity of praying at three "times of the day," Origen addeth: "yet neither shall we spend the nocturnal time without this manner of prayer, as it is related concerning Paul in the Acts that he with Silas in Philippi prayed at night" [^448].
*(Orig. p. 95)*
*St. Cyprian* already elaborateth carefully the symbolism of the prayer hours of the day. Perceiving together with Tertullian in the threefold number of the hours the mystery of the Holy Trinity, St. Cyprian discerneth the same signification also in the three-hour intervals separating these hours one from another; in particular, St. Cyprian discerneth the significance of the 3rd hour in the descent of the Holy Spirit, of the 6th in the prayer of the Apostle Peter which decided the reception of the Gentiles into the Church, and of the 6th and 9th in that

"the Lord, crucified at the 6th hour, until the 9th washed away our sins with His blood... For us, however, beloved brethren, beyond the hours observed from of old, the times (*spatia*) of praying and the mysteries have now increased. For it is meet to pray also in the morning, that by morning prayer the Resurrection of the Lord may be glorified. At the setting of the sun and the conclusion of the day it is necessary again to pray; since Christ is the true Sun and the true Day, therefore at the setting of the sun and the conclusion of the day, when we pray that light may come upon us, we entreat (*praecamur*) the coming of Christ, Who will impart the grace of eternal light... And if we abide always in Christ, that is, in the light, then even at night we ought not to cease from prayer... Let not the darkness which we have escaped hinder us; let there be no omission of prayer in the nocturnal hours (*nulla sint horis nocturnis precum damna*) from slothfulness and neglect" [^449].

Thus, all the most important ecclesiastical writers of the 3rd century make mention of the hours of prayer, and all alike designate as such hours the 3rd, 6th, and 9th, noting that besides these morning and evening were dedicated unto prayer, and that prayers at night were likewise in custom. Apparently, at these hours private prayer is presupposed, yet the analogy of these hours with the morning and evening assemblies for divine worship, as well as the designation of nocturnal prayers in Tertullian as "assemblies" (*convocationes*), permitteth us to think that in certain places and at certain times small prayer gatherings were held at these hours. Thus the writers of the first half of the 3rd century know already, not counting Matins with the Liturgy and Vespers, up to 6 prayer hours (and with these services—8): morning prayer, the 3rd, 6th, and 9th [printed: 8th] hours, evening prayer, and nocturnal prayer, perchance even more than one (St. Cyprian: "nocturnal hours"). The prayers of the 3rd, 6th, and 9th [printed: 8th] hours consequently bore approximately the same character as the morning and evening prayers. Hence even now among certain Eastern Christians (for example, the Armenians), who have preserved an exceedingly ancient ecclesiastical practice, morning and evening prayers are accounted an ecclesiastical service on a par with the others (as likewise in certain ancient Greek and Slavonic Horologia). Remarkable is the testimony of St. Cyprian that "now the times of praying and the mysteries have increased": before his very eyes there was taking place, as it were, both the multiplication and the complication of these secondary ecclesiastical services.

#### Prayer Hours according to Canonical Monuments of the 3rd Century

Naturally, the canonical monuments of the 3rd century, which belong rather unto its second half than unto the first (upon which fall the aforementioned *(Orig. p. 96)* testimonies), know already both a somewhat greater number of prayer hours and a more communal, liturgical character attending them. The testimonies of canonical monuments concerning the prayer hours are important for us also in that they speak of the practice of diverse Churches: Syrian, Egyptian, and Roman, and nonetheless indicate a uniform practice. The slight difference in this practice among the diverse Churches may testify that this practice was elaborated independently. In view of the particular importance of this epoch for the elaboration of the ritual of the liturgical hours, the first foundations whereof were now being laid, we shall present in parallel all the prescriptions of this kind in the canonical monuments of the 3rd century. Let us begin with the *Testamentum*, as providing more succinct indications.

The *Testamentum* in its prescriptions concerning the prayer hours makes a distinction between the clergy (more specifically, the bishop and presbyter) and the laity, requiring from the former greater zeal and diligence in observing these hours. Herein the passage concerning the episcopal and presbyteral hours of prayer in the *Testamentum* exhibiteth in the Syriac manuscript and in the Arabic translation for the Coptic Church characteristic variants (marked by us in italics):

1. *The "Testamentum Domini Nostri Jesu Christi" in the Syriac Recension:*

Let the bishop be constantly at the altar, abiding long in prayers and at night, especially in the prescribed nocturnal hours, namely, at the first, at midnight, and at the first hour of dawn, when the morning breaketh. In addition unto this, in the morning (?), at the third hour, at the sixth hour, at the ninth hour, at the twelfth hour, and at the hour of the lighting of the lamp. If he prayeth for the people and for himself at all times continually, he doeth well. And let him be alone in the building of the church. Yet if he hath one or two companions, it is good if he abideth with them for united, concordant prayer in the word. For where two or three are gathered in My name, as ye remember I said unto you, I also will be in the midst of them. If he cannot continually abide the entire night, at least let him remain (in the temple) at the aforementioned hours. For then the Angels visit the church [^450].

2. *The "Testamentum" in the Arabic Translation for the Coptic Church ("Arabic Didascalia"):*

Let the bishop be constantly at the altar and free for prayer by day and by night,—especially at the hours wherein prayer is appointed: at the beginning of the day, and at the time of going unto sleep, and at midnight, and at the time of dawn, and then at the first hour of the day, as also at the 3rd, 6th, and 9th, and at dusk. If he prayeth for himself and for all the people at all times, he acteth well; and let him be alone in the church. Yet if he hath one or two companions and it pleaseth him that they be with him, let him arrange that they assist him in every work, especially in prayers and supplications, which must be performed attentively and in harmony, forasmuch as the Lord said: Where two or three are gathered in My name, there am I in the midst of them. If he cannot perform prayers continually day and night, let him pray at those hours which we have indicated. Then the Holy Angels will visit the church and minister unto it [^451].

*(Orig. p. 97)*
3. *The Testamentum (concerning the hours of prayer for the laity):*

Let the people always take care to pray unfailingly at the very dawn, as soon as they arise from their bed and wash their hands; and thereafter let them go unto whatever work each pleaseth.
*(Orig. p. 98)*
Let all take care to pray at the third hour with sorrow and labor, either in church, or if they cannot go unto church, at home. This is the hour at which the Only-Begotten was led unto the Cross.

In like manner let there be prayer with sorrow at the sixth hour, for then the day was divided by darkness. Let there therefore be a voice that would imitate the prophets and the suffering creation.
Likewise also at the ninth hour let a prayer with doxology be extended, as it were in imitation of the souls of those who praise the God of truth, Who remembered His holy ones [^452] and sent His Word and His wisdom for their illumination. For at this hour life was opened unto the faithful, and blood and water flowed from the side of the Lord.
*(Orig. p. 99)*
In the evening, since it is the beginning of the following day and representeth an image of the (final) resurrection, (God) hath made it that we should praise (Him).
At midnight let them arise, praising and extolling God for (the Lord's) Resurrection. It is necessary that a believing husband, having an (un?)believing wife, should go and perform prayers at the appointed hours.
*(Orig. p. 100)*
At dawn let them glorify with psalmody, forasmuch as Christ, having arisen, glorified the Father amid the singing of the apostles. Let those who are pure not omit any of the indicated hours of prayer [^453].

4. *The Canons of Hippolytus*

All who belong unto the order of Christians ought to pray first of all at the time when they arise from morning sleep. When they gather to pray, let them wash their hands. The same let them do before each of their affairs.
If in the Church there is an assembly for the word of God, let each hasten thither unto this assembly, and let him know that the hearing of the word of God must be set far above enjoying all the splendor of this world, and that he will suffer great loss whomsoever necessity ever hindereth from hearing the word of God. Let them endeavor more frequently, being freed from affairs, to gather in church and firmly cast away from themselves hatred toward an enemy, especially if anyone is literate. All the more will he receive benefit if he heareth that which he knew not, for the Lord is present in the place where the remembrance of (His) majesty is celebrated, and the Spirit descendeth upon those assembled, pouring out His grace upon all. Whosoever among them is a man of divided heart (courage?), in them He resteth, even as ye have heard concerning their appointment (ordination?) in the Spirit. Those, however, who are moved by their own mind (following only its promptings?) (and remaining) at home, follow not that which they hear in church. Therefore let each endeavor with great zeal to visit the church on all days whereon prayers are celebrated. And on whatever day they pray not in church, take the Scripture and read therein. Let the sun in the morning see the Scripture upon thy knees.
*(Orig. p. 98)*
Let them pray also at the third hour, since at this time the Savior was willingly crucified for our salvation, that He might grant us freedom.
Then pray at the sixth hour, since at this hour all creation was brought into turmoil on account of the dreadful crime committed by the Judeans.
At the ninth hour again let them pray, since at this hour Christ prayed and yielded up His spirit into the hands of His Father.
*(Orig. p. 99)*
And at the hour when the sun setteth let them pray, since this is the completion of the day.
And thereafter at the lighting of lamps in the evening let him pray, even as David saith: "By night I speak."
And thereafter at midnight let him pray, even as David likewise did. Paul and Silas, the servants of Christ, prayed at midnight and praised God [^454].
Therefore, we ought to remember God at every hour.
And when anyone lieth down upon his bed for sleep, he ought to pray in his heart, doing this in such manner (a prayer is missing, perchance the Lord's Prayer) [^455].
Whosoever is bound by marriage, whenever he desireth to arise from the side of his wife, let him pray. For marriage defileth not. And after regeneration a bath is not needed, excepting the washing of hands and nothing besides this, since the Holy Spirit scenteth the body of the believer and cleanseth it entirely.
Let each endeavor with great zeal to pray at midnight, for our fathers said that at this hour all creation is ready for service unto the glory of God, the orders of Angels and the souls of the righteous bless God, as the Lord testifieth, saying concerning this: **"At midnight a cry arose: Behold, the Bridegroom cometh; go ye out to meet Him"** (*polunoshchi zhe vopl' byst': se Zhenikh gryadet, iskhodite vo sreteniye yemu*).
*(Orig. p. 100)*
And thereafter at the time when the cock croweth, prayers ought to be established in the churches, even as the Lord said:

**"Watch, for ye know not at what hour the Son of Man cometh, at cockcrow or in the morning"** (*bdite yako ne veste, v kiy chas Syn chelovecheskiy priidet, v petloglasheniye ili zautra*) [^456].

*(Orig. p. 97)*
5. *The Egyptian Canons*

All the faithful, men and women, having arisen in the morning from sleep, before they set about any work, let them wash their hands and pray unto God, and only then go forth unto their affairs.
Yet if an instruction in the word of God takes place, let each prefer to go unto that place, taking into consideration that God will hear when he shall speak (with Him) through the instructor. For, having prayed in church, he will be able to avoid the unpleasantnesses of the day. The God-fearing man must remember that it is a great loss not to go unto the place where they teach, especially if he can read. Or (?) if he hath come to learn, let none of you be (come?) last in church, unto the place where instruction is imparted. Then it is meet to grant unto the preacher to propose what is profitable for all, and thou shalt hear that whereof thou didst not think, and shalt receive benefit from that which the Holy Spirit will give through the instructor. In this manner thy faith will be confirmed in that which thou shalt hear. Furthermore, in that place it will be told thee also that which thou oughtest to do at home. Therefore let each be zealous in visiting the church, the place where the Holy Spirit flourisheth. If on any day there be no instruction, let each at home take the holy book and read to his heart's content therein that which seemeth unto him profitable.
*(Orig. p. 98)*
And if thou art at home, pray at the third hour and praise God. If, however, a man findeth himself in another place and this hour arriveth, pray in thy heart unto God. For at this hour Christ was seen (appeared) nailed unto the Cross. Therefore also in the Old Testament the Law commanded to place at every hour the showbread (loaves of proposition) as a prefiguration of the Body and Blood of Christ, and (commanded) the slaughter of the irrational lamb, which is a prefiguration of the perfect Lamb, for the Shepherd is Christ; He is the Bread that came down from heaven.
In like manner pray again at the sixth hour. For when Christ was nailed unto the Cross, that day was divided and a great darkness appeared. Therefore at this hour let them pray with mighty prayer, imitating the voice of Him Who prayed when all creation grew dark from the Judean unbelief.
And furthermore, a great prayer and great praise ought to be performed at the ninth hour, that thou mayest know how the soul of the righteous praiseth the Lord, the true God, Who remembered the saints and sent unto them His Son, Who is His Logos, that He might enlighten them; for at this hour Christ was pierced in the side with a spear, and blood and water flowed forth, and thereafter He enlightened yet the remainder of the day until evening.
*(Orig. p. 99)*
Therefore thou also, going to sleep, oughtest to begin the day and make it an image of the Resurrection.
Pray further before thou restest upon the bed of thy sleep.
And at midnight, rising upon thy bed, wash thyself and pray; yet it is necessary to wash with pure water. If thou hast a wife, pray together alternately. If she be not yet a believer, having withdrawn apart, pray alone and return again unto thy bed. Thou art bound by marriage not in order to neglect prayer; for ye are not defiled; they who are washed have no need to wash again, for they are pure and blameless; having breathed upon thy hand and signed thyself with the moisture of thy lips, thou art entirely pure unto thy feet. For this is the gift of the Holy Spirit, and the drops of baptism (the drops serve as drops of baptism) descending upon the fountain, that is, the heart of the believer, cleanse him who hath become a believer. It is necessary for us to pray at this hour, for the elders (Greek text: *presbyteros*, πρεσβύτερος) handed down unto us this custom and taught us so to wash ourselves. At this hour all creation resteth, blessing *(Orig. p. 100)* God. The stars, trees, and waters stand as it were still; the entire host of Angels celebrateth ministry with the souls of the righteous; they bless Almighty God at this hour; therefore whosoever believeth, let him pray at this hour. The Lord likewise spake thus, testifying concerning this: **"At midnight a cry arose: Behold, the Bridegroom cometh; go ye out to meet Him"** (*polunoshchi vopl' byst': se Zhenikh gryadet; iskhodite v sreteniye yemu*). And He added: **"Watch therefore, for ye know neither the day nor the hour wherein the Son of Man cometh"** (*sego radi bdite, yako ne veste dne ni chasa, v on' zhe Syn chelovecheskiy priidet*).
In like manner, rising at the hour when the cock croweth, pray. For at this hour the children of Israel denied Christ, Whom we, believing in Him, have known through faith, looking full of hope unto the day of eternal light, which will shine upon us forever in the resurrection of the dead [^457].

Comparing all these testimonies one with another, one cannot fail to notice first of all that the *Testamentum* imparteth unto the hours of prayer in part that character which they possess now in the Catholic Church, being obligatory only for the clergy (*horae canonicae*), although it requireth the arrangement at these hours of at least small prayer assemblies. The latter two monuments, however—the *Canons of Hippolytus* and the *Egyptian Canons*—insist more upon the unfailing observance of the hours of prayer by all the faithful. Characteristic is the indication of these monuments regarding the very frequent, well-nigh daily celebration of the morning divine service, wherein the reading of Holy Scripture is recognized as its most important part. Amid the rarity of copies of the Bible at that time, the church was the sole place where one could study it, the most accessible school of theology. It appeareth incomprehensible that the monuments require attendance at the morning divine service especially from "those who know how to read": perchance the latter more than others neglected these assemblies, deeming the domestic reading of Holy Scripture sufficient. The *Egyptian Canons* note especially the broad development of preaching (not without reason do they share a common homeland with Origen). The *Testamentum* and the *Egyptian Canons* single out from among the other hours of prayer the ninth, indicating for its prayers pre-eminently *(Orig. p. 101)* a joyful and laudatory character. Such a character the service of this hour beareth even now. The *Testamentum*, comparatively with the *Canons of Hippolytus* and the *Egyptian Canons*, possesseth new liturgical orders. Thus in the Syriac recension it indicateth in the evening, besides the hour of the lighting of lamps (Vespers) and the "first hour" of the night, corresponding unto the service of retiring unto sleep of the other monuments or our Compline, yet the 12th hour of the day as a prayer hour, placing it before the lighting of lamps. An echo of this practice is that in the present Coptic Horologion "Compline" precedeth Vespers [^458]. The Arabic recension of the *Testamentum*, omitting the service of the 12th hour, possesseth another, superfluous in comparison with the *Canons of Hippolytus* and the *Egyptian Canons*—namely, the *first hour (of the day)*. It is possible that the Syriac *Testamentum* likewise pointeth unto this service by the word "in the morning" (if a comma be placed after it). Characteristic is that insistence wherewith the *Testamentum*, yet only in the Syriac text, requireth the observance of the *nocturnal hours* of prayer: either because these hours were more neglected, or by reason of their special favorableness for a prayerful disposition. Certain ancient Horologia, as we shall see subsequently, possess an entire system of "nocturnal hours," equalizing them in number with the diurnal ones and bringing both quantities separately up to 12.

Thus already in the 3rd century there exist positively all our present ecclesiastical services under the form of prayer at the corresponding hours, while of these services: the Liturgy, Matins, Vespers, and the 3rd, 6th, and 9th Hours trace their origin back unto the apostolic age.

#### The Order of the Hours of the 3rd Century

The monuments of the 3rd century do not indicate for the prayer hours any definite order. Consequently, herein everything was left unto the freedom of the believer. Yet already in the 2nd century, as we have seen, the indispensable accompaniment of the prayer hours then observed was the Lord's Prayer. That this was so in the 3rd century as well is clearly evident from the fact that Tertullian, precisely in his treatise *On Prayer*, speaketh of the prayer hours, as likewise from the fact that well-nigh every significant writer of the 3rd century left a commentary upon this prayer (Tertullian, Origen, St. Cyprian). To what extent the Lord's Prayer was considered basic, all-exhaustive, and necessary at every prayer, and consequently in honoring the sacred hours of the day, is demonstrated by the tone of defense wherein Tertullian speaketh concerning other prayers: "since there exist petitions corresponding unto the circumstances of each, then, having premised the established and ordinary prayer (that is, the Lord's Prayer, as the context demonstrateth) as a foundation, as it were, we have the right to express accidental (*accidentium*) desires, the right, as it were, to pass beyond the bounds of petitions" [^459]. These "supplementary" prayers unto the *Our Father* *(Orig. p. 102)*, presumably, did not yet possess ready models anywhere, judging from the fact that the *Testamentum*, so rich in prayers, provideth no such models; yet the "prayer of the widows" at midnight in that same *Testamentum* may be regarded as the first attempt to formulate prayers also for the liturgical hours.

Tertullian permitteth us to say yet more concerning the prayer ritual of the liturgical hours. Immediately after speaking concerning these hours, remarking that "a brother who hath entered the house must not be sent away without prayer," he saith: "those more zealous in prayer have the custom of subjoining unto prayers the alleluia and psalms in such manner that by their concluding words those present may respond (unto him)." With this testimony of Tertullian one may compare the following prescription of the *Testamentum*: "unto him who singeth in church, let the virgins and boys respond. If also at home two or three sing privately, in like manner alternately let those who sing respond; likewise also the men" [^460]. Both there and here there is clearly question of that semi-private, semi-public prayer which the prayer "hours" represent in the canonical monuments of the 3rd century; and as an accompaniment of this prayer, that is, of the then order of the hours, there are already indicated, as also now, both psalms and the alleluia (now with us concluding the psalms of the Hours), and the singing or other public recitation of the most expressive verses of the psalms (cf. our present prokeimenon, the refrains unto the troparia of the hour, and the "verse" of the hour). — The same Tertullian in the same treatise acquainteth us with a whole series of rites in use at these semi-public prayers, whereof certain he disapproveth, while others he recommendeth, and which in greater or lesser degree have been reflected in our present divine service in general, and in particular in that of the Hours. Of these rites the most customary and necessary in Tertullian appeareth genuflection: "every day we ought to prostrate ourselves before God, at least at the first prayer wherewith we greet the day; on fasts and stations, however, no prayer can be without genuflection" [^461]. Well-nigh equally necessary at every prayer was the "kiss of peace" [^462] (preserved with us only at the Liturgy). It was customary likewise to lift up and spread forth the hands [^463], and to wash the hands before prayer [^464]. Tertullian expresseth disapproval concerning the customs of taking off the outer garment at prayer and sitting down after it [^465]. Tertullian makes no mention in this enumeration of rites of the sign of the *(Orig. p. 103)* cross, yet in another place he speaketh concerning it: "at every departure (*progressum*) and movement, at every entrance and exit, at putting on clothes and shoes, at washing, at table, at the lighting of lights, at bed, at sitting down, and in every action we trace (*terimus*) upon the forehead the sign (*signaculo*) of the cross" [^466]. But the *Canons of Hippolytus* and the *Egyptian Canons* speak of the sign of the cross immediately after the discourse concerning the liturgical hours and in connection therewith.

*The Canons of Hippolytus:*

We, however, together with the catechumens, will instruct one another concerning the service of God; then the demons cannot grieve us when in every prayer we remember Christ.
Sign thy forehead with the sign of the cross for victory over Satan and for the glorification of (God) for faith. This did Moses likewise with the blood of the lamb, wherewith he smeared the doorposts and the lintels of the doors... [^467].

*The Egyptian Canons:*

Ye, however, all believers, if ye perform these (prayers at the appointed hours) and keep them in memory, teaching one another and the catechumens to do this, then nothing shall cause you to stumble, and never shall ye fall, if at all times ye remember Christ.
At every hour receive (in thy mind) this name, that thou mayest seal (*sphragizein*, σφραγίζειν) thy forehead in fear. For this is a known and manifest sign whereby the devil is destroyed. When thou doest this in faith, thou manifestest thyself (as a Christian) not only before men, but also in thine own conscience, wherein thou art comforted as a pursuer (of the devil), forasmuch as the adversary the devil looketh only upon the strength of the heart, and when from within he seeth a man that he is discerning, being sealed with the seal of the word of God outwardly and inwardly, then he fleeth immediately, being pursued by the Holy Spirit Who abideth in the man who hath given Him a place in himself. This did Moses likewise... [^468].

Characteristic is the view of the sign of the cross as an adjuration against the devil.

*(Orig. p. 104)*

#### Constituent Parts of Divine Worship

In order that the picture of the daily cycle of divine worship in the 3rd century may be complete, it is necessary to make several further general observations concerning the character of the services of that era and their internal content—that is, to examine more closely the common and indispensable constituent elements of every divine service: the reading of Holy Scripture, prayer, and singing in the 3rd century. Then, in addition to the structural composition of the services of that time, we shall fully comprehend their entire content.

#### The Reading of Holy Scripture

Frequent though the aforementioned testimonies of 3rd-century monuments concerning the reading of Holy Scripture at divine worship may be, they do not leave everything clear on this point. Above all, they do not specify the cycle of sacred books that were read. One must bear in mind that the New Testament canon of sacred books was not yet fully defined at that time. Not all the sacred books currently regarded as divinely inspired were recognized everywhere, in all Churches, as such even in the 4th century, as shown by the classification of certain of these books by St. Athanasius and Eusebius of Caesarea into the category of *antilegomena* (ἀντιλεγόμενα, disputed) or merely *anagignōskomena* (ἀναγιγνωσκόмеνα, readable—that is, permitted to be read at divine worship as edifying alongside the divinely inspired books). Such hesitation in the 4th century existed regarding the Epistle to the Hebrews, the majority of the Catholic Epistles, and the Apocalypse. Judging from the fact that into the category of such books "disputed" with regard to their canonicity in the 4th century were placed also certain venerable ancient writings subsequently decisively recognized as uninspired—such as the Epistle of Barnabas, the *Shepherd* of Hermas, and the like—one may think that in the 2nd and 3rd centuries the scope of Holy Scripture read at divine worship was broader than ours: that is, that alongside the present canonical books of the New Testament there were read and not sharply distinguished from them the writings of the Apostolic Fathers, and in certain Churches probably even apocrypha. A trace of this practice hath been preserved unto the present day in the Abyssinian Church, where as Holy Scripture at divine worship there is read, for example, the Book of Enoch [^469]. In our divine worship, a trace of this practice is the reading of the non-canonical books of the Old Testament: the Wisdom of Solomon and the Wisdom of Jesus son of Sirach as paremias alongside and on a par with the canonical books, as well as, in part, the reading of the Acts and Apostolic Epistles as it were on a par with patristic readings at the All-Night Vigil before the Six Psalms.

#### Pericopes

For the first time from the 3rd century we possess testimonies regarding the liturgical division of the New Testament for reading. The *Arabic Didascalia*, as we have seen [^470], makes mention of pericopes (*zachala*). The testimony of this canonical monument, *(Orig. p. 105)* regarding whose attribution unto the 3rd century doubt is possible, is confirmed by writers of the 3rd century. Origen makes mention of pericopes in his commentary upon the Book of Kings: "that which hath been read is very extensive; and since it is necessary to speak of that which is divided into two pericopes, and there hath been read in order concerning Nabal..." [^471]. It is noticeable at times how the daily pericope compelleth Origen in a homily to dwell upon sections of Scripture little conducive unto edification, such as genealogies or the enumerations of the Hebrew encampments in the wilderness [^472]. All this likewise permitteth the conclusion that the division of Scripture for liturgical reading must have been continuous, without omissions. The poverty of the church year (in sacred commemorations) excluded the need for any departures from the continuous readings. Nevertheless, for existing commemorations, special readings must have been selected; this is evident from the fact that the same Origen in his commentary upon the Book of Job speaketh of reading it on fast days in honor of Christ's Passion: "in the church assembly the suffering of Job is read on holy days, on days of fasting, on days of abstinence, on days wherein those fasting and abstaining as it were suffer together with that marvelous Job, on days wherein by fasting and abstinence we follow the holy Passion of our Lord Jesus Christ... Not without reason (*merito*) even now on days of suffering, on days of sanctification, on days of fasting is the suffering of the blessed Job read; upon it do they meditate, and it do they unceasingly investigate" [^473].

#### The Reader

At the beginning of the 3rd century the reading of all Holy Scripture without distinction was assigned unto the reader, the view of whose office was of the highest order: it was accounted honorable even for a confessor. "So also was it meet," writeth St. Cyprian regarding the appointment as readers of the confessors Aurelius [printed: Avraamiy] and Celerinus, "for them to begin from the office of reader. Nothing is more becoming for a voice that hath confessed the Lord with a glorious proclamation than to resound in the performance of divine readings; after the lofty words which martyrdom for Christ hath uttered, to read the Gospel of Christ, through which martyrs are made" [^474]. "What else ought to have been done for one who hath come unto us with such a commendation (*dignatione*) from the Lord, who was renowned for the admiration of the very one who persecuted him, than to elevate him unto the ecclesiastical ambo (*tribunam*), that, standing upon the height of the elevated place, visible unto the entire multitude by the glory of his station (*honoris*), he might read the precepts and the Gospel of the Lord, which this confessor steadfastly and faithfully followeth? Let that voice which hath confessed the Lord be heard daily in that which the Lord hath spoken. Let this confessor see whether there existeth a higher degree which he might attain in the Church. There is nothing wherein *(Orig. p. 106)* a confessor could be so profitable unto the brethren as that, when the Gospel reading is heard from his mouth, everyone who heareth may imitate the faith of the reader" [^475]. These passages clearly demonstrate that in Carthage in the middle of the 3rd century the reader read the Gospels as well (although already the 2nd century singled out the latter as a pre-eminently sacred book). But the *Testamentum* already entrusteth the reading of the Gospel unto a presbyter or deacon [^476].

#### Homilies

With regard to homiletics, the 3rd century is important in that now for the first time those homilies are committed unto writing which were delivered in church in explanation of the read sections of Holy Scripture (Origen, Hippolytus). Thereby was laid the foundation of that patristic literature which subsequently yielded such rich material for liturgical patristic readings. Yet from among the writers of the 3rd century our Typikon hath selected none for liturgical use.

#### Prayers

With regard to the prayers at the daily cycle of divine worship, the 3rd century likewise takes a significant step in comparison with the 2nd. There, formulas of Eucharistic prayers appear for the first time (in the *Teaching of the Twelve Apostles* / *Didache*); here, similar prayer formulas appear for the other principal daily services, at least for Matins, and at least themes for the prayer of the Hours.

St. Cyprian reproacheth a heretic in that, "having despised the bishops and forsaken the priests of God, he dareth to set up another altar, to offer another prayer with unauthorized words" [^477].

#### Melodies

Liturgical singing, as we have seen, received significant development in the 2nd century in comparison with the 1st, if one crediteth the tradition that St. Ignatius the God-Bearer was the initiator of antiphonal singing in the Christian Church. In the 3rd century it takes a no less significant step: the necessity is recognized of regulating the very melody (not the order alone) of Christian chant. Consequently, in the matter of chant the 3rd century penetrateth deeper than the 2nd. We have in mind the considerations expressed by Clement of Alexandria regarding music appropriate for Christians and their divine worship. Above all, Clement directeth attention unto the distinction of Christian divine worship from Jewish and pagan worship in musical terms: "we for the glorification of God employ exclusively the peaceful word, and no longer employ either the ancient psaltery, or the trumpet, or the timbrel, or the flute" [^478]. Yet not all genres even of vocal singing, in Clement's view, may be accepted by Christians and *(Orig. p. 107)* were accepted by the Church of his time: "Music must be resorted to for the embellishment and education of morals. For even at a banquet (the agape?) we drink for mutual singing, chanting our cherished (hope) and glorifying God for the ungrudging gift of human enjoyments and for the constant provision of everything necessary for the growth of both body and soul. That music must be rejected which is superfluous (*perittē*, περιττὴ), which breaketh the soul, which runneth into variety, now mournful (*thrēnōdē*, θρηνώδη), now unrestrained and voluptuous (*akolaston kai hēdypathē*, ἀκόλαστον καὶ ἡδυпаθῆ), now frenzied and raving (*ekbakcheuomenēn kai manikēn*, ἐкβαкχευομένην καὶ μανικὴν)" [^479].

Dwelling upon the genres of vocal Greek music existing in his time—which had captivated the attention of the entire world of that day, had long since penetrated Eastern peoples, and must have everywhere displaced national melodies—Clement findeth several of these genres utterly unacceptable for a Christian and the Church: "We ought to choose melodies imbued with dispassion and chastity; melodies that enervate and relax the soul cannot harmonize with our manly and magnanimous frame of mind and disposition. The art expressed in vocal modulations through diverse flourishes is a false art; it fostereth a propensity toward an indolent and disordered life. By austere and sober melodies, however, shamelessness and drunkenness are averted in the very bud (presumably the agapai are meant). One must surrender chromatic harmonies (*chromatikas harmonias*, printed *χρωατικὰς ἁρμονίας*) unto shameless (*achrōmois*, ἀхрώμοις) carousals and the music of bouquet-bearing courtesans" [^480]. "The diverse venoms of enervating songs and mournful verses of the Carian muse are equally destructive unto morals, captivating them through intemperate and artless (*kakotechnō*, κακοτέχνῳ) music into the passion of such a revel" [^481]. Yet concerning certain genres of contemporary Greek music Clement speaketh approvingly, apparently finding in them something in common with the sacred music of the ancient Hebrews: "David may furnish a model for music, singing and prophesying, praising God melodiously (*emmelōs*, ἐммелῶς). For the Dorian harmony precisely there is most suitable such an enharmonic mode (*genos enharmonion*, γένος ἑναρμόνιον), and for the Phrygian—the diatonic (*diatonon*, διάтоνον), as Aristoxenus saith; and thus the harmony of the barbarian Hebrew psaltery, revealing within itself something venerable as the most ancient, becometh, especially in Terpander (the Greek musician), a model for the Dorian harmony, when he praiseth Zeus in the following manner: Zeus is the beginning of all, the leader of all; this beginning of hymns do I raise unto thee, Jupiter" [^482]. The next of the Greek melodies, the Carian, Clement characterizeth as too plaintive and somber for Christian use; further concerning it [printed: *o nam*] nothing is known unto us. As regards the chromatic, enharmonic, and diatonic melodies, however, *(Orig. p. 108)* their very structure is known unto us. Their difference depended upon the magnitude of each of the three intervals in the tetrachord (a system of 4 strings or notes) which formed the foundation of Greek music. The total magnitude of the intervals in a tetrachord equaled 2 1/2 tones, and the simplest structure of a tetrachord was that in which it consisted of two whole intervals or tones and one half-tone; such a structure was called diatonic (through tone). A more artificial structure was that in which the tetrachord consisted of a tone and a half and two semitones; such a structure was called chromatic (colorful, varied). Still more artificial was the structure in which the tetrachord was composed of a double tone and two quarter tones: "Such a tetrachord was probably not used in vocal singing practice owing to the impossibility of precise execution by the voice and distinction by the ear of quarter tones, but was practiced in the realm of instrumental music" [^483]. This latter structure of the tetrachord was called enharmonic. But Clement, apparently, by an enharmonic melody understandeth some other (unison?), since he regardeth it as simpler than the diatonic and assigneth it unto Dorian melodies, which subsequent writers class with the diatonic genre of music on a par with the Phrygian.

All these remarks of Clement concerning music were evidently prompted by the lack of discrimination among Alexandrian Christians (naturally, highly educated in general and musically in particular) toward diverse genres of music. Clement was thus the first among the Teachers of the Church to arrive at the thought of regulating the liturgical singing of Christians with regard unto its very melody, and he declared himself decisively against the admission into the Church of the most artificial and passionate melodies. Subsequent organizers of church chant—in the West, Saints Ambrose and Gregory the Great, and in the East, St. John of Damascus—excluded the chromatic chant from their system of Tones, completely in accordance with Clement's indications, and adopted the Dorian and Phrygian chants of a diatonic character.

#### The Development of Hymnody

Writers of the 3rd century consider themselves entitled to boast before pagans of the abundance of hymns in their divine worship and to compete with them in this regard. Clement of Alexandria saith unto a pagan that upon the "God-beloved, cleanly shaded mountain" (in the Church) they "abandon themselves unto rejoicing (*bakcheuousi*, βακχεύουσι); yet not Maenads (priestesses)..., but daughters of God, fair lambs, celebrating (*theaspizousai*, θεασπίζουσαι) the venerable solemn mysteries (*orgia*, ὄργια) of the Word, forming a sober-minded (*sōphrona*, σώφρονα) choir; the choir here is the righteous; here is singing, here is a hymn unto the King of all; maidens sing, Angels glorify, prophets speak" [^484]. Tertullian saith: "If dramatic art delighteth anyone, we have an abundance of Scrip-*(Orig. p. 109)*tures, an abundance of verses, an abundance of maxims, an abundance of songs (*canticorum*), an abundance of singing (*vocum*); and not fable, but truth; not strophae, but simplicity" [^485]. Origen, in response to Celsus' observation that Christians would honor God if they sang praises unto the Sun and Minerva, saith: "We utter (*legomen*, λέγομεν) hymns only unto the one God of all and unto His Only-Begotten Word God; we chant praises (*hymnoumen*, ὑмνοῦмен) unto God and unto His Only-Begotten, even as the sun, moon, stars, and all the heavenly host sing praises unto Him" [^486].

The great growth of liturgical singing literature encountered even a reaction among certain bishops. In the encyclical letter directed against Paul of Samosata, bishop of Antioch (who was carried away by the heresy of Artemon), in the second half of the 3rd century, the bishops denounce him, among other things, because "he abolished the psalms unto the glory of our Lord Jesus Christ, as being of recent origin (*neōterous*, νεωτέρους) and the compositions of modern men; whereas in the midst of the church, on the great day of Pascha, he commanded songs to be sung in honor of himself (*psalōdein eis heauton*, ψαλωδεῖν εἰς ἑαυтὸν), and for this purpose appointed women, whom hearing one could not but shudder" [^487].

#### Hymnographers and Hymns of the 3rd Century

Notwithstanding so rich a hymnographic activity in the 3rd century, scarcely any compositions of this genre, or even the names of their authors, have reached us from that era. This is explained by the destruction of Christian books by pagans and by the fact that Christians concealed their teaching—which was contained, among other things, in hymns (*hymnoi theologountes*, ὕμνοι θεολογοῦντες), especially the dogma of the Holy Trinity, brought forward principally by the 3rd century—not only from pagans, but also from catechumens (*disciplina arcani*), on which account Christians presumably feared to write down their hymns (as also the Creed) [^488]. Nevertheless, from the 3rd century there have survived not only several names of hymnographers, but also several of their works. Eusebius citeth from the work of Dionysius of Alexandria *On the Promises* a passage wherein this hierarch, reproving Nepos, bishop of the Egyptian Pentapolis († 246), for chiliastic views, praiseth him for "an abundance of spiritual songs, wherewith even unto now many of the brethren are delighted" [^489]. — Clement of Alexandria concludeth his *Paedagogus* with a hymn unto the Shepherd—that is, unto the Savior; it is possible that this hymn had a liturgical use, and in any case it *(Orig. p. 110)* can provide an idea of the character of the ecclesiastical poetry of that time. The hymn, beginning with the words: "Tamer of untamed colts," consisteth entirely of a long series (up to 30) of rapturous and tender titles (epithets) for Christ (for example: wing of nestlings, King, Word, Bestower of wisdom, Savior, husbandman, rudder, bridle, fisher of men), and a supplication unto Christ to gather His children for His praise and to lead them along His path. The conclusion of the hymn is accounted the most poetic: "O heavenly milk, poured forth from the glorious breasts of the graced Virgin—that is, of Thy Wisdom! We, Thy children, nourished with tender lips, filled with the gentle breath of the maternal bosom, sing all together simple songs and innocent hymns unto Christ the King, as a holy reward for the doctrine of life; we sing simply the mighty Child." The hymn consisteth of four strophes; it is written in anapests, spondees, and dactyls, with verses not everywhere regular and uniform. The hymn is consequently characteristic as the first attempt at applying Greek versification unto Christian song.

— The allegorical dialogue of Hieromartyr Methodius, bishop first of Patara (in Asia Minor) and subsequently of Tyre († 311), *The Banquet of the Ten Virgins* (presumably written in counterpoise to Plato's *Symposium*, demonstrating the superiority of virginity over marriage), concludeth with a "Hymn of the Virgins unto Christ God" in 24 strophes (in imitation, perchance, of the alphabetical psalms), with a refrain wherewith the choir responds unto the address of each virgin unto Christ. In the hymn, which begins: "From above, O virgins, a voice resoundeth...", the virgins summon one another, in view of the approaching voice that awakeneth the dead, to hasten forth unto the meeting of the approaching Bridegroom;

they express their self-forgetting devotion unto Christ, animating themselves by the example of "the Forerunner, who suffered for love of the truth," and of the Mother of the Bridegroom, "the graced, blameless, unapproachable, pure Virgin who was subjected to suspicion regarding her virginity"; the hymn concludeth with a prayer unto the Father with the Son to receive the virgins "into the portals of eternal life" [^490]. The hymns of Clement and St. Methodius resemble also the subsequent Akathist—the former by its multiplicity of epithets and acclamations, and the latter by its 24-strophe division. Yet in spirit and content both represent something inimitable for subsequent times: so much immediacy of religious feeling is in them, as yet untouched by theological reflection, such intimacy, so to speak, in communion with God, and such power of love for Christ, possible only in those centuries.

From among our present liturgical hymns, the most akin unto these hymns is the canticle **"Gladsome Light"** (*Svete tikhiy* / *Phōs Hilaron*). Judging from the fact that St. Basil the Great speaketh of it as "ancient" [^491], its composition cannot be placed later than the 3rd century. It is remarkable that all these monuments of liturgical poetry of the 3rd century possess an exclusively or predominantly (**"Gladsome Light"**) Christological *(Orig. p. 111)* content: of such a character, as we have seen, were the ecclesiastical hymns in the 2nd century as well [^492]. In this respect prayers differed from hymns: following the model of the Lord's Prayer, and in view of the constant mention by the Savior, in His precepts concerning prayer, of the Father (that prayer ought to be directed unto Him), the prayers that have survived from the 3rd century are for the most part addressed unto the Father. In the 4th century this even prompted a special decree of the Council of Hippo: "When they stand before the altar, prayer must always be directed unto the Father" [^493]. This custom and decree could have been prompted also by the endeavor to protect the dogma of the Trinity from a tritheistic interpretation and to emphasize in this dogma the concept of monarchy (*monarchia*).

From among our present liturgical hymns one may assign unto the 3rd century (judging from the fact that it is found in 4th-century codices of Holy Scripture) the **"Great Doxology"** (*Slavosloviye velikoye*). Just as the hymns of Clement, Methodius, and the hymn **"Gladsome Light"** are models of original 3rd-century Christian creativity, so this hymn is a model of skillful compilation from Holy Scripture. Its versification is Hebrew: parallelism of members. The first three hymns may serve as models of those songs which, according unto the testimony both of the Apostle Paul and later of Tertullian, were sung by individual persons at divine worship (being improvised or composed beforehand) by turn; the latter, perhaps, is a model of hymns for that congregational performance which, according unto the statement of the Neocaesareans unto St. Basil the Great, was introduced into their church by St. Gregory the Wonderworker († 270) [^494], and of which 4th-century writers make increasingly frequent mention. An echo of this distinction between the two genres of hymns (for individual and for congregational use) hath been preserved in our present Typikon in its requirement that **"Gladsome Light"** be pronounced by the superior, whereas for the singing of the **"Great Doxology"** both choirs assemble together. By the special character of the first genre of hymns is explained, perhaps, the fact that not all of them entered into divine worship even from subsequent centuries (neither the poems of Gregory the Theologian nor the hymns of St. Ephrem the Syrian entered into liturgical worship, just as the hymns of Clement and Methodius did not).

#### The Church Year of the 3rd Century: Feasts and Weekdays

Regarding the church year in the 3rd century in comparison with the 2nd, one must note above all a greater distinction and setting apart of feast days from weekdays. Although the Alexandrian school of theology did not approve of such separation [^495], *(Orig. p. 112)* it is manifested, for example, in that on Sunday and during Pentecost work, fasting, and genuflections are now for the first time prohibited: "We," saith Tertullian, "as we have received by tradition, on the day of the Lord's Resurrection alone ought to refrain not only from kneeling, but from every manner of anxiety and toil, deferring our ordinary business lest we give place unto the devil" [^496]. "On the Lord's day we account it unlawful (*nefas dicimus*) to fast or to pray on bended knees" [^497]. "The non-bending of knees on the Lord's day," saith Pseudo-Justin, "is a symbol of the Resurrection, through which by the grace of Christ we have been delivered from sins and from death slain by Him; this custom received its beginning from apostolic times, as saith the blessed Irenaeus, martyr and bishop of Lyons, in his treatise on Pascha" [^498].

#### Sunday

Tertullian is thus the first to make mention of rest or freedom from labors as a mark of a Christian feast, and in particular of Sunday. Yet the Alexandrians—Clement and Origen—in agreement with writers of the 2nd century (especially Saints Justin and Irenaeus), speak only of rest from worldly pursuits and insist that a Christian feast ought not to resemble the Jewish Sabbath with its absolute idleness [^499]. Characteristic is the view of Origen regarding the commemoration associated with Sunday, expressed in the following passage of his: "Now, since there is much people (in church) on account of Friday, and especially on the Lord's day, which is a commemoration of Christ's Passion (for the Lord's Resurrection is celebrated once a year, and not always after seven days), let everyone pray unto God that His word may come unto us" [^500]. Such a view of Sunday is reflected also in our Typikon, when it appointeth for Sunday, besides the Sunday Canon, also the Canon of the Cross and Resurrection, and when it appointeth heirmoloi for the canon of general edifying content rather than dedicated unto the historical event, and the like.

#### Saturday

Although in this manner there continueth the polemic begun in the 2nd century against the Jewish Sabbath, and writers of the 3rd century like those of the 2nd all agree in the conviction regarding its complete non-obligatoriness for Christians [^501], nevertheless from the very beginning of the 3rd century, with the waning of antagonism toward Judaism, there ariseth a tendency toward some manner of honoring Saturday, distinguishing it from the series of ordi-*(Orig. p. 113)*nary days; and this tendency toward the end of the century and the beginning of the 4th century leadeth unto Saturday being honored in certain Churches almost equally with Sunday. Thus Tertullian, immediately preceding the aforementioned passage concerning the honoring of the Resurrection, saith: "In the matter of genuflection also prayer suffereth variety in view of those few who on Saturday abstain from kneeling. Since this exception is stubbornly defended in the Churches, may the Lord grant His grace that they may either give it up or follow their opinion without causing scandal unto others" [^502].

It is remarkable how those passages of the *Syriac Didascalia* where it speaketh of honoring the Lord's day are interpolated by the compiler of the *Apostolic Constitutions* in the sense of celebrating Saturday.

1. *The Didascalia:*

On the Lord's day, leaving all things aside, gather together in church. For whereby shall he be justified before God who goeth not to hear the saving word and to be nourished with divine food which abideth unto the ages?

2. *The Apostolic Constitutions:*

Assemble thither ("into the Lord's house") especially with greater diligence on the Sabbath day and on the day of the Lord's Resurrection, to send up praise unto God, Who created all things through Jesus and sent Him unto us, Who permitted Him to suffer and raised Him from the dead. For whereby shall he be justified before God who will not go to hear the saving word concerning the Resurrection on such a day, when we also perform three prayers standing in remembrance of Him Who arose on the third day, and when there take place readings of the prophets, the proclamation of the Gospel, the offering of the sacrifice, and the gift of sacred food [^503].

The insertion regarding Saturday is made here purely mechanically: the discourse doth not subsequently return unto it. (These parallels are important also as an indicator of how the ritual of Sunday service and the view of the Eucharist developed). Unto another passage of the *Didascalia*, however, where it speaketh of honoring the Lord's day, the *Apostolic Constitutions* make no addition concerning Saturday, although they likewise rework it (the text of the *Didascalia* is marked in italics): "On the Lord's day of the Lord, that is, on the *Kyriakē* (Κυριακή), assemble steadfastly, giving thanks unto God and confessing wherewith God hath favored you through Christ" [^504]. The *Testamentum of Our Lord Jesus Christ* appointeth for Saturday a liturgy with mystagogy, as for Sunday, Pascha, Pentecost, and Epiphany [^505], and prescribeth that at the Eucharist on *(Orig. p. 114)* Saturday three loaves be offered in the image of the Trinity, and on Sunday four—in the image of the Gospel [^506].

#### Wednesday and Friday

Among the other days of the week, Wednesday and Friday continued in the 3rd century to be honored with fasting. The true "gnostic" according unto Clement "knoweth the riddle (*ainigma* [printed: *μύνημα*]) of fasting on those days, that is, on Wednesday and Friday" [^507]. According unto Origen, "we have the 4th and 6th days of the week, on which we are accustomed to fast" [^508]. Origen prizeth Friday especially highly, juxtaposing it with Sunday [^509], and even with Pascha and Pentecost [^510]. The *Syriac Didascalia* speaketh of the fast on Wednesday and Friday in connection with the Paschal fast (in the section on fasting): "He said unto us, teaching us: 'Do ye fast for My sake in these days, or have I need that ye should afflict your soul? Nay, for the sake of your brethren (the Jews—for the pardon of their sin against Christ) have ye done this, and so do ye in the days wherein ye fast—on Wednesday and on Friday—continually, as it is written in Zechariah: the fast of the fourth day and the fast of the fifth, that is, Friday' [^511]."

The *Canons of Hippolytus* regard those who do not fast on Wednesday and Friday as adversaries of God, Who fasted for our sake [^512]. The 69th Apostolic Canon already threateneth a cleric with deposition and a layman with excommunication for non-observance of these fasts.

The *Testamentum*, in the prescription that "the sacrifice (Eucharist) must be offered on Saturday and Sunday only and on a day of fasting" [^513], apparently hath in view the weekly fasts.

#### Fasting in General

This latter passage showeth that fasting was viewed as a kind of feast, a solemnity. Yet there existed also an opposite tendency in the view of fasting, mentioned disapprovingly by Tertullian, which leaned toward the opinion that the fast is broken by the reception of the Eucharist: "Many think that on the days of the stations [^514] they ought not to attend the prayers of the sacrifices, *(Orig. p. 115)* because upon receiving the Body of the Lord the station would be broken. What then? Doth submission unto the Eucharist release a man from a vow unto God? Will not thy station be more solemn if a man stands at the altar of God? When the Body of the Lord hath been received and reserved [^515], then both will be salvific—both participation in the sacrifice and the fulfillment of duty. If the station received its name from a military example (for we also are soldiers of God), then indeed no joy or sorrow occurring in military camps breaketh the station of the soldiers; for joy makes the fulfillment of discipline more pleasant, and sorrow makes it more diligent" [^516].

The fast continued until the ninth hour. The Orthodox reproached the Montanists, among other things, for extending the day's fast beyond this hour. "They (the Orthodox) look upon our stations as unworthy," saith Tertullian, having become a Montanist; "some of them (the stations) they even accuse of novelty, as having been introduced later, saying also that this duty (of fasting) cannot be performed arbitrarily and prolonged beyond the 9th hour, asserting this, of course, on the ground of their custom" [^517].

Apart from Wednesday and Friday and the Paschal fast, of which we shall speak presently, other fasts did not yet exist; yet public fasts on occasion of calamities, such as drought, were customary. Such fasts are touchingly described by Tertullian. "When there are no rains, and famine threateneth in consequence," saith Tertullian unto the pagans, "ye, daily sated and ever ready to eat..., seek heaven at the Capitol and await clouds from the ceilings, having turned away from God Himself and from heaven itself. But we, dried up with fasts, enfeebled with abstinence, withdrawn from every pleasure of life, clad in sackcloth and sprinkled with ashes, knock at heaven and touch God; and when we have obtained mercy, Jupiter is honored" [^518].

#### Prolongation of the Paschal Fast

The forty-day fast before Pascha, which replaced in the 3rd century—though not yet everywhere—the earlier, shorter fast, in its origin and character hath something in common with the fasts of this latter kind. If it did not arise, it at least lengthened unto 40 days undoubtedly under the influence of the practice of the catechumenate, from the desire to cooperate through fast and prayer in the preparation of catechumens for baptism. Concerning the custom of fasting with the catechumens, monuments of the 2nd century already speak. According unto the words of St. Justin, those converting unto Christianity "are taught to ask of God with prayer and fasting the remission of their former sins, and we *(Orig. p. 116)* pray and fast with them" [^519]. "Before baptism let them fast," prescribeth the *Teaching of the Twelve Apostles*, "the baptizer and the one being baptized, and, if they can, certain others. But command the one being baptized to fast beforehand one or two days" [^520]. "Those approaching unto baptism," saith Tertullian, "must pray with frequent prayers, with fasts, genuflections, and vigils, with confession of all former sins" [^521]. Since in the 3rd century baptism was assigned unto Pascha, this fast turned out to be pre-Paschal. The *Testamentum* acquainteth us with the very first stage in the existence of the 40-day fast before Pascha, with its inception. It speaketh of it in such a connection. From among those receiving catechesis, the term of which is appointed by the *Testamentum* at 3 years, those already prepared for baptism are chosen and "are exorcised from that very day wherein they are chosen (apparently, daily), and are baptized on the days of Pascha. During the 40 days of Pascha the people abide in the temple watching, praying, listening to the Scriptures, hymns, and discourses of instruction" [^522]. There followeth a description of the baptism, chrismation, and communion of the newly baptized. The fast of the Forty Days (Четыредесятница / Lent), if only "40" is not a later insertion [^523], is represented here as that fellowship of the faithful in prayer and fasting with those preparing for baptism which the *Teaching of the Twelve Apostles* requireth and of which Justin the Martyr speaketh. Thus also according unto Tertullian, "a solemn day for baptism is Pascha, when the Passion of the Lord was accomplished, into which we are baptized... In view of the fact that the Savior fasted after His baptism 40 days, someone will say that it behooveth us rather to fast after baptism. But what restraineth, if not the necessity of joy and thanksgiving?" In these latter words of Tertullian there already clearly floateth the idea of a 40-day fast before baptism, and consequently before Pascha. (At the same time they shed light also upon the original meaning of exemptions in Pentecost from fasting and genuflection). But although the fast of the Forty Days arose in connection with baptism, already in the 3rd century it is viewed as something of intrinsic value. Such it appeareth in part in the testimony of the *Testamentum* concerning it. The *Canons of Hippolytus*, moreover, speak of it even without reference unto baptism, although immediately after the order of baptism: "On the days of fasting which are established in the canons for the fourth day of the week, and for the sixth, and the Forty Days... (corrupt) whoever joineth other fasts unto them shall receive a reward. But whoever resisteth this, and whom sickness, calamity, or necessity doth not excuse therein, resisteth God, Who fasted for our sake" [^524]. Finally, Origen makes mention of the Forty-Day Fast: "We have the days of the Forty Days consecrated unto fasting" [^525].

*(Orig. p. 117)*

Yet not in all Churches had the pre-Paschal fast acquired a 40-day duration. Concerning that same Alexandria where Origen lived and labored, and from the very era of Origen, we have testimony that the pre-Paschal fast was restricted unto several days. St. Dionysius, bishop of Alexandria (246–265), was queried by Bishop Basilides as to when the Paschal fast ought to be ended—whether on Saturday evening, or on Sunday morning at cockcrow, as was done in Rome. Having expressed his view regarding the various times for the end of the fast, the Alexandrian bishop addeth: "and the six days of the fast are not observed by all equally and alike; for some pass all the days without food, while others pass not even one; unto those who are exceedingly enfeebled by the prolonged fast and well-nigh perish from exhaustion, an earlier taking of food is pardonable; but if others during the four preceding days of the fast not only did not fast without intermission, but even lived luxuriously, and then, when the final two days arrive—that is, Friday and Saturday—fast continuously and think that they accomplish something great and glorious if they abstain until morning, I think that they have not engaged in such an ascetic struggle as those who exercised themselves for more days" [^526].

The contradiction between Dionysius and Origen can be reconciled by the fact that Origen, having lived long in Palestine, speaketh of the practice of the Church there. The lengthening of the fast unto 40 days could originally have occurred in Palestine; and since the Church of Jerusalem enjoyed great authority, from thence the 40-day fast could easily have spread throughout the entire Christian world. At the very beginning of the 4th century, as we shall see, we find it already everywhere; consequently it must have arisen no later than the 3rd century [^527]. A transition from *(Orig. p. 118)* a one-week fast unto a 40-day fast could have been a two- or three-week fast—a term unto which the pre-Paschal fast was limited in some places even in the 4th century, according unto the testimony of the historian Socrates [^528]. A three-week fast is prescribed by the *Testamentum* for a bishop and presbyter after their ordination [^529].

#### Pascha According to 3rd-Century Writers

Pascha in the 3rd century continued to remain that sorrowful-joyful fast in honor of Christ's Passion which, according unto the testimony of St. Irenaeus, it was in the 2nd century; but the termination of this fast on the night after Saturday is now invested with special solemnity and thus giveth beginning unto Pascha with its present character, although it is not yet fully separated from the preceding fast.

Characteristic is the complete silence concerning fasting in such a writer as Clement of Alexandria. Unto Origen's heart as well the feast of Pascha speaketh little. Explaining the prescriptions of the Book of Exodus concerning the institution of the Passover and the Gospel passages concerning the Savior's celebration of the Old Testament Passover, Origen makes no mention whatever of an analogous Christian feast, insisting solely upon the thought that our Pascha is Christ [^530]. Yet Origen nevertheless twice makes mention of the Christian feast of Pascha. Proving unto Celsus that Christianity is higher not only than pagan, but also than Jewish feasts, Origen remarketh: "If anyone object that among us also something similar is done on the Lord's day (Sunday), Friday, Pascha, and Pentecost, one may answer that the perfect Christian, abiding in words, deeds, and thoughts with the Word, God by nature, ever liveth on Sunday, ever passeth Sundays (the Lord's days)" [^531]. Another mention by Origen of Pascha we have seen above [^532]. Tertullian knoweth, apparently, only a fasting Pascha. The words of God at the institution of the Old Testament Passover, "it is the Lord's passover" [Ex. 12:11], Tertullian explaineth: "that is, the Passion of Christ" [^533]. Although in one passage Tertullian expresseth himself concerning Pascha that "we celebrate (*celebramus*) it annually in the first month" [^534], this "celebration" in other passages he reduceth unto a vigil and strict fasting. Demonstrating unto a Christian woman the inconvenience of having a pagan husband, Tertullian saith: "at the solemnities (*solennibus*) of Pascha will he bear with indifference thy *(Orig. p. 119)* absence by night (*abnoctantem*)?" [^535]. Disapproving the custom of abstaining in fasts from the kiss customary at prayer, Tertullian remarketh: "but on the day of Pascha, when fasting is a common and as it were public religious duty, we rightly abstain from the kiss of peace" [^536].

#### Pascha According to Canonical Monuments of the 3rd Century

Of the canonical monuments of the 3rd century, the *Canons of Hippolytus* and the *Egyptian Canons* speak of Pascha more briefly than the others. Apparently, the prescription concerning Pascha in one canon collection constituteth a reworking of the other, or both have behind them a common original source. Therefore a comparison of the passages pertaining hereto from both monuments is not without interest for the history of the feast.

##### The Canons of Hippolytus

The week in which the Jews keep the Passover must be observed by the entire people with great diligence; especially let them beware during these days of fasting to leave aside every passion, so that even in all conversation they may speak not with merriment, but with sadness, since it is known that the Lord of all, being impassible, suffered for our sake at that time, that we might patiently endure tribulations whereby we may be delivered from the torments deserved by us for our sins—and also that we, having become partakers of the tribulations which He accepted for our sake, might become partakers also of His kingdom. The food which is proper unto the time of Pascha is bread with salt and water. If anyone be afflicted with sickness, or dwell in a village where he knoweth no Christians, so that he passeth the time of Pascha in rejoicing, not knowing its appointed time, or be constrained thereto by severe sickness, let all such fast after the Forty-Day Fast and devoutly observe Pascha, that it may be manifest that we had not in the depth of our heart the intention, having cast off fear and neglected the fast, to establish for ourselves our own Pascha, laying another foundation than that which is laid... [^537].

The night of the Resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ must be observed with the greatest diligence; for He Himself is the greatest. *(Orig. p. 120)* Let no one therefore sleep in this night until dawn; then wash the body with water before approaching unto Pascha, and let the entire people be in light. For in this night the Savior obtained freedom for all creation; and then do heaven and earth and all that is in heaven and on earth keep festival, since He arose from the dead and ascended into heaven and sitteth at the right hand of the Father, whence He will come in the glory of the Father and of His Angels to render unto each according unto his works: unto those who have done good, in the resurrection of life; and unto those who have done evil, in the resurrection of judgment, as it is written.

##### The Egyptian Canons

Concerning that it is unseemly for anyone to taste anything on Pascha earlier than the hour at which it is lawful to eat. The fast cannot be imputed unto him who doth not abstain until the hour which constituteth the end of the fast. But if anyone be sick and have not strength to fast two days, let him at least fast on the day of Saturday, but let him be content with bread, salt, and water. If anyone be on a voyage and know not the day of Pascha, let him, when he learneth it, defer his fast unto after Pentecost. For that is not the Passover which we observe; that which constituteth the type hath passed away. For this reason we said not: in the second month [^538]; but when he learneth with certainty (the day of Pascha), let him enter upon the fast [^539].

*(Orig. p. 120)*

For both monuments Pascha is a fast in honor of Christ's Passion, but for the former into its concept there enters already the solemn release from the fast in the night of the Resurrection.

Another and, apparently, more complex phase in the development of the Paschal ritual is represented by the *Syriac Didascalia*. Remarkable is the tenderness and animation wherewith it speaketh of Pascha, which are absent from the *Canons of Hippolytus* and the *Egyptian Canons*. Interesting likewise is that redaction unto which the prescriptions of the *Didascalia* concerning Pascha were subjected in the *Apostolic Constitutions*. Besides the fact that the latter supplement Pascha with an entire cycle of new feasts and fasts—the Nativity of Christ, Theophany, the Forty-Day Fast, Thomas Sunday, Ascension, Pentecost, and the one-week fast after Pentecost (the Fast of the Holy Apostles / Peter's Fast)—the very tone of the prescriptions of the *Didascalia* concerning Pascha in the *Apostolic Constitutions* hath changed, and not everywhere for the better.

#### The Synoptic Comparison: Syriac Didascalia and Apostolic Constitutions

##### 1. The Syriac Didascalia

Therefore the believer must not swear by the sun, nor by any of the other heavenly signs or elements, nor mention with his mouth the name of idols, nor utter from his mouth reviling, but blessings and the psalms of the Lord and the divine Scriptures, which are the foundations of our faith, and especially the days of Pascha, wherein all the faithful fast throughout the entire world. Even as our Lord and Teacher said, when they asked Him: "Why do the disciples of John fast, but Thine fast not?" And He answered them, saying: "Can the children of the bridechamber mourn while the bridegroom is with them? But the days will come when the bridegroom shall be taken away from them, and then *(Orig. p. 121)* shall they fast" [^540]. Now indeed He is with us by His works, but in His visible appearance He is far off, because He hath ascended unto the height of heaven and sitteth at the right hand of His Father [^541].

From the second day of the week (Monday) fast ye six days until the night after Saturday, and this shall be accounted unto you a week. On the tenth day, however (that is, of the first spring month)—since the beginning of My name is *Yod* (*Iota*) [^542]—the day on which there was a renewal of fasts (a mandate to intensify the fast?), not according unto the custom of the former people (the Jews), but according unto the New Covenant which I have established for you: fast ye also on the fourth day of the week (Wednesday) for their sake, because on the fourth day of the week they began to destroy their souls and apprehended Me... Again also on Friday fast ye for their sake (the Jews), because they crucified Me in the midst of the feast of their unleavened bread, as was foretold by David: "In the midst of their feast they have set up their banners and knew not" [^543]. Ye, however, continually in these days fast at every time, and especially those who are of the house of the Gentiles (Christians from the Gentiles). For the people (the Jews) obeyed Me not, and them have I delivered from the blindness and error of idols and accepted them, that for your fast and that of those who are of the house of the Gentiles, and for your ministry on those days when ye pray and make supplication for the error and perdition of the people, your prayers and petitions may be accepted before My Father Who is in heaven, as though proceeding from a single mouth of all the faithful upon earth, and that all that they have done against Me may be forgiven them. For this reason also in the Gospel I said: "Pray for your enemies"; and blessed are they who mourn over the perdition of the unbelieving.

Therefore know, brethren, that our fast wherewith we fast at Pascha ye shall fast for the obstinacy of our brethren... [^544]. *(Orig. p. 122)* Therefore ye must pity and fast and pray for them... [^545]. Therefore pray for them and make petition, and especially on the days of Pascha [^546].

Ye must, brethren, carefully determine the days of Pascha and perform your fast with all diligence. Begin then when your brethren who are of the people (Christians from the Jews) keep the Passover, because our Lord and Teacher, having eaten the Passover with them, was betrayed by Judas after that hour, and we immediately began to mourn, since He was taken from us. By the reckoning of the moon, according unto our calculation, the calculation of the faithful Jews, on the tenth day of the moon on the second day of the week the priests and the elders of the people assembled and came into the court of Caiaphas the high priest and took counsel together to seize Jesus and slay Him... Jesus however on that day was in the house of Simon the leper [^547]. Therefore from the tenth day, which is the second day of the week, on the days of Pascha ye shall fast and use only bread and salt and water at the ninth hour until the fourth day of the week; on Friday and Saturday fast ye completely, tasting nothing [^548].

*(Orig. p. 123)*

Assemble together, and watching without sleep the entire night, praying and entreating and reading the prophets and the Gospel and the psalms with fear and trembling and diligent supplication until the third hour of the night after Saturday, and then break your fast. Thus also we fasted when our Lord suffered, for a testimony of the three days, and watched in prayers and supplications for the lost people, because in error they believed not our Savior... Especially strictly must ye fast on Friday and Saturday, and watch and keep vigil on Saturday, and read the Scriptures and psalms, and pray and entreat for those who have sinned, and wait and look for the Resurrection of our Lord Jesus until the third hour in the night after Saturday. And thereafter offer your sacrifices, and then eat and rejoice and be glad and exult (*exsultate*), because Christ, the pledge of our resurrection, is risen; and let this be unto you an ordinance forever unto the consummation of the age. But apart from Pascha it is not permitted to fast those 3 hours of the night which are between Saturday and the first day of the week, since it is the night of the first day of the week [^549].

*(Orig. p. 120)*

##### 2. The Apostolic Constitutions

It is forbidden also to swear by idols and to utter their abominable names with the mouth, or to worship them and fear them"—and thereafter followeth a detailed development of these thoughts without the mention, corresponding unto the *Didascalia*, of prayers on the days of Pascha and of Pascha itself [^550].

*(Orig. p. 121)*

"Let there be preserved among you the fast of the Forty Days (Четыредесятница / Lent), containing the commemoration of the life and legislation of the Lord; and perform ye this fast before the Paschal fast. After these days, having completed the fast, begin ye the Holy Week of Pascha, fasting therein all of you with fear and trembling, praying in these days for those who are perishing [^551].
