Or: "Enter into the church, behold the poor remaining here from midnight until day; behold the sacred vigils uniting day with night; behold the Christ-loving people, fearing neither by day nor by night the tyranny of sleep nor the constraint of poverty." "All-night and continuous standings" Chrysostom contrasts with daytime standings, which are interrupted and imperfect: "In them, imitating the angelic choral standing, we offer unceasing praise unto the Creator. O marvelous gifts of Christ! On high the angelic hosts sing praise; upon earth men by their choir standings in the churches imitate this doxology; above, the Seraphim cry aloud the Thrice-Holy hymn; below, the multitude of men sends it up; a festival common unto earthly and heavenly beings is instituted; one thanksgiving, one rejoicing, one joyful choral dance" [^652]. From this one may deduce that the angelic hymn: **"Glory to God in the highest"** (*«Слава в вышних Богу»*) and the Seraphic hymn: **"Holy, holy..."** (*«Свят, свят...»*) entered into the composition of the vigil.

*(Orig. p. 150)*

#### Sunday Worship According to Cassian

It is possible, however, that in certain localities vigils were celebrated also on the eve of Sundays. In favor of this may speak both the fact that in St. John Chrysostom they appear as an already very customary and frequent phenomenon, and the fact that at the beginning of the 6th century we find them in the practice of not only the Monastery of St. Sabbas. Nevertheless John Cassian, as a peculiarity of Sunday divine worship in the East (apparently, predominantly in Palestinian and Mesopotamian monasteries), states that "on Sunday before the midday meal there takes place only one gathering, wherein, for the honor of the communion of the Lord, with great solemnity and attentiveness executing the psalms and prayers, they combine the Third and Sixth Hours; thus in the sequences of prayer nothing is diminished; and yet in honor of the Resurrection of the Lord there is granted unto the brethren some relaxation and indulgence in comparison with other days" [^653]. Conforming unto this, in the 4th-century Church of Jerusalem (according unto the *Pilgrimage*), wherein there was no office of the Ninth Hour, after the Liturgy there was celebrated a service in place of the Sixth and Ninth Hours [^654].

#### Days of the Liturgy and Communion

The Divine Liturgy in the majority of churches was celebrated, besides Sunday, only on Saturday. So it was in Alexandria, according unto the testimony of its Archbishops St. Athanasius and Timothy (380–385) [^655]; in the neighboring churches and monasteries of Egypt and the Thebaid, according unto the testimony of Socrates [^656] and John Cassian [^657]; in Asia Minor, according unto the testimony of the Council of Laodicea [^658]; in Constantinople, according unto the testimony of Socrates [^659]. According unto Basil the Great: "We communicate four times each week—on Sunday, Wednesday, Friday, and Saturday, and also on other days of the week if the commemoration of a martyr happens; but it is good and profitable every day to partake of and receive the Holy Body and Blood of Christ" [^660].

From this last passage it is evident that in the 4th century all communicated at every Liturgy. But certain passages from the homilies of Chrysostom demonstrate that many, under the pretext of their unworthiness, not only ceased to communicate at every Liturgy, but restricted themselves unto receiving communion once or twice a *(Orig. p. 151)* year [^661]. Unto such the holy father says, not without irony, that if they be unworthy, they ought not to approach the Holy Mysteries even once a year [^662]. St. Macarius of Egypt says unto a woman who had fallen under the influence of sorcery: "Never neglect to visit the church; never withdraw thyself from communion of the Mysteries of Christ; misfortune befell thee because thou hast not approached the most pure Mysteries of our Saviour for five weeks already" [^663].

More firmly maintained was the custom of daily communion in the West. According unto St. Jerome, in his time this custom existed in Rome and in Spain [^664]. But judging by the fact that various persons addressed letters unto St. Jerome and Augustine concerning the expediency of this custom [^665], it was already close in the West, as in the East, unto waning. Pseudo-Ambrose says: "If the Bread is daily (*quotidianus*), why dost thou receive It after a year, as the Greeks are accustomed to do in the East? Receive daily that which is daily necessary unto thee" [^666].

The cessation of general communion at every Liturgy had this influence upon the elaboration of the liturgical typikon, that it elevated Vespers and Matins unto a height close unto that of the Liturgy, creating the view of them as services equally necessary and obligatory as the latter [^667].

#### Litanies

Speaking of church services of the 4th and 5th centuries, one cannot fail to mention the so-called litanies (*litaneiai*, λιτανεῖαι). These were solemn processions, cross-bearing processions from one temple unto another, or unto the city square, or outside the city, taking place at the translation of relics or other remains of a martyr, on commemorations of martyrs unto the places of their sufferings or unto their churches from the principal church, as well as on occasions of public calamities. Their origin was laid down already in the 3rd century; but in that era, so arduous for Christians, these processions were restricted unto instances of the translation of martyrs' remains and were conducted for the most part at night [^668]. Only in the 4th century did they receive wide application *(Orig. p. 152)* and become public and more solemn. "A few days before this," says St. Chrysostom, "on account of torrential rains there were litanies and supplications, and our whole city, like a torrent, rushed unto the apostolic shrines; we supplicated, calling upon St. Peter and the blessed Andrew, this pair of apostles, as well as Paul and Timothy" [^669]. Basil the Great speaks of litanies as a new but profitable institution: "In his time," that is, under Gregory the Wonderworker († 270), Bishop of Neocaesarea, he writes unto the Neocaesareans, "there were not even litanies such as ye perform now; and I speak this not by way of accusation against you, for I would desire that all of you live in tears and unceasing repentance" [^670]. Concerning Epiphanius, Bishop of Ticinum (*Ticiensis*, in Italy) in the 4th century, his biographer Ennodius (5th century) relates that he "decreed (*censuit*) that at every pestilential contagion (*aeris errore*) processions should be conducted (*procedendum*)" [^671]. The Emperor Theodosius the Great, before the war with Eugenius, arranged a litany through the city: in haircloth, with priests and people, he made the circuit of all the places of prayer, lying prostrate before the tombs of the martyrs and apostles, entreating of the saints help for himself [^672]. The same was done by the Emperors Theodosius the Younger and Marcian [^673]. The Greek writer Marcus the Deacon (5th century) in his *Life of St. Porphyrius, Bishop of Gaza* († 420), relates concerning a Litiya on the occasion of drought: "Having taken the sign (*signo*) of the Precious Cross which preceded us, we went forth with hymns unto the ancient church situated unto the west of the city. Porphyrius himself followed (walked behind), bearing the Holy Gospel and having around him the pious clergy"; further on the author indicates also the number of prayers at this Litiya before different temples [^674]. Frequently also litanies in honor of martyrs are mentioned. Thus Sidonius Apollinaris, Bishop of Clermont (*Arvernorum*, in Gaul) in the 5th century, speaks of a "pre-dawn procession" unto the tomb of the Martyr Justus [^675]. Few ritual particulars concerning such litanies have been preserved. Sozomen, concerning the procession at the translation of the remains of the Martyr Meletius unto Antioch, remarks that it was performed amid "the alternate singing of psalms" [^676]. St. Augustine says that in the procession at the translation of the remains of St. Stephen the bishop walked in the midst of the people [^677].

Thus the Litiya or litany in the 4th century—that is, from its very origin—receives a dual character: on the one hand, it is a mournful, penitential supplication in times of public calamities or for their averting; on the other hand, it is attached unto the commemoration of the saints. Such a character it retains throughout all subsequent time, both in the Eastern and in the Wes*(Orig. p. 153)*tern Church; such an impress does it bear even now among us [^678]. At the same time, from its very origin the litany or Litiya appears as something supplementary unto the ancient church offices, more precisely unto the vigil: it is celebrated after the vigil (as in the account of Marcus the Deacon) or before it (as in Sidonius Apollinaris). Such a place with respect unto church services the Litiya occupies also now among us. But in the practice of the 4th-century Church of Jerusalem, as we have seen, it already coalesces more closely with other church services (Vespers and Matins), although it loses not its fundamental character—as an addition unto them.

#### Elements of Divine Worship in the 4th and 5th Centuries

In order that the picture of divine worship in the 4th and 5th centuries may be complete, it is necessary to characterize in greater detail the constituent elements of the divine worship of that era—that is, prayer, psalmody, reading, and instruction—for which purpose it is necessary to assemble from the writers of this period the accounts concerning these elements of divine worship. These testimonies are important also because they familiarize us with the practice of different Churches (St. Basil the Great—the Asia Minor Church, St. Chrysostom—the Antiochian and Constantinopolitan, St. Jerome—the Roman, St. Augustine—the African, etc.).

#### Prayer

As regards prayer during divine worship in the 4th and 5th centuries, among the writers of the 4th and 5th centuries we find nothing that substantially supplements the information concerning it provided by the cited complete orders of divine worship of that era (in the *Apostolic Constitutions* and the *Pilgrimage*). Yet these latter data are so complete that in this respect there is nothing more to be desired. We possess therein both the very text of the prayers of that time, and detailed indications of the place occupied by them in divine worship, and the manner of their celebration. In comparison with later and present prayers they are distinguished, naturally, by greater brevity, but in divine worship they occupied a far more prominent and significant place than today: owing unto the fact that they were not, as now, silent, they must have occupied no less than half of each church service, if not more: according unto the *Pilgrimage* attributed unto Sylvia, the first part of the service, before the arrival of the bishop, consists of alternating psalms, hymns, and prayers, while the second half of the service—with the bishop—as it were consists entirely of prayers. In the divine worship of the *Apostolic Constitutions*, prayers occupy such a dominant position that the author passes over the other elements of divine worship in complete silence.

Unto the holy fathers of the 4th and 5th centuries are attributed many of the prayers in use today. Thus a whole series of prayers at the present Hours, as we shall see, including the prayer **"Thou Who at all times"** (*«Иже на всякое время»*), is attributed unto Basil the Great, *(Orig. p. 154)* as are the prayers of Pentecost (some of which were previously used at every Vespers, the so-called sung office). Several morning and evening prayers, as well as prayers before and after communion, are attributed unto St. John Chrysostom and St. Macarius the Great. The prayer **"Spotless, undefiled, incorrupt..."** (*«Нескверная, неблазная...»*) is attributed unto St. Ephrem the Syrian [^679]. If these ascriptions are not always reliable (frequently they contradict one another in different monuments), they nevertheless bear witness unto the fact that the 4th and 5th centuries were from ancient times venerated as the most normative in regard unto church prayers.

#### Chant

Chant during divine worship in the 4th and 5th centuries received far more room in comparison with the 3rd century. At the Matins of the *Testamentum* it fills only what appears to be a necessary intermission between two long sequences of prayers; whereas unto the services described by the 4th-century pilgrim the title of "sung offices" (*asmatikai akolouthiai*) could well be applied.

##### The Psalter

The musical portion of the office was composed, as it is now, of biblical material and hymns of Christian composition. The former, both in the examined monuments and in the writers of that period, is reduced almost exclusively unto the psalms. Of the other canticles of Holy Scripture mention is made, as we have seen, of the liturgical use of the Canticle of the Three Youths and the Canticle of Simeon the God-Receiver [^680]. The liturgical use of the Psalter was no narrower than that of the present day: "In our assemblies," says St. John Chrysostom, "David is first, middle, and last" [^681]. "David is our Simonides, Pindar, Alcaeus, Flaccus, Catullus, and Serenus," says Blessed Jerome [^682]. From the temple the Psalter penetrated also into domestic use: according unto Socrates, the Emperor Theodosius the Younger with his sisters performed psalmody daily [^683]. According unto Blessed Jerome, "the farmer at the plow sings Alleluia; the reaper, covered with sweat, consoles himself with psalms; and the vine-dresser with his pruning-hook sings something of David" [^684]. The choice of psalms for singing at divine worship still depended in large measure upon the presiding bishop: "we prepared for ourselves a short psalm, which we bade the lector chant," says Blessed Augustine [^685].

##### Methods of Psalmody

As regards the method of chanting the psalms, responsorial and antiphonal singing was spreading more and more, apparently, in place of congregational singing.

*(Orig. p. 155)*

##### Unison Singing

The passage cited above from the letter of St. Basil the Great unto the clergy of Neocaesarea [^686] seems to give it to be understood that the Neocaesareans considered the first two methods of singing an innovation. From the words of St. John Chrysostom:

"once the whole congregation sang with one voice, as we do even now" [^687], one may likewise conclude that this was the primitive method of singing, and that it had now begun to give way unto others. Blessed Augustine likewise mentions such a method of chanting the psalms: "We sang the psalm with one voice (*una voce*), encouraging one another, saying with one accord: **'Come, let us rejoice'**" [^688].

##### Solo Chanting

The opposite unto this method of singing was constituted by that wherein a psalm (or canticle, or hymn) was sung solely by a choir of chanters or by a single chanter without the participation of the worshipers. It has been observed that St. Cyril of Jerusalem, referring unto the psalms that had been chanted in his catechetical lectures, never expresses himself: "as we or you have sung," but always: "as you have heard" [^689]. The Council of Laodicea even forbids anyone to sing in church except the "canonical chanters" [^690]. According unto John Cassian, among the Egyptian monks the psalm was always sung by one of the brethren, while the rest sat and listened [^691]. Characterizing this mode of psalm execution in greater detail, John Cassian gives it to be understood that it was performed with an even chant (*parili pronunciatione*), in some monasteries without interruption verse after verse (*contiguis versibus*) [^692], in others with their division into two or three sections (*intercisiones*) with intermediate silent prayers [^693]. From the custom of continuous singing of a psalm by a single chanter there arose in the West a method of executing psalms unto which was attached somewhat later the name *psalmus tractus* (*tractim dicere*—to speak without interruption), and which consisted in this, that the psalm or a verse thereof was sung by a single chanter without any response made unto him by the choir (according unto the definition of Amalarius, a 9th-century writer) [^694]. From such singing of psalms has arisen our present reading of them, which is properly speaking a recitative chant.

##### Responsorial or Hypophonic Chant

Alongside the unbroken singing of the psalm by the whole people or by a single chanter, 4th- and 5th-century writers frequently mention the responsorial chanting of the psalm. "The Fathers established," says St. John Chrysostom, "that the people, when they knew not *(Orig. p. 156)* the whole psalm, should chant as a refrain (*ὑπηχεῖν*) from the psalm a forceful verse containing some sublime doctrine, and thence draw the necessary instruction" [^695]. What a powerful impression this singing produced is shown by the well-known incident with St. Athanasius: when during divine worship soldiers entered the church to arrest St. Athanasius in order to bring him to trial (at the demand of the Arians), he ordered the psalm to be sung with the refrain: **"For His mercy endureth for ever"** (*«Яко в век милость Его»*), executed by the whole people, and this enabled St. Athanasius to escape from the soldiers [^696]. According unto Sozomen, at the translation of the relics of the Hieromartyr Babylas unto Antioch the people chanted in response unto each verse of the psalm: **"Confounded be all they that worship carved images, that boast themselves of idols"** [^697]. At times such refrains were very long, embracing two verses from the psalm. Thus, in his exposition of the 18th Psalm, Blessed Augustine speaks of the singing by the whole people of its 13th and 14th verses: **"Who can understand his lapses? Cleanse Thou me from my secret faults..."** [^698] The entire psalm in such a method of execution must have been sung or read by a single chanter. "The chanter (*ὁ ψάλλων*) sings (*ψάλλει*) alone, although all chant the refrain (*ὑπηχοῦσι*), as if the voice were sent up from a single mouth" [^699]. (Concerning the reading of psalms, St. Ambrose remarks: "you heard today how it was read (*lectum*): **'Be ye angry, and sin not'**" [^700]; and Blessed Augustine: "best of all was that which they related concerning Athanasius, the Bishop of Alexandria, that he so instructed the reader to chant the psalms that he seemed not so much to sing as to read" [^701]). The *Pilgrimage* of Sylvia speaks, apparently, predominantly of responsorial psalmody. Unto the wide dissemination of this method of singing there contributed, as we have seen from the words of St. Chrysostom, the imperfect knowledge of the text of the psalms among the people and, in all likelihood, the rarity of written manuscripts thereof. Out of responsorial psalmody arose our prokeimena and the Roman Catholic responsories [^702]: instead of entire psalms, there were selected for singing with a refrain at first, in all probability, certain sections of them, and subsequently merely a few verses (at first four, whence the Great Prokeimenon, and later two). Yet the testimonies from the 4th and 5th centuries still presuppose the integral singing of the psalm with a refrain. Such singing of an entire psalm with a refrain unto each verse has been preserved in our present Typikon only for Psalm 135 (LXX; Masoretic Ps. 136), and that because the refrain *(Orig. p. 157)* (**"For His mercy endureth for ever"**) is placed here after every verse in the biblical text itself.

##### Antiphonal Chant

Still more complex was the antiphonal method of singing. It is not known with certainty what kind of singing was designated by this term in the 4th and 5th centuries. Originally, in all probability, this was the name given unto the alternating singing of the verses of a psalm between two halves of the worshipers. If so, then the initial occasion for the introduction and spread of such singing could have been the increase in the number of believers: unison singing of the psalm by all amid an excessively large number of worshipers could disturb the harmony of the chant. Unto this precise method of singing St. Basil points in the passage cited above from his epistle unto the clergy of Neocaesarea [^703]. Socrates, who traces, as was pointed out above [^704], the origin of antiphonal singing unto Antioch and regards as its founders the presbyters Diodore and Flavian (4th–5th cc.), speaks of singing by two choirs (consequently, by trained singers, and not by the general people).

By the same term there was designated, apparently, another method of singing somewhat distinct from this, namely that wherein before the psalm or after the psalm, executed alternately by two choirs, there was sung a particular verse of this psalm or of some other; this verse, closely related unto the content of the psalm, was called an antiphon (an echo, a reverberation) [^705]. According unto the definition of the aforementioned Amalarius: "until the symphony of the antiphon, the psalm is sung by two choirs, and at the antiphon itself the choirs unite" [^706]. Such antiphons must have been borrowed not only from the psalms and from Holy Scripture in general, but could also be of independent Christian composition. Sylvia, as we have seen, noticeably distinguishes them from the psalms, as well as, indeed, from the hymns. Yet Socrates in that same passage expresses himself: *ἀντιφώνους ὕμνους* ("it is necessary to state also whence the custom of antiphonal hymns in the Church took its origin" [^707]). Blessed Augustine, attributing unto St. Ambrose the introduction into Milan of the Eastern method of singing, apparently has in mind antiphonal singing of this very latter kind, since responsorial singing in general was already widely disseminated everywhere, while antiphonal singing in the broad sense (the first of the aforementioned modes) did not differ essentially from it. "Then," says Blessed Augustine concerning the episcopate of St. Ambrose in Milan, "it was established that singing should be performed according unto the custom of the Eastern regions, lest the people languish in weariness" [^708]. Today both among us and in the Roman Catholic Church antiphons are precisely designated as special verses, not always drawn from the psalms [^709] and not always *(Orig. p. 158)* (among us) united with the singing of psalms; among us, however, antiphons also designate the alternating chanting of the verses of a psalm (thus, for example, the divisions of the Kathismata are termed antiphons [^710]); a remnant of the antiphonal execution of a psalm by the entire assembly of worshipers is preserved among us in the chanting of **"Let my prayer be set forth"** (*«Да исправится»*) at the Liturgy of the Presanctified Gifts [^711].

#### Eastern Hymnographers

If the term "antiphon" possessed the sense of an independent addition unto a psalm at its beginning and end (or an addition unto a specific division of a psalm), then it formed a transition from the psalms unto those canticles and hymns which already in the 3rd century had acquired a significant place in divine worship. As in the 3rd century, the revival of hymnographic activity in the Church was fostered by the attempts of certain heretics to disseminate their doctrine by means of hymns. This was done in Syria by the followers of Bardesanes [^712]; under the name of Arius there was known a collection of hymns entitled *Thalia* (*Θάλεια*) [^713] (one of the Muses); under the name of Apollinaris, the *New Psalter* [^714]; the Donatists likewise made use of hymns for the propagation of their doctrine [^715]. In combating this heretical hymnography there attained renown Saints Athanasius the Great, Ephrem the Syrian, Gregory the Theologian, and John Chrysostom. But the first and the last of these fought rather by way of the organization of divine worship. Unto St. Chrysostom tradition attributes the introduction into divine worship of troparia-antiphons [^716], wherein there may perhaps be kept in view merely their transference from Antioch unto Constantinople [^717]. Saints Ephrem and Gregory, on the other hand, emerged as renowned hymnographers. Unto the former († 373 / 378) the Syrians and Copts attribute twelve to fourteen thousand hymns; but the majority of such hymns bear traces of later composition and merely imitate the authentic hymns of Ephrem [^718]. In the *Acts (Life) of St. Ephrem* it is stated that "by his sublime and spiritual canticles (*odas*) he delivered instruction concerning the Nativity of Christ, the Baptism, the Fast, the Passion (of Christ), the Resurrection, the Ascension, and the other mysteries of that divine Providence; unto these he joined also other hymns—concerning the martyrs, concerning repent*(Orig. p. 159)*ance, and concerning the departed" [^719]. (Let us note that the cycle of feasts given in this enumeration conforms entirely unto the 4th century). The canticles of St. Ephrem for feasts in their character strongly recall the later *stichera*; thus, for example, the canticle for the Nativity of Christ depicts the inner disposition of the Righteous Joseph at the sight of the Divine Infant: "Who hath given unto me as a son the Son of the Most High?... Vain was my suspicion toward Mary... David, place the crown upon His head..." [^720] Certain of the hymns of St. Ephrem for feasts are used even today by the Maronites (Syrian Monothelites). Unto St. Ephrem are also attributed about fifty canticles in honor of the Mother of God, the majority of which are likewise used today among the Maronites; there is an account [^721] that from these canticles of St. Ephrem Paul of Akmoreia (in the 11th–12th cc.) extracted his stichera unto the Most Holy Theotokos, appointed in our Octoechos at **"Lord, I have cried"** (*«Господи воззвах»*) at Sunday Vespers "where there is no Menaion." The hymns of St. Ephrem, notwithstanding the warmth of religious feeling, did not enter into our church use, in all probability because they were written in the Syriac tongue. Unto Gregory the Theologian († 389 / 390), a rather prolific poet, are attributed about twelve hymns, the finest among which are: the "Hymn to God," rather close in content unto the **"Te Deum Laudamus"** (*«Тебе Бога хвалим»*) [^722], and the "Hymn to Christ after Silence (Fasting) at Pascha," wherein, however, there is glorified not the Resurrection, but the creative and providential working of God and the Incarnation. The hymns of St. Gregory are of a somewhat abstract content and on that account were not received into divine worship (it cannot be maintained, however, that they were not used in divine worship in antiquity). On the other hand, a number of passages from the orations of St. Gregory were transformed by later hymnographers into church canticles (for example, **"Christ is born"** [*«Христос рождается»*]). Marked by even greater abstraction are the hymns of Synesius of Cyrene, which are somewhat imbued with Neoplatonism [^723].

#### Latin Hymnography

The West in this period brought forward more illustrious hymnographers: Hilary of Poitiers († 367), Pope Damasus († 384), St. Ambrose of Milan († 397), Blessed Augustine († 430), Prudentius (Aurelius Prudentius Clemens, b. 348), Sedulius (Coelius Sedulius, first half of the 5th c.), and Fortunatus (Venantius Fortunatus, † c. 609). Unto this same epoch belongs in the West *(Orig. p. 160)* the hymn **"Te Deum Laudamus"** (*«Тебе Бога хвалим»*) (judging by the mention made thereof by 6th-century writers [^724]), superscribed in Roman Catholic liturgical books with the names of Saints Ambrose and Augustine. According unto one tradition, it was composed by St. Ambrose in thanksgiving for the definitive victory over Arianism. According unto other traditions, it was chanted under divine inspiration (improvised) by St. Ambrose and Blessed Augustine at the baptism of the latter by the former, when they both stood in the baptismal font; St. Ambrose sang one verse, and Blessed Augustine another; the final verse: **"In Thee, O Lord, have I hoped..."** (*«На Тя, Господи, уповах...»*) was concluded by Blessed Augustine [^725]. Unto St. Ambrose and Blessed Augustine this hymn cannot belong, because it is not mentioned in their writings (whereas other hymns of theirs are mentioned) and differs from their undoubtedly authentic hymns.

In hymnographic terms the 4th and 5th centuries, consequently, were more fruitful in the West than in the East: they contributed unto Roman Catholic worship no less material than perhaps all subsequent centuries combined. Hence Roman Catholic worship prides itself before ours on the antiquity of its hymns, as well as on their poetic form (the aforementioned are written for the most part in unrhymed iambics). Yet the Latin hymns of the 4th and 5th centuries, which served as models also for subsequent Latin hymnography, in comparison with the later Eastern *stichera* that entered into our divine worship, are of a very abstract and general character—they are not attached unto the sacred commemorations of the day (recalling in this respect, from Eastern hymnography, the contemporary compositions of St. Gregory the Theologian and Synesius) [^726]. Such a development of hymn-writing in the 4th and 5th centuries in all likelihood provoked the decrees in the East of the Council of Laodicea against the liturgical use of "private psalms" (*ἰδιωτικοὺς ψαλμοὺς*) and non-canonical books [^727], and in the West of the Fourth Council of Toledo of 633, which permitted the use of hymns only of Saints Hilary and Ambrose, as well as the Lesser and Greater Doxologies [^728].

#### Melodies and Modes

If in the 3rd century the melody of church canticles engaged the care of pastors, then in the present period these concerns were bound to intensify. However, no reliable reports upon this point have been preserved from this period. There exists an account concerning St. Basil the Great († 379) that he applied unto church canticles the melody of Pindar's epinicia [^729]. Unto the name of St. Ambrose is superscribed an Antiphonary set to musical notation of later *(Orig. p. 161)* origin [^730]. It contains four melodies based upon the four Greek musical modes: Dorian, Phrygian, Lydian, and Mixolydian; the distinction of these melodies was grounded in the fact that they began from different pitches of the octachord: the first on D, the second on E, the third on F, and the fourth on G, and therefore their reciting tone (dominant), attached unto the first degree of the octachord (in the second melody unto the sixth, since on the fifth degree stood the variable B), occurred on different notes. Thus arose the four authentic modes (unto which were later added another four plagal modes) [^731]. These modes bear the name of Ambrosian; in the composition of the present Roman Catholic (Gregorian) Octoechos they correspond unto modes 1, 3, 5, and 7. Among our Byzantine-Ruthenian Tones, the first three of them are close unto Tones 1, 2, and 3.

#### Liturgical Reading in the 4th and 5th Centuries

Liturgical reading in the 4th and 5th centuries, in comparison with the 3rd century, underwent significant changes in regard unto the volume of that which was read, the assignment of readings unto one or another service, and the selection of readings.

##### Formation of the Canon

In the first respect, a sharp boundary was definitively drawn between canonical and non-canonical sacred books. Apparently, at the very beginning of the 4th century there was still some hesitation in this regard, but from the second half of this century the canon of sacred books everywhere received its present composition. Thus Eusebius of Caesarea († c. 339 / 340) still hesitates in recognizing the Apocalypse as a canonical book, as well as in the authenticity of the Catholic Epistles of James, Jude, 2 Peter, and 2 and 3 John [^732]. St. Athanasius († 373) [^733], as well as the Councils of Laodicea (second half of the 4th c.) [^734] and Carthage (419) [^735], know the canon already in its present form (the Council of Laodicea does not name, however, the Apocalypse in its list of canonical books). The precise establishment of the canon could not fail to elevate the authority of biblical literature, nor to intensify, so to speak, the sense of its divine inspiration and reverence toward it. The reading of sacred books during divine worship now definitively receives that sacramental significance which was attributed unto it in part also in earlier times (not without the influence of the synagogue). At the same time—in comparison with the 3rd century—the Old Testament is now pushed more and more into the background in liturgical reading.

##### Number of Readings from the Old and New Testaments

At the beginning of this period there is noticeable still a certain uniformity in the reading of both Testaments at divine worship. Thus the *Apostolic Constitutions* appoint *(Orig. p. 162)* (for the Liturgy, at which alone at that time readings were held) two readings from the Old Testament [^736]: from the Law and the Prophets [^737], and two or three from the New: from the Acts, the Epistles of Paul, and the Gospels [^738]. Later, or in other churches, there was, apparently, one reading from the Old Testament and two from the New. St. John Chrysostom in his homilies delivered at Constantinople says: "Let us touch today upon what was read... And blessed David draweth unto himself our ministration, as doth the apostolic word spoken unto Timothy; and Isaiah philosophizeth concerning human nature; and our Master Jesus, conversing with His disciples: **'The harvest is plenteous...'**" [^739] "The reader begins: 'The prophecy of Isaiah,' and no one attendeth... Then he crieth aloud: 'Thus saith the Lord,' and no one attendeth" [^740]. "In vain entering hither did one prophet speak, did one apostle converse with us, and concerning what?" [^741] St. Basil the Great in his homily unto those preparing for baptism mentions the reading on that day after the psalms from Isaiah, Chapter 2, Acts, Chapter 2, and Matthew 11 [^742]. In another homily mention is made of reading "at the morning hour" after the psalms from Proverbs, the Apostle, and the Gospels [^743]. Cf. in the Armenian Liturgy—*lectio prophetica*, *Apostolus*, *Evangelium* [^744]. So it was also in the Western churches. Maximus, Bishop of Turin (in Italy, in the 5th c.), speaks of readings on a single day from Isaiah, the Gospel of Matthew, and John [^745]. Blessed Augustine sometimes speaks of readings only from the Epistles and the Gospels [^746], but sometimes also from the Prophets, for example Isaiah (57:13) [^747]. The most ancient manuscripts of the Western liturgies—Gallican [^748], Ambrosian, Mozarabic (in Spain)—and the most ancient lectionary of the Spanish Church, the *Liber Comicus* [^749] (c. 6th c.), have an Old Testament reading (*lectio*) before the apostolic (*epistola*) and the evangelical (*lectio sancti evangelii*) [^750]. On the contrary, the most ancient manuscripts of the Roman Liturgy in the *Sacramentarium Gregorianum* (attributed unto St. Gregory the Great, † 604) and the most ancient Gallican lectionaries, which do not ascend higher than the 8th century (*Comes ab Albino emendatus* under Charlemagne, and others), have only New Testament readings—*Apostolus* and *(Orig. p. 163)* *Evangelium* [^751]. Thence scholars conclude that in the Roman Liturgy there were never Old Testament readings [^752]. According unto Walafrid Strabo († 849), Pope St. Celestine I (422–432) first introduced an Old Testament element into the Liturgy by prefixing unto the apostolic and gospel readings the Introit antiphons (*ad introitum*): "before his time prior to the oblation only the reading of the Apostle and the Gospel was read" [^753]. (Cf. below the testimony of John Cassian). It may be that under the influence of Roman practice Old Testament readings were gradually abolished also in the Eastern liturgies. In the 6th century there are no longer Old Testament readings in the Greek Liturgy: they are not mentioned in the acts of the Council of Constantinople of 536, nor in the *Life of St. Sabbas the Sanctified* composed by Cyril of Scythopolis, where mention is made of the Liturgy and its readings [^754]. St. Sophronius, Patriarch of Jerusalem, although he speaks in his work *On the Sacred Vestments and the Liturgy* of "prophetic words" at the Liturgy "after the first supplication" (the litany), understands by them the antiphons [^755]. Other Eastern liturgies, although they lack Old Testament readings even in their most ancient manuscripts, yet in the fact that they have four entire New Testament readings, may preserve a trace of the former existence of Old Testament readings. Thus the Coptic (Jacobite) and Ethiopian liturgies have readings from the "Apostle," that is, the Epistles of St. Paul; from the "Catholic," that is, the Catholic Epistles; from Acts; and from the Gospel [^756]. In the Nestorian Liturgy there are likewise four readings and all from the New Testament; for example, for the Ascension of the Lord: 2 Corinthians 2:14–17; 3:1–3, and Acts 1:1–14; then 1 Timothy 1:8–11; 3:14–16, and Luke 24:36–53 [^757]. (The Acts, like the Gospel, is preceded by an Epistle of the Apostle!). Old Testament readings in this liturgy were abolished only in the 7th century (by Patriarch Mar Aba c. 614 [^758]). A similar development, consequently, may be supposed also concerning the Coptic-Ethiopian liturgy.

The Old Testament readings removed from the Liturgy were not, of course, abandoned altogether, but were transferred unto other services, specifically unto Vespers, as the service which had taken the place of the former evening Liturgy and was therefore closest unto it in structure. Yet from the 4th and 5th centuries there is no information concerning the existence of readings at Vespers (excluding the obscure indication in the *Pilgrimage* of Sylvia [^759]). But there are reports that Old Testament readings were assigned predominantly unto weekdays, on which for the most part the Liturgy was not celebrated. Thus John Cassian states that in the Egyptian monasteries at weekday offices (which ones, he specifies not) there is one reading from the Old Testament and one from the New Testament, whereas on Saturday and Sunday both readings are from the New Testament (naturally, at *(Orig. p. 164)* the Liturgy, since on both these days almost everywhere the Liturgy was celebrated, as we have seen, of which readings had been an indispensable constituent since the 2nd century); likewise throughout the entire Pentecostarion period [^760]. Remarkable is the restriction which was made for weekdays in regard unto New Testament readings, an echo whereof may be seen in the requirement of the Council of Laodicea that on Saturday there should be read "(also) the Gospel with (*μετὰ*) the other scriptures" [^761]: in all likelihood on weekdays the Gospel was not read.

The *Pilgrimage* of Sylvia speaks of the reading of the Gospel only at Sunday Matins and at the services of great feasts (and of Holy Week); more frequently she speaks of "readings" in general [^762]. However, it must be noted that since reading was from ancient times attached unto the Liturgy, in certain localities, on days when there was no Liturgy, there were no readings either. Cassian calls reading at weekday worship something "supererogatory, only for those who desire it" [^763].

##### Pericopes

As regards the selection of readings, there occur in this period even more than in the 3rd century [^764] mentions of "pericopes," of "readings" (*lectiones*). But just as in that era, these pericopes were not attached unto specific days of the year, but were read continuously one after another at divine worship, excluding the great feasts and in part Great Lent, for which there were special readings. "Your Holiness remembers," says Blessed Augustine, "that we customarily examine the Gospel of John according unto the order of the readings. But since now the celebration of the holy days has arrived, for which definite readings from the Gospel are appointed, and they are annual, so that there can be no others, we must of necessity interrupt the adopted order, though we abandon it not entirely" [^765]. Certain passages in St. John Chrysostom sound, however, as if the pericopes were already distributed among the liturgical days of the year, among the Sundays. "We frequently indicate unto you many days in advance the subject (*ὑπόθεσις*) of the discourse, so that you in the intervening time may take the book into your hands and examine the pericope" [^766]. "Let each person several days in advance on any day of the week, even on Saturday, take and read at home continuously (*συνεχῶς*) the pericope of the Gospel that is about to be read" [^767]. But Chrysostom could speak thus also in the event that the pericopes were not fixed unto specific calendar days, but followed in the continuous order of the Gospel [^768].

The presiding bishops enjoyed a certain freedom in the choice of pericopes for reading. "For this reason did we bid (*fecimus*)," says Blessed Augustine, "that there be read that very reading from the Gospel wherein the Lord was tempted with the words *(Orig. p. 165)* of the psalm which you have just heard" [^769]. Sometimes the theme planned by the preacher determined the selection of the reading: "remember our promise," says Blessed Augustine, "we ordered that corresponding readings from the Gospel and the Apostle be brought forward" [^770]. If the sermon had to be continued at the following service, the reading was likewise repeated at it: "Your charity remembers that last Sunday we conversed concerning spiritual rebirth; this reading we ordered to be read again, in order to complete that which was not stated then" [^771].

##### Euthalius

From the 4th and 5th centuries there has been preserved an attempt at dividing the biblical New Testament text for liturgical use, belonging unto Euthalius, according unto some manuscripts a deacon (of Alexandria), according unto others Bishop of Sulca (*Σούλκης*, an unknown locality in Egypt), perhaps at first a deacon and later a bishop. In his "edition" (*ἔкθεσις*) of the Acts [^772], the Epistles of St. Paul, and the Catholic Epistles, Euthalius first of all divides the biblical text into verses (*stichoi*), placing in each verse as many words as a reader is able to pronounce in a single breath, yet conforming therein unto the sense; next he divides the text into 57 readings (*ἀναγνώσεις*), indicating (in the *Ἀνακεφαλαίωσις*) with which words each reading begins and how many chapters it contains (the chapters being of nearly the present size, sometimes smaller); the Acts is divided into 16 readings, Romans and 1 Corinthians into 5 readings each, 2 Corinthians into 4 readings, Hebrews into 3 readings, James, 1 Peter, 1 John, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, 1 Thessalonians, and 1 Timothy into 2 readings each, and the remainder into 1 reading each. (In regard unto the Epistles of St. Paul, Euthalius made use of the division into chapters that existed prior to him). For each chapter its citations and parallels from other sacred books and apocrypha are indicated, and a summary of the contents is given. Today scholars dispute the attribution of this work in its entirety unto a single individual and disagree in determining the time of his life. Under Athanasius, unto whom the author dedicates his work, some understand the famous Archbishop of Alexandria, others Archbishop Athanasius II of Alexandria (490–496). Scholars find that the work could have originated in the 4th century (under St. Athanasius the Great), but that certain elements in it, and among others the division into liturgical readings, constitute a later accretion, since they correspond unto no division of the ecclesiastical year (a division, it is thought, that had in view private or monastic use) [^773]. If Euthalius directed his labor upon the Apostle, then, one may think, the Gospel already possessed a division into liturgical lections—although attempts at such a division from the 4th and 5th centuries have not survived.

*(Orig. p. 166)*

##### Scope of the Pericopes

All these accounts concerning the division of the biblical text for liturgical use and the traces of such division demonstrate that in the present period the sacred books were read at divine worship without omissions. Unto the same effect speak also the surviving homilies of the 4th and 5th centuries, which for the most part expound the sacred book in its entirety, verse by verse. St. John Chrysostom says in one homily: "Whoso regularly attendeth church, even if he read not at home, but merely listeneth here unto that which is offered, for him one year sufficeth for the acquisition of rich knowledge; for we read not here today one scripture and tomorrow another, but always the same and continuously (*diapantos*)" [^774]. Since such readings—that is, divine services with the reading of Holy Scripture—occurred for the most part no less than twice a week (on Saturday and Sunday), sometimes thrice [^775] or daily [^776], the pericopes for continuous reading must have been only slightly larger than our present lections (*pericopes* / *zachala*), so that the entire New Testament without omissions could be read through in the course of a year [^777]. The Old Testament, of course, was not read in its entirety (as was the case also in the synagogue [^778]).

##### Festal Readings

If ordinary weekdays and even Sundays in the year did not yet possess fixed pericopes, feasts, Great Lent (*Tessarakoste* / the Forty-Day Fast), and Pentecost in certain localities at least already possessed them. During Great Lent, Genesis was read. Chrysostom says in one of the homilies on the statues, which were delivered during the fasting season: "today I shall examine the reading set before us," and he expoundeth Genesis 1:1 [^779]. The second series of homilies on Genesis (67 in number) was delivered during Great Lent of another year, and the third (9 homilies) in a third year [^780]. The homilies of St. Basil the Great on the Hexaemeron were likewise delivered during the Fast: in them there is an indication that they were spoken in springtime [^781]. The reason why Genesis was read at this time could consist in this: that the ecclesiastical year in certain localities began with the spring [^782]. St. Ambrose in his Paschal greeting writeth: "ye heard how the Book of Job was read, which was completed (*est decursus*) at the solemn office (*munere*) and in solemn season" [^783]. The homilies on the Book of Job attributed unto St. John Chrysostom begin: "The annual sufferer of mankind hath *(Orig. p. 167)* arrived today" [^784]. St. Ambrose mentioneth the reading of the Book of Jonah during Holy Week: "on the following day the Book of Jonah was read according unto custom: and that was the day wherein the Lord gave Himself up for us, when in the church repentance (the fast) is relaxed (*relaxatur*—Holy Thursday or Holy Saturday)" [^785].

The *Pilgrimage* of Sylvia, indicating for each day of Holy Week, beginning with Lazarus Saturday, a definite Gospel reading, and for certain days several such readings, speaketh also "of readings from the prophets" in this week [^786]. Yet in regard unto the reading of the Passion of the Lord in the ancient Church there was diversity. In Jerusalem, according unto Sylvia, on Great and Holy Friday all the Evangelists were read: first all the passages concerning the Passion, then concerning the judgment of Pilate, and finally, at the sixth hour (12 noon by our reckoning) on Golgotha there was read "from the Gospel where He suffered" [^787]. In Africa, on the contrary, according unto the testimony of Blessed Augustine, the Passion of the Lord was read only according unto Matthew; and when Augustine in one year took it into his head to read the Passion according unto John, the people were troubled (thinking that ancient tradition was being violated and preference given unto the custom of another church), and he was obliged to return unto the adopted order [^788].

Equally in both the Eastern and Western Churches the Acts of the Apostles were read during Pentecost. In St. John Chrysostom there is a special homily in explanation of this establishment [^789]. Blessed Augustine saith concerning the Acts that they are read "at the annual solemnity (*anniversaria solemnitate*) following the Passion of the Lord" [^790], and that their reading "beginneth from the Sunday of Pascha" [^791]. Concerning readings for other feasts we find no mentions in the writers of the 4th and 5th centuries, with the exception of indications in the *Pilgrimage* of Sylvia of readings on the Meeting of the Lord (*Hypapante*), the Sunday of Palms, the Sunday of Antipascha, and Pentecost, corresponding unto the festal Gospel pericopes (at Pentecost—from Acts concerning the Descent of the Holy Spirit, and from the Gospel concerning the Ascension [^792]); passages concerning other fixed feasts besides the Meeting of the Lord have not survived in the manuscript. On multi-day feasts, such as Pascha was, there was a special reading for each day. Blessed Augustine saith in words delivered on Pascha: "Concerning the Resurrection of our Lord, in these days it is customary to read from all the books of the Holy Gospel" [^793]. "Concerning the Resurrection of the Lord it was read today also, but from another book of the Gospel, namely according unto Luke; for at first it was read according unto Matthew, yesterday according unto Mark, today according unto Luke; such is the order of the Evangelists. As His Passion is described by all the Evangelists, so these seven or eight days afford room for reading concerning the Resurrection of the Lord according unto all the Evangelists. The Passion, however, since it is read on a single day, is commonly read only according unto Matthew" [^794].

*(Orig. p. 168)*

##### Lectionaries

Scarcely in this period did there exist written designations of festal and fasting pericopes in biblical codices (at least in the codices of Holy Scripture surviving from the 4th and 5th centuries—the Sinaitic, Vatican, and Alexandrian—there are no such designations), and still less anything resembling the later "Evangelistaria," "Lectionaries," and "Festal Gospels": the order of readings was preserved by tradition. From this period we possess reports only concerning the first attempts at Lectionaries. According unto the testimony of Gennadius, a presbyter of Marseilles (*Massiliensis*), who lived at the end of the 5th century, Musaeus, likewise a presbyter of Marseilles (c. 458), at the urging of St. Venerius (*Venerii*), extracted from Holy Scripture the readings for the festal days of the whole year, as well as responsorial verses of the psalms adapted unto the season and the readings (*responsoria etiam psalmorum capitula temporibus et lectionibus apta*) [^795]. A second report likewise cometh from Gaul: Sidonius Apollinaris, Bishop of Clermont (*Arvernorum*) in the 5th century (mentioned above), in an epitaph unto Claudianus, the brother of Claudianus Mamertus [^796], saith that the latter "prepared (*paravit*) for the annual solemnities (*solemnibus*) readings suitable unto each season" [^797].

##### Ceremonial Aspect of the Readings

More than for the distribution of readings across the ecclesiastical year was accomplished by the 4th and 5th centuries, apparently, for the elaboration of the ceremonial aspect of liturgical reading. At least, from these centuries we find not only the first accounts concerning the preparatory and concluding rites and acclamations for the liturgical readings, but the majority of such rites and acclamations have been preserved in unchanged and even unaugmented form unto this day.

##### The Persons Who Read

First of all, in regard unto the persons who read, a more precise regulation was introduced. Specifically, the reading of the Gospel was almost universally assigned unto the higher ranks of the clergy, beginning with the deacon and not excluding the bishop. Whereas in the 2nd century—in Justin Martyr—the task of the bishop is the homily following the reading [^798], which was performed by a lector—according unto the *Testamentum Domini Nostri Jesu Christi* [^799] and the *Apostolic Constitutions* [^800] the Gospel is read by a deacon and a presbyter. The *Pilgrimage* of Sylvia frequently assigneth the reading of the Gospel unto the bishop [^801]. *(Orig. p. 169)* In other places, principally, it seems, in the Western Church, the reading of the Gospel was regarded as the prerogative of the deacon (as is the case today in the Roman Church and in part among us): Blessed Jerome remindeth the deacon Sabinian that he "in the capacity (*quasi*) of a deacon continually read (*lectitabas*) the Gospel" [^802]. Socrates speaketh of the reading of the Gospel by a deacon (Sabbatius) at every liturgical assembly [^803]. According unto the words of Sozomen, in Alexandria the Gospel was read only by the archdeacon, in other places by deacons, in many places only by presbyters, and in some places on great feasts by bishops, for example, in Constantinople on the first day of Pascha [^804]. In rare localities there was preserved the former right of the lector to read all Holy Scripture, not excluding the Gospel, as may be inferred from the decree of the First Council of Toledo in 400: "penitents shall not be admitted unto the clergy, except only out of necessity and for the benefit of the work, and in such case let them be numbered among the lectors, yet so that (*ita ut*) they read neither Gospels nor Epistles" [^805].

##### The Acclamation "Peace Be Unto All"

The reading of Holy Scripture was preceded by a series of acclamations, and first of all by the acclamation:

**"Peace be unto all"** (*«Мир всем»* / *Pax vobiscum*).

St. John Chrysostom calleth this acclamation "the common preface in all ecclesiastical actions: when the primate entereth into the church, he immediately saith: **'Peace be unto all'**; when he ariseth for the sermon, he beginneth not to speak unto the people before he imparteth peace unto all; when the priests perform the blessing (at Matins and Vespers before the prayer), they preface it with this; when he biddeth greeting to be given—**'Peace be unto all'**; when the Sacrifice is accomplished—**'Peace be unto all'**" [^806]. In the West likewise, judging by Blessed Augustine, this greeting was pronounced by the bishop before the readings. Describing a service whereat a miracle of healing took place, Blessed Augustine saith: "joy was complete, joyful voices sounded forth: 'Thanks be to God, praise be to God' (*Deo gratias, Deo laudes*); no one kept silence; on every side they cried aloud; I greeted the people, and again they exclaimed (*clamabant*) with the same ardent voice; and when at last silence was restored, there took place the solemn reading of the divine scriptures" [^807]. That this "greeting" of the bishop unto the people upon entering the church before the reading consisted in the imparting of peace is evident, besides the cited passage of Chrysostom, also from several other passages of his homilies, which indicate likewise the response of the people unto the greeting: "Upon entering the church, we immediately *(Orig. p. 170)* according unto this law (in conformity with the Savior's commandment concerning reconciliation with one's neighbors before prayer) say: **'Peace be unto you'**, and you reply: **'And with thy spirit'**" [^808]. "What is more perverse and senseless," Blessed Augustine reprehendeth the Donatists, "than for lectors and those who read the Epistles to say 'peace be unto thee' (*pax tecum*), and yet to separate themselves from the peace of those churches unto which these Epistles were written?" [^809] From these passages it is evident at the same time that the practice of the Eastern and Western Churches on this point was identical: in both places the reading was preceded by the imparting of peace; the formula, apparently, was not yet firmly fixed and everywhere uniform. Peace was imparted by the primate of the assembly, that is, for the most part by the bishop. But from the fact that the Council of Carthage of 419 forbiddeth lectors to "greet (*salutent*) the people" [^810], one may conclude that originally this peaceful greeting was pronounced by the lector himself [^811], and only when there was attached unto it a sacramental-intercessory significance was the right unto it transferred unto the bishop or presbyter.

##### Let Us Attend

St. John Chrysostom mentioneth the acclamation **"Let us attend"** (*«Вонмем»* / *Proschomen*) before the reading: "There stands the deacon, the common minister, crying aloud and saying: 'Let us attend'; and this frequently... after him the lector begins: 'The prophecy of Isaiah'; then he pronounceth aloud (*eis epekoon*): **'Thus saith the Lord'** [^812], while the standing deacon stoppeth the mouths of all by the imposition of silence (evidently by the acclamation: 'Let us attend'), he speaketh this, rendering honor not unto the lector, but unto Him Who speaketh with all through him" [^813]. Concerning this imposition of silence mention is made also by St. Ambrose [^814] and Blessed Augustine [^815]. Of acclamations following the readings, even after the reading of the Gospels, monuments of the 4th and 5th centuries make no mention [^816].

*(Orig. p. 171)*

The fact of the emergence of all these acclamations beareth witness unto the reverence which the reading of Holy Scripture inspired at divine worship [^817].

##### Rites of the Reading

Unto the same reverence testifieth the setting wherein the reading took place. Here first of all one must note the almost universal custom of standing during the reading of Holy Scripture (in contrast unto the sitting of the synagogue), noted for the first time by monuments of the 4th and 5th centuries [^818], yet still contending with the custom of sitting during these readings. The contest was resolved by standing being assigned unto the Gospel reading, and sitting unto the rest. Already the *Apostolic Constitutions* prescribe: "When the Gospel is read, let all presbyters, deacons, and the entire people stand in complete silence" [^819]. But St. John Cassian saith that Egyptian monks during the readings customarily sat upon low benches, and he noteth no difference in this regard for New Testament readings [^820]. Sozomen noteth as something strange (*xenon*) in the Alexandrian Church—something he neither knoweth nor hath heard of in others—that the bishop does not rise during the reading of the Gospel [^821]. Philostorgius (4th–5th cc.) relateth concerning Theophilus, an Arian bishop, that upon arriving in India he "corrected many things that were performed there contrary unto the order (*ouk euagos*), for there they listened unto the Gospel reading sitting, and permitted certain other things not allowed by the Divine law (*hon me theios thesmos epestatei*)" [^822]. In the *Life of St. Anastasius I*, Pope of Rome (398–402), it is related that he established that "each time the Gospel is read, the priests should not sit, but stand bowed (*curvi*)" [^823].

Unto the reproach of the presbyter Vigilantius, who contended against the veneration of martyrs, that the Church permitteth the kindling of lamps in daylight at the tombs of martyrs, Blessed Jerome remarketh: "even apart from the relics of martyrs, *(Orig. p. 172)* throughout all the churches of the East, when the Gospel is about to be read, lights (*luminaria*) are kindled, even when the sun is shining—not, indeed, to banish darkness, but as a token of joy, so that under the figure of material light there may be represented that Light whereof we read in the Psalter: 'A lamp unto my feet is Thy law, and a light unto my paths'" [^824]. Consequently, this custom was not yet universal, but was hardly new: it had been preserved from the time when the Gospel was always read in the evening or at night—at the Liturgy, which in antiquity was celebrated in the evening with the agape, and later (from the 2nd century) in the deep morning, its preparatory portion merging with the dawn Matins [^825].

##### Reading of Non-Canonical Books

Alongside the canonical books of Holy Scripture, there were still read at divine worship in this period certain non-canonical sacred books. The distinction between the two consisted in this: that the canonical books were regarded as divinely inspired and therefore served as the rule of faith and piety, whereas the non-canonical books were regarded merely as pious compositions and were appointed for reading unto converts and catechumens [^826]. Blessed Jerome saith concerning the books of Judith, Tobit, Maccabees, the Wisdom of Solomon, and Sirach: "as the Church readeth the books of Judith, Tobit, and Maccabees, yet receiveth them not among the canonical scriptures [^827], so also these two volumes [^828] (Wisdom and Sirach) she readeth for the edification of the people (*ad aedificationem plebis*), yet not for establishing the authority of ecclesiastical dogmas" [^829]. Other writers of this period express themselves in similar fashion concerning these books, placing alongside them certain compositions of the Apostolic Fathers and ancient Christian writings as non-canonical books of the New Testament. St. Athanasius, having enumerated the canonical books of the Old and New Testaments, remarketh: "but for greater exactness, writing this also out of necessity, I subjoin that besides these there are others also, not included in the canon, which nevertheless have been appointed by the Fathers to be read unto those newly arriving (*anaginoskesthai tois arti proserchomenois*) and desiring to be instructed in the word of piety: such are the Wisdom of Solomon, the Wisdom of Sirach, Esther, Judith, Tobit, the so-called Teaching (*Didache*) of the Apostles, and the Shepherd" [^830]. According unto *(Orig. p. 173)* Rufinus (presbyter of Aquileia, † 410), "there are also other books which by our ancestors were called not canonical, but ecclesiastical (*ecclesiastici*), such as the Wisdom of Solomon and the other Wisdom called of the Son of Sirach; of the same rank are the Book of Tobit and Judith and the Books of Maccabees; and in the New Testament the book called the Shepherd, or Hermas, and that called The Two Ways, or the Judgment of Peter (*Duae Viae sive Judicium Petri* = the 'Teaching of the Twelve Apostles', which beginneth with the words: 'Two ways...'); all these books they willed indeed to be read in the churches (*quae omnia legi quidem in ecclesiis voluerunt*), yet not to be brought forward for confirmation of faith therefrom" [^831]. Concerning the reading of the *Shepherd* in the churches Eusebius likewise makes mention: "it, as we know, hath been publicly read in the churches (*en ekklesiais ismen auto dedemosieumenon*)." In addition, he speaketh of the liturgical reading also of the Epistle of St. Clement, Bishop of Rome:

"it is known that it was publicly read (*epi tou koinou dedemosieumenen*) both in antiquity and now among ourselves" [^832]. When the canon was definitively established, the reading of these books at divine worship had either to cease or to take on a character distinct from the reading of canonical books. In certain churches, apparently, the former occurred. Thus St. Cyril of Jerusalem admonished: "one must have nothing in common with apocrypha (so he calleth all non-canonical books); that alone must one study which we read openly (*meta parresias*) in church... but that which is not read in church, read not even in private" [^833]. Nevertheless Sozomen speaketh (disapprovingly) of the reading in certain Palestinian churches of the apocryphal Apocalypse of Peter (on Great and Holy Friday) [^834]. In the majority of churches, however, not only did the reading of non-canonical books continue, as the above-cited testimonies demonstrate, even after they had been decisively recognized as non-canonical, but after their example there began to be read also the writings of later teachers of the Church, with only a sharp distinction drawn between the readings of divinely inspired scriptures and these latter. Restricting liturgical reading unto canonical scriptures, the Council of Carthage forbiddeth the reading of other books not unconditionally, but "under the name of divine scriptures" [^835]. Blessed Jerome said concerning St. Ephrem the Syrian: "Ephrem, deacon of the Church of Edessa, wrote much in the Syriac tongue and attained such renown that in certain churches his compositions are read publicly after the reading of the scriptures" [^836]. "If a presbyter," decreeth the Council of Vaison (in Gaul) of 529, "on account of any infirmity cannot preach himself, let the homilies of the holy fathers be read by the deacons" [^837]. The biographer placeth into the mouth of Caesarius, Bishop of Arles (6th c.), these words: "if the words of the Lord, of the prophets, and of the Apostles are read by presbyters and deacons, *(Orig. p. 174)* why should not presbyters and deacons read the words of Ambrose, of Augustine, or of my humble self, or of every one of the saints?" [^838]

The custom of reading the acts of the martyrs at divine worship, having begun perhaps already in the 2nd and 3rd centuries [^839], now attained widespread dissemination, although in certain localities it provoked legislative restrictions and prohibitions on account of the corruption of these acts. Eusebius of Caesarea referreth unto "memoirs concerning the martyrs" and unto the "book concerning the martyrs" or "collection of martyrdoms" (*he ton martyron synagoge*) composed by himself [^840]. Blessed Augustine repeatedly mentioneth readings of this kind at divine worship: "in the passion which was read unto us today" [^841]. The Council of Carthage of 397 decreeth: "it shall be lawful also hereafter (*liceat etiam legi*) for the passions of the martyrs to be read, when their annual commemorations (*dies*) are celebrated" [^842]. Only in the Roman Church by the decree of Pope Gelasius at the Council of seventy bishops in 494 was the reading of the acts of the martyrs forbidden, which "out of singular caution, according unto ancient custom, are not read in the holy Roman Church, because the names of those who wrote them are for the most part unknown, and in them, it is thought, much that is superfluous and incongruous with the matter hath been written by unfaithful simpletons (*idiotis*), such as, for instance, the passions of a certain Quiricus and Julitta, as also of Gregory and others, composed manifestly by heretics" [^843]. Nevertheless this same decree mentioneth the reading in many Roman churches, though not in the Lateran, of the acts of the holy Pope Sylvester.

It was also in custom to read in church and, of course, at divine worship the decrees of Councils. Blessed Augustine saith that in many African churches it was customary annually during the days of the fast, that is, in Great Lent prior unto Pascha, when the strictly fasting people have greater leisure, to read through the acts of the Council of Carthage (*eadem gesta collationis*) in their entirety from beginning to end in order [^844].

Since in the order of the Liturgy given by the *Apostolic Constitutions* [^845], as in all the so-called apostolic liturgies, which in their fundamentals ascend unto the 4th century and earlier [^846], reading is indicated only from the canonical books (the Law, the Prophets, the Gospels, Acts, and the Epistles), all other readings must have taken place at other services, as is the case today. If so, then *(Orig. p. 175)* already in the 4th century did the so-called rubrical readings (*ordo*-mandated lections / *ustavnye chteniya*) at Vespers and Matins take their origin.

##### Preaching in the 4th and 5th Centuries

Preaching at divine worship in the 4th and 5th centuries occupied no less significant a place than in former centuries, owing unto the liveliness of theological controversies and the elevation of the general level of education among the clergy (many church figures of the 4th and 5th centuries had received an education in the finest secular schools of that epoch). Scarcely any period brought forth a longer series of illustrious preachers or furnished more material for our present rubrical readings. In the East there attained renown: Eusebius of Caesarea, Saints Athanasius the Great, Basil the Great, Gregory the Theologian, Cyril of Jerusalem, Gregory of Nyssa, Macarius the Great, Ephrem the Syrian, John Chrysostom, Proclus Patriarch of Constantinople, Cyril of Alexandria, Epiphanius of Cyprus, and Blessed Theodoret; in the West: St. Ambrose, Blessed Augustine, Peter Chrysologus, Leo the Great, and Caesarius Bishop of Arles. The majority of the homilies preserved from this period represent expositions of Holy Scripture; a significant number are devoted unto dogmatic controversies; fewer are of a purely edifying character, and a comparatively small circle is constituted by festal panegyrics. Of sermons of the first kind there entered into our present divine worship in the widest measure the homilies of St. John Chrysostom, and in part of St. Basil the Great; the second kind of sermons of this period, having had a temporary character, entered not at all into our divine worship. Of the third kind there entered the discourses of St. Ephrem; of the fourth, the majority of the few works of this kind.

Preachers of this period not infrequently note the zeal wherewith their instructions were attended, and at times were compelled to contend even with an exaggerated appraisal of the place and importance of preaching within the composition of divine worship. "Preaching," saith St. John Chrysostom, "is everything unto you. You say: what is there to do in church if there is no sermon? That is an entirely perverse view. What need is there of a preacher? It was properly on your account that he became necessary. Why a sermon? All is clear from Holy Scripture" [^847]. "Often have I sought at that sacred hour (of the Eucharist) for so numerous an assembly as is now gathered here, and found it nowhere; and deeply did I sigh that you listen unto your fellow-servant speaking unto you with such zeal, yet when Christ appeareth upon the mystical table, then the church is empty" [^848]. However, in that same hierarch there occur lamentations also concerning the inattention of the listeners, and concerning their departure from the church prior unto the conclusion of the instruction: "many of those standing and hearing me yawn, scratch their head, and grow weary... while others depart before I finish speaking" [^849]. Caesarius of Arles (early 6th c.), after fruitless exhortations not to leave the sermon, commanded for the duration *(Orig. p. 176)* thereof that the church doors be locked [^850]. In general, in the East preaching at divine worship occupied far more room than in the West, as is evident both from these latter testimonies, and from the catalogue of preachers here and there, and finally, from the manifestly exaggerated yet characteristic testimony of Sozomen, that in Rome "neither the bishop nor anyone else teacheth in church" [^851].

##### Time of Preaching

The principal moment for preaching remained as before the Liturgy, and specifically its preparatory portion, the Liturgy of the Catechumens, as is demonstrated by a whole series of homilies of St. John Chrysostom and others, who frequently remind their hearers of the liturgical acclamations and prayers they have just heard. But sometimes and in certain localities preaching took place also at other services. Thus the homilies on the Hexaemeron of St. Basil were delivered two in a day—at the morning office and at the evening office ("when you were present at the brief morning [*heothen*] discourse, we stumbled upon such concealed depth of thought that we despaired of that which followed, etc.") [^852]. According unto Socrates, "in Caesarea of Cappadocia and in Cyprus on Saturday and Sunday always in the evening at the lighting of the lamps (*meta tes lychnapsias*) the presbyters and bishops expound the Scriptures" [^853]. The homilies of St. John Chrysostom on Genesis were delivered in the evening ("we expound unto you the Scriptures, yet you, turning your eyes away from us, have directed your attention unto the lamps, unto him who was kindling the lamps") [^854]. "Turn your attention unto the continuation of the psalm whereof we spoke at Matins," Blessed Augustine inviteth his hearers [^855]. Since preaching was considered an indispensable constituent of the Liturgy [^856], it must, one must think, have taken place obligatorily on those days when the Liturgy was celebrated, and as frequently as the latter was celebrated in any locality. But during Great Lent (*Tessarakoste*) and Pentecost, especially during the former—in view of the catechumens—they preached for the most part daily. Thus in the homilies of St. John Chrysostom on Genesis and "On the Statues," as well as in the discourses of Blessed Augustine on the psalms, references unto "yesterday's" discourse constantly occur. In monastic communities, moreover, at least in certain ones, as we shall see, the abba daily instructed the brethren throughout the entire year.

##### Persons Who Preached

As regards the persons who preached, following the example of the Apostles and the practice of the 2nd and 3rd centuries [^857], the true minister of the word was considered to be the bishop. "The proper office (*proprium munus*) of a bishop is to teach the people" [^858]. According unto St. John *(Orig. p. 177)* Chrysostom, the ability to teach in a bishop "ought to be before all else" [^859]. Preaching talent in that era most of all advanced persons unto episcopal sees, as the examples of Eusebius of Caesarea, Saints Gregory the Theologian, John Chrysostom, and Blessed Augustine demonstrate. But in ecclesiastical teaching presbyters also took part far more than in former times. Already in the 3rd century so illustrious a preacher as Origen was merely a presbyter. The *Apostolic Constitutions* prescribe: after the readings, and in particular after the Gospel, "let the presbyters severally, and not all at once, exhort the people, and after them all the bishop, who is like unto a helmsman" [^860]. In conformity with this, in the Church of Jerusalem according unto the description of the *Pilgrimage* attributed unto Sylvia, on the Lord's Day "of all the sitting presbyters whosoe'er desireth preacheth, and after them all the bishop preacheth" [^861]. St. John Chrysostom preached in Antioch precisely in the rank of presbyter in the presence of his bishop Flavian, who sometimes added his own exhortation unto his sermon [^862]. Unto Blessed Augustine, when he was a presbyter, his aged bishop Valerius, who possessed poor command of the Latin tongue of his flock, committed preaching in church; and when the bishop was reproached for this, he appealed unto Eastern custom of this kind [^863]. Consequently, in the West prior unto that time preaching had been the prerogative of the bishop alone. But already Blessed Jerome saith concerning this: "it is a very bad custom that in certain churches the presbyters keep silence and speak not in the presence of the bishops, as though the latter envied them or disdained to listen unto them" [^864]. In cases of necessity or extraordinary circumstances, deacons also were admitted unto preaching. Already in the 3rd century, according unto the testimony of St. Cyprian, during persecutions which at times deprived the Church of presbyters, the right of preaching was granted also unto deacons [^865]. One of the most renowned preachers of the 4th century, St. Ephrem, possessed only the rank of deacon. St. Gregory the Great, Pope of Rome († 604), during illness commissioned deacons to read his homilies [^866]. Above we saw that deacons were commissioned with the reading at divine worship of the homilies of the holy fathers [^867]. Even laymen were admitted unto preaching, but only in the most exceptional cases. Thus it was already in the 3rd century according to the testimony of Eusebius, when Origen withdrew from Alexandria to Caesarea of Palestine, "here the local bishops (Alexander of Jerusalem and Theoctistus of Caesarea) requested him to discourse and expound the Holy Scriptures publicly in church, notwithstanding the fact that at that time he was not yet ordained unto the presbyterate"; and unto the reproach on the part of Demetrius, Bishop of Alexandria, "that it had never been heard of and was not now the custom *(Orig. p. 178)* for a layman to preach in the presence of a bishop," they appealed unto a whole series of former examples in diverse countries [^868]. But from the 4th and 5th centuries such examples are no longer known, if one discount the speech of Emperor Constantine the Great unto the First Ecumenical Council. On the contrary, when certain monks in the East began to arrogate unto themselves the right of church preaching, Pope Leo I the Great (440–461), unto whom, perhaps, even the preaching of a presbyter in church was unfamiliar, wrote against this unto Maximus, Bishop of Antioch, and Theodoret, Bishop of Cyrrhus, saying in his letter unto the former: "beside the priests of the Lord, let none dare to preach, whether he be monk or layman, under whatsoever name of learning (*cujuslibet scientiae nomine*) he may be renowned" [^869]. But the Council of Carthage of 399 decrees: "let not a layman (*laicus*) dare to teach in the presence of clerics, unless they themselves request him so to do" [^870].

Only unto woman, as ever since apostolic times [^871], was preaching unconditionally forbidden. That same Council decrees: "A woman, however learned and holy, let her not presume (*non praesumat*) to teach men in the assembly" [^872]. In the Eastern Churches, however, deaconesses were permitted to engage in the catechization of women preparing for baptism, yet not publicly, but privately [^873]. In this regard certain heretical communities differed sharply from the Catholic Church, not only permitting the preaching of women, but possessing prophetesses, such as were Prisca and Maximilla among the Montanists, and elevating women unto the episcopal and presbyteral ranks, as among them Quintilla and Priscilla [^874]. The same was true among the Collyridians of the 4th century, among whom women celebrated sacred rites in honor of the Most Holy Virgin Mary, as also among the Cataphrygians [^875].

##### Acclamations and Rites Accompanying Preaching

Inasmuch as preaching, serving as an exposition of Holy Scripture and wholly grounded upon it, was likewise regarded, in some measure, as the word of God, so also was preaching framed with rites and acclamations almost identical unto the reading of Holy Scripture. Thus before the sermon the deacon invited those present unto silence and attention [^876], perhaps with the acclamation **"Let us attend"** (*Proschomen*). Before the instruction the preacher offered a prayer, presumably secretly [^877].
