Meanwhile there hath come down unto us a document that was, so to speak, a living witness of the gradual establishment of the forty-day fast in place of the former shorter one in one of the most prominent Churches of antiquity: the so-called *Festal Letters* of St. Athanasius of Alexandria, a contemporary of that very Council of Nicaea, one of whose canons is regarded as the first authentic testimony in time concerning the Forty-Day Fast. In the first of these epistles, of the year 329, the Forty-Day Fast is not mentioned at all, and the beginning of the "holy fast" is assigned unto the Monday of Holy Week. Inasmuch as the fourth and fifth epistles of 332–333 likewise *(Orig. p. 242)* presuppose this order, whereas in the two preceding ones (the 2nd and 3rd) the Forty-Day Fast also hath a place beside or before Holy Week, one cannot conclude from the first epistle that the Forty-Day Fast was not yet known in Egypt at that time. The fluctuation showeth only that the Church there was in a stage of transition from the former order unto the new. Complete certainty is imparted unto this supposition by the epistle of St. Athanasius unto Serapion, appended unto the 11th Festal Letter and written in the year 340 from Rome. Unto the Bishop of Thmuis, unto whom during the absence of the Alexandrian Archbishop the oversight of the entire Egyptian Church was entrusted, in this epistle it is proposed "to proclaim unto the brethren the forty-day fast and to add an exhortation unto it, so that, while the whole world fasteth, we alone who dwell in Egypt may not become a laughingstock for our non-fasting and for surrendering ourselves unto rejoicing in these days." In the 19th Festal Letter of the year 346 the observance of the Forty-Day Fast is already presented by St. Athanasius as an indispensable condition for a worthy celebration of Pascha, saying: "Whosoever disregardeth the Forty-Day Fast, entering as it were heedlessly and uncleansed into the Holy of Holies, that man doth not celebrate the feast of Pascha." [^1248]

Where the six-week fast was adopted, they commenced it on the Monday of the second week of the present Orthodox fast. Consequently, the present First Week of Great Lent in such a practice was not included in the fast. As a memorial of such a practice, which is no longer followed even by its principal ancient adherent, the Roman Church, there hath remained in this latter Church the fact that the Secret Prayer of this Monday—which now in the Roman Church is already the sixth day of the fast—commenceth with the words: *Sacrificium quadragesimalis initii solemniter immolamus* ("We solemnly offer the sacrifice of the beginning of the Forty-Day Fast"). [^1249] The lengthening of the forty-day fast unto seven weeks was caused by the circumstance that among the number of fasting days there were not to be included not only the Sundays falling during the Forty-Day Fast, but, according unto the view of the Eastern Church, Saturdays as well. When, following the emergence in the West of fasting on Saturday, Eastern ecclesiastical legislation began to prohibit it with particular insistence, [^1250] then those Eastern Churches which hitherto had maintained a six-week fast before Pascha likewise adopted a seven-week fast. In that very Jerusalem Church, in which Eusebius and Cyril of Jerusalem (who said on Great and Holy Friday: "these elapsed days of the Forty-Day Fast" [^1251]) know a forty-day fast, the Aquitanian pilgrim lady of the IV century already witnesseth eight weeks of the pre-Paschal fast; [^1252] yet Peter, Patriarch of Jerusalem (524–544), testifieth [^1253] unto a seven-week fast in his church.

*(Orig. p. 243)*
### The Manner of Fasting

In that same historian Socrates, who acquaints us with the gradual lengthening of the pre-Paschal fast from a one-week fast into a forty-day fast, we find also information concerning the development undergone by the very form of fasting.

> "The divergence," saith Socrates, "doth not concern solely the number of fasting days, but also the conception of abstinence from foods; for some abstain from the eating of every kind of animal, while others of all animate creatures partake only of fish, and certain ones > together with fish eat birds also, saying that birds, according unto the narrative of Moses, likewise proceeded from water. Some abstain even from fruits and eggs, others feed only upon dry bread, certain ones do not partake even of that, while others, fasting until the ninth hour, partake thereafter of any food." [^1254]

Sozomen, who generally repeateth Socrates, doth not note this difference in the fasting of the Forty-Day Fast, pointing only unto the difference in its duration. Thus, very soon after there was accepted in the Church, as one of the possible forms of fasting, abstinence from flesh-meat, an exception was made for certain kinds of meat—and in this regard not only for fish, as now, but for birds as well. Yet this latter kind of exception, possessing no foundation for itself, soon fell away, and only the former remained. In permitting the use of fish during a fast they could be guided by the following considerations: 1) the curse of God following upon the Fall was directed specifically upon the earth, and not upon the waters or their inhabitants; 2) fish pertain unto the element with which baptism is connected; 3) in the narrative of creation it is said: "The Spirit of God moved over the water" (Gen. 1:2). [^1255]

The next degree of abstinence in fasting Socrates considereth the non-consumption of "fruits and eggs"; consequently, not everywhere was a distinction yet established between the one and the other. As a trace of this there hath remained among us the Cheese-fare Week (*Sedmitsa Syrnaya*).

The concluding words in the testimony of Socrates demonstrate that what was regarded as essential in fasting even in the V century was not the kind of food, but the duration of complete abstinence therefrom, that is to say, the hour of partaking thereof. In other words, what was essential in fasting was that on a fasting day there was no midday meal (*ἄριστον*, *prandium*), but solely dinner or supper (*δεῖπνον*, *coena*—among the ancients the midday dinner was not distinguished from supper). This is apparent also from other writers of that same epoch. "Wait a little (with food): soon is the end of the day," said St. Ambrose during Lent. [^1256] "Thou waitest for evening to take food, yet spendest the entire day in the lawcourts," reproached St. Basil the Great his listeners during the fast. [^1257] "Let us not think that the mere non-eating until evening is sufficient for us unto salvation," said in like manner at that time St. John Chrysostom; "what profit is there from fasting, tell me, if thou dost not eat for whole days, yet surrenderest thyself the whole day unto games, jesting, and even *(Orig. p. 244)* perjury and evil-speaking?" [^1258] "In the days of fasting," exhorteth Blessed Augustine, "that which we would consume for dinner, let us bestow upon the poor, and not upon the preparation of sumptuous suppers with delicacies for the most refined tastes." [^1259] "By as much as it drieth up in the body," reproacheth contemporaries Peter Chrysologus, "by so much is it fuller in" wallet; rather, fasting, let us bestow our dinner upon the poor." [^1260] In agreement with this our present *Typikon* likewise accounteth as an indispensable condition of a fast "a single meal" (*odnu trapezu*). [^1261] In monasteries, moreover, where throughout the entire year they were accustomed to take food once a day [^1262] in the evening, [^1263] during the Forty-Day Fast they did not eat for several days together. The pilgrim lady, reputed to be Sylvia, saith concerning the Jerusalem monks (*apotaktites*) that certain of them during the Forty-Day Fast, "having tasted food on Sunday after the Liturgy, that is to say, at the fifth or sixth hour, do not eat until Saturday"; on this day they taste food in the morning after the Liturgy, which on their account is celebrated before daybreak; "those who cannot spend an entire week in fasting eat in the middle thereof on Thursday; those unable to do even this fast for two days together throughout the entire Forty-Day Fast; and whosoever cannot accomplish even this tasteth food from evening unto evening." [^1264]

Originally, perhaps, upon the expiration of the day in the evening they partook during a fast of every kind of food, only, of course, in moderate measure. [^1265] Yet very soon, by the time of Socrates (V century), they arrived at the conception of the necessity of restricting oneself in fasting by the kind of food. Since the kinds and degrees of this restriction strikingly coincide with the anchoritic practice of fasting, [^1266] which antedated *(Orig. p. 245)* the establishment of the Forty-Day Fast, it is indubitable that we have here a borrowing thence. Since, furthermore, the most accepted food among the ascetics was bread and vegetables, such food soon became everywhere customary for the Forty-Day Fast as well. Sylvia saith concerning the Jerusalem monks that in the days of the Forty-Day Fast they "taste neither a crumb of bread, nor oil, nor tree fruit, but only water and a little flour gruel." [^1267] Gradually such food became customary during the fast for the laity as well: the Council of Laodicea requireth "to fast throughout the entire Forty-Day Fast with xerophagy (*νηστεύειν ξηροφαγοῦντας*)." [^1268]

The lengthening of the fast unto forty days posed for ecclesiastical practice a difficult task: how to act regarding the Sundays falling during the fast, upon which fasting would be unfitting, and regarding Saturdays, which in that epoch were honored in certain places almost equally with Sundays. The answer unto this was given already in the III century by St. Hippolytus of Rome. In the inscriptions upon his statue (with the chair) discovered in Rome there is also this rule: "the fast must be interrupted when a Sunday occurreth." [^1269] "During the Forty-Day Fast they fast throughout whole days, except for Saturday and Sunday," saith St. Ambrose. [^1270] St. Basil the Great saith that they fasted only five days in the week. [^1271] St. John Chrysostom calleth Saturday and Sunday days of rest for the strivers of the fast. [^1272] Yet unconditionally this rule was observed so long as fasting was placed in the duration of non-eating and not in the kind of food—that is to say, so long as it was accounted permissible in the evening on a fasting day to eat anything. When, however, the kind of food was restricted for the fast as well, naturally on the days of mitigation of the fast (Saturday and Sunday), as also at the hours of this mitigation (the ninth hour or evening), they came to partake only of certain kinds of food (bread, vegetables, fish, and in certain places perhaps milk). [^1273]

### Divine Worship of the Forty-Day Fast

Besides fasting, the days of the Forty-Day Fast were honored by a distinctive divine worship. Now for the first time, seemingly, it was acknowledged unfitting for fasting days to celebrate the Liturgy, [^1274] as is evident from the explicit canon of the Council of Laodicea concerning this: "that except for Saturday and Sunday, during the Forty-Day Fast it is not permitted to offer bread (*ἄрτον προσφέρειν*)." [^1275] The proximate cause of such a prohibition was that the Liturgy in certain places continued to be united with the agape, and consequently was accompanied by a more *(Orig. p. 246)* or less abundant and sumptuous meal. In Egypt, where the agape was retained especially long, the Liturgy was celebrated on every Wednesday and Friday without Communion, [^1276] which could have served as the germ of the Presanctified Liturgy. Yet the first testimony concerning this latter pertaineth unto Patriarch Sophronius of Jerusalem (VII century). [^1277] The non-celebration of the Liturgy during the Forty-Day Fast had perforce to elicit its compensation by other services. According unto the testimony of the pilgrim lady, reputed to be Sylvia, in the Jerusalem Church, with the exception of Saturday and Sunday, "during the Forty-Day Fast there was no offering (*oblatio*)," and as if in place of the Liturgy, unto the customary services of the day—Matins, the Sixth Hour, Ninth Hour, and Vespers—there was added the Third Hour: "at the third hour they go again (after Matins) into the Anastasis (the church), and everything is performed that throughout the whole year is performed at the sixth hour, since during the days of the Forty-Day Fast there is added also this: that they go into the church at the third hour." [^1278] In that same Jerusalem Church, according unto the witness of the same monument, on all Saturdays of the Forty-Day Fast there was celebrated a solemn vigil, commencing on Friday immediately following the Ninth Hour and Vespers and continuing until Saturday morning, when the Liturgy was joined directly unto it: "throughout the whole night there are sung alternately now psalms, now antiphons, and there are alternately diverse readings, and all this continueth until morning." [^1279] The other services of the Forty-Day Fast in the Jerusalem Church did not differ from the customary ones. The pilgrim lady noteth only a certain peculiarity in the divine worship of Wednesday and Friday of the Forty-Day Fast: the Ninth Hour was celebrated in the Church of Sion (and not in the Church of the Anastasis). [^1280] In general the Forty-Day Fast in the Jerusalem Church was distinguished by divine services so solemn that its days were as if a continuous festival: they were called *eortae*, "paschal"; concerning them the pilgrim lady expresseth herself that they "are celebrated" (*celebrantur*). [^1281] Whereas the Council of Laodicea enacteth "that during the Forty-Day Fast one ought not to celebrate the birthdays of the martyrs, but to perform their commemorations on Saturdays and Sundays," [^1282] in the Jerusalem Church the commemorations of the martyrs falling during the Forty-Day Fast were celebrated at their proper time, and for them certain peculiarities of the fasting service were abrogated (for example, the aforesaid celebration of the Ninth Hour on Sion). [^1283] During the Forty-Day Fast ecclesiastical preaching was intensified: according unto the witness of the Jerusalem pilgrim lady, there during the Forty-Day Fast, "in order that the people might ever be instructed in the Law, the bishop and the presbyters preach unceasingly (*assidue*)." [^1284] By the luminaries of ecclesiastical *(Orig. p. 247)* preaching in the IV–V centuries the greatest number of their finest homilies was delivered during the days of the Forty-Day Fast.

### The Catechumenate during the Forty-Day Fast

Considerable peculiarities were imparted unto the divine worship of the Forty-Day Fast by assigning the catechumenate unto its days. The catechumenate, which in that epoch lasted about three years, [^1285] was solemnly brought to conclusion during the Forty-Day Fast. The principal acts of this conclusion were the naming of the candidate preparing for baptism (*competens*) at the beginning of the Forty-Day Fast, his daily exorcism (from evil spirits) throughout the entire fast, [^1286] final instruction in the truths of the faith, the learning and exposition of the Creed (*traditio symboli*), and lastly, baptism itself on Great and Holy Saturday; certain of these acts formed part of the daily round of divine services, while others were appended thereto, by virtue whereof the entire divine worship of the Forty-Day Fast was as it were concentrated around the catechumens and might be called the liturgy of the catechumens. Nor is this surprising, in view of the fact that the Forty-Day Fast itself arose out of the fast of the catechumens and of the faithful with them and on their behalf prior unto baptism. [^1287] Sylvia thus describeth the catechumenate during the Forty-Day Fast:

> "He that declareth his name doth this before the day of the Forty-Day Fast, and the presbyter recordeth the names of all; this takes place eight weeks beforehand, during which, as I have said, the Forty-Day Fast continueth. [^1288] When the presbyter hath recorded the names of all, on the following day—the day of the Forty-Day Fast itself, that is to say, from which the eight weeks of the fast commence—a cathedra is set for the bishop in the midst of the great church, that is to say, in the Martyrium; on either side the presbyters sit upon chairs, and all the clerics stand; then those seeking baptism (*competentes*) are brought forward one by one: if they be men, they come with their fathers (sponsors); if women, with their mothers (sponsors). And then the bishop questions one by one the neighbors of him that hath entered, saying: whether he leadeth a good life, whether he honoreth his parents, whether he be not a drunkard or a boaster; and he questioneth concerning all the vices that are more grievous in man. And when he is convinced that he is blameless in all things, he inscribeth his name with his own hand. Those who approach unto baptism, during the forty days of the fast, early in the morning > the clerics exorcise, as soon as the morning dismissal takes place in the Anastasis. Immediately following this a cathedra is set for the bishop in the great church, in the Martyrium, and all who approach unto baptism, both men and women, sit around the bishop, while the fathers and mothers stand; in like manner, of the people, all who wish to listen enter and sit down, but only the faithful. A catechumen doth not enter thither at the time when the bishop instructs them (who are prepared for baptism) in the Law. Thus, beginning from Genesis, throughout these forty days he traverseth all Scripture, first expounding it carnally (literally), and *(Orig. p. 248)* then explaining it spiritually. In like manner also during these days they are instructed concerning the resurrection and concerning everything pertaining unto the faith, and this is called catechesis (*cathecisis*). And when five weeks have elapsed from the beginning of instruction, then they receive the Creed (*traditio symboli*); the meaning of this Creed in its individual words the bishop explains unto them in like manner as the meaning of the Scriptures, first carnally, then spiritually; so also he explains the Creed. And it cometh to pass that in these places all the faithful follow the Scripture when it is read in church, since all are instructed during these forty days, beginning from the first until the third hour, for the catechesis continueth three hours. And the Lord knoweth, reverend sisters, that the faithful who enter to hear the catechesis attend with greater attention unto that which is spoken and explained by the bishop than when he sitteth and preacheth in church concerning individual passages interpreted in such manner. Upon the conclusion of the catechesis, at the third hour, immediately they conduct the bishop with hymnody into the Anastasis, and the dismissal of the third hour takes place: and thus, for the space of three hours they are instructed daily throughout seven weeks. But in the eighth week of the Forty-Day Fast, that is to say, which is called the Great Week, their instruction ceaseth, in order that that which is more momentous may be accomplished. In the Great Week (doubtless on Monday) the bishop comes in the morning into the great church, into the Martyrium; behind the altar in the apse a cathedra is set for the bishop, and thither they approach one by one—a man with his father, a woman with her mother—and recite (*reddet*, return) the Creed unto the bishop. Following the reading of the Creed unto the bishop, he addresseth all" [^1289] with a brief exhortation.

Thus the catechumenate was conducted in other churches also (for example, in the Roman and African churches). At the recitation (*redditio*) of the Creed in certain churches a promise was exacted to recite it daily in the morning, at midday, and in the evening. [^1290] In the history of divine worship this rite of the catechumenate is significant in that it fixed permanently in the Liturgy the litany for the catechumens, and in Great Lent also that for those preparing for illumination (baptism). In addition, it gave rise unto a special ancient service during the Forty-Day Fast, specifically for the catechumens: the *tritekte*, so named from the time of its celebration (*τριτέκτη*, "third-sixth," between the 3rd and 6th hours) and related on the one hand unto the service of the Hours, especially the Third, and on the other unto the Liturgy of the Catechumens; this service achieved full development by the IX century, yet its origin may be placed in this epoch, and its germ accounted to be the Third Hour celebrated in Jerusalem only during the Forty-Day Fast and probably adapted unto the catechesis taking place during this service, albeit in another church (in the Martyrium); at all events Psalm 24 [MT 25], which formeth part of the Third Hour, is entirely suited unto the rite of the catechumenate. [^1291] *(Orig. p. 249)*

### Penance and Communion during the Forty-Day Fast

Having assigned unto the Forty-Day Fast, as unto the most sacred season of the year, the catechumenate and baptism, the Church relegated unto this season also the administration of two other mysteries which demanded no less purifying preparation. So it was first of all with penance, this second baptism. The discipline of penance, so complex and rigorous in the first centuries, was most conveniently applied in the pre-Paschal fast. Already the Council of Ancyra (314–315 AD) appointeth Pascha as the time both for receiving the penitent into the Church and for transferring him from a lower order of penance unto a higher: "let them be received into the rank of those that hear the Scriptures until the Great Day of Pascha," it enacted regarding those who had partaken of idol-sacrifices during the persecutions. [^1292] According unto St. Gregory of Nyssa († after 394 AD), "on the day of Pascha we not only lead unto God those who are transformed by regeneration in the font of grace, but also those who through repentance and conversion from dead works approach unto eternal life." [^1293] Thus the present custom of preparing for Communion (*govet'*) in Great Lent arose already in this epoch. Thence deriveth also the predominantly penitential content of divine worship in Great Lent. (As a memorial of such an appointment of the Forty-Day Fast there serveth in the Roman Church the rite of the so-called "blessing of ashes" on the first day of the Roman Catholic Lent, on the Wednesday of the first week of our fast). Under the influence of this ancient assignment of penitential discipline unto the Forty-Day Fast, subsequently all the faithful came to be regarded during this fast as being in the status of penitents (and in part of catechumens), and upon this ground were deprived of the full Liturgy. [^1294] When the custom of weekly Communion of all the faithful was abandoned, the Forty-Day Fast became a preparation also for the worthy reception of this mystery, which was assigned now unto the day of its institution by the Saviour—Great and Holy Thursday—now unto Pascha. "Formerly many," saith St. John Chrysostom, "approached the Holy Mysteries thoughtlessly and without discernment, even on that day whereon Christ instituted Them. Therefore, seeing how much harm ariseth from indiscreet approach unto Them, the fathers came together and appointed forty days of fasting, prayers, hearing of the word of God, and assemblies, in order that throughout all these days, being thoroughly cleansed by prayers, almsgiving, fasting, vigils, tears, confession, and all else, we might approach (unto the Mysteries) with a pure conscience according unto our ability," [^1295] "so that, *(Orig. p. 250)* being purified from the sins cleaving unto us in every manner throughout the year, we might with spiritual vigilance become partakers of this unbloody sacrifice." [^1296] Blessed Jerome saith: "The Lord Himself, the true Jonah sent to preach unto the world, fasteth forty days, and leaving us the heritage of fasting, prepareth by this ascetic struggle our souls for the eating of His Body." [^1297]

### Civil Legislation concerning the Forty-Day Fast

Secular legislation for its part met the Church halfway in the sanctification of the Forty-Day Fast. Emperor Theodosius the Great issued two edicts concerning the Forty-Day Fast. According unto one of them, "during the forty days which through the performance of diverse rites prepare for the season of Pascha, all examination of criminal cases is suspended" (doubtless because it was accompanied by judicial torture), and according unto the other, "in the consecrated days of the Forty-Day Fast there shall be no corporal punishments that might end in death." [^1298] A similar ordinance on a particular occasion was made by Emperor Valentinian, according unto the words of St. Ambrose. [^1299] An exception unto the aforementioned laws of Theodosius the Great was made by Theodosius the Younger for cases involving the Isaurian brigands. [^1300]

### The Penultimate Week of the Forty-Day Fast

Among the weeks of the Forty-Day Fast in the Jerusalem Church, the penultimate week likewise was distinguished by a special station of divine worship (upon Sion). [^1301]

### Holy Week

The final, pre-Paschal week of the fast was everywhere named the "Great Week" (*Hebdomas Magna*). [^1302] The fast during this week was intensified. The *Apostolic Constitutions* prescribe for it the strictest fast upon bread, salt, and vegetables, advising total abstinence from food on Friday and Saturday. [^1303] According unto the testimony of St. Epiphanius of Cyprus, "these six days of Pascha all the people (*πάντες οἱ λαοί*) customarily spend in xerophagy (*ξηροφαγία*), that is to say, they partake towards evening only of bread with salt and water; while certain ones zealously extend their abstinence (*ὑπεрτίθενται*, literally postpone, that is to say, the partaking of food) unto two, three, and four days; and others even spend the entire week without food until cockcrow on Sunday." [^1304] *(Orig. p. 251)*

### Lazarus Saturday

Unto the Great Week there were reckoned in the Jerusalem Church the penultimate Saturday, whereon was commemorated the resurrection of Lazarus, and the final Sunday, whereon was commemorated the Entry of the Lord into Jerusalem. The divine worship of these days is described in detail by the Aquitanian pilgrim lady:

> "In the morning, at the daybreak of Saturday, the bishop officiates (*offert*) and celebrateth the Liturgy (*oblationem*) so that the dismissal may take place earlier. The archdeacon proclaims, saying: 'Let us all be ready today at the seventh hour (1:00 PM) at the tomb of Lazarus.' And then, upon the arrival of the seventh hour, all assemble at the tomb of Lazarus (in Bethany). On the way from Jerusalem unto the tomb of Lazarus, approximately five hundred paces from that place, there is a church upon the road at the place where Mary, the sister of Lazarus, met the Lord. And when the bishop arrives thither, all the monks go forth to meet him there, and the people enter thither: a hymn is sung there and one antiphon, and there is read the corresponding passage from the Gospel where the sister of Lazarus met the Lord (John 11). Then, after the saying of the prayer and the blessing of all, they proceed thence unto the tomb of Lazarus with hymns. Hymns are sung, as also antiphons adapted unto the day and place; readings likewise are read suitable unto the day. And then, when the dismissal takes place, Pascha is proclaimed: that is to say, a presbyter ascendeth unto a high place and reads that passage where > it is written in the Gospel: **'Jesus therefore six days before the passover came to Bethany'** (*Iisus zhe prezhde shesti dney Paskhi priide v Vifaniyu*) [^1305] and the rest (John 12). Thus, upon the reading of this passage and the proclamation of Pascha, the dismissal takes place. And this is performed on this day because, as it is written in the Gospel, this occurred in Bethany six days before the passover: and from Saturday until Thursday, when after the Supper the Lord was taken, six days are reckoned. Thus all return into the city, directly into the Anastasis, and there Vespers takes place according unto custom." [^1306]

### Palm Sunday

> "On the following day, that is to say, on Sunday, which formeth the entrance into the Paschal Week, called here the Great Week (*septimana major*), at cockcrow the customary service is celebrated (Matins until morning in the Anastasis or at the Cross). In the morning on the Sunday day there takes place the customary procession (*proceditur*—litany) in the great church, which is called the Martyrium. Upon the conclusion of the service in the great church, before the dismissal, the archdeacon proclaims, saying first: 'Throughout the entire week, that is to say, beginning from tomorrow, at the ninth hour let us all gather in the Martyrium, that is to say, in the great church.' Then he proclaims a second time, saying: 'Today at the seventh hour let us all be ready on the Mount of Olives.' Thus, upon the dismissal of the Liturgy in the great church, that is to say, in the Martyrium, the bishop is escorted with hymns into the Anastasis. Upon the completion of all that is customarily performed on Sundays in the Anastasis after the dismissal in the Martyrium (the lity), [^1307] each person, returning unto his own home, *(Orig. p. 252)* hasteneth to eat, so that at the beginning of the seventh hour (1:00 PM) all may be ready in the church situated upon the Mount of Olives, that is to say, on the Mount of Olives, where is that cave wherein the Lord taught." [^1308]

> "At the seventh hour all the people ascend the Mount of Olives, that is to say, the Eleon, unto the church, together with the bishop; hymns and antiphons suitable unto this day and place are sung, and readings likewise are read (the Ninth Hour). And when the ninth hour arriveth, they proceed with hymns unto the Imbomon, that is to say, unto that place (of the Mount of Olives) from which the Lord ascended into heaven, and where all sit down (for the readings), for all the people, in the presence of the bishop, receive an invitation to sit, and only the deacons ever stand. There also hymns and antiphons suitable unto the > place and day are sung, and readings and prayers are likewise inserted. And when the eleventh hour arriveth, there is read that passage from the Gospel where the children with branches and palms met the Lord, saying: **'Blessed is He that cometh in the name of the Lord'** (*Blagosloven gryadyy vo imya Gospodne*) (Vespers). And immediately the bishop and all the people arise, and then from the summit of the Mount of Olives all proceed (a procession / lity) on foot. And all the people go before him with hymnody and antiphons, continually responding: **'Blessed is He that cometh in the name of the Lord.'** And all the children, as many as there be in these places, even those that cannot walk because they are very tender, and whom their parents carry in their arms, all hold branches—some of palms, others of olives; and thus they escort the bishop, singing refrains, and they go slowly that the people may not grow weary; therefore already in the evening they arrive at the Anastasis. And when they arrive thither, even though it be quite late, Vespers is celebrated; then a prayer (litany) is said at the Cross, and the people are dismissed." [^1309]

Thus the ancient custom of the Procession on the Foal of an Ass on Palm Sunday and our present universal custom of using (and blessing) palms and willow branches on this Sunday received their beginning in the Jerusalem Church. [^1310]

### The First Days of Holy Week

The first three days of Holy Week in the Jerusalem Church were distinguished by an exceptionally solemn service of the Ninth Hour. It was celebrated in the Martyrium (and not in the Church of the Anastasis), where in general more solemn services were celebrated (for example, the Liturgy on Sundays), and continued from the 9th hour until the 1st hour of the night (= from 3:00 PM unto 8:00 PM). Besides hymns and antiphons there were readings at it suitable unto the day and place, alternating continually with prayers. After the Ninth Hour, Vespers was celebrated, which concluded already at night and ended with a litany (consisting, as customarily, of hymnody, prayer, and the blessing of the catechumens and faithful) of the bishop into *(Orig. p. 253)* the Church of the Anastasis. [^1311] On Great Tuesday and Wednesday this solemn evening service received yet a new addition: another litany (of the same structure)—on Tuesday unto the Mount of Olives, unto the aforementioned cave (where the Lord taught the disciples), and on Wednesday unto the cave of the Church of the Anastasis; at this litany the Gospel was read: on Tuesday from St. Matthew, the discourse of the Saviour concerning the signs of the Second Coming (**"Take heed that no man deceive you"** [*Blyudite, da nikto zhe vas prel'stit*]), doubtless delivered on Tuesday from the Mount of Olives; and on Wednesday the Gospel concerning the betrayal of Judas, which, the pilgrim lady remarketh, was listened to with affecting cries and groans. [^1312] These Gospel readings are assigned unto those same days of Holy Week by our *Typikon* as well.

### Great and Holy Thursday

Great and Holy Thursday was regarded as a festal day of Holy Week. The canon of the Council of Laodicea: "during the Forty-Day Fast, in the final week, one ought not to dissolve (*λύειν*, that is to say, from the fast) Thursday (*τὴν πέμπτην*), and thereby dishonor the entire Forty-Day Fast, but one ought to fast throughout the entire Forty-Day Fast and be content with xerophagy," [^1313] demonstrateth that there was an opposite custom, and at least from xerophagy they relaxed on Great Thursday. In the Calendar of Polemius Silvius, Bishop of Sion in northern Italy (435–455 AD), [^1314] on March 24 there is indicated *Natalis calicis*—the commemoration of the Chalice (the day of Christ's death was assigned unto March 25, and of the Resurrection unto March 27). In monuments of the VI and VII centuries this day is directly styled a feast (*solemnitas*, *festum*). [^1315] On this day the Liturgy was to bear an especially solemn character; it was celebrated late in the evening (in imitation of the Saviour), and in certain places in addition also in the morning. Blessed Augustine, in reply unto the question of Januarius: "whether to celebrate the offering (the Eucharist) on Great Thursday in the morning, and then again after dinner? To fast and after the Eucharist to dine, as we customarily do?" writeth:

> "Unto certain ones there is exceedingly pleasing a certain plausible reason for this: that on one determinate day of the year, whereon the Lord delivered the Supper, it is permissible as if by a special commemoration to celebrate the Eucharist and receive the Body and Blood of the Lord after the taking of food. Yet I account it more fitting to celebrate it at such an hour that those who have fasted may approach unto the offering, but after the refection which takes place at the ninth hour. By this we compel no one on the day of the Lord's Supper to breakfast, yet neither do we dispute with any; in general I do not criticize this practice, declaring only that the majority or almost all in most places are accustomed on this *(Orig. p. 254)* day (only) to dine (*coenare*); and since certain ones observe also the fast, in the morning the offering of Christ is celebrated on account of those who breakfast, since they cannot endure at once both fasting and the bath, and in the evening on account of those who fast." [^1316]

Blessed Augustine, thus, noteth a twofold practice: on Great Thursday some celebrated the Liturgy in the morning as well, so that there might be possible was breakfast (the dissolution of the fast), and in the evening (in commemoration of the Supper of Christ); others only in the evening; yet of these latter—some before the taking of food, others after taking it. Blessed Augustine inclines toward the latter practice. And the Council of Carthage of 419 AD permits on Great and Holy Thursday the celebration of the Liturgy after the taking of food. [^1317]

Two Liturgies were celebrated on Great and Holy Thursday in the Jerusalem Church as well, which for this day had elaborated a very complex ritual. Matins, the Third and Sixth Hours here were served in the Church of the Anastasis in the customary manner, while the Liturgy was celebrated (by whom is not stated) first in the Martyrium from the eighth unto the ninth hour (= 2–3 o'clock in the afternoon), and then

> "he (the bishop?) goes behind the Cross; [^1318] there only a single hymn is sung, a prayer is pronounced, the bishop makes the offering there, and all receive Communion; with the exception of this single day, throughout the entire year the Liturgy is never celebrated behind the Cross, save only on this day. Thus, following the dismissal there, they go into the Anastasis (a litany); a prayer is pronounced, the catechumens are blessed according unto custom, then the faithful, and the dismissal takes place. And then everyone hastens to return unto his own house to partake of food, because immediately after food all go unto the Mount of Olives, unto that church wherein is the cave in which the Lord was on this day with the apostles. And there, until approximately the first hour (7 o'clock in the evening), hymns or antiphons suited unto the day and the place are continually sung, and readings are also read; they alternate with prayers; passages from the Gospel are likewise read wherein the Lord conversed with the disciples on this day, seated in that cave which is located in the church. And thence, at approximately the sixth hour of the night (12 o'clock midnight), with hymns they ascend unto the Imbomon, unto that place from which the Lord ascended into heaven. And there again in like manner there are readings, hymns, and antiphons suited unto the day; prayers are likewise pronounced, which the bishop reads, reading ever such as are adapted unto the day and the place. At the first crowing of the cocks (2 o'clock in the night) they descend with hymns from the Imbomon and arrive at that place where the Lord prayed, as it is written in the Gospel: **'And He was withdrawn from them about a stone's cast, and kneeled down, and prayed'** (*i Sam otstupi ot nikh yako verzheniye kamene, i molyashesya*) and the rest [Luke 22:41]. At this place there is an elegant church: into it enter the bishop and all the people; there is pronounced here a prayer suited unto the place and the day; yet another hymn is sung, and the corresponding passage from the Gospel is read where He said unto His disciples: **'Watch and pray, that ye enter not into temptation'** (*bdite, da ne vnidite v napast'*) [Matt. 26:41] > (the Gethsemane prayer). And the entire passage is read through there, and again a prayer is pronounced. Thence likewise all, even the young children, descend with hymns into Gethsemane; on account of so great a multitude of the crowd, *(Orig. p. 255)* exhaustion from the vigils, and fatigue from the daily fasts, being obliged to descend from so high a mountain, they proceed unto Gethsemane amidst hymns very slowly. And an abundance of church candles and lanterns is prepared to provide light for all the people. And when they arrive at Gethsemane, first a suitable prayer is pronounced, then a hymn is sung, and that passage from the Gospel is read where the Lord was taken. And when this passage is read, all the people with weeping raise such an outcry and lamentation that perchance this groaning of all the people is heard in the city. Following this hour they go with hymns on foot into the city; they arrive at the gates at the hour when man begins to recognize man; then they pass through the midst of the entire city, all to a man—elders and youth, the wealthy, all assembled here, and especially on this day no one withdraws from the vigil until morning. In this manner they escort the bishop from Gethsemane unto the gates, and thence through the whole city unto the Cross. And when they arrive at the Cross, daylight is already beginning to appear. Here again that passage from the Gospel is read where the Lord is brought unto Pilate; everything is read which, as is written, Pilate spoke unto the Lord and unto the Jews. Then the bishop addresses a discourse unto the people, encouraging them—since they have labored the entire night and must yet labor during the day—that they should not grow weary, but should place their hope in the Lord, Who for this labor will render a great reward. And having encouraged them as best he can, he, addressing the people, says: 'Go for the present each unto his own house, sit down a little while, and around the second hour be ready here, in order to be able from that hour until the sixth to behold the Holy Wood of the Cross, each believing that it will profit him unto his salvation. From the sixth hour (12 o'clock noon) it is necessary for us all to assemble in this place, that is to say, before the Cross, in order to labor in readings and prayers until nightfall.'" [^1319]

Thus our present Rite of the Holy Passion arose in the Jerusalem Church already in this epoch: at the vigil continuing from Thursday evening until Friday morning, in the intervals between hymns and prayers there was a series of Gospel readings, and precisely concerning those events which took place with the Saviour at those hours when the readings take place and in those places whither the service of the vigil is transferred in solemn litany; and the litany halted and the Gospel was read at five stations: in the cave on the Mount of Olives (the beginning of the vigil), at the Imbomon (that is to say, the place of the Ascension), at the site of the Gethsemane prayer, at the place of the taking of the Lord by the soldiers, and upon Golgotha.

Unto Great and Holy Thursday there was likewise assigned in certain places the most solemn act among those preparatory unto baptism—the recitation of the Creed (*redditio symboli*). According unto the decree of the Council of Laodicea, 'those being baptized must learn the Creed and on Thursday of the Great Week recite (*ἀπαγγέλλειν*) [it] unto the bishop or unto the presbyters'; [^1320] in Constantinople the recitation of the Creed was assigned unto this day only by Patriarch Timothy (511–518 AD), according unto the testimony of Theodore the Lector (VI century); [^1321] yet in Rome this was done on Great and Holy Saturday. [^1322] *(Orig. p. 256)*

### Great and Holy Friday

Great and Holy Friday was the day of the most rigorous fast and sorrow: 'a day of bitterness (*amaritudinis*), on which we fast.' [^1323] The *Apostolic Constitutions* enjoin those who are able to spend it in absolute fasting, without food. [^1324] Pope Innocent I (402–417 AD) states: 'It is well known that the apostles during these two days (Great Friday and Saturday) were in sorrow and were hiding for fear of the Jews, and it is indubitable that they fasted on these days, so that ecclesiastical tradition likewise requires that the Mysteries, that is to say, the Liturgy, should not be celebrated at all on these days.' [^1325] Neither was there any Liturgy on this day in the Jerusalem Church, where divine worship on this day consisted of: (a) the veneration of the Wood of the Cross of the Lord, discovered under Constantine the Great, and the kissing thereof, which took place from the second until the sixth hour of the day (7 o'clock in the morning until 12 noon); (b) a service resembling in composition our Royal Hours—from the sixth until the ninth hour (= from 12 noon until 3 o'clock in the afternoon); and (c) the customary Great Lenten Ninth Hour and Vespers (from 3 o'clock in the afternoon). Thus the entire day was spent, as was also the whole preceding night, in divine service. Here is its description by the pilgrim lady:

> 'After the dismissal (of the Vigil of the Passion) at the Cross, before the rising of the sun, all go forth immediately with zeal unto Sion to pray at that column at which they scourged the Lord. Returning thence, they sit down for a little while in their own homes, and immediately all are ready. Then upon Golgotha, behind the Cross, a cathedra is placed for the bishop, which stands there now; upon this cathedra the bishop seats himself; a table covered with a linen cloth is placed before him, around the table stand the deacons, and there is brought a gilded silver reliquary casket in which is the Holy Wood of the Cross; it is opened and taken forth; there is laid upon the table both the Wood of the Cross and > the title inscription (*titulus*). And so, when this has been placed upon the table, the bishop sitting holds with his hands the extremities of the Sacred Wood, while the deacons, standing around, keep guard. It is guarded in this manner because there exists a custom according unto which all the people, approaching one by one, both the faithful and the catechumens, bow down before the table, kiss the Sacred Wood, and then pass on. And since, as they relate, I know not when, someone bit off and stole a particle of the Sacred Wood, on that account now the deacons standing around keep watch, lest anyone among those approaching should dare to do the like. And thus all the people pass by one by one, all bowing down and touching the Cross and the title inscription first with the forehead, and then with the eyes; then, having kissed the Cross, they pass on; but no one stretches out his hand to touch it. And when all have kissed the Cross and passed by, a deacon stands holding the ring of Solomon and that horn from which the kings were anointed; they kiss and venerate the horn and the ring... (lacuna) save the second... (lacuna) until the sixth hour all the people pass by, entering through one door and going forth through another, because this takes place in that place where on the eve, that is to say, on Thursday, the Liturgy was celebrated. And when the sixth hour arrives (12 o'clock noon), they proceed unto the Cross, whether there be rain or heat, because this place is not covered and rep-*(Orig. p. 257)*-resents as it were an exceedingly spacious and beautiful courtyard situated between the Cross and the Anastasis; there all the people assemble, so that it is impossible to open the lattice screen. A cathedra is placed for the bishop before the Cross, and from the sixth until the ninth hour nothing takes place save readings, in the following order: first there is read from the Psalms where the sufferings of the Lord are spoken of; passages are read from the Apostle, whether from the apostolic Epistles or from the Acts, where they speak of the sufferings of the Lord, as also from the Gospels the passages where He suffers; in like manner (*item*) there is read both from the Prophets where they say that the Lord will suffer, and from the Gospels where the sufferings are narrated. Thus, from the sixth hour until the ninth hour (3 o'clock in the afternoon) continually in such order readings take place and hymns are sung, in order to show unto all the people that everything foretold by the Prophets concerning the sufferings of the Lord is proved, both through the Gospels and through the writings of the Apostles, to have been accomplished. Thus, during the space of these three hours all the people are instructed that nothing came to pass that had not been foretold, nothing that had not > been entirely fulfilled. With the readings there continually alternate prayers which are adapted unto the day, and at every reading and prayer there is such sorrow and such groaning among all the people as to elicit wonder, for there is no one, neither old nor young, who on this day, during these three hours, does not weep so much as cannot even be imagined, contemplating that which the Lord endured for our sake. Following this, at the beginning of the ninth hour, that passage is read from the Gospel according unto John where He gave up the ghost; upon the reading of this, there is a prayer and a dismissal. And after the dismissal before the Cross, immediately all assemble in the great church, in the Martyrium; there is performed everything that throughout the entire week was performed from the ninth hour, when they assemble in the Martyrium, until evening (Vespers). But upon the dismissal in the Martyrium, they proceed (a litany) into the Anastasis, and when they arrive thither, that passage is read from the Gospel where Joseph asks of Pilate the Body of the Lord and lays It in a new tomb. Upon the reading of this, a prayer is pronounced, the catechumens are blessed, and then the dismissal takes place. On this day no announcement is made of a vigil in the Anastasis, because it is known that the people are exhausted; yet there is a custom of keeping vigil there; thus whoever among the people desires and is able keeps vigil, while he that is unable does not keep vigil there until morning; but of the clerics those keep vigil there who are stronger and younger, and throughout the whole night hymns and antiphons are sung there even until morning. The greater part of the people keep vigil, some from evening, others from midnight.'" [^1326]

### Great and Holy Saturday

Great and Holy Saturday in the *Apostolic Constitutions* is accounted an even more rigorous fast than Friday: unto those unable to remain without food during these two days together it is enjoined to fast in this manner at least on Saturday. [^1327] Whereas customarily the fast concluded in the evening or at the ninth hour, the fast of Great and Holy Saturday concluded at midnight or even on the following morning (on Sunday). [^1328] On Great and Holy Saturday *(Orig. p. 258)* the baptism of catechumens was administered, but it took place already at the nocturnal vigil from Saturday unto Pascha, and therefore pertained unto the divine worship of Pascha. Consequently, nothing in divine worship disturbed the strict and austere fast of this day, which was not mitigated by the proximity of the great festival. Even in the Jerusalem Church the divine service of this day was distinguished by simplicity and was the ordinary fasting office. First of all, the vigil here preceding this day, as we have just seen, was not obligatory, and not everyone came unto it in the evening, others only from midnight. Besides this vigil or—what in this case is the same thing—Matins, on Great and Holy Saturday in the Jerusalem Church there were celebrated only the Third and Sixth Hours: 'at the third hour, likewise at the sixth hour, it is done (*fit*) according unto custom,' remarks the pilgrim lady; 'at the ninth hour, however, there is no (service) on Saturday, but the Paschal Vigil is prepared in the great church, that is to say, in the Martyrium.' [^1329] Consequently, on Great and Holy Saturday in the Jerusalem Church there was not only no Liturgy (on account of the fast), but neither was there the Ninth Hour or Vespers (in view of the vigil). Neither was there on this day any Liturgy in the Roman Church, according unto the witness of Pope Innocent. [^1330]

### Pascha

With regard unto Pascha the present epoch was characterized first of all by the almost definitive resolution of the question concerning the time of its celebration. Unto what sharpness the controversies concerning this arrived in the IV century is evident from the fact that, by the admission of contemporaries, they agitated the Church no less than the great Christological question of that day, [^1331] while in the expression of Socrates, Christians, although on account of this 'did not sever communion, yet by reason of the discord conducted this festival more sorrowfully.' [^1332] The Nicene Ecumenical Council, according unto the testimony of Sozomen, was convoked as much for the resolution of this liturgical dispute as on account of the Arian heresy. [^1333] In its epistle unto the Alexandrian Church the Nicene Council, following upon its discussion concerning Arius and the Melitian schism, writes:

> 'We inform you that through your prayers the matter has been resolved concerning the concordant celebration of Pascha likewise, so that all the Eastern brethren who formerly celebrated Pascha together with the Jews shall henceforth celebrate it in agreement with the Romans, with us, and with all who from ancient times observe it after our manner.' [^1334]

Emperor Constantine, moreover, dispatched a special epistle unto the churches concerning this enactment of the Council, wherein he says that at the Council 'it was deemed good for all and everywhere to celebrate Pascha on one and the same day,' not together with the Jews, who are guilty of the murder of the Lord and of patricide, so as not to be obligated unto them even in this, all the *(Orig. p. 259)* more so since they err in this also, inasmuch as sometimes they happen to have two Paschas in a single year—and above all, so that there might be no discord concerning such a 'feast of faith,' regarding the time whereof concord already reigned among Rome, Italy, Africa, Egypt, Spain, Gaul, Britain, Libya, and the whole of Greece. [^1335] How the aforesaid countries determined the day of Pascha is indicated neither by the Council in its epistle nor by the Emperor. On this point certain light is shed by the following testimonies: the rule of the holy Apostles: **'If any bishop, presbyter, or deacon shall celebrate the holy day of Pascha before the vernal equinox with the Jews, let him be deposed from the sacred order'** (*ashche kto yepiskop ili presviter ili diakon sv. den' Paskhi prezhde vesennyago ravnodenstviya s iudeyami praznovati budet, da budet izverzhen svyashchennago china*); [^1336] and the injunction of the *Apostolic Constitutions*:

> 'With accuracy observe the return of the vernal equinox, which occurs on the twenty-second day of the month of Dystros (March), observing until the twenty-first moon, lest the fourteenth day of the moon should fall into any other week (that is to say, lest the fourteenth of Nisan should fall prior unto the vernal equinox occurring on the twenty-second of Dystros) and lest ye celebrate the Resurrection of the Lord on any other day than the Lord's Day (Sunday).' [^1337]

The distinction between the universal practice in the celebration of Pascha and the local practice against which the Nicene Council contends, therefore, lay in this: that the latter did not harmonize the lunar year with the solar year, [^1338] by virtue whereof Pascha could turn out to fall prior unto the vernal equinox and not upon a Sunday. The Council doubtless demanded the celebration of Pascha upon the first Sunday following this equinox. Concerning the day of Pascha the bishops of the principal cities made annual announcements through special encyclical epistles. There has been preserved a series of such 'Festal Epistles' (*Paschal Epistles*) from St. Athanasius of Alexandria. In one of them the limits of the Paschal cycle are indicated:

> 'The Romans maintain that they possess a tradition from the Apostle Peter forbidding Pascha to transgress the limits on the one hand *(Orig. p. 260)* of the twenty-sixth of Pharmouthi (the Egyptian month corresponding unto April, doubtless = April 23), and on the other of the thirtieth of Phamenoth (doubtless March 26).' [^1339]

The conception of the festival of Pascha among the writers of this epoch is higher than in the III century. [^1340] St. Gregory the Theologian styles it 'the queen of days, the feast of feasts and triumph of triumphs, surpassing, as the sun surpasses the stars, not only all human and earthly festivals, but even the festivals in honor of Christ,' and St. John Chrysostom 'the longed-for and saving feast.' [^1341] Among the emperors there was a custom, unto which Valentinian I gave beginning in 367 AD, of releasing on the day of Pascha (by a special edict, termed *indulgentia paschalis*) those imprisoned in jail, except for heinous criminals and recidivists. [^1342]

An indispensable attribute of Pascha was accounted, as in the III century, the vigil in the night thereof. According unto St. Epiphanius of Cyprus, 'vigils until dawn (*ἀγρυπνοῦσι... ἐπιφώσκουσαν*) [al. *ἀγροπνοῦσι... ἐπεφώσκουσαν*] in certain places are celebrated only from (Great) Thursday unto Friday and on the eve of the Sunday (of Pascha).' [^1343] According unto the narrative of Socrates, when the Novatians, adherents of Sabbatius, who had begun to celebrate Pascha with the Jews, on Pascha 'were celebrating their customary all-night vigil (*παννυχίδα*), a kind of demonic panic seized them (before an imaginary assault on the part of the bishop from whom Sabbatius had separated), and they by night, shut up in a narrow space, began so to crush one another that upward of seventy persons perished.' [^1344] Lactantius and Blessed Jerome point out as the foundation for the Paschal Vigil the expectation of the Second Coming precisely in the Paschal night. [^1345]

> 'This is the night wherein a vigil is celebrated among us in view of (*propter*) the coming of our King and God; the significance (*ratio*) of this night is twofold—that in it He received life when He suffered, and thereafter will receive the kingdom over the universe.' [^1346]

> 'Among the Jews there is a tradition that Christ (the Messiah) will come at midnight, in like manner as in the days of the Egyptians, when the Passover was celebrated and the destroyer came, and the Lord passed over the dwellings, and by the blood of the lamb the lintels of our doorposts (*frontium*) were consecrated. For this reason I hold that it is an apostolic tradition—on the day of the Paschal Vigil before midnight not to dismiss the people awaiting the coming of Christ, and only when this hour has passed, having secured safety, let all celebrate the festival.' [^1347]

As in the III century, the focus of the Paschal Vigil was the baptism of catechumens. St. John Chrysostom and his biographer Palladius, Bishop of Helenopolis, describing the barbarian assault upon the basilica during the Paschal divine service for the arrest of St. Chrysostom, recount among other cruelties of the soldiers also *(Orig. p. 261)* this: that they forced women who had already undressed for baptism to flee naked, and with the blood from their wounds stained the water in the baptisteries; nevertheless in that night approximately three thousand persons were baptized. [^1348] In general the ritual of the Paschal divine worship remained the same as in the III century; as we have seen, in the *Apostolic Constitutions* the Paschal Vigil is described [^1349] very closely unto the Syriac *Didascalia* and consists, as there, of 'prayers and supplications' (= Matins), 'readings of the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms' (= the Liturgy of the Catechumens), and the baptism of the catechumens, all of which took place 'until the crowing of the cocks'; then, 'following the reading of the Gospel (doubtless concerning the Resurrection of Christ) and the corresponding discourse,' with a prayer for the conversion of Israel, the vigil, and with it the Paschal fast, concluded, and there doubtless followed the Eucharist with the agape. Such approximately was the composition of the Paschal Vigil in other places as well, as is shown by the description of the Aquitanian pilgrim lady:

> 'In Jerusalem,' says she, 'the Paschal Vigil is celebrated in the same manner as among us; only here there is added furthermore this: the children who have received baptism, clothed as they came forth from the font, are conducted together with the bishop into the (church of the) Anastasis. The bishop goes behind the lattice screen into the Anastasis (into the sanctuary, into the cave of the Lord's Sepulchre); a single hymn is sung; then the bishop pronounces a prayer for them, and thereafter goes with them into the great church (the Martyrium), where according unto custom all the people are keeping vigil (*vigilat*); there is performed that which customarily takes place among us also (the Paschal Vigil and the Liturgy continue), and upon the completion of the oblation the dismissal takes place. And following the dismissal of the vigil in the great church, immediately with hymns they proceed into the Anastasis, and there again a passage from the Gospel concerning the Resurrection is read; a prayer takes place, and again (*denuo*) [al. *demuo*] there the bishop makes the offering (the Liturgy; two Liturgies, as also on Great and Holy Thursday), but more expeditiously (*totum ad momentum*), in order not to detain the people; and only then are the people dismissed. The dismissal of the vigil on this day takes place at the same hour as among us.' [^1350]

The Paschal Vigil was distinguished by an exceptional abundance of illumination. According unto the narrative of Eusebius, Emperor Constantine the Great, during the days of the 'saving festival, intensifying his pious activity, celebrated the divine triumph with all the strength of his soul and body, and ordered the celebration in this manner: the sacred night spent in vigil he transformed into the light of day, for persons appointed thereunto throughout the entire city kindled tall columns of wax, like fiery lamps illuminating every place, so that this mystical night became brighter than the brightest day.' [^1351] St. Gregory the Theologian on Pascha spoke: 'Splendid was our torch-bearing and procession of lights yesterday (*λαμποφορία καὶ φωταγωγία*) [al. *φωταγογία*], which we celebrated both privately and publicly, almost the entire human race and every rank of dignity (*ἀξία πᾶσα*) [al. *ἀγία πᾶσα*], illuminating the night with abundant fire, an image of the Great Light... But today's (light) is more glorious and more excellent: for yesterday's light was the herald of the rising *(Orig. p. 262)* Great Light and as it were a joyful forefeast thereof; today, however, we celebrate the Resurrection itself, not as yet expected, but already accomplished and having gathered unto itself the whole universe.' [^1352] These last words show that the feast of Pascha itself was reckoned from morning, with the relaxation of the fast upon the conclusion of the vigil.

### Bright Week (The Paschal Week)

Now for the first time the celebration of Pascha was extended from a single day unto an entire week, in correspondence unto the week of the Passion of the Lord. St. John Chrysostom preached daily throughout this week: 'Throughout the course of the seven subsequent days we hold assemblies and set before you a spiritual table'; 'seven of these days together all enjoyed instruction at the assemblies.' [^1353] 'Throughout the entire Great Week and in that following upon it let not slaves labor, because the former is the week of the Passion, and this latter of the Resurrection, and it is necessary to receive instruction.' [^1354] Emperor Theodosius the Great prohibited judicial proceedings throughout the entire Paschal week, [^1355] and Theodosius the Younger banned theatrical and circus spectacles. [^1356] Blessed Augustine styles these days 'the eight days of the neophytes' (the newly baptized). [^1357] In the Jerusalem Church, says the Aquitanian pilgrim lady, 'the Paschal days are observed (*attenduntur*) as among us, and according unto their order there are masses (*missae*) for eight days; the decoration and arrangement here are the same (*hic autem ipse ornatus est et ipsa compositio*) during the eight days of Pascha as at Theophany—both in the great church, and in the Anastasis, and at the Cross, and in Bethlehem, as also at the tomb of Lazarus.' [^1358] The most solemn services were (in the Jerusalem Church) on the first three days of Pascha and on the eighth, judging from the fact that on these days the service was in the Martyrium (the great church), whence the litany proceeded into the Anastasis; on the remaining days they served in turn in the other churches: on Wednesday on the Mount of Olives, on Thursday in the Anastasis, on Friday on Sion, on Saturday at the Cross. Daily in the afternoon there was a litany with the participation of the newly baptized children and the monks (*apotaktites*) unto the Mount of Olives, upon which 'hymns and prayers were performed' (doubtless Vespers or an office in place thereof) in two places: in the cave and on the Imbomon, whence the Litiya proceeded into the Church of the Anastasis already 'at the hour of the lighting of the lamps (*lucernae*).' On the first day of Pascha and on the eighth (= Thomas Sunday) this solemn afternoon service or Vespers, celebrated in three places, received a special addition—a litany upon Sion, where true Vespers was celebrated (likewise, indeed, not so called, yet more resembling Vespers than the described afternoon office): hymns adapted unto the day were sung, a prayer was pronounced, and the Gospel concerning Thomas was read (that is to say, concerning the event which took place precisely at the site of the service), moreover on the first day of Pascha *(Orig. p. 263)* only as far as the words **'I will not believe'** (*ne imu very*) [John 20:25], and on the eighth 'the entire reading' (precisely as among us at present); then there were prayers over the faithful and the catechumens. The service concluded at the second hour of the night (= 7 o'clock in the evening).

### Thomas Sunday

The Sunday following upon Pascha was likewise marked by a special celebration in other churches. In St. Gregory the Theologian, St. John Chrysostom, and Blessed Augustine there are discourses and homilies upon this day; in the first two they are inscribed: 'Upon the New Sunday' (*καινὴ* or *διακαινήσιμος*), and in the latter 'Upon White Sunday' (*dominica in albis*). It is unknown whether these inscriptions belong unto the authors themselves, and whether in this epoch there arose the custom which gave occasion unto the latter appellation—namely, that the newly baptized (*neophytes*) from this Sunday exchanged the white garments placed upon them at baptism for ordinary attire. [^1359]

### The Ascension

Upon the Ascension the earliest homilies are in St. Gregory of Nyssa and St. John Chrysostom. Blessed Augustine testifieth that the festival is honored everywhere, and Socrates styleth it a 'universal (*πάνδημος*) festival.' [^1360] The *Apostolic Constitutions* designate the Ascension as a festival free from labor. [^1361] Unto the establishment of the festival the erection by Empress Helena upon the Mount of Olives of a magnificent basilica [^1362] (destroyed by the Saracens) could have contributed; besides it, upon the very place of the Ascension there was a church [^1363] (which existeth even now). Yet it is remarkable that upon the Mount of Olives, judging from the description of the Aquitanian pilgrim lady, no service was celebrated upon this festival, which by the pilgrim lady is not even styled 'the Ascension,' but 'the 40th day following upon Pascha.' In anticipation of this day, already upon Wednesday in the Bethlehem cave of the Nativity of Christ there was a vigil, unto which they proceeded from Jerusalem 'after the sixth hour' (= 12 o'clock midday); upon the following day in this same place there was a Liturgy with appropriate homilies by the presbyters and the bishop, so that they returned unto Jerusalem late. [^1364]

### Pentecost

By Pentecost, as also in the III century, was accounted either the fifty-day period from Pascha, or the concluding day thereof, the Day of Pentecost. Pentecost in the sense of a period was a season of unceasing festival and joy. [^1365] Therefore during this period, as also upon Sundays, fasting and kneeling at prayer were prohibited: [^1366] 'Throughout all the fifty days of Pentecost neither doth genuflection take place, nor is fasting enjoined *(Orig. p. 264)* (*οὔτε προσετάκται* [al. *προστέτακται*]).' [^1367] Yet this custom did not as yet possess universal dissemination. 'Since there are certain persons who bend the knee upon the Lord's Day and during the days of Pentecost, therefore, in order that all things may be observed uniformly across all dioceses, it hath seemed good unto the Holy Council that prayers be offered unto God standing.' [^1368] Blessed Augustine saith: 'I know not whether it be observed everywhere that one prayeth standing during these days (of Pentecost) and upon all Sundays.' [^1369] According unto the testimony of St. John Cassian, in Egypt 'throughout all the days of Pentecost no one whatsoever bendeth the knee or observeth a fast until the ninth hour,' yet Cassian had not seen 'that this was observed with such strictness in Syrian monasteries'; and in Egyptian monasteries the abolition of fasting during Pentecost was expressed only in this: that 'food was partaken of at the sixth hour (= 12 o'clock midday) instead of the ninth hour, while the quantity and quality thereof were not altered.' [^1370] According unto the words of the Aquitanian pilgrim lady, in Jerusalem 'from Pascha unto Pentecost absolutely no one fasteth, not even the *apotaktites* (monks)'; yet the service there during Pentecost did not differ from the customary non-fasting office, except on Wednesday and Friday, when the stational procession (*proceditur*) [al. *oriceditur*] customary upon these days unto Sion was performed in the morning, since there was no fast; and there took place 'a Mass (Liturgy?) according unto its order.' [^1371]

Pentecost in the strict sense was accounted a festival solely in honor of the Holy Spirit. 'Honor the Day of the Spirit,' exhorteth St. Gregory the Theologian in his oration upon this festival. [^1372] Perhaps in view of this and by virtue of the connection between baptism and chrismation there existed the custom, mentioned already in the III century by Tertullian, [^1373] of administering baptism at Pentecost. In Blessed Augustine there is an address upon Pentecost unto the newly baptized, wherein he saith unto them, among other things: 'That which you see taking place here before you upon the altar of God, you have already seen also in the preceding night'; [^1374] consequently, in the night preceding the festival there was a vigil at which baptism was administered. Emperor Theodosius the Younger prohibiteth theatrical spectacles 'at Pascha and Pentecost, so long as the white baptismal garments are worn and the commemoration of the apostolic suffering (the Acts of the Apostles) is read.' [^1375] In the Jerusalem Church Pentecost possessed, according unto the description of the Aquitanian pilgrim lady, an eminent divine service as well. On this day, saith the pilgrim lady, 'there is great labor for the people.' The festival openeth, however, with the customary Sunday Matins with the identical Gospel in the Church of the Anastasis, beginning, as doth daily Matins, from the crowing of the cocks. With the advent of morning in the Martyrium the Liturgy is celebrated with homilies by the presbyters and the bishop; *(Orig. p. 265)* by reason of the impending stational processions the dismissal is hastened and takes place before the third hour (= 9 o'clock in the morning). Immediately following upon the dismissal the people escort the bishop with hymnody unto Sion, where in the church upon the place of the descent of the Holy Spirit the passage from the Acts of the Apostles concerning this event is read, and homilies are delivered by the presbyters upon the same theme; 'then according unto its order the Mass takes place, and an offering is made here also (*offertur*—the Liturgy).' The people are dismissed for the midday meal. Following upon the meal divine worship takes place upon the Mount of Olives—namely, first of all Vespers (though not so named) upon the Imbomon (the place of the Ascension):

> 'There sit down [^1376] the bishop, the presbyters, and all the people; readings take place, and interspersed there are sung hymns and antiphons suited unto the day and place; the prayers which are inserted always possess such content as fitteth the day and place (concerning the descent of the Holy Spirit); that passage from the Gospel is likewise read wherein the ascension of the Lord into heaven following upon the Resurrection is recounted; [^1377] upon the conclusion the catechumens are blessed, then the faithful, and they descend thence at the ninth hour and with hymns proceed unto the Eleona Church over the cave wherein the Lord sat and taught the Apostles. Upon arriving there already after the tenth hour (= 4 o'clock in the afternoon) Vespers (*lucernare*) is celebrated there; prayer is offered; the catechumens are blessed, and thereafter the faithful also (this is properly speaking only a stational litany unto the Vespers celebrated upon the Imbomon). [^1378] Thence all the people unto the last man descend with the bishop with the singing of hymns and antiphons appropriate unto this day, and proceed slowly toward the Martyrium. When they approach the city gates it is already night (after 6 o'clock in the evening), and they bring forth to meet the people a multitude of church lanterns; and since it is rather far from the gates unto the Martyrium, they arrive thither at approximately the second hour of the night (= 7 o'clock in the evening), for they proceed slowly and that entirely for the sake of the people, lest they become exhausted. All the people with the bishop enter with hymns into the Martyrium through the great doors which open from the side of the public square. Upon entering into the church, hymns are sung, prayers are pronounced, the catechumens are blessed, and after them the faithful (the second stational litany unto the Vespers begun upon the Imbomon). And thence once again with hymns they proceed into the Anastasis; and when they arrive in the Anastasis, in like manner hymns and antiphons are sung, prayer is pronounced, the catechumens are blessed, and after them the faithful (the third stational litany unto the same Vespers). The like is performed at the Cross (the fourth stational litany). And thence once again the entire Christian populace unto a single man escort the bishop with hymns unto *(Orig. p. 266)* Sion; when they arrive thither there take place appropriate readings, psalms and antiphons are sung, prayer is offered, the catechumens are blessed, after them the faithful, and the dismissal takes place (the fifth stational litany, the most solemn, with readings—that is to say, doubtless an entire Vespers). Following upon the dismissal all approach the hand of the bishop, and then each returneth unto his own home at approximately midnight.' [^1379]

Thus the divine service of Pentecost in the Jerusalem Church of the IV century in the number of its stational processions and duration recalleth the service of Great Thursday night into Friday, save that the former occupied an entire day, whereas the latter took place at night.

### The Week of Pentecost and the Fast Thereafter

The *Apostolic Constitutions* enjoin celebrating Pentecost for an entire week. [^1380] Yet in the Jerusalem Church, according unto the words of the Aquitanian pilgrim lady, 'from the day following upon Pentecost all fast according unto custom, as throughout the entire year, each as he is able, excepting Sabbath days and Sundays'; [^1381] and the customary divine services are restored. 'Following upon it (Pentecost) fast for one week, for it is just that you should both rejoice concerning the gift of God and fast following upon the relaxation,' [^1382] enjoin the *Apostolic Constitutions*. In this manner there arose in this very epoch the beginning of the Apostles' Fast (Peter's Fast), as a solemn restoration of the customary fasts of the year following upon their fifty-day abolition.

### The Immovable Feasts

Having elaborated almost unto its present composition the cycle of the most important movable feasts, the period under consideration accomplished less for the immovable feasts; the most significant development in this latter regard was the introduction of three new festivals: the Nativity of Christ, the Meeting of the Lord, and the Exaltation of the Cross.

### The Nativity of Christ and Theophany

The festival of the Nativity of Christ became segregated from Theophany (*Epiphany*) by reason of the fact that this latter festival embraced an excessively complex series of commemorations. The destinies of these two festivals are intimately connected, and they share a common history. — Having originated in the III century, but not possessing at that time universal dissemination, [^1383] the festival of Theophany (*τὰ θεοφάνεια* or *ἐπιφάνεια*) was now introduced into the most remote lands: it is mentioned in Thrace in 304 AD, in Gaul in 362 AD, and in Spain in 380 AD; [^1384] only the Donatists in Africa rejected it as an innovation. [^1385] By a law of circa 400 AD circus performances were banned upon Theophany, yet from judicial proceedings this day was rendered exempt *(Orig. p. 267)* only under Justinian. [^1386] Yet not everywhere were identical commemorations attached unto this festival. According unto the *Apostolic Constitutions* (Syria) [^1387] and the most ancient Coptic calendar [^1388] this festival was dedicated unto the Baptism of the Lord. [^1389] Blessed Augustine in his six sermons upon this festival speaketh solely of the adoration of the Magi. [^1390] For almost the entire East until the close of the IV century, however, it was a festival in honor of the Nativity of Christ. [^1391] From the description of Theophany in Jerusalem in the Aquitanian pilgrim lady it is evident that it was a festival in honor of the Nativity of Christ. The opening of the description hath not been preserved, and the surviving portion thereof speaketh already of the return of the stational procession unto Jerusalem from Bethlehem with the chanting of **'Blessed is He that cometh in the Name of the Lord'**; the procession approached Jerusalem already before dawn; consequently, throughout the entire night preceding the festival there was a vigil in the Bethlehem church, which upon the departure of the procession was continued there by the clergy and monastics; the procession with the bishop entered into the Anastasis, 'where countless lamps were already burning; there a psalm is sung, prayer is pronounced, and first the catechumens and then the faithful receive a blessing from the bishop.' At the second hour (= 7 o'clock in the morning) the Liturgy takes place in the Martyrium with a homily and readings, and following upon it they proceed with singing into the Anastasis, and the dismissal takes place at approximately the sixth hour (= 12 o'clock midday). Vespers is the daily office. Upon the second and third days of the festival the service is likewise held (*proceditur*) in the Martyrium (upon Golgotha) of equal duration until the sixth hour and of equal joy (*laetitia*); upon the fourth day they celebrate in like manner (*celebrantur*) in the Eleona Church, upon the fifth day in the Church of Lazarus, upon the sixth on Sion, upon the seventh in the Anastasis, and upon the eighth again in the Martyrium. Throughout all these days an equally solemn service is celebrated in Bethlehem also by the local clergy and monastics resident there. The pilgrim lady noteth the lavish adornment of the churches upon this festival:
