> 'There one seeth nothing save gold, precious gems, and silk; whether thou lookest upon the vestments, they are of pure silk embroidered with gold; whether thou lookest upon the curtains, they are likewise of pure silk embroidered with gold (consequently, the temple was draped with fabrics, as is done at present in St. Peter's Basilica in Rome for solemnities); and the vessels all brought forth upon this day are of gold, embellished with gems.' [^1392]

That this festival, which the pilgrim lady in another passage styleth 'Theophany' (*epiphania*), [^1393] was dedicated unto the Nativity of Christ, was apparent from the intimate and extensive connection of the festal *(Orig. p. 268)* divine worship with Bethlehem, as well as from the fact that forty days following upon this festival the Meeting of the Lord (*Hypapante*) was commemorated. [^1394]

Not in Jerusalem alone by this epoch (the close of the IV century) had the Nativity of Christ as it were overshadowed the other commemorations associated with the festival of Theophany. Such was the case throughout the entire East. St. Epiphanius of Cyprus demonstrateth (in controversy with the Alogi) that the birth of the Saviour occurred on January 6, and His Baptism on November 8. [^1395] According unto the testimony of St. John Cassian, in Egypt under Theophany 'they understand the Baptism of the Lord and His Nativity according unto the flesh, and for this reason celebrate the solemnity of both mysteries not upon two separate days, as in western regions, but upon a single day.' [^1396] The Armenian Church even unto this day celebrateth the Nativity of Christ on January 6. Even after the East, under western influence, separated the Nativity of Christ from Theophany, men continued to apply unto the former the designation of Theophany. St. Basil the Great saith concerning the Nativity of Christ: 'Let us designate this festival of ours Theophany.' [^1397] St. Gregory the Theologian saith: 'Now we celebrate Theophany, or the feast of the Nativity.' [^1398]

Earliest of all did the festival of the Nativity of Christ separate from Theophany in the Roman Church. According unto the testimony of John, Bishop of Nicaea (IX century), based upon grounds unknown, this church began to celebrate the Nativity of Christ on December 25 under Pope Julius (337–352 AD). [^1399] In a composite calendar-chronographic monument brought down unto the year 354 AD and bearing diverse titles (*Anonymus Cuspiniani*, *Catalogus Bucherianus*, *Calendarium Furii Philocali*), [^1400] in the section *Depositio martyrum* (the demise days of the martyrs) at the eighth of the Kalends of January (= December 25) there is indicated 'the day of the birth of Christ in Bethlehem,' while in the section *Annales* there is the note: 'In the consulate of Caesar Augustus and Aemilius Paulus, Christ was born on the eighth of the Kalends of January, on a Friday, on the 15th day of the new moon.' Consequently, the Nativity of Christ in Rome came to be celebrated on December 25 prior unto 354 AD, and doubtless long before that year. Pope Liberius (352–366 AD), upon consecrating as a nun Marcellina, the sister of St. Ambrose of Milan, pointed out unto her the significance in the coincidence of this event *(Orig. p. 269)* of her life with the day of the Nativity of the Saviour from the Virgin, and in doing so mentioned the miracles of the changing of water into wine at Cana and the feeding of the four thousand. [^1401] This demonstrateth that, on the one hand, in Rome there existed already an independent festival of the Nativity of Christ not identical with Theophany (with which latter St. Hippolytus of Rome connecteth the commemoration of the Baptism alone), [^1402] while on the other hand that this festival was still associated in the consciousness of Roman Christians with Theophany (the miracle at Cana and the miracle of the feeding being Theophany commemorations). [^1403] The earliest discourse upon the Nativity of Christ *(Orig. p. 270)* among Western fathers is that of St. Zeno of Verona (†380 AD). — In the East the festival first became known in Cappadocia: unto St. Basil the Great (†379 AD) there already belongeth, as we have seen, a homily inscribed 'Upon the Holy Nativity of Christ'; it may be that unto him belongeth also the initial introduction of this festival in the East. [^1404] The friend of Basil the Great, St. Gregory the Theologian, planted the festival in Constantinople. When following upon the death of Valens and the accession unto the throne of Theodosius the Great the Orthodox in Constantinople breathed freely from Arian oppressions, they received in the person of the Isaurian solitary Gregory the Theologian, formerly Bishop of Sasima, their first bishop; his ministry he began in a private church which he named Anastasia; in it he for the first time in Constantinople in 379 AD on December 25 celebrated the feast of the Nativity of Christ. [^1405] Thus the first act of the restoration of Orthodoxy in the capital was the introduction of the new festival. The activity of St. Gregory the Theologian in Constantinople was of brief duration (until 381 AD); upon his departure his innovation could have been discontinued, and therefore it is not surprising that one account, albeit rather late (in John of Nicaea, IX century), assigneth the introduction of the feast of the Nativity of Christ in Constantinople unto the era of Emperor Arcadius (395–408 AD): Emperor Honorius, having visited his mother and brother, inclined them toward establishing this festival after the example of Rome. [^1406] In Antioch St. John Chrysostom, on the commemoration of the Martyr Chrysogonus [al. St. Philogonius] on December 20, 386 or 388 AD, [^1407] stated that on the approaching December 25 the Nativity of Christ would be celebrated here for the first time—that in the West this festival had been known from antiquity, whereas unto Antioch reports concerning it had penetrated approximately ten years previously; that he himself had long desired and even secretly prayed that this festival might be celebrated in Antioch as well. [^1408] The festival which arrived a few days thereafter gathered a multitude of people, and in his homily unto them Chrysostom again touched upon the history of the feast. He stated that concerning the festival there had been much contention in Antioch, some regarding it as an innovation, while others pointed out that it had anciently been celebrated in the West from Thrace unto Cadiz; upon three grounds Chrysostom exhorteth his hearers unto veneration of the festival: (a) by reason of the rapidity wherewith it was spreading:

> 'Although ten years have not yet elapsed since this day became known unto us, nevertheless, as if delivered unto us from antiquity and many years ago, it hath so flourished through your zeal; for even as noble plants, when planted in the earth, quickly attain unto great height and are laden with fruit, so also this day... hath suddenly so grown and brought forth so great fruit, that, as may now be seen, our court is filled, and the entire church is thronged with a multitude of people'; (b) that December 25 is the day of the Nativity of the Saviour, *(Orig. p. 271)* according unto Chrysostom, is confirmed by the documents preserved in Rome concerning the census under Augustus; (c) this is apparent also from the fact that the conception of the Saviour according unto the Evangelist Luke followed six months after the apparition of the Archangel Gabriel unto Zechariah, and this latter must have taken place in the month of Tishri (= September) upon the Day of Atonement; [^1409] and if the conception of the Saviour was in March, then His Nativity must fall in December. [^1410] — Somewhat later the new festival received recognition in two other centers of the Christianity of that epoch: Alexandria and Jerusalem. Whereas during the stay of Cassian in Egypt (circa 380 AD) there was as yet no feast of December 25 there, [^1411] in 432 AD (in the patriarchate of St. Cyril of Alexandria) in Alexandria a sermon upon the Nativity of Christ was delivered on the 29th day of the Egyptian month of Choiak (= December 25) by the visiting Bishop Paul of Emesa. [^1412] — As regards Jerusalem, where, as we have seen, the Aquitanian pilgrim lady (circa 385 AD) celebrated the Nativity of Christ on January 6, according unto the testimony of Basil of Seleucia, 'Juvenal (425–458 AD, Bishop of Jerusalem), who now occupieth the glorious and weighty throne of James, began to celebrate the day of the Nativity of the Lord.' [^1413] In accord with these trustworthy reports are in general also the later traditions, embellished in favor of the Roman Church and not free from anachronisms, [^1414] concerning the introduction of the feast of the Nativity of Christ in the East. According unto one of these traditions, Bishop Cyril of Jerusalem, according unto another, Juvenal, in an epistle unto Pope Julius complained of the inconvenience of celebrating the Nativity of Christ and the Baptism upon the same day: 'One cannot go at one and the same time unto Bethlehem and unto the Jordan,' and requested that he examine and determine the day of the Nativity of Christ; the Pope recommended the practice of his own church—the celebration of the Nativity of Christ on December 25. St. Basil the Great commissioned St. Gregory the Theologian to establish this celebration at the Council of Constantinople. St. John Chrysostom likewise gave his consent unto this. From Cyprus Epiphanius was summoned, that he, as a native Jew, might confirm the day upon the basis of the Scriptures. Patriarchs Theophilus of Alexandria and Flavian of Antioch accepted the new festival. In view of such unanimity, even heretical sects followed in this instance the Catholic Church. — Unto the majesty of the commemorated event the new festival was of course indebted for its success. Yet its introduction required no little time and did not occur without struggle. Already St. Epiphanius of Cyprus, who accounted the day of the Saviour's birth to be January 6, upon the basis of the observation of St. Luke that at His Baptism the Saviour was about thirty years of age [^1415] persistently *(Orig. p. 272)* proveth ('many times have I been compelled to say') that the Nativity of the Saviour could not have been upon the same day of the month as His Baptism [^1416]. Against this identification Chrysostom likewise objecteth: 'Not that day wherein the Saviour was born ought one to style Theophany (*ἐπιφάνεια*), but that wherein He was baptized; not following upon His birth did He become known unto all, but when He was baptized' (there followeth a citation of John 1:33); [^1417] and in passing Blessed Jerome remarketh: 'In His Nativity the Son of God appeared unto the world secretly, but in His Baptism manifestly.' [^1418] The custom of celebrating the Nativity of Christ and the Baptism upon a single day was not abandoned in certain localities in the East even in the VI century. Cosmas Indicopleustes (circa 530 AD) remarketh that whereas the Nativity of Christ is everywhere celebrated in December, the Jerusalemites alone 'by a credulous conjecture (*στοχασμοῦ*)' celebrate it together with Theophany. [^1419]

With the segregation of the Nativity of Christ into a distinct festival, in the East there remained for Theophany the sole commemoration of the Baptism. For the *Apostolic Constitutions* Theophany is a festival exclusively in honor of the Baptism. [^1420] St. Ephrem the Syrian also in his hymns upon Theophany speaketh of the Baptism of Christ and of the catechumens. [^1421] Simultaneously with the division of the festivals men in the East must have assigned the baptism of catechumens unto January 6, in connection with which there arose at this very time the custom of a special veneration of the water sanctified on this festival for the baptism of catechumens. St. John Chrysostom in his homily upon the Baptism of the Lord saith:

> 'Christ was baptized and sanctified the nature of waters, and therefore upon this festival all, having drawn water (*ὑδреυσάмеνοι*) [al. *ὑδρεσάμενοι*] at midnight, carry it home and preserve throughout the entire year the moisture (*τὰ νάματα*) from the waters sanctified today; and there occurreth a manifest sign: the nature of those waters is not corrupted by duration of time, but for an entire year, and frequently two or three years, the water drawn today remaineth incorrupt and fresh (*ἀκεραίου καὶ νεαроῦ*) [al. *ἀκερκίου καὶ νεαроῦ*], and following upon such an interval doth not yield unto waters newly drawn from a fountain.' [^1422]

### The Meeting of the Lord

The Jerusalem Church, according unto the testimony of the Gallic pilgrim lady, already in this epoch celebrated the day of the Meeting of the Lord (*Hypapante*). The festival possesseth no distinct name in the pilgrim lady, but is designated 'the 40th day from Theophany,' and her turn of phrase ('it is celebrated here with great honor') apparently makes it understood that in the homeland of the pilgrim lady this festival did not exist.

> 'Upon this day the service takes place in the Anastasis (not in the Martyrium, as upon the greatest festivals and as the Liturgy upon the Lord's Day), and all things are performed according unto order with the greatest solemnity, as if at Pascha (!); all the presbyters preach, and *(Orig. p. 273)* thereafter the bishop, expounding always upon that passage of the Gospel where upon the 40th day Joseph and Mary brought the Lord into the Temple.' [^1423]

### The Exaltation and Dedication of the Church of the Anastasis

In the same Jerusalem Church there now took its origin also the festival of the Finding (and Exaltation) of the Precious Cross, which stood in intimate connection with the festival of the Dedication of the Church of the Anastasis, even as these events themselves are directly linked one with another. Emperor Constantine, as soon as he became sole ruler, resolved to erect a church upon the Sepulchre of the Lord, which the pagans, according unto the testimony of Eusebius, had buried, leveled with the ground, and erected over it a temple of Venus; the cave of the Sepulchre was discovered deep beneath the earth, and over it a magnificent temple was constructed. [^1424] Eusebius recounteth also the visit by Constantine's mother, St. Helena, unto the holy places, and her lavish gifts unto the churches erected by her son in Bethlehem and upon the Mount of Olives. Concerning the finding of the Cross Eusebius makes no mention. Of the latter Socrates and Sozomen already speak. [^1425] According unto their narrative, they determined which was the Cross of the Lord among the three discovered by the miracle of healing wrought through laying it upon a terminally ill woman, while according unto later accounts (for example, in St. Paulinus of Nola, VI century) [^1426] by the miracle of a resurrection from the dead. Socrates erroneously placeth the finding of the Cross after the Council of Nicaea, since Helena reposed in the year of the latter; more accurately the year of the event is indicated by the Alexandrian Chronicle: the year 320; the chronographer Theophanes dateth it yet earlier. Beyond Jerusalem the festival in this epoch scarcely had any dissemination; no one mentioneth it: it could exist perhaps in churches that had received a portion of the Precious Wood (for example, in Constantinople); an ecumenical veneration it began to receive, doubtless, only upon the restitution unto Emperor Heraclius of the portion of the Wood seized by the Persian King Chosroes. The day of this latter event, May 3, came in the West to be celebrated earlier (from the VII century) than September 14. [^1427]

Understandably, in Jerusalem the day of the Finding (Exaltation) of the Cross was a supreme festival in an epoch when the memory of the event was still fresh. Here is the description of the festival in the pilgrim lady:

> 'The Day of Dedications (*Encaenia*) is the name given unto that season when the holy church upon Golgotha, which is called the Martyrium, was consecrated unto God; and the holy church in the Anastasis—that is to say, in that place where the Lord rose following upon His Passion—it also was consecrated on this day unto God. The Dedication of these holy churches is celebrated with supreme honor because on this day the Cross of the Lord was found. Therefore was it so arranged that the day of the first dedication of the aforesaid churches should be the very day when the Cross of the Lord was discovered, in order that all things together might be celebrated upon one and the same day with all joy. And in Holy Scripture we find that the day of dedication is that day when holy Solomon, upon completing the House *(Orig. p. 274)* of God which Solomon had built, stood before the altar of God and prayed, as it is written in the Books of Chronicles [Paralipomenon]. And so, when these days of dedications arrive, they are kept for eight days: many days prior, people begin to assemble from every quarter—not only of hermits or apotactites from various provinces, that is to say from Mesopotamia, and Syria, and Egypt, and the Thebaid, where there are many hermits, but likewise from all diverse places and provinces; for there is none who upon this day doth not hasten unto Jerusalem unto so great a joy and unto such venerable days; and laymen, both men and women of faithful spirit, in like manner assemble in these days from all provinces unto Jerusalem, for the sake of the holy day. In these days also there assemble in Jerusalem the bishops—when they are few—to the number of more than forty or fifty; and with them come many of the clergy. And what need is there to say more? Whoever takes no part in so great a solemnity during these days accounteth himself to have fallen into the greatest sin, unless there be some hindering necessity which keepeth a man from his good intention. In these days of dedications the adornment of all the churches is the same as that which obtaineth at Pascha and at Theophany; and each day the service is celebrated in diverse holy places even as at Pascha and at Theophany. For upon the first and second days the service is celebrated in the great church which is called the Martyrium. On the third day—upon the Mount of Olives, that is to say in the church which is upon the mount from whence the Lord ascended into heaven following upon His Passion, in which church is the cave wherein the Lord taught the Apostles upon the Mount of Olives. On the fourth day... [defect in manuscript]' [^1428]

Likewise, according unto the testimony of Sozomen, from the time of the consecration of the Martyrium under Constantine the Great, 'the Jerusalem Church celebrateth this festival annually and with exceeding solemnity, such that the mystery of baptism is then conferred and the church assemblies continue for eight days; by occasion of this solemnity there flock thither, for the visiting of the holy places, many from almost the entire inhabited world.' [^1429]

### Theotokion Feasts: The Dormition and the Annunciation

With the waning of paganism—the struggle against whose mythical elements had previously precluded dwelling upon the details of the earthly origin of the Saviour—Christianity was able to render due veneration, after Christ, unto His Mother as well. Constantine the Great erected three churches in Her honor in the new capital. In Rome, prior unto the construction of the Liberian Basilica (which until recent times was regarded as the most ancient church), there existed, as recent investigations have revealed, a church dedicated unto the Most Holy Theotokos (*Santa Maria Antiqua*). The consort of Emperor Marcian (450–457 AD), Pulcheria, erected in the Constantinopolitan suburb of Blachernae the church of the Theotokos that was subsequently to become so renowned [^1430], as well as churches unto Her of the Hodegetria and in Chalcoprateia. *(Orig. p. 275)* The Council of Ephesus (431 AD) took place in the Church of the Most Holy Mary [^1431]. Unto Her likewise was dedicated the Church of the Spoudaioi in Jerusalem [^1432]. In the encomium of Theodore upon St. Theodosius (circa 500 AD) it is stated that in the Palestinian monasteries there is celebrated annually with great solemnity the commemoration of the Theotokos (*Θεοτόκου μνήμη*) [^1433], that is to say, in all probability Her Dormition. If the homilies upon the Annunciation of Patriarch Proclus of Constantinople († 446 AD) and of Peter Chrysologus of Ravenna († 450 AD) are genuine, then in this same epoch there arose also the Feast of the Annunciation; in favor of this testifieth likewise its intimate chronological correlation with the Nativity of Christ.

### Commemorations of Martyrs

The cessation of persecutions, by relegating the martyrs into the sacred distance of the past, could not but intensify their veneration. Festivals in their honor arose all the more naturally in that their relics and sepulchres were before the eyes of all [^1434], and the exact days of their demise were known. Every local church possessed an extensive roll of martyrs, and men now began to take care to gather into a unified whole the records concerning the time and place of their suffering and to celebrate their memory without omission. In every significant church there was formed its own Menologion of saints. Its compilation was rendered all the easier by the fact that regarding many martyrs there were preserved either official judicial transcripts [^1435] of their interrogation and trial, or else records penned by Christian eyewitnesses themselves during the passion and immediately following upon the death of the martyr [^1436]. It was necessary merely to classify these materials, and this began to be done already in the III century, with the work in certain churches receiving the most painstaking and systematic execution [^1437]. In view of this, *(Orig. p. 276)* it is not surprising that in the IV century local churches came to possess Menologia of their own martyrs.

### The Ancient Menologia

#### a) The Philocalian Calendar

Originally these Menologia were appended unto pagan calendars, wherein alongside the pagan festivals there were designated the Christian solemnities; or else lists of saints venerated in a given locality were simply subjoined unto the pagan calendar by way of an appendix unto the calendar wherein the pagan festivals were recorded. Such, for example, is the calendar in the aforementioned Chronograph belonging unto Furius Dionysius Philocalus [^1438]. This is a purely pagan calendar for the year 354 AD; but subjoined unto it are: a list of twelve Roman popes (from Lucius unto Julius I, from 252 AD unto 352 AD) with the designation of the day of their burial (the list beareth the title *Depositio episcoporum*), and an analogous list of Roman martyrs (*Depositio martyrum*, extending down unto 304 AD), comprising 22 commemorations. Into this latter list were entered likewise the holy popes who died as martyrs (Sixtus, Fabian, Callistus, Pontian); there are mentioned also several non-Roman martyrs (Cyprian, Perpetua, and Felicitas—from the African Church, a daughter church in relation unto Rome); apart from the martyrs there are only two commemorations of the Apostles (February 22, 'the Chair of Peter at Antioch,' and June 29, Peter and Paul) and one festival of the Nativity of Christ—December 25. Beside the names there is no title of 'martyr' or 'saint'—of the 22 commemorations of martyrs in this calendar, 16 entered into our church calendar (the most important, apart from those already mentioned: Agnes on January 21 and Laurence on August 10).

#### b) The Calendar of Polemius Silvius

Of a similarly purely local and semi-pagan character is the calendar of Polemius Silvius, bishop of Sion (*Sedunum* / *Sitten*) in northern Italy (435–455 AD). In it are indicated pagan festivals (53 in all, whereas in Philocalus there are more than 100): *Carmentalia*, *Lupercalia*, *Terminalia*, *Quinquatria*, *Lavatio Cereris* (the washing of Ceres), *feriae servorum* (the festival of slaves, December 18 = Saturnalia), *feriae *(Orig. p. 277)* ancillarum* (the festival of handmaids, July 7), *natales* (birthdays) of the Caesars, of Cicero, and of Virgil, days of the sessions of the Senate, and circus games; and side by side—Christian commemorations: Theophany, the Death of Christ on March 25, His Resurrection on March 28, the Nativity of Christ, and six festivals of saints: *depositio Petri et Pauli* on February 22 (not June 29), Vincent, the Maccabees, Hippolytus, Stephen, and Laurence. Consequently, this was a calendar intended both for secular and for ecclesiastical use [^1439].

#### c) The Syriac Martyrology

Among purely Christian Menologia the most ancient is the Syriac Martyrology preserved in a manuscript (of Nitrian origin) of the year 411 AD, bearing the heading: 'The names of our lords the confessors and victors, and their days wherein they received their crowns' [^1440]. It was compiled in 380–400 AD. It consisteth of two distinct parts: the martyrology proper, concluding with the words 'here end the confessors of the West,' and an appendix unto it bearing the title: 'The names of our lords the confessors slain in the East,' wherein no longer according unto the days of the month, but according unto hierarchical orders there are indicated the bishops, presbyters, and deacons who suffered martyrdom in Persia (Persia was thus accounted at that time to be the Christian East). In the martyrology, which begins with December (though December 1–25 is defective), there are commemorations for more than half the days of the year. Before the name of a martyr there is designated for the most part the place of his suffering; for hierarchical persons their dignity is stated. Apart from the martyrs, among whom are found also the Maccabees, there occur commemorations of bishops: one of Rome, two each of Alexandria, Antioch, and Palestine, and two of unspecified cities; moreover, for certain of these non-martyrs there is added: 'commemoration.' Among the Apostles: 'Stephen the Apostle and Coryphaeus of Martyrs' on December 26 [^1441], John and James on December 27, Paul and Peter 'the Coryphaeus of the Apostles' on December 28; of dominical festivals only Theophany on January 6, while the Nativity of Christ is lacking through manuscript defect; 'on the Friday following upon Pascha the commemoration of all the martyrs.' Consequently, the Menologion is almost exclusively martyrological. Certain martyrs are distinguished by the martyrology into the category of 'ancient'; these are in all probability all those who suffered prior unto Diocletian. Regarding the geographical distribution of the commemorations, the Nicomedian saints predominate: the name of Nicomedia is mentioned 32 times; Antioch 24, Alexandria 19, Constantinople, Rome, and Jerusalem twice each; in all probability the martyrology was originally compiled in Nicomedia and gradually moved eastward, becoming enriched with local commemorations, and in Persia received the mechanical addition of the second part. It representeth, therefore, the type of a local Menologion in the earliest stages of its evolution into *(Orig. p. 278)* an ecumenical one [^1442]. It shareth many common commemorations with the Pseudo-Hieronymian Martyrology of the VII century and with our own (for example, Ignatius, Polycarp, Agnes, Perpetua, Babylas, Pamphilus, Chionia, Agatha, Plato, Romanus, Pelagia, and others), though for the most part assigned unto different days of the month.

#### d) The Carthaginian Calendar

Another local Menologion of the same epoch is the Carthaginian Calendar, bearing the title: 'Here are contained the passions of the holy martyrs and the depositions of the bishops whom the Church of Carthage celebrateth annually' [^1443]. The latest commemoration dateth apparently from the beginning of the V century. The calendar begins with Pascha on April 19 and breaketh off at February 16; it containeth commemorations for 80 days; unto the names are appended titles: *martyr*, *holy martyr*, *apostle*, *evangelist*. Of festivals: the Nativity of Christ and Theophany (*Epiphania*); there are commemorations of the Maccabees, John the Baptist, the Innocents slain by Herod, the Apostles Andrew, James 'whom Herod slew,' Luke, Stephen, eight Carthaginian bishops, and of the martyrs fifteen are common with our own calendar.

#### e) The Gothic Calendar

From the same epoch (prior unto the middle of the V century) there hath survived a fragment of a Gothic (Arian) calendar for October 23 – November 29 [^1444], containing exclusively Gothic names (it is strictly national—for instance, there are no commemorations of Clement or Cecilia); on November 14—the Apostle Philip; on November 29—the Apostle Andrew.

### Orders of Saints in the Menologia

A survey of this series of calendars demonstrateth sufficiently that these were strictly martyrological Menologia, and only rarely and by degrees did other commemorations enter into them—first and foremost those of the Apostles, chiefly as the primary martyrs [^1445]. One may conclude that of the Apostles *(Orig. p. 279)* the majority already in this epoch attained a place in the calendars of those churches which regarded them as their founders or wherein their relics had been discovered (in Rome—Peter and Paul; in Jerusalem—James; in Alexandria—Mark [^1446]). Very soon, however, earlier than those of the martyrs, apostolic commemorations must have become universal throughout the Church. Emperor Constantine the Great erected in Constantinople the 'Church (*μνήμη*) of the Apostles' [^1447], wherein he himself was entombed [^1448]. Among individual Apostles, in this epoch the commemoration of the Apostles Peter and Paul attained universal observance throughout the Church. The same may be said concerning the commemoration of John the Baptist and St. Stephen [^1449].

The calendars examined demonstrate that alongside their own martyrs the local churches venerated the memory of their bishops; yet it is characteristic that the days dedicated unto the latter were designated by a different term: not *natalitia* ('birthday,' that is to say 'passion'), but 'commemorations' (the Syriac Martyrology) or 'depositions' (the Carthaginian Calendar). According unto Sozomen likewise, each autonomous local church (for instance, Maiuma, Gaza) 'celebrateth its own solemnities (*πανηγύρεις*) of the martyrs and commemorations (*μνείας*) of the priests who had been among them' [^1450]. The departed hierarchy of the local church was thus placed almost in the same category with the martyrs, and in all probability in its entirety (in the Carthaginian Calendar there are eight local bishops) [^1451]. *(Orig. p. 280)* Later and more slowly than all others, Old Testament saints and angels entered into the Menologia. The former entered in all probability in proportion as their relics were discovered. Sozomen mentioneth the finding of the relics of the Righteous Zechariah [^1452]; Blessed Jerome mentioneth the translation of the bones of the Prophet Samuel from Judea unto Constantinople [^1453]; subsequent records (Synaxaria, Menologia) speak of the discovery of the relics of the Prophet Isaiah, of Nicodemus, the Prophet Daniel, the Maccabees and their mother, Zechariah the father of the Forerunner, the Bethlehem Innocents, and Simeon the God-receiver [^1454]. Yet of these saints during the present period veneration was accorded only unto the Maccabees, as we have observed from the Calendars of Polemius Silvius, the Syriac, and the Carthaginian, and the Innocents, named by this last calendar (St. John Chrysostom hath a homily upon the memory of the Maccabees, and Blessed Augustine two sermons). Thus the veneration of Old Testament saints penetrated very slowly into the Church and developed later; the Western Church hath them not in its calendar. As regards the Angels, their veneration in this epoch is sufficiently attested by the church erected by Constantine the Great in a suburb of Constantinople unto the Archangel Michael, at which, according unto the testimony of Sozomen who recounteth this, many healings were wrought [^1455]. In certain localities it was necessary even to contend against excesses in the veneration of Angels, as for example in Phrygia and Pisidia, where the worship of Angels, already rebuked by the Apostle Paul [^1456], elicited the decree of the Council of Laodicea 'that Christians ought not to forsake the Church of God and depart and invoke angels (*ἀγγέλους ὀνομάζειν*) and hold assemblies in their honor (*συνάξεις ποιεῖν*)' [^1457]. It is self-evident that of the veneration of monastic ascetics (*venerable fathers*) there could as yet be no question.

### The Services for Saints

The veneration of saints, that is to say for the most part of martyrs, was expressed by the celebration of a vigil on the eve of their commemoration day, and on the day of the feast itself by the Liturgy with an agape, or at least general communion. At the divine service an encomium upon the martyr was pronounced, and the account of his passion was read. The service was celebrated for the most part upon the tombs of the martyrs themselves, consequently outside the city walls. All this is evident from a series of homilies by the Holy Fathers upon the memory of the martyrs. 'Consider how ridiculous it is,' saith Chrysostom in a homily upon the day of the martyrs, 'after such an assembly (*σύνοδον*), after vigils (*παννυχίδας*), after hearing the Holy Scriptures, after partaking of the Divine Mysteries, and after spiritual bounty (*χορηγίας*—almsgiving unto the poor or an agape for them on the occasion of the feast), to behold a husband and wife spending whole days *(Orig. p. 281)* in a tavern' [^1458]. Sidonius Apollinaris, bishop of the Arverni (= Clermont in Gaul) in the V century, thus describeth the feast of St. Justus:

> 'We assembled at the tomb of St. Justus. The procession was before dawn, the solemnity annual, an enormous multitude of both sexes which the spacious basilica could not contain, though surrounded moreover by extensive cryptoporticos. Upon the conclusion of the office (*cultu*) of the vigil, > which was celebrated by monks and clerical psalmists with alternating sweetness of song (*alternante mulcedine*), each departed unto his own abode, yet not far off, so as to return again by the third hour (9 a.m.), when the divine service (*res*) was to be celebrated by the priests.' [^1459]

Commemorations of martyrs occurred every week about twice, and in all probability each time were celebrated with the like solemnity. Chrysostom saith: 'Lately (*πρῴην*) the blessed Babylas with the three youths gathered us hither; today two holy soldiers (the Martyrs Juventinus and Maximinus) have arrayed in battle order the host of Christ' [^1460]. According unto Blessed Theodoret, 'unto the shrines of the martyrs we assemble not once, nor twice, nor five times in the year, but frequently celebrate their solemn festivals (*πανηγύρεις*)' [^1461]. With the like solemnity were celebrated the memories of those few saints whom the Menologia of that age contained apart from the martyrs, as for example the Maccabees, and the Innocents slain by Herod. It could not be otherwise, for the Church looked upon these saints in the very same manner as upon martyrs. St. Chrysostom remarketh the singular zeal wherewith upon the day of the Maccabees the people assembled [^1462] in Antioch, the site of their suffering, where there was a basilica in their honor [^1463]. Blessed Augustine calleth their festival *solemnem diem* [^1464]. As for the Innocents, their commemoration in the majority of churches must have been celebrated together with the Feast of Theophany or the Nativity of Christ, judging from the fact that mention of them is found only in sermons and homilies upon this festival [^1465]. With no less, if not still greater solemnity was celebrated the memory of the Apostles where festivals were held in their honor. According unto the description of Prudentius, who visited Rome in 405 AD, on the feast of SS. Peter and Paul the entire city was in prayerful motion (*Romam per omnem cursitant orantque*); a vast multitude formed two enormous waves pouring into the two churches of the two Apostles (situated over their sepulchres and considerably distant one from another), in each of which on that day the bishop officiated [^1466]. This festival *(Orig. p. 282)* in the V century had in Rome even an eight-day post-festive period, if one may credit the title of a Sermon of Pope Leo I: *in octavis ss. apostolorum* [^1467].

### The Day of All Saints

In view of the fact that during the mass executions of Christians in certain persecutions the names, as well as the days of demise, of many of those who suffered remained unknown, and moreover each local church honored chiefly its own martyrs, in order that not one of these latter might remain in the Church without commemoration, there arose in this same epoch a festival in honor of all the martyrs, which subsequently was transformed into the feast of All Saints. We have seen that in the Syriac Martyrology such a festival is assigned unto the Friday following upon Pascha. According unto Chrysostom, however, who hath a homily upon this day, it hath its place, even as at present, on the first Sunday after Pentecost:

> 'Eight days have not yet passed since we celebrated the sacred solemnity of Pentecost, and once again the choir of the martyrs hath received us—or rather an army and host in no wise inferior unto the host of Angels seen by Jacob, but vying with and equal unto it.' [^1468]

### Commemoration of the Departed

In intimate connection with the commemorations of the saints stood the commemoration of ordinary departed Christians. In the III century, as we have seen [^1469], no marked distinction was as yet drawn between the former and the latter. Now it is otherwise. Blessed Augustine saith:

> 'In the heavenly fatherland there is no place for prayer, but only for praise. Why then is there no place for prayer? Because in nothing is there any lack. Whatsoever is thought upon there is present; whatsoever is hoped for is possessed; whatsoever is longed for is attained. Yet even in this life there is a certain perfection: it is that which the martyrs have attained. Therefore the Church requireth, as the faithful know, when the martyrs are named (*recitantur*) before the altar of God, not to pray for them, but to pray for the other departed who are commemorated. For it is an insult unto a martyr to pray for him (*injuria est enim pro martyre orare*), for one unto whose prayers we ought to commend ourselves. For he strived against sin even unto blood.' [^1470]

The *Apostolic Constitutions*, however, do not as yet draw so sharp a line between the saints and ordinary reposed Christians: 'Assemble in the cemeteries, performing the reading of the sacred books and singing psalms for the reposed martyrs and for all the saints from the beginning of the world, and for your brethren who have fallen asleep in the Lord' [^1471]. In a later section of the *Apostolic Constitutions* there are indicated likewise the present days of commemoration:

> 'Celebrate also the third day (*τρίτα*) of the departed in psalms, readings, and prayers, for the sake of Him Who rose on the third day; and the ninth day (*ἔναта*) in remembrance of those who are here reposed; and the fortieth day (*τεσσαράκοста*) according unto the ancient *(Orig. p. 283)* pattern, for even so the people of Israel mourned for Moses; and the annual anniversary in memory of the reposed. And let there be distributed from his estate unto the poor in memorial of him.' [^1472]

St. Ambrose, on the occasion of the fortieth-day memorial (*sorokoust*) of Emperor Theodosius the Great, remarketh: 'Some are accustomed to observe the third day and the thirtieth; others the seventh and the fortieth' [^1473]. There was a prolonged hesitation between adopting the 7th or 9th day, and the 30th or 40th, which depended, in all probability, upon the nationality of the local church; the ancient Greeks offered sacrifices for the dead on the 3rd, 9th, and 30th days; the Romans—on the 9th day [^1474]. Blessed Augustine censured the observance of the 9th day as a pagan custom [^1475]. In Palestine even in the VI century the 7th day was observed [^1476]. The Syrians, according unto the testimony of St. Ephrem the Syrian, observed the 30th day [^1477]. Gradually in the East the 3rd, 9th, and 40th days were adopted, while in the West the 7th and 30th days prevailed [^1478].

### Commemorations of Earthquakes, Victories, and Episcopal Consecrations

In order that the picture of the liturgical year in the IV–V centuries may be complete, it is necessary to name several additional festivals and fasts which were not incorporated directly into our present Typikon, but which influenced it indirectly or were characteristic of the epoch. Thus days were celebrated that had been marked by special benefactions of God, such as deliverance from flood, earthquake, or military victories. According unto the testimony of Sozomen, when Alexandria during the reign of Julian was threatened with inundation by a sea flood, which nevertheless soon subsided, 'the day on which this occurred the Alexandrians denominated the "memorial of the quake" (*γενέσια τοῦ σεισμοῦ*), and even unto this day honor it with an annual festival; this latter they celebrate with solemnity and devotion, kindling throughout the entire city a multitude of lamps and offering unto God prayers of thanksgiving (*χαριστηρίους λιτάς*)' [^1479]. Cf. in our calendar October 26. Concerning festivities in honor of victories Eusebius speaketh: upon the overthrow of Licinius, for Christians 'there dawned joyful and festive days of celebration; all things were filled with light... throughout the cities and villages were heard choirs of praiseful hymns, wherewith Christians glorified, as they had been taught, first of all God the King of all, and then the pious Emperor with all his God-beloved children' [^1480].

Cf. in our calendar June 27, December 25, and the chanting of Many Years at the conclusion of Vespers, Matins, and the Liturgy. As a distinct festival *(Orig. p. 284)* there was celebrated annually, at least in the West, the day of the bishop's consecration, denominated, like the day of a sovereign's coronation, his 'birthday' (*natalis*). Concerning such a festival mention is made in the letters of St. Ambrose, St. Hilary, and St. Paulinus of Nola [^1481]. There have survived also several sermons of Blessed Augustine and of Pope Leo I upon their *natales episcopi* or *episcopatus*, testifying unto the deep compunction which this festival awakened in the bishop himself, and unto how this day was honored by all the people and how greatly it strengthened the bond of the bishop with his flock [^1482].

### The Ember Days (Fasts of the Four Seasons)

Of fasts, apart from the chief and ancient ones indicated above, there arose in this epoch in the West the 'fasts of the four seasons of the year' (the Ember Days). Pope Leo I (440–461 AD) mentioneth them: 'Throughout the entire year the fasts are distributed so that the law of abstinence is prescribed for all seasons of the year: namely, the spring fast is kept in the Forty Days (Lent), the summer fast at Pentecost, the autumn fast in the seventh month, and the winter fast in the tenth'; as the foundation for these fasts St. Leo indicateth gratitude unto God for the gathered fruits of the earth [^1483]. The present dates of these fasts (for the 1st—the 1st week of Great Lent; for the 2nd—the week of Pentecost; for the 3rd—the 3rd week of September; for the 4th—the 3rd week of Advent) were definitively determined under Pope Gregory VII [^1484]. The foundation for these fasts was laid by Pope Callistus (217–222 AD), who 'instituted a fast on three Saturdays of the year according unto the prophecy concerning corn, wine, and oil' [^1485]. Parallel unto these Western fasts, in all probability in the East as well the annual fasts were brought unto the number of four.

### The Movement Against the Veneration of Martyrs and Monasticism

Summing up the accomplishments of the IV–V centuries in the domain of divine worship, one must recognize as paramount in this endeavor the rapid enrichment of the liturgical year with commemorations, and the transformation of divine worship and of the very conception thereof under the influence of monasticism, which stood in intimate connection with the extensive development of this latter. Neither the one nor the other, it must be observed, passed without opposition on the part of the puritans of the Church in that age. Blessed Jerome left a polemical treatise (composed in 406 AD) against the Gallic presbyter Vigilantius, *(Orig. p. 285)* which acquainteth us with the contemporary movement within Christianity (which enjoyed the sympathy even of certain bishops) against the veneration of martyrs and the spread of monasticism.

> 'We see,' Blessed Jerome citeth the words of Vigilantius, 'that after the manner of pagan rites, under the pretext of piety, there hath been introduced into the churches—even while the sun is still shining—the kindling of a multitude of candles; everywhere likewise kissing they venerate a certain powder (*pulvisculum*—in all probability dust from the tombs of martyrs or ashes from cremated bodies), I know not what, in a small precious vessel, wrapped in a towel. As though, forsooth, such men render great honor unto the most blessed martyrs, whom they deem in need of being illuminated, whereas they are illuminated by the Lamb Who sitteth upon the throne with all the brightness of His majesty!'

Concerning the vigils in honor of the martyrs, Vigilantius thought 'that they ought not to be permitted, lest they appear frequently to celebrate Pascha' (unto which Blessed Jerome replieth: 'Therefore also on the Sunday day sacrifices ought not to be offered unto Christ, lest they frequently celebrate the Pascha of the Resurrection of the Lord'), and in view of 'abuses of them (the vigils) on the part of youths and wanton women, frequently observed at night' (Blessed Jerome retorteth: 'even at Paschal vigils something similar is frequently observed'); Vigilantius likewise said, having in view vigils for martyrs, that 'except for Pascha, Alleluia ought never to be sung.' An adversary of monasticism and asceticism, Vigilantius 'at secular banquets preached against the fast of the saints, and philosophizing over the wine cups and feasting on pastries, he delighteth in the melody of the psalms, so that only over banquets doth he deign to listen unto the songs of David and Asaph and the sons of Korah' [^1486]. Against monasticism and asceticism in general, the former monk Jovinian also arose (in Rome and Milan); in his treatise against him (composed in 392 AD), Blessed Jerome attributeth unto him, among others, the following theses: 'virgins, widows, and married women, once washed in Christ, if they differ not among themselves in other works, possess equal merit'; 'between abstinence from meats and the receiving of them with thanksgiving there is no difference whatever' [^1487]. Directed against the ascetical tendencies of the time was likewise the Council of Gangra (mid-IV century). The very impotence of these movements and their lack of lasting result (concerning Vigilantius we know solely thanks unto Jerome) demonstrated their incompatibility with the spirit of Christianity [^1488]. — No less important an achievement of the IV–V centuries in the domain of divine worship was the unification of the forms thereof throughout the entire Christian world. Such unity in divine worship had not existed in Christianity either before or after. Eusebius falleth into no ordinary rhetorical exaggeration of his when he thus characterizeth the liturgical services of Constantine the Great: 'Now the inhabitants of the West are edified by his Godly instructions at the selfsame hours of time with the dwellers of the East, and they that populate the North sing the selfsame hymns with the inhabitants of the South' [^1489].
*(Orig. p. 286)*

## VI–VIII Centuries

### Character of the Period

These centuries may be denominated the most decisive and definitive period in the formation of our liturgical Typikon. Both the daily office (the diurnal and nocturnal cycle) and the church year now receive in all essentials their present form. Unto the share of subsequent times there remained only the elaboration of both in secondary particulars. Yet our information concerning the energetic labor of this period in the realm of the church rule is exceedingly meager, yielding substantially unto the periods preceding and subsequent (from the IX century onwards).

The chief, if not exclusive, agent in the development of the liturgical Typikon became now monasticism. Being so characteristic a phenomenon of church life in the IV–V centuries, it now acquireth an even stronger influence upon that life; from it, chiefly, are replenished the ranks of the higher hierarchy; it nourisheth enlightenment and literature; it exerteth an influence upon the resolution of the most weighty theological questions. If the monasticism of this period no longer displayeth such giants of the spirit as in its nascent era, it nevertheless continueth to astonish the world with ascetical feats (St. Mary of Egypt, † 522 AD; St. Symeon of the Miraculous Mountain, † 596 AD), inventeth new forms thereof (holy folly for Christ's sake—St. Symeon the Fool, † 590 AD; hesychasm and holy silence—St. John the Hesychast, † 558 AD), and revealeth examples of martyrdom unknown unto the former period (the slaughter of the fathers in Sinai and Palestine) [^1490]. All of this, together with the extraordinary numerical growth of monasticism, renders it a mighty power in the Church, the chief nerve of her life. But almost the greatest influence of monasticism out of all church life was destined to be felt upon divine worship. It is not surprising, therefore, that all the information that hath reached us from this epoch concerning divine worship is confined precisely unto monastic worship. — If a comparative evaluation be made of contemporary monasticism according unto the regions of its dissemination, the first place must be assigned unto Palestinian and Sinaitic monasticism. How much more significant these centers were in comparison with others (for example, with Constantino*(Orig. p. 287)*nople), is evident from the fact that they alone left behind a literary monument. Whereas concerning the monasteries of other places from this epoch we possess almost no information, Sinaitic and Palestinian monasticism of the VI–VII centuries possesseth its own patericon in the form of the *Spiritual Meadow* (*Pratum Spirituale*) of John Moschos, and Palestinian monasticism possesseth a most detailed history covering almost this entire period. The latter, moreover, attracted unto itself the attention, favor, and lavish donations of the Byzantine emperors. Consequently, if the monasticism of this era took upon itself the development of Christian divine worship, then the greatest contribution here was destined to be made by the Palestinian monasteries. Among these latter, the central figure of this epoch is St. Sabas the Sanctified (*prp. Savva Osviashchennyi*). It is not surprising if literary tradition traceth back unto him, above all others, our present type of divine worship.

### St. Sabas the Sanctified

St. Sabas the Sanctified († 532 AD) is the representative of that new type of asceticism and monasticism which preferred active life unto the contemplative ('by action hast thou attained unto contemplation', according unto the expression of the church hymn): the expansion of a network of monasteries and their good ordering—materially, juridically (through petitioning the civil authorities for privileges on their behalf), and internally (in discipline and preeminently in liturgical order)—were the work of his entire life. The *Life of St. Sabas* was described by his disciple, the Palestinian monk of the VI century, Cyril of Scythopolis [^1491]. By origin a wealthy Cappadocian, St. Sabas began his monastic life in an Asia Minor monastery, where he 'learned the Psalter and the structure of the cenobitic rule'; but having visited Palestine when already eighteen years of age, he became a disciple of St. Euthymius, who according unto his custom entrusted him for his initial formation unto the cenobium of St. Theoctistus. Upon the death of the latter, Sabas (now thirty years of age), with the blessing of St. Euthymius, began a solitary life (without quitting the cenobium of St. Theoctistus), spending five days at a time without food in complete solitude; and after the death of Euthymius he chose for his director St. Gerasimus, who received him immediately as a cell-dweller (*kelliotes*) into his lavra. When St. Sabas was keeping one of the Great Fasts in the desert after the example of SS. Theoctistus and Euthymius, the site for his ascetical labors and for his future famous lavra was revealed unto him by a vision: it was a cave situated upon a sheer precipice of rock, such that one had to ascend into it by a rope. After five years of solitary life here, hermits began to flock unto St. Sabas, and when their number reached seventy, he erected a tower and a small church (*eukterion*) with a consecrated altar, in which an invited presbyter celebrated. Soon, however, by a vision there was revealed unto St. Sabas not far from the lavra 'a great and marvelous cave, having within the appearance of a church of God; for on the eastern side there is a God-fashioned apse (*konche theoktistos*—for the sanctuary), and on the northern side a large chamber in the form of a diaconicon, while from the south there is a wide entrance admitting sufficient light; having embellished through God's assistance this *(Orig. p. 288)* cave, he instituted therein divine worship (*ton kanona*) on Saturdays and Sundays.' This church existeth even unto this day, dedicated in honor of St. Nicholas. When the number of the brethren reached one hundred and fifty, a regular administrative economy was established in the lavra, facilitated by large donations. In the *Life of St. Sabas* it is not stated that he subjected those entering his monastery unto a probationary trial (especially unto so severe a testing as was practiced in Egypt); the consequence of this, in all probability, was that a portion of the monks began to act willfully and petitioned the patriarch to give them another hegumen; but the patriarch, instead of doing so, ordained Sabas a presbyter. Following this, there occurred two further instances of rebellion among the brethren against Sabas, after the first of which Sabas was compelled to withdraw temporarily from the monastery, and after the second, sixty monks departed from the lavra and founded another monastery. Perhaps under the influence of these occurrences, St. Sabas instituted in his lavra, after the example of SS. Euthymius and Gerasimus, a cenobium for novice monks, from whence he transferred them unto the status of cell-dwellers (*kelliotai*) only after they had mastered the Psalter and the rule of psalmody (*kanon tes psalmodias*). Gradually St. Sabas founded three lavras: besides the first, the Great Lavra, also the New Lavra, founded near Tekoa by the disciples of St. Sabas who had willfully departed, but subsequently subjected by him unto his authority; and the Lavra of the Seven Mouths (*Heptastomos*), so named after the torrent beside which it stood; and in addition four cenobia. Attached unto the lavras and cenobia, Sabas established large hospices (*xenodochia*); these latter he founded likewise in Jerusalem (where for this purpose he purchased the cells of the *spoudaioi*, when a monastery was constructed for them by the patriarch) and in Jericho. Besides rich donations (even on the part of the emperors), St. Sabas expended upon this also the entire estate handed over unto him by his mother when the latter embraced the monastic state. St. Sabas was appointed archimandrite of all the Palestinian lavras, and as the most prominent figure in the monasticism of that age, he was twice sent successfully by the patriarchs on missions of the Jerusalem Church unto Constantinople—unto Emperors Anastasius and Justinian.

### The Structure of the Sabbaite Monasteries

Concerning the internal organization of the Sabbaite monasteries there are very few data in his *Life* by Cyril of Scythopolis. Mentioned as officials are: the superiors (*archegoi*) of the monasteries (§ 58), the steward or bursar (*oikonomos*, § 59), and the canonarch, who, among other duties, struck the wooden semantron (*krouein*) for divine service (§ 43) and apparently administered economic affairs jointly with the steward (§ 59). All of them performed all things with the knowledge and counsel of St. Sabas (*ibid.*). He enjoyed such veneration that monks of other monasteries, upon meeting him, would fall down at his feet; he would bless them, raise them up, and embrace them; such was the case, at least, at the first meeting of St. Sabas with Gregory of Scythopolis (§ 75). The striking for service was performed with his knowledge and permission (*gnome*), but at appointed hours (§ 43). The services (*kanon*, *kanon tes psalmodias*) were celebrated by a numerous multitude (*plethos*) of brethren with sweet chanting (*meta melous hedyphonou*), with incensations, and the kindling of candles (*ibid.*). Among the services there is mentioned a certain nocturnal office (§ 43, designated simply as *kanon*—office), apparently Matins, unto which is applied the designation *ta lychnika* (§ 60, see below); there is mentioned next the Third Hour: while residing in *(Orig. p. 289)* the palace as an ambassador of the patriarch unto Emperor Justinian, when the emperor was discussing with the quaestor the petition of the patriarch and Sabas, the latter, 'withdrawing a little distance, was reading secretly the psalms of David and celebrating the divine office (*leitourgian*) of the Third Hour'; and unto the reproach of his deacon for his lack of attention unto the sovereign, he replied: 'They, my son, are doing their business, and we likewise must do ours' (§ 73). Consequently, there were also services of the Sixth and Ninth Hours. They communicated, apparently, daily at the Ninth Hour, after which followed the common table and Vespers: when St. Sabas, with the hegumens of the Monastery of St. Euthymius and of the Patriarchal Monastery at Jericho, attended the last days of the life of Patriarch Elias of Jerusalem († 517 AD), the latter daily from the dismissal of Matins (*apo men tes ton lychnikon apolyseos*) did not show himself unto them until the ninth hour, but around the ninth hour came forth and communicated (*ekoinonei*) with them, partook of food, and after Vespers (*to lychnikon*) retired once again (§ 60). When Armenians began to enter the Lavra of St. Sabas, he initially assigned unto them for divine worship in their native tongue the small church (the first of those constructed), but upon the erection and consecration of the great church (the third church, dedicated in honor of the All-Praised Mother of God and Ever-Virgin Mary), he

> 'transferred them from the small church for the performance of the rule of psalmody into the God-fashioned (second) church, bidding them to recite (*legein*) among themselves, at the Armenian synaxes (*synaxesin*), the Gospel (*to megaleion*) [^1492] and the rest of the order of service, but at the time of the Divine Oblation (*proskomides*) to go unto the Greeks for the reception of the Divine Mysteries; when, however, certain of them > ventured to utter the Trisagion hymn with the addition contrived by Peter surnamed the Fuller: "Who wast crucified for us", the divine elder, filled with indignation, commanded them to chant this hymn in Greek, according unto the tradition of the Catholic Church' (§ 32).

Here the discourse is clearly concerning the Liturgy of the Catechumens, which consequently appeared as something completely independent alongside the Liturgy of the Faithful. 'Sabas ordained that on Saturday the assembly should take place in the church created by God, and on the Sunday day in the church of the Mother of God, and decreed that in both churches on every Sunday day and Lord's feast there should unfailingly be a vigil from evening until morning (*aparaleiptos apo opse heos proi agrypnian*)' (*ibid.*). On the Sunday day, after the divine service (*he tou Theou leitourgia*), for the fathers assembled from the cells situated in the vicinity of the monastery, a repast (*diaklysma*) was offered by the steward of the lavra, consisting of bread, olive oil, honey, cheese, and other victuals (§ 59).

Among the festivals, mention is made of the commemorations of St. Anthony the Great, St. Euthymius on January 20, Palm Sunday, and Pascha:

> 'As St. Euthymius had the custom on the fourteenth day of the month of January to withdraw into the deep desert and there spend the Forty Days' Fast, so also Sabas, having modified this custom slightly, went forth from the lavra after the passing of that day on which the memory of St. Anthony is celebrated, celebrated the memory of the great Euthymius, which is observed on the twentieth day, and after this departed into the deep desert. There until the feast of Palms he was removed from all intercourse with men. And this he did almost every year.'

Together with him there went forth for the same purpose other ascetics of the lavra *(Orig. p. 290)* inclined toward solitude. 'During all the days of the fast Sabas remained without food, contenting himself with the communion of the Holy Mysteries on Saturday and the Sunday day', and spending all his time in prayer and in the fulfillment of 'his rule of psalmody' [^1493]. On the Feast of the Dedication of the Church of the Resurrection, 'according unto the custom of the hegumens', St. Sabas was accustomed to go with certain brethren of his lavra unto Jerusalem; here on one of the Sundays an anathema against heretics was pronounced: the bishops and hegumens ascended the ambo and proclaimed: 'If anyone receiveth not the four Councils, and likewise the four Gospels, let him be anathema', or 'Anathema unto Severus and his accomplices.' (This ceremony was celebrated in the Jerusalem Church of St. Stephen the Protomartyr, because that church could contain all the assembling monks, who numbered up to ten thousand; § 56).

### St. Theodosius the Cenobiarch

As his fellow-laborer in planting monasticism in Palestine, St. Sabas had St. Theodosius the Cenobiarch († 529 AD). Likewise a Cappadocian, formerly a reader, who had received a blessing for monastic life from St. Symeon the Stylite, St. Theodosius founded his cenobium not in caves, like SS. Chariton and Sabas, but in an open place, six versts from Jerusalem and from the principal Lavra of St. Sabas: the cenobium of St. Theodosius was more populous than the Great Lavra of St. Sabas, having in his time up to seven hundred monks and distinct churches for the Greeks, the Bessi [^1494], the Armenians, and the possessed; the 'rule of psalmody' was celebrated in each church seven times a day, but the Liturgy only in the Greek church. The successor of St. Theodosius, Abba Sophronius, quadrupled his monastery. In the XII century, unto the Russian pilgrim Daniel it presented the appearance of an entire city [^1495], but was definitively destroyed by the Crusaders, whereas the Lavra of St. Sabas existeth even unto this day. During the lifetime of St. Theodosius, who was appointed alongside St. Sabas as superior of all Palestinian cenobia, his cenobium was a noble rival and complement unto the lavras of St. Sabas, leaving its imprint upon monastic life. Sabas and Theodosius, in the words of the biographer of the latter [^1496], 'were *(Orig. p. 291)* of one soul and one mind, breathing each other's presence more than the air, so that the inhabitants of Jerusalem, seeing their unanimity and accord in relation unto God, denominated them a new apostolic pair, like unto the pair of the Apostles Peter and John' (in character St. Sabas resembled the Apostle Peter, and Theodosius—John). Yet at the same time Sabas was wont to say unto Theodosius: 'Thou art hegumen of boys (*paidion*), whereas I am hegumen over hegumens; for each of my disciples is an independent ascetic and is hegumen of his own cell' [^1497].

Thus the *Life of St. Sabas* confirmeth the later tradition concerning his composition of the so-called Jerusalem Typikon only by: 1) the report that he introduced Sunday and festal vigils which lasted in his monastery from evening until morning, and not merely from midnight, as was the practice in secular churches (for example, in the Jerusalem Church of the Resurrection and in other monasteries, even the austere Egyptian ones); the rule hitherto had known such all-night vigils for the most part only two or three times a year [^1498]; 2) the notice concerning the unfailing exactitude wherewith the liturgical hours were observed under St. Sabas. If this be so, then by St. Sabas was laid the foundation at least for two distinctive features of the later Jerusalem Typikon.

### The Testament of St. Sabas

From St. Sabas there have survived also written rules of monastic life, in all probability those which, according unto his biographer, he delivered before his death unto his successor Melitas: 'he gave him a testament inviolably to preserve the rules (*paradoseis*) introduced by him in his monasteries, delivering them unto him in writing (*engraphos*, § 76).' These rules are of interest as being among the most ancient ktetorial typika given unto monasteries by their founders, which served as models for our Typikon. These rules are placed in a XII-century manuscript Jerusalem Typikon (Sinai Library, No. 1096; and in a XV-century manuscript, No. 531) between its menaion and triodion sections, and fully corresponding unto the data of the *Life of St. Sabas*, they may be recognized as authentic, with the exception of certain interpolations (for example, the addition of 'venerable' unto the name of Sabas, etc.) [^1499]. The rules bear the title: 'The Pattern, Rule, and Law (*Typos kai paradosis kai nomos*) of the Honorable Lavra of St. Sabas.'

> 'It is necessary to observe the rules established by our venerable and blessed father Sabas. — In no case is there to be received into the Lavra either a beardless youth or a eunuch; and women are not permitted to enter for prayer not only into the Lavra, but even into the metochia [^1500], and especially into the second door of the great *(Orig. p. 292)* metochion. Whosoever among the monks of the Lavra shall be observed entering the monastic gynaeceum for the purpose of eating or drinking, or remaining there either under the pretext of guarding it, or for the tonsure, or for confession of thoughts (*logismous*), or who writeth unto women and receiveth letters from them, and in general hath familiarity (*gnosin*) with women, or contracteth spiritual kinship (*synteknias*), such a one must be expelled from the brotherhood, as a cause of offense (*skandalon*) not only unto Christians, but also unto pagans. — Neither Georgians (*Iberas*), nor Syrians, nor Franks (*Phrangous*) [^1501] shall have the right to celebrate the full Liturgy in their churches; but unto those assembling therein it is permitted to chant the Hours and the Typika (*ta typika*), to read the Epistle and the Gospel in their native tongue, and after this to gather in the great church and communicate together with the entire brotherhood of the divine, immaculate, and life-creating Mysteries. — Over the tomb of the saint (that is, of Sabas) the pro-liturgy (*proleitourgian*) is to be celebrated by the presbyter appointed for this purpose. — No one at all shall have the right to depart from the Lavra on Saturday in view of the all-night vigil that is to be celebrated, except for monastic necessity and business; but after the vigil, with the consent of the superior or the ecclesiarch, let him go according unto his necessity. Unto him that was not present at the preceding vigil nothing > is accepted as an excuse, because the entire preceding week was sufficient for him to attend unto his needs; and this (departure on business), if possible, is to be done once a month. — Those departing into the desert and dwelling therein, if they do so with the consent and blessing of the superior, are to be received according unto their needs; but if they have withdrawn willfully and out of a desire to live according unto their own will (*ex idiorrhythmias*), then upon their return they are not to be received. — Whosoever, by the Providence of God and by the judgment of the patriarch, should be elected either as metropolitan, or as bishop, or as hegumen unto another monastery, or elevated unto whatever rank of the Great Church, shall not have the right to sell or donate outright the cell belonging unto him in the Lavra or in the metochion; but they belong unto the holy monastery, and brethren who are worthy and needy may receive them from the hegumen. This same order must be observed also with regard unto deceased brethren: without the consent and will of the hegumen, no one (among the brethren) hath the right to bequeath unto his disciple his own cell. — If discord should arise among certain of the brethren and the evil should so increase therefrom that someone should dare to strike others and lay hands upon them, then such persons, if they do not reconcile, and even if they do reconcile, yet if it be necessary in the interests of the monastery, are to be cast out as disturbers of peace and adversaries of the commandment of Christ; for "the servant of the Lord must not strive", as saith the divine Apostle [2 Tim. 2:24]. — Whosoever among the brethren shall be detected in drunkenness, or in quarrels with anyone, or in insults against anyone, or in forming cabals (*hetairias*) and factions (*systrophas*), such a one must either be corrected, or else expelled from the monastery. In like manner also he who, during the performance of a monastic obedience, should be detected in theft, must be removed from his *(Orig. p. 293)* obedience, with the assigning unto him of a penance for correction and repentance, and he must not go forth from his cell, except at the appointed hours of liturgical assemblies (*ton synaxeon*) and prayers. — Concerning those who intend to practice hesychia and not appear in church, and likewise concerning those received for complete reclusion, we desire that they assemble with the rest of the brethren solely at all-night vigils; but in cities, villages, at the shrines of holy > men, and in other notable places, let them be in complete solitude, for silence in deed can bring profit far better than in words. — Guests coming from without, (especially) if any of them desire to make a beginning in the Lavra, we shall receive and in every way console for the space of seven days; if, however, the guests be of those dwelling in the city (that is, Jerusalem) or of the surrounding inhabitants and have come for veneration, then three days are sufficient for them; the cleansing (of the monastic buildings is necessary), in view of the multitude of poor folk arriving daily. — Inasmuch as demons are accustomed to cause harm during the elections of hegumens, and to stir up strife and contentions between the two nationalities, that is, between the Greeks (*Rhomiaioi*) and the Syrians, giving birth therefrom unto scandal, we therefore decree: let no one henceforth from among the Syrians be elevated unto the rank of hegumen; but we ordain and agree that as stewards and docharioi (that is, those having charge of the property of the monastery) and in other obediences, Syrians be preferred, as men capable thereof and active by their very nature' [^1502].

### The Fate of the Sabbaite Lavra and Its Liturgical Significance

The Lavra of St. Sabas even after his death did not lose its central and leading significance in Palestinian monasticism, and consequently in monasticism in general, although it experienced not a few internal and external tribulations. Thus Origenism almost penetrated into it in the person of Hegumen George in the VI century. In 614 AD it was plundered by the armies of the Persian King Chosroes, during which the monks were tortured to extract where the treasures of the lavra were hidden, and forty-four of them were slain; the monks who escaped from the Persians restored the lavra with the assistance of Modestus, Archimandrite of the Cenobium of St. Theodosius (subsequently Patriarch of Jerusalem), who consoled them with the passage from the Wisdom of Solomon, Chapter 3, concerning the untimely demise of the righteous (a passage that formed a paroemia at the service for venerable fathers). Nevertheless, after the Persian devastation, information concerning the lavra until the VIII century almost ceaseth; from this period, however, there is one not unimportant piece of news concerning it: that its Archimandrite John was the first to sign the epistle of the Palestinian monks unto Pope Martin on the occasion of the Lateran Council of 649 AD convened by him against the Monothelites [^1503]. But during this period of its life the lavra rendered the greatest of its services unto the Church, and in particular unto the liturgical Typikon, by nurturing the most renowned hymnographers: St. Andrew of Crete († ca. 712 AD), St. John of Damascus († ca. 780 AD), *(Orig. p. 294)* St. Cosmas, Bishop of Maiuma († ca. 787 AD), Stephen the Sabaite († ca. 807 AD) and Theophanes the Branded (*Graptos*, † ca. 850 AD).

### The Sunday Vigil on Sinai and in Palestine: The Visit to Nilus by Moschus and Sophronius

The Life of St. Sabas, like all accounts concerning Palestinian monasticism—in contrast unto reports concerning, for example, Egyptian monasticism—containeth absolutely no data concerning the divine services there. This can apparently be explained solely by the fact that the latter in Palestinian monasteries, as is directly known concerning the Syro-Mesopotamian monasteries [^1504], followed the customary rite, the order of secular parish churches. And this latter rite, as we have seen, even in the V century was already quite close unto the present one. For example, at Vespers there was already Ps. 140, the Great Litany and the Litany of Supplication, **"O Gladsome Light"** (*Phos Hilaron / Svete Tikhiy*), **"Vouchsafe, O Lord"** (*Kataxioson, Kyrie / Spodobi Gospodi*), **"Now lettest Thou"** (*Nyn apolyeis / Nyně otpushchayeshi*); at Matins, Ps. 62 and Ps. 50, certain Old Testament and New Testament canticles, the Lauds (*Ainoi / Khvalitny*) psalms, **"Glory to God in the highest"** (*Doxa en hypsistois Theo / Slava v vyshnikh Bogu*), and the same litanies. Unto these invariable portions was conjoined a series of hymns, sometimes termed troparia, corresponding unto the given day, as well as corresponding readings from the Old and New Testaments [^1505]. Such, at least, was the order of the divine office in the churches of Syria and Palestine—that is, precisely those in whose bosom arose that branch of monasticism which is regarded as the progenitor of the present Typikon. Into this already established order of divine worship, monasticism needed only to insert the Psalter, inasmuch as the Psalter from antiquity was regarded as the handbook for the monk. This insertion could be effected either in such manner that the hitherto existing psalm element in divine worship might be stretched and expanded, or, without disturbing that element, the Psalter could be externally inserted into divine worship, fashioning from it as it were a distinct monastic office upon the ordinary secular service. The former was accomplished in the liturgical rite of the Western Church; the latter, in the Eastern Typika by the system of kathismata and the kanon (understanding by the latter the Biblical canticles). As unto how this addition was originally effected in the VI century, a precious report concerning this hath been preserved in the narrative of the visit unto the Sinaitic Abba Nilus [^1506] by the Palestinian monks John Moschus, author of the *Spiritual Meadow* (*Pratum Spirituale*), and Sophronius, subsequently Patriarch of Jerusalem—a visit which took place ca. 606 AD. This narrative hath been preserved in certain ancient Paterika (in manuscripts of the Vatican Library) [^1507] and in Nikon of the Black Mountain [^1508]. We cite the narrative in the first recension, with variants from Nikon in parentheses (*italics denote that which is absent in Nikon*):

"Abba John and Abba Sophronius related unto us: before the holy Sunday (*at the dawning of the Lord’s *(Orig. p. 295)* Day*), we went unto Abba Nilus upon Mount Sinai. The elder was up upon the summit of the mountain with two disciples. Inasmuch as we arrived for Vespers, the elder began: **"Glory to the Father"** (*Slava Ottsu*), and the rest; and after they had said: **"Blessed is the man"** (*Blazhen muzh*) and **"Lord, I have cried"** (*Kyrie ekekraxa / Gospodi vozzvakh*) without troparia, and **"O Gladsome Light"** (*Phos Hilaron / Svete Tikhiy*), and **"Vouchsafe, O Lord"** (*Kataxioson, Kyrie / Spodobi Gospodi*), they began **"Now lettest Thou"** (*Nyn apolyeis / Nyně otpushchayeshi*) and the rest. Upon the conclusion of Vespers he set before us a refection. After the refection we began the kanon (rule); and after the Six Psalms (*Hexapsalmos*), having said **"Our Father Who art in the heavens"** (*Otche nash, Izhe yesi na nebesech*), they began the psalms chanted melodiously. And when they had said the first stasis of 50 psalms, the elder began **"Our Father Who art in the heavens"** (*+ the elder began to recite the Epistle*), fifty times **"Lord, have mercy"** (*Gospodi pomiluy*); and when they had sat down, one of his disciples read the Catholic Epistle of James. Rising up, we again began the second stasis of 50 psalms; and upon the completion of the 50 psalms he gave [the book] unto another brother, and that one read from the same book the Catholic Epistle of Peter. And rising up, they began the 3rd stasis; and upon the completion of the 150 psalms, and after they had said **"Our Father"** and **"Lord, have mercy"**, they sat down, and the elder gave me the book, and I read the Catholic Epistle of John. And rising up, they began the Canticles (*ōdas*) of Moses (softly) chanted melodiously without troparia; and neither at the third nor at the sixth did they make an intercalary hymn (*mesōdion*), but **"Our Father"** and **"Lord, have mercy"**; and having said the Lauds (*Ainoi / Khvalitny*) psalms without troparia, they began **"Glory to God in the highest"** with the **"I believe"** (*+ in one God*) and **"Our Father"** and **"Lord, have mercy"**. The elder then added: 'O Son and Word of God (*+ Lord*), Jesus Christ, our God, have mercy upon us, and help, and save our souls!' And when we said 'Amen', we sat down. And I say unto the elder: 'Why, Abba, dost thou not preserve the order of the Catholic and Apostolic Church?' And the elder saith unto me: 'He that preserveth not the order of the Catholic and Apostolic Church, let him be anathema both in this age and in that which is to come!'
