According unto the Ambrosian rite, the Psalter is chanted not once a week, but once in two weeks; from Ps. 109 onward it is sung, as in the Roman rite, at Vespers and the daytime Hours; up to Ps. 108, however, it is divided into 10 decuries, each of which comprises 16–8 psalms, and which are sung in turn at the weekday Matins of two weeks, with the exception of Saturday and Sunday; Matins of these latter days, as well as of feasts, has biblical canticles in place of the Psalter; likewise the weeks before the Nativity of Christ and Pascha have proper psalms at Matins; the Psalter is in a different translation than in the Roman rite—the one in which it is used also among the canons of St. Peter's in the Vatican. The customary opening of the offices never contains the Symbol of Faith, but only **"Our Father"** and the *Ave Maria*. At Matins, before the psalms, in the introductory part there is also the Canticle of the Three Holy Children: **"Blessed art Thou, O Lord God of our fathers"** (*"Blagosloven esi, Gospodi Bozhe otets nashikh"*) and *Kyrie eleison*. After the psalms, which are sung continuously, at Matins there are only 3 readings: on Sunday from homilies upon the Gospel, on weekdays from the Scripture, and on feasts from the life of the saint or festal discourses; only at the Nativity of Christ and Theophany are there three nocturns and 9 readings, and on Friday 6 readings, the last 3 of which are the Passions according unto Mark, Luke, and John, with Matthew at the Liturgy. At *Laudes*, after the opening verse **"O God, come to my assistance"**—the Canticle of Zechariah (*Benedictus*), in place of which on the Sundays of Advent, the Nativity of Christ, Circumcision, and Theophany, there is sung the Canticle of Moses: **"Give ear, O ye heavens"** (*"Slyshi, nebo"* / Deut. 32); then on Sundays and feasts of saints an antiphon unto the Holy Cross 5 or 7 times and a secret prayer; the Canticle of Moses **"Let us sing unto the Lord"** (*Cantemus Domino* / *"Poim Gospodevi"*) with an antiphon and *Kyrie eleison* thrice, and another secret prayer; the Canticle of the Three Children **"Bless the Lord, all ye works"** (*Benedicite omnia opera* / *"Blagoslovite, vsia dela"*), in place of which on Saturday is sung Ps. 117, and on weekdays Ps. 50 with an antiphon and *Kyrie eleison* thrice; a prayer aloud; the Praises psalms (Lauds), a *capitulum*, an antiphon, *Kyrie eleison* thrice, *Dominus vobiscum*; a psalm simply by two choirs together (*directus*) and a hymn according unto the day; *Kyrie eleison* 12 with *Dominus vobiscum*, a *psallenda* (an antiphon repeated with 'Glory' and several verses), and on weekdays—a responsory called *in baptisterio* (in the baptistery; cf. below in the Greek 'Choral/Sung Vespers and Matins'), a *commemoratio* of the saint with an antiphon, *Kyrie eleison* 12, a verse and a prayer aloud, *Kyrie eleison* thrice, and *Dominus vobiscum* with the dismissal (*procedamus in pace*—'let us go forth in peace'). The Hours have 3 psalms each without antiphons; at the 1st Hour: Ps. 53 [LXX 53 / MT 54] and 2 divisions of Ps. 118; at the 3rd, 6th, and 9th Hours: 3 divisions of Ps. 118; a hymn, a *capitulum*, a responsory, *Kyrie eleison* thrice, a prayer, and the dismissal. Vespers has: *Lucernarium* (a verse with a responsory), a hymn, then: on feasts *Responsorium in choro*, on weekdays and lesser feasts—an antiphon and 4 psalms, and on great feasts an antiphon and 2 psalms; thereafter on feasts *Notitia* (a proper commemoration), *Psallenda* or *Responsorium in baptisterio* (on weekdays), *commemorationes* (with an antiphon and *Kyrie eleison* 12), *Kyrie eleison* thrice, a prayer, and the dismissal. Compline: **"Our Father"**, the *Ave Maria*, **"O God, come to my assistance"**, a hymn, Pss. 4, 30, 90, 132, and 133 without antiphons, a *capitulum*, the Canticle of Simeon (**"Now lettest Thou Thy servant depart"** / *Nunc dimittis*), *Kyrie eleison* thrice, an antiphon unto the Theotokos, a prayer, and the dismissal [^1542]. Remarkable is the conjunction on feast days of Vespers with Matins or the Liturgy.

### The Mozarabic Rite

The Mozarabic rite has no continuous chanting of the Psalter in course; the psalms are proper unto the days. At Matins (in Spanish *matutinum*, elsewhere *nocturni*) the customary opening: *Kyrie eleison*, *Christe eleyson*, *Kyrie eleison*; **"Our Father"**; *Dominus sit semper vobiscum* ('The Lord be always with you'); a verse proper unto the feast, an antiphon from a psalm with a responsory (*responsus*), a canticle from the Prophets or New Testament with an antiphon and Alleluia (in the Forty Days [Great Lent] without it), another antiphon with Alleluia, a responsory, and a verse, the Blessing (*Benedictio*—the Canticle of the Three Holy Children), the 'sono' (*sonus*—a solemn chant), the Praises psalms (*Laudes*—Pss. 148–150), *capitula* (brief prayerful invocations), a hymn, and petitions (*preces*), resembling our litany-like petitions. *(Orig. p. 318)*
The Hours have a hymn, 3 psalms with antiphons, a responsory, *capitula*, *preces*, **"Our Father"**, and a dismissal prayer. At Vespers (*vesperum*), after the bringing in of the light, the deacon or cleric says in a low voice: '*Kyrie eleyson, Christe eleyson, Kyrie eleyson*. **Our Father**'; the priest: 'The Lord be always with you', the clergy: 'And with thy spirit'; then loudly and drawn out: 'In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, light with peace', and the response: 'Thanks be to God'. At the conclusion of the offices—**"Our Father"** with the response 'Amen' unto each petition, and unto the 4th petition concerning bread—'For Thou art God'; then a prayer for the diverse needs of the faithful (longer at *Laudes* and Vespers than at the remaining offices); the deacon: 'Bow down for the blessing' (*Humiliate vos ad benedictionem*); the priest—three petitions with the response 'Amen' unto each, and the verse: 'In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ let us go forth in peace' (*In nomine Domini Jesu Christi procedamus in pace*), response: 'Thanks be to God' (*Deo gratias*) [^1543]. In general, Mozarabic divine worship is distinguished by great originality, a wealth of hymns and poetic compositions of Christian authorship, and an abundance of ceremonial actions which the Roman rite doth not possess, while some of them recall Eastern practices. Thus at the daily offices, besides the bringing in of the light: a) the chanting of an 'Alleluiarium' before the readings (cf. among us the Alleluia before the Gospel); b) the washing of hands by the priest before the blessing at the end of the office; the priest washes his hands with the words: 'With a pure heart and pure body may we be accounted worthy to offer unto Thee, O Lord, this blessing'; c) the *laus*, during the singing of which the church is censed, sung with a verse in memory of the saint at nocturns and Vespers, very strongly recall the Eastern choral office of three-antiphon structure.

### The Gallican or Lyonese Rite

The Gallican or Lyonese rite (*Lugdunensis*) follows the Roman in the use of the Psalter, with minor departures at Prime and *Laudes*; the most important differences from the Roman: the non-use of hymns except at Compline, the customary opening consisting of the Lord's Prayer alone (also at Compline), and at Matins on weekdays 1 nocturn with 3 readings. *(Orig. p. 319)* on feasts 3 nocturns and 9 readings; *Laudes* begins directly with the psalms (there are no opening verses nor the Canticle of Zechariah); at all the Hours the psalms are sung continuously under a single antiphon and with a single 'Glory' at the end; at the Hours there are no hymns, while the *capitulum* and responsory are sung only on feasts; the Psalter at the 1st Hour is distributed differently than in the Roman rite: on weekdays from Pss. 11 to 14 and 2 divisions of Ps. 118, and on Saturday and Sunday from Pss. 99 to 117; consequently at the 1st Hour in that same period, instead of Ps. 117, Ps. 92 is used; on weekdays at the 1st Hour Ps. 53 (**"Save me, O God, by Thy name"**) and 2 divisions of Ps. 118, and on Sunday Pss. 9, 21–25, 117, and 2 divisions of Ps. 118. The Hours conclude with the psalm **"Out of the depths"** (*De profundis* / Ps. 129 [LXX 129 / MT 130]) with a collect for the departed, and the antiphon of the Most Holy Virgin closing the Roman Hours is sung only at the 9th Hour and Compline. At Vespers the *Magnificat* on certain feasts has an antiphon intercalated 8 times between the verses (cf. among us **"More honorable than the Cherubim"**). Compline has no introductory reading, but begins with **"Our Father"** and the verses: **"Turn us, O God"** and **"O God, come to my assistance"**, and has no *capitulum*; the conclusion is as at the Hours, with the addition of the antiphon of the Most Holy Virgin. On certain days at *Laudes*, Vespers, and other offices there are special petitions (*preces*), litanies, and processions [^1544].
*(Orig. p. 320)*

### The Church Year

The condition of the Church Year in the 6th–8th centuries is sufficiently characterized by: a) the menologia and martyrologies that have come down unto us from this era; b) the activity of ecclesiastical hymnographers.

#### Martyrologies: a) The Pseudo-Hieronymian

The most ancient of such martyrologies is the so-called Hieronymian Martyrology (*Martyrologium Hieronymianum*), attributed unto Blessed Jerome, preserved in 8th-century manuscripts, and dating back no later than unto the second half of the 7th century [^1545]. The martyrology received its definitive redaction in Gaul and, in all likelihood, in Auxerre (this town is named 30 times, and all its bishops are included with the exception of one, whereas those of Lyons, for example, are far from all included, etc.). The martyrology contains within itself 6,000 names [^1546]. The majority of days have more than 10 commemorations, frequently 30–40, sometimes more than *(Orig. p. 321)* 1,000 commemorations, and once (June 2) 240; yet there are also days with only 3–4 names (Feb. 3, Oct. 26). The martyrology manifestly strives, in contrast unto the most ancient calendars, to embrace the entire universal Church, whereas sacramentaries even of the 9th–15th centuries intended for Gaul and Germany contain for the most part only Roman saints; in this regard all subsequent Western martyrologies follow the Hieronymian Martyrology (those of Ado, Usuard, Notker, and Rabanus Maurus). The commemorations of Eastern saints are in the same scope as in the 4th-century Syriac martyrology, and either the author utilized it or they shared a common primary source; the Roman martyrs, apparently, are taken from the *Depositio martyrum* (see above, p. 307); of Roman popes there are 4 more than in Philocalus (see *ibid.*), beginning with Cornelius (251) and ending with Leo I († 461); for some of them the day of consecration is also indicated; the author also used the Carthaginian calendar; there are many Gallic saints; beside the names the hierarchical rank is frequently indicated; the city is indicated for the most part, sometimes only the country; very often the designation: 'in Africa' (without specifying a city); sometimes—*alibi* ('elsewhere'). Of Old Testament saints: Haggai—Jan. 4, Habakkuk—Jan. 15, Job—May 9, the Three Holy Children—Apr. 24, Aaron—July 1, Elisha—Aug. 29, the Sacrifice of Isaac—March 25 (likewise the day of Christ's death), and the exit of Noah from the Ark—April 28. There are Symeon the God-Receiver on January 6, Martha and Mary on Jan. 7, the Conception of John the Baptist on Sept. 24, and his Nativity and Repose as among us. Of the Apostles, only Matthew is missing; James, the Brother of the Lord, on March 25, because he was slain at Pascha; on Jan. 25 'the Translation of Paul' (today his 'Conversion'). Of the venerable fathers: Anthony the Great on Jan. 17, Symeon the Stylite on Jan. 5. All the Twelve Great Feasts are present, except the Transfiguration and the Entry of the Theotokos; furthermore—the Departure of Jesus from Egypt on Jan. 7, and the Beginning of the Lord's Preaching on May 1.

#### b) The Lesser Roman and c) Silos Martyrologies

The further development of the martyrology in the West proceeded (in contrast unto the East) by way of its abbreviation; the reason was the absence of all information concerning the majority of the saints in the Hieronymian Martyrology, which excited doubt as unto their existence, and furthermore—its inconvenience for liturgical use. Thus considerably briefer than the Hieronymian Martyrology is the so-called Lesser Roman Martyrology (*Martyrologium Romanum Parvum*), first cited by Ado in the 9th century (see below) and attributed by him unto an unknown Roman pope. Judging by the fact that it shows the Feast of All Saints on November 1, but still as a local Roman feast—a feast established by Pope Gregory III (731–741)—the martyrology is no earlier than this period. It exhibits, on the one hand, traits of greater antiquity in comparison with the Hieronymian, and on the other—marks of significant development. Thus the majority of names do not possess the title 'St.' or 'Bl.'; 7 days have no commemorations; daily there are 2–3 commemorations; vigils occur only for the Nativity of Christ and the Martyr Laurence; there are Apostles of the Seventy *(Orig. p. 322)* and Apostolic Fathers; more Old Testament saints; and the Exaltation of the Holy Cross on Sept. 14 is present [^1547]. This must be a very ancient local martyrology (Spanish? on account of the vigil for Laurence), later supplemented in places. Another remarkable local Western martyrology is that preserved in a manuscript no later than the 10th century, which belonged unto the Monastery of St. Sebastian in Silos (central Spain) [^1548] and containing a lectionary compiled, in all likelihood, c. 650, and a martyrology of 925–1000. The lectionary is an important monument of the ancient Spanish rite, distinct both from the Roman and from the South-Spanish Mozarabic: there is the practice of catechumenate; on the Saturdays of the Forty Days [Great Lent] there is no fasting; the Sundays after Theophany and after Pentecost are not indicated; the Apostle James is absent (in Spain!); the Annunciation is on December 28, in accordance with canon 1 of the Tenth Council of Toledo (656); the 'Crushing' (*allisio*) of the Holy Innocents is on January 8 (not December 27 or 29); the Feast of the Holy Cross is on May 3 (not September 14). The martyrology, although later than the lectionary, bears the imprint of great antiquity. Beside certain names the title is not 'saint' (*sanctus*) but *domnus* (4 of them Toledan); of feasts of the Theotokos there are only the Annunciation and the Dormition (*assumptio*) on August 15 [^1549].

#### d) The Constantinopolitan Martyrology of the Eighth Century

Of the same local type is the most ancient Constantinopolitan 'Menologion of the Festal Gospels of the Whole Year' (*Μηνολόγιον τῶν εὐαγγελίων ἑορταστικῶν*) in a Greek codex of Gospel *(Orig. p. 323)* lections. In favor of its Constantinopolitan provenance speaks the mention of local sites, local commemorations (May 11 [Foundation of Constantinople] and October 26 [Great Earthquake]), and 29 patriarchs from Metrophanes (306–326) unto Paul the New (either Paul III, 686–693, or Paul IV, 780–784). This last commemoration indicates likewise the date of compilation; that it took place immediately following the first Iconoclastic persecution is shown by the absence of commemorations of the champions of the holy icons of this era as being very recent, even Patriarch Germanus († 740), John of Damascus, and others. The menologion contains commemorations for 143 days, for the most part 2, rarely 2–3; in February there are 6 commemorations, in March and April 4 each (Lent). After Constantinopolitan saints, the most numerous are those of Asia Minor; the most renowned patriarchs and saints of the entire East are present, even Anastasius the Persian († 625, January 22); popes are absent; of Western saints there are only Laurence, Gervasius, and Protasius. The commemorations almost all fall on our present dates (only the Holy Innocents on December 31) and diverge from Roman dates. For the first time appear SS. Constantine and Helen on May 21; Justinian and Theodora likewise occur on November 14 (the day of Justinian's death), but without the title 'saint'. There are no Constantinopolitan bishops prior unto Metrophanes. For the Annunciation, the Dormition, and St. John Chrysostom (November 11) a *pannychis* (*παννυχίς*) is appointed; on the eves of the Nativity of Christ and Theophany—a *paramone* (*παραμονή* [vigil / eve]) [^1550].

In the 6th–8th centuries, similarly unto the Greek and Roman, the calendars of the Nestorians, Armenians, Copts, and Abyssinians, who had separated from the Eastern Church, likewise assumed nearly their present form.

### The Nestorian Church Year

The Nestorian church year possesses only a few immovable feasts; consequently, the church year is determined by Pascha unto a greater degree than among us. The beginning of the year among the Nestorians is reckoned from the Nativity of Christ, properly speaking from the 4 preparatory Sundays preceding it (as among the Roman Catholics), which are called Annunciation Sundays (the Annunciation is celebrated during these Sundays, whereas under March 25 there is merely a calendar notice of the event), and the New Year is celebrated on the first of these 4 Sundays. The feast of the Nativity of Christ is the most solemn and constitutes with Theophany a special festal period of 12 days (as among us). Commemorations of saints among the Nestorians, in order to avoid coinciding with Sundays and feasts, are assigned unto the Fridays of almost the entire year: the first Friday after the Nativity of Christ is dedicated unto the Holy and Blessed Lady Mary (cf. among us the Synaxis of the Most Holy Theotokos); the 1st Friday after Theophany—unto John the Forerunner (preceded by a three-day fast); the 2nd—unto the Apostles Peter and Paul; the 3rd—unto the 4 Evangelists; the 4th—unto the Protomartyr Stephen; the 5th—unto the three Greek Doctors: Diodore, Theodore, and Nestorius; the 6th—unto the three Syriac Doctors: Ephrem, Narsai, and Abraham; the 7th—unto the patron saint of the church; the 8th—unto Adam *(Orig. p. 324)* and all the departed. After the Sundays of Epiphany, of which there may be 5 to 8 (if fewer than 8, then on Fridays two commemorations are combined), follow the Sundays of Great Lent, three weeks before which the Nestorians observe the Fast of the Ninevites (on Monday, Tuesday, and Wednesday of our Week of the Publican and Pharisee, which for this reason is made fast-free among us). After Pentecost follow the 7 Weeks of the Apostles; on the Friday of the 3rd of these weeks occurs the 'Feast of God' or 'Thou Shalt Wash Me' (named after a special ceremony) in honor of the Holy Trinity (while Pentecost is solely in honor of the Descent of the Holy Spirit; cf. among Roman Catholics the Feast of the Holy Trinity on the 1st Sunday after Pentecost). Following the 7 'Weeks of the Apostles' come the 7 'Weeks of Summer', after them the 7 'Weeks of the Prophet Elias', 1 to 3 (the number depending on the Paschal cycle) 'Weeks of St. Moses', and 4 Weeks of the 'Dedication of the Church' or 'Entrance into the Temple', so named because on the first Fridays of each cycle one of these three commemorations is celebrated. The year thus always comprises 42 weeks or 364 days; the days lacking to complete the full solar year are supplemented by an intercalary week every 7 years. The immovable feasts are: the Transfiguration of the Lord on August 6; the 'Passing of the Virgin' on August 15; the 'Nativity of the Lady Mary' on September 8; the 'Finding of the Cross' on September 13; the Holy Martyr George on April 24 (if it coincides with Bright Week, the Friday of Renewal Week, or Sundays, it is transferred unto the 1st Friday after the Dormition). Thus of our Twelve Great Feasts only the Entry into the Temple is absent (as well as the Conception). Every Wednesday is dedicated unto the Most Holy Virgin, Friday unto the Sufferings of Christ, and Saturday unto the Veneration of the Cross. The services of the diverse days of the year possess very little in common with one another: not only doth each Sunday have a proper service, but almost every day of the week as well; in total there are approximately 220 services [^1551].

### The Armenian Church Year

The principal peculiarity of the Armenian menologion in comparison with the Greek is that the majority of commemorations in it are movable. Specifically, the Transfiguration is celebrated on the 7th Sunday after Pentecost and together with the Sunday of Arachavorats (corresponding unto our Sunday of the Publican and Pharisee) forms the Paschal cycle of the year (Pascha falling, as among us, between March 22 and April 25), consisting of 24 weeks; for the remaining 28 weeks the reckoning is by the feasts and fasts that occur in this period: first come the Sundays after Transfiguration, then the Sundays after the Assumption [Dormition], after the Exaltation, then after the Fast of Hisnakats (the 'Pentecost' Fast, beginning on the Sunday nearest November 18), and after the Nativity of Christ or Theophany. The Assumption and the Exaltation are celebrated on the Sundays nearest unto our dates for these feasts. The remaining feasts are immovable: the Nativity of Christ and Theophany [Baptism] on January 6; the Meeting of the Lord [Hypapante] on February 14; the Annunciation on April 7; the Nativity of the Most Holy Theotokos, the Entry into the Temple, and the Conception, as among us; feasts in honor of the Savior, the Cross (apart from the Exaltation: the Finding and the Apparition), the Church (the Dedication of the Cathedral of Etchmiadzin), and the Theotokos (apart from our Twelve Great Feasts: the Conception, the Deposition of the Robe, and of the Cincture) are accounted dominical (*derunakan*), possessing *(Orig. p. 325)* a forefeast or vigil and an 8-day afterfeast; the afterfeast is almost equal in solemnity unto the feast itself and unto Sunday, so that there are 140 'dominical' days in the year (on all of which marriages are prohibited). The feasts of the saints are all movable, because they must not be celebrated on dominical days or during fasts; during the course of the week, therefore, saints may be celebrated only on Monday, Tuesday, Thursday, and Saturday; during multi-day fasts—only on Saturday; throughout the entire period of Pentecost saints are not celebrated at all, with the exception of the commemoration of the Beheading of the Forerunner on Holy Saturday (at the Liturgy only; the Nativity of John the Baptist is celebrated in January) and the commemoration of Elias on Trinity Sunday [^1552]. The most important commemorations of saints—St. Elias, the Apostle James, and Gregory the Illuminator of Armenia—are preceded by fasts. There occur such commemorations as: the Creation of the World on Great Monday; the Destruction of Sodom on Great Wednesday; and the Old Testament Ark and the New Testament Church on the eve of the Transfiguration [^1553].

### The Copto-Abyssinian Church Year

The Coptic and Abyssinian menologia, closely related to one another, diverge considerably from the Greek and Latin both in their present form and in antiquity [^1554]. Their Monophysite character is discernible in that they contain, and that several times a year, the commemoration of Severus, Patriarch of Antioch, as well as of other Monophysite teachers. Their most sharp and conspicuous distinction from the Orthodox and Western calendars is a different system of chronology, by virtue of which all Julian and Gregorian calendar dates fall upon different days of the Coptic and Abyssinian months. The latest of the Orthodox saints in the Copto-Abyssinian calendars are Symeon the Stylite († 596) and Thomas, Patriarch of Constantinople (601–611). Yet of the ancient saints of the Greek Church many are absent from the Coptic calendars: absent, for example, in the most ancient of them are Ignatius the God-Bearer, John Chrysostom, and Ephrem the Syrian (whereas in the later ones they are present). The Twelve Great Feasts are all present as among us, with only the Entry into the Temple lacking (among the Copts). In the most ancient Coptic calendar the 'Feast of the Theotokos' occurs on the 21st day of the following months: January, March, May, July, and October; in another calendar—on the 21st day of every month; the Nativity of the Theotokos on April 26 and September 7; certain Apostles (for instance, both Jameses) likewise occur twice a year; the Archangel Michael 8 times a year; the Martyr or 'Apostle' Thecla 5 times. This peculiarity of the Coptic calendar is developed still further by the Abyssinian, which repeats the principal commemorations every month: thus on the 12th day (= the 8th according unto our reckoning) of each month occurs the commemoration of the Archangel Michael; on the 19th—of the Archangel Gabriel and the other incorporeal powers; on the 21st—of the Mother of God *(Orig. p. 326)*; on the 28th—of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob; on the 27th—the Crucifixion ('Salvation of the World'); on the 29th—the Nativity of Christ. There are commemorations of the Angels Raphael, Uriel, Raguel, and of the following Old Testament personages: Adam and Eve, Noah, Samson, Solomon, Sirach, Esther, Judith, Susanna 'the Pure', Pilate and his wife; the 4 Apocalyptic Living Creatures and the 24 Elders. The following events are likewise celebrated: the Translation of Enoch unto heaven, the Entrance of Noah into the Ark and his Departure therefrom, the Standing Still of the Sun by Joshua the Son of Nun, the Annunciation unto Joachim concerning the Birth of the Virgin, the Purification of Anna on the 80th day after the Birth of the Most Holy Virgin, the Journey of Jesus Christ into Egypt, the Flight of Jesus Christ from Mehs to Qosqam in Egypt, the Miracle in Cana of Galilee, the Imprisonment of John the Baptist, the Translation of the Head of John the Baptist, the Synaxis of the Apostles with the Savior, and the Second Repose of Lazarus [^1555].

### The Cycle of the Principal ("Twelve Great") Feasts

A review of the menologia of the 6th–8th centuries hath demonstrated that the church year both of the East and of the West had already formed down unto the minutest details of its present aspect; it remained for it subsequently only to receive into itself later saints. The natural consequence of the multiplication of commemorations—with which, in all likelihood, all the days of the year were now everywhere occupied (as in the most ancient of the menologia of this era, the Pseudo-Hieronymian; while in the Constantinopolitan of the 8th–9th centuries half the days of the year are occupied, because there not only commemorations but also Gospel lections are indicated)—was the necessity of establishing a certain gradation in the celebration of these commemorations, the need to render certain of them, a select few, more solemn. When these commemorations were so few in the course of the year, as in the 4th–5th centuries, it was possible to celebrate them all with identical solemnity, which was indeed done at that time: there was no marked distinction between the manner of honoring a martyr and the greatest events from the life of the Savior. Nonetheless, already unto the Fathers of the 4th–5th centuries are attributed by later writers attempts to single out from among all commemorations the feasts in honor of the Savior into a category of special solemnity. In the homily on the Ascension attributed unto St. Epiphanius of Cyprus, 4 great feasts are enumerated (the Nativity of Christ, Theophany, the Resurrection, and the Ascension) [^1556]. St. Proclus, Patriarch of Constantinople († 447), enumerates 5 of them (adding the Descent of the Holy Spirit) [^1557]. In the words placed into the mouth of St. John Chrysostom by George Hamartolos (9th century), there are 7 such feasts (adding: the 'Saving Passion' and the 'Seventh Great, Unceasing, Awaited Day of the Universal Resurrection of the Dead') [^1558]. John, Bishop of Euboea (8th century), enumerates 11 principal feasts: all *(Orig. p. 327)* the present Twelve Great Feasts, excluding the Entry into the Temple, the Dormition, and Palm Sunday, with the addition of the Conception; in another passage he adds unto these feasts the Dormition as well [^1559]. Thus this era was already close unto distinguishing the feasts in honor of the Savior and the Mother of God into a category of the highest rank, and was even approaching the concept of the sacred number 12 for them. Nevertheless, even now these feasts were not yet separated from the others so sharply as they were subsequently. This is evident from the Festal Gospel (written in gilded letters) of the Sinai Library, wherein, alongside all our present 12 feasts (excluding Palm Sunday), there are Gospels appointed for a whole series of other days in the year: September 1, December 24, January 6, February 7 (St. Peter, in all likelihood the patron saint of the monastery), March 9, April 23, May 8, May 10 ('Dedication of the Theotokos of our Monastery'), June 29, August 29, and all Sundays; in a certain festal Apostolos of the 8th century several of these commemorations are absent (apart from special ones: September 8, March 9, and June 29 are lacking), but there are added: October 26, November 1 and 8, December 6 and 26, and June 24 [^1560].

The expansion and elevation of certain feasts was fostered likewise by the civil authority. Thus Emperor Justinian in 534 renewed the prohibition of judicial proceedings for December 25 and January 6 [^1561]. In 542 the same emperor, in all likelihood, celebrated for the first time in Constantinople the Feast of the Meeting of the Lord [Hypapante] and made it mandatory for the entire empire, in thanksgiving for the deliverance of Constantinople from a three-month pestilence and Antioch from an earthquake [^1562]. Unto Emperor Maurice (582–602) is attributed the introduction of the feasts of the Nativity of the Theotokos, the Annunciation, and the Meeting of the Lord (for the latter two, in all probability, their renewal) [^1563]. Of the Twelve Great Feasts, there originated in this era the Transfiguration (the earliest authentic homilies for this feast being those of St. Andrew of Crete), the Nativity of the Theotokos (likewise), and the Entry into the Temple (present in a Festal Gospel of 715).

### The Nativity Fast

In this same era the Nativity Fast received its origin in the East and its universal dissemination in the West. Its kernel, as we have seen, could have been the 4th of the 'fasts of the four seasons' [Ember fasts]. Yet from the 5th century there are reports for the West regarding a fast specifically preparatory unto the Nativity of Christ. Thus concerning Perpetuus, Bishop of Tours († 491), Gregory of Tours relates that from St. Martin's Day on November 11 until the Nativity of Christ he fasted on Mondays, Wednesdays, and Saturdays [^1564]. The Second Council of Tours (567) prescribes that monks fast *(Orig. p. 328)* on all days in December until the Nativity of Christ (canon 27). The Council of Mâcon (*Concilium Matisconense*, in Gaul) in 581 prescribes fasting on Mondays, Wednesdays, and Saturdays from November 11 until the Nativity of Christ, and the offering throughout all this time of the Sacrifices (*sacrificia*) according unto the order of the Forty Days [canon 9]. Later the fast was adopted in Rome and Italy. Augustine and Leo I make no mention of it, yet the series of homilies of Gregory the Great begins with discourses for the second Sunday of Advent (such being the name given unto the Nativity Fast, as a preparation for the coming, *adventus*, of the Savior). The Sacramentary of Pope Gelasius, assigned unto the 6th century, provides 5 masses (that is, for 5 weeks) of Advent; the ancient Spanish Silos Lectionary has the same number, whereas the Milanese and Mozarabic rites possess 6 weeks of Advent (42 days, corresponding unto our 40). However, the 7th-century Lectionary of Luxeuil (*Lectionarium Luxoviense*) and the so-called *Missale Gothicum* (*Gotico-Gallicanum*) begin with the vigil of the Nativity, and consequently have no Advent. Pope Gregory VII in the 11th century reduced the number of weeks of Advent unto 4 (in all likelihood, corresponding unto the 4,000 years according unto Roman chronology prior unto the Nativity of Christ). In the East the first indication of the Nativity Fast (from November 15) occurs in a Coptic calendar of the 8th century [^1565]. In the 9th century, as we shall see, the obligatoriness and duration of this fast were still disputed here.

### Ecclesiastical Chant

With the development of the church year in the 6th–8th centuries is closely linked the activity of the Eastern hymnographers of that era. On the one hand, it was evoked and expanded by this development; on the other hand, it contributed unto it, elevating ecclesiastical commemorations by hymns extolling them. Therefore this activity, no less than the history of menologia, may serve as an index of the growth and enrichment of the church year during this period.

### The Troparion and Sticheron (Venerable Auxentius)

Properly speaking, only from the 6th century did hymnographic creation in the East achieve immortality, since not a single hymn prior unto this time hath come down unto us, at least under its author's name. Evident it is that only now did such creative labor enter upon the true path. Remarkable it is that precisely in this era hymnography completely languished in the West, and local councils there, as we have seen, attempted definitively to bar its access unto church services. If we compare the Eastern hymns of that era with the Western, the cause of this difference will become manifest: Western compositions continued to content themselves with general, indefinite themes; Eastern hymns responded vividly unto the rapid development of the church year, striving to exhaust each ecclesiastical commemoration. Therefore Eastern hymnography could not cease so long as this development continued. A special invigoration of it is observable precisely toward the beginning of the 6th century in Constantinople, and for this invigoration it was indebted unto the above-mentioned *(Orig. p. 329)* St. Auxentius. From him date the most ancient forms of ecclesiastical song that have come down unto us: the troparion and the stichera. This Bithynian ascetic († 470), according unto the words of his biographer, for the people gathering at his cave 'composed troparia of two or three clauses, exceedingly pleasant and profitable, though simple, and caused them to chant them in a voice most simple and artless. When one verse had been repeated several times in alternating chant, they began at the command of the blessed one to chant the second, then the third, and the others in order.' The biographer cites specimens of these troparia of Auxentius: one of these specimens hath as its theme the angelic doxology of the Lord; another, God's creation of the world; the third, redemption; the fourth and fifth are of a penitential character; the sixth is a glorification of the saints (**"Rejoice in the Lord, O ye righteous, and pray for us. Glory to Thee, O Christ, God of the saints!"**). The biographer likewise observes that some remained at this common singing until the 3rd hour (of the morning), others until the 6th hour (9:00 a.m. and 12:00 noon), and that with special solemnity the venerable father himself pronounced the Canticle of the Three Holy Children with the refrain of the people: **"Praise and exalt Him supremely unto all ages"**, concluding this canticle with his own homily [^1566]. In this narrative is found an indication of the original manner of chanting troparia: each strophe was chanted twice by both choirs; an echo of this practice remains in our present chanting of the entire troparion twice or thrice, and on great feasts in the identical execution of the majority of stichera, irmoses, and troparia. In this same manner psalms were chanted in the 4th–5th centuries.

### The Kontakion

Yet very soon such singing was abandoned both for psalms and for the troparion. If for psalms it was abandoned under the influence of the desire to chant as great a number of them as possible (ascetics chanted the entire Psalter within twenty-four hours), for troparia it was abandoned owing unto the multiplication of these hymns. Then the thought arose, in place of the solemn congregational chanting of each verse in a troparion, to chant in this manner only its final verse as a refrain unto an entire series of troparia. With the change in the manner of chanting the troparion (*τρέπω* = I turn; *τρόπος* = among other things, melody, tune), the designation likewise had to change: such hymns came to be called *kontakion* (*κοντάκιον*), a corruption of *κονδάκιον* (a scroll [^1567], from *κόνταξ*—a rod or stick), in all likelihood because they drew after themselves an entire series of other hymns; these latter, supplementary unto the kontakion and of longer length, were called *oikos* (*οἶκος*—house, temple, household, or the 12th part of the zodiac [^1568]).

### Venerable Romanos and Other Authors of Kontakia

The founder of this genre of ecclesiastical song is considered to be St. Romanos the Melodist (6th century), a Syrian and chanter of Hagia Sophia in Constantinople; and his first kontakion *(Orig. p. 330)*, according unto tradition chanted by a special heavenly inspiration, was the kontakion for the Nativity of Christ, **"Today the Virgin giveth birth unto the Transcendent One"** (*"Deva dnes' Prekushchestvennago rozhdaet"* / *Ἡ Παρθένος σήμερον τὸν ὑπερούσιον τίκτει*): in a Greek Kondakarion of the 12th–13th centuries according unto MS No. 437 of the Moscow Synodal Library, unto this kontakion are appended 24 ikoi with the same conclusion as in the kontakion: **"A little child, God before the ages"** (*"Otrocha mlado prevechnyi Bog"*), bearing the acrostic: *τοῦ ταπεινοῦ Ῥωμανοῦ ὕμνος* ('A hymn of humble Romanos'); the number 24 corresponds unto the quantity of letters in the Greek alphabet and hath a parallel in Ps. 118 [LXX 118 / MT 119], which consists of 22 sections beginning in order with all the letters of the Hebrew alphabet. Even more closely corresponds unto the structure of this psalm the kontakion and ikoi of the Annunciation, constituting the so-called Akathist, arranged alphabetically and attributed by diverse scholars either unto St. Romanos, or unto Sergius I, Patriarch of Constantinople (610–638), or unto his referendary and deacon of Hagia Sophia, George of Pisidia [^1569]. In addition unto the kontakion and ikoi for the Nativity of Christ, such hymns bearing the name of Romanos in the acrostic have survived for other feasts as well. Thus in that same Kondakarion the name of Romanos is borne by the kontakia and ikoi for Pascha (**"Though Thou didst descend into the grave"** / *"Ashche i vo grob snizshel esi"* / *Εἰ καὶ ἐν τάφῳ κατῆλθες*), for Meatfare Sunday (**"When Thou comest, O God, upon earth with glory"** / *"Egda priideshi Bozhe"*), and for Meatfare Saturday (the 1st kontakion not being the present one)—comprising 1 kontakion and 24 ikoi each; for January 6, December 17 (the Prophet Daniel), June 29, the Sunday of the Veneration of the Cross, Great Friday, the Ascension, and Pentecost—comprising a kontakion and 18 ikoi each, including those lost (as indicated by the missing letters of the acrostic); for February 2 and Palm Sunday—a kontakion and 16 ikoi; for All Saints—a kontakion and 13 ikoi; and for November 1—a kontakion and 4 ikoi. In other Kondakaria there occur, bearing the name of St. Romanos in title or acrostic, kontakia and ikoi for the following feasts and in the following numbers: September 1—28; January 6—13; Great Monday—20; Great Tuesday—23; Great Wednesday—20; Great Thursday—25; on the Denial of Peter (at the Passions)—24; Great Friday (another set)—24; the Sunday of Antipascha [Thomas Sunday]—21; August 29—20; September 8—12; December 6—26; November 1—14. The number of ikoi in the first collection corresponds more or less unto the importance of the feast. As regards the ikoi in the other collections, the attribution of certain of them unto St. Romanos may be questioned, even if his name appears in the acrostic [^1570]; yet their very quantity demonstrates that they arose in that era when kontakia and ikoi occupied the same position in divine worship as in the days of St. Romanos, that is, during the predominance of the kontakion-based structure of liturgical services. Furthermore, the Akathist on the occasion of the deliverance of Constantinople from the invasion of the Avars under Emperor Heraclius, which constituted *(Orig. p. 331)* an entire all-night service, was not an extraordinary office, but an ordinary one for that period; unusual in it was only that it was heard entirely standing upright.—St. Romanos naturally found imitators, new creators of kontakia and ikoi, and these imitations could continue throughout the entire period of the kontakion-based liturgical system, until such time as the 'kanon', a new genre of hymnography, supplanted this system, just as the kontakion in its turn had once supplanted the troparion (while the troparion had perhaps arisen to replace the antiphon). In that same Kondakarion there occur in like quantity ikoi bearing the names of other authors, notably in an acrostic bearing the name of Cosmas (for the Dormition, the kontakion **"The Mother of God, vigilant in prayers"** / *"V molitvakh neusypaiushchuiu Bogoroditsu"* and 21 ikoi), the renowned creator of kanons, for whom it was natural to begin his hymnographic activity by imitating older models. In similar quantity (around 20) kontakia and ikoi were composed occasionally by other later hymnographers, such as George (9th century), author of kanons for the Entry into the Temple (23 ikoi); and especially numerous ones by a certain Studite. Yet the majority of ikoi in the most ancient Kondakarion are without the names of authors, the number of ikoi for each feast conforming unto its solemnity, as partly with Romanos: thus for the Transfiguration an unknown author provides the kontakion (the present one) and 22 ikoi; on the Sundays of Antipascha and All Saints the present kontakia and 11 ikoi each; for the Exaltation and November 8 the present kontakia and 10 ikoi each; on September 26, October 26, and January 7, besides the kontakion, 5 ikoi; on September 8 and July 20—4 ikoi; on September 1, July 1 and 27, August 2 and 29, and on the 1st Saturday of Lent—3 ikoi; there are also sets of 2 and 1.

vigilant in prayers** and 21 ikoi), the renowned creator of kanons, for whom it was natural to begin his hymnographic activity by imitating older models. In similar quantity (around 20) kontakia and ikoi were composed occasionally by other later hymnographers, such as George (9th century), author of kanons for the Entry into the Temple (23 ikoi); and especially numerous ones by a certain Studite. Yet the majority of ikoi in the most ancient Kondakarion are without the names of authors, the number of ikoi for each feast conforming unto its solemnity, as partly with Romanos: thus for the Transfiguration an unknown author provides the kontakion (the present one) and 22 ikoi; on the Sundays of Antipascha and All Saints the present kontakia and 11 ikoi each; for the Exaltation and November 8 the present kontakia and 10 ikoi each; on September 26, October 26, and January 7, besides the kontakion, 5 ikoi; on September 8 and July 20—4 ikoi; on September 1, July 1 and 27, August 2 and 29, and on the 1st Saturday of Lent—3 ikoi; there are also sets of 2 and 1.

### The Authors of Kanons

The first creator of kanons was, in all likelihood, St. Sophronius, Patriarch of Jerusalem († 644), a native of Damascus. He composed triodia [three-ode kanons] of a penitential character for all the days of the Forty Days [Great Lent] and for the Resurrection of Christ, which are no longer in use today (having been supplanted, in all probability, by Studite compositions); thus the original form of the kanon was the triodion, perhaps even the diodion [two-ode kanon], just as at Matins originally not all biblical canticles were chanted, but only several (as hath survived unto this day in Armenian and Roman Catholic worship). Apart from triodia, St. Sophronius wrote Anacreontic verses and epigrams for many feasts (evidently not intended for liturgical use). Under his name are inscribed in the most ancient manuscripts the Royal Hours of Great Friday, the Eve of the Nativity of Christ, and the Order of the Great Blessing of Water at Theophany. St. Andrew († c. 712) of the Lavra of St. Sabbas, subsequently Archbishop of Crete, was in all likelihood the first to write complete kanons [nine-ode kanons], yet he began with triodia, which he composed for all the days of Holy Week (now chanted at its Complines, having been supplanted at Matins by the triodia of Cosmas), with the exception of Holy Saturday; for the more solemn feasts he wrote complete kanons—those presently in use being: the Great Kanon, that for the Raising of Lazarus, the Sunday of the Myrrh-bearers, Mid-Pentecost, the Nativity of the Theotokos, *(Orig. p. 332)* the Conception of Anna, June 24 [Nativity of the Forerunner], and December 20 unto St. Ignatius the God-Bearer; those not presently in use: for the Exaltation, the Meeting of the Lord, June 29, July 23 (unto the Martyr Trophimus and his companions), and August 1 (unto the Maccabees). St. Germanus, Patriarch of Constantinople, who died in exile for the veneration of the holy icons (the son of an executed senator, previously Bishop of Cyzicus), composed kanons presently in use: for the Forefeast of the Exaltation, May 30 unto St. Isaacius, and June 17 unto the Martyr Hermias. St. Cosmas, Bishop of Maiuma, the elder foster-brother and fellow ascetic in the monastery of St. Sabbas of St. John of Damascus, who died shortly after him, wrote kanons or triodia or tetraodia [four-ode kanons] (the latter on Lazarus Saturday and Great Saturday having been transformed by others into complete kanons) for all the days of Holy Week from Lazarus Saturday and for the Twelve Great Feasts, except Pascha, the Ascension, the Nativity of the Most Holy Theotokos, the Entry into the Temple, and the Annunciation; in addition, kanons for December 26 unto the Ancestors of God, and April 23 unto the Great-Martyr George. St. John of Damascus († c. 780), at first a minister of the Caliph of Damascus, later a monk of the Monastery of St. Sabbas, a Jerusalem preacher, and a confessor for the holy icons, composed the Sunday kanons of the Octoechos for the 8 tones and kanons for the Twelve Great Feasts, except the Exaltation, the Entry into the Temple, the Meeting of the Lord, and Palm Sunday (for the Annunciation—a tetraodion or diodion); furthermore, kanons for Thomas Sunday; September 1 for the Beginning of the Indiction; September 13 for the Dedication; May 7 for the Apparition of the Cross; September 23 for the Conception of John the Forerunner; June 24 for his Nativity; August 29 for his Beheading; February 24 for the Finding of his Head; June 29 for the Apostles Peter and Paul; May 8 for John the Evangelist; November 30 for the Apostle Andrew; December 27 for the Archdeacon Stephen; October 1 for the Apostle Ananias; then unto saints (by choir): unto Righteous Job on May 6; unto prophets: Elias on July 20, Elisha on June 14, Isaiah on May 9; unto hierarchs: Righteous Lazarus (not in use), Hippolytus on January 30, Paul of Constantinople on November 6, Basil the Great on January 1, Gregory of Nyssa on January 10, John Chrysostom (two kanons) on January 27, Epiphanius of Cyprus on May 12; unto martyrs: Babylas on September 4, Autonomus on September 14, Euphemia on September 16, Thecla on September 24, Sergius and Bacchus on October 8, Epimachus on October 31, Cosmas and Damian (two kanons) on November 1, Akepsimas on November 3, Menas on November 11, Eustratius on December 13, Cyrus and John on January 31, Theodore the Recruit [Tyro] on February 17, Proterius on February 28 (not in use), the Forty Martyrs on March 9, George on April 23, Leontius on June 18, Julian of Cilicia on June 21; unto venerable fathers: Paul of Thebes on January 15, Arsenius on May 8, John the Dwarf [Colobos] on November 9, Onuphrius on September 8, Symeon of the Admirable Mountain on May 24, Maximus the Confessor on January 21. St. Stephen the Sabaite, that is, a monk of the Monastery of St. Sabbas († c. 807), wrote kanons for the Circumcision; Cyriacus the Hermit on September 29; the Venerable Fathers Slain at the Monastery of St. Sabbas on March 20; and St. Barbara and John of Damascus on December 4.—All these authors of kanons composed stichera likewise for certain commemorations. From this same period other hymnographers are known, such as Theodore of Sykeon, Bishop of Anastasiopolis (8th century), George, Bishop of Syra*(Orig. p. 333)*cuse († c. 669), and others, who left behind them several stichera and kanons.

### The Metrical Structure of Ecclesiastical Song

Greek ecclesiastical chant in all the indicated genres (troparion, kontakion, kanon, sticheron) of this era, as of subsequent periods, is constructed according unto a special poetic system: not the ancient metric system based upon the quantity (length and brevity) of syllables, but upon the so-called rhythmic system, based upon the number of syllables in a verse and the placement of accents upon them; this because the distinction between letters according unto their length and brevity had by that time already vanished from spoken speech. A certain Greek grammarian (Theodosius of Alexandria) states that whoever wishes to compose a canon must write troparia possessing the identical number of syllables and the identical accentuation as the Heirmos. In this manner accentuation plays the principal role in the construction of Greek hymns. For example, in the kontakion of the Nativity of Christ:

Ἡ παρθένος σήμερον  
Τὸν ὑπερούσιον τίκτει  
Καὶ ἡ γῆ τὸ σπήλαιον  
Τῷ ἀπροσίτῳ προσάγει…  

in the 1st and 3rd lines there are 7 syllables each, in the 2nd and 4th lines 8 each; in the 1st and 3rd lines accents fall upon the 3rd and 5th syllables, in the 2nd and 4th upon the 4th and 7th syllables. (In the translation into Church Slavonic, understandably, the rhythm is not preserved). For the purposes of this rhythm grammatical liberties are likewise permitted: thus in disyllabic particles, prepositions, and pronouns (*ἀλλά*, *παρά*, *ἐγώ*) the shifting of the accent unto the first syllable is allowed; trisyllabic words with accents upon the first or last syllable are in case of necessity recognized as possessing two accents, both upon the first and upon the last syllable (as is done likewise in Russian versification): *πόлемос*, *τάπεινος*. The poetic meter of Greek ecclesiastical hymns is confirmed likewise by the fact that many of them possess an acrostic (Slavonic: *krayegranesiye*) and rhyme; for example, in St. Romanos in the kontakion for the Nativity of Christ *σήμερον* rhymes with *σπήλαιον*, and *δοξολογοῦσι* with *ὁδοιποροῦσι* ("today" — "the cave", "they give glory" — "they travel") [^1571]. Yet it must be observed that the canons of St. John of Damascus for the Nativity of Christ (**"He saved the people"** [*Spase liudi* / *Ἔσωσε λαόν*]), Theophany (**"He traverses the sea"** [*Shestvuyet morskuyu* / *Στείβει θαλάσσης*]), and Pentecost (**"Covered by divine protection"** [*Bozhestvennym pokroven* / *Θείῳ καλυφθείς*]) are written in ancient classical *(Orig. p. 334)* meter, namely iambic trimeter, and their acrostics in dactylic hexameter (the latter being exceedingly difficult).

### Western Hymnography

Concerning the West, in view of the above-noted unfavorable attitude of ecclesiastical authority toward hymns during divine worship, only a few new hymns appeared in this era; their authors are either entirely unknown or doubtful (thus several hymns are attributed unto St. Gregory the Great).

### The Octoechos

With regard unto ecclesiastical chant, the present era accomplished especially much likewise in that only now was the cycle of liturgical chants definitively established both in the West and in the East. In the West this achievement is attributed unto Pope St. Gregory the Great; in the East, unto St. John of Damascus. According unto the words of his biographer, the Deacon John (9th century), St. Gregory assembled the melodies that had arisen across centuries in the Church, removed the less valuable, corrected the remainder, and supplied what was lacking; from the material thus obtained he compiled a new Antiphonary [^1572]. On the basis of this testimony the present Antiphonary of the Roman Church and the system of tones adopted therein are denominated Gregorian. A still later tradition attributes the ordering of ecclesiastical melodies in the East unto St. John of Damascus: unto his name and that of his teacher Cosmas is inscribed a musical treatise bearing the title 'The Hagiopolite' (*Sviatogradets*) [^1573]. As we have seen (see above, pp. 160–161), the ordering of church melodies must have begun far earlier than both Gregory the Great and John of Damascus; and tradition links the beginning of this ordering in the West with the name of St. Ambrose, whereas unto Gregory the Great is attributed solely the addition unto the 4 Ambrosian tones existing prior unto him—at the foundation of which lay the Dorian, Phrygian, Lydian, and Mixolydian modes (see *ibid.*)—of four new melodies kindred unto them, the 'plagal tones' (*toni plagales*), namely: the Hypodorian, beginning upon A and having its dominant upon the 6th degree; the Hypophrygian, beginning upon B with its dominant upon the 7th degree; the Hypolydian, upon F with its dominant upon the 6th degree; and the Hypomixolydian, upon D with its dominant upon the 7th degree. Thus were obtained 8 tones (subsequently a 9th was added, representing a mixture of the 2nd and 8th—*tonus peregrinus sive irregularis*). An identical number of tones and with an identical musical character was established, according unto tradition, by John of Damascus in the Eastern Church, only the reckoning of tones here is different: first come all the authentic tones, and *(Orig. p. 335)* then their plagal (*πλάγιοι*) counterparts, whereas in the West each authentic tone is followed immediately by its plagal:

| Tradition | Tone 1 | Tone 2 | Tone 3 | Tone 4 | Tone 5 | Tone 6 | Tone 7 | Tone 8 | Tone 9 |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Greek** | αʹ | βʹ | γʹ | δʹ | πλ. αʹ [*] | πλ. βʹ | βαρύς [**] | πλ. δʹ | — |
| **Slavonic** | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 | 8 | — |
| **Latin** | 1 | 3 | 5 | 7 [orig. 8] | 2 | 4 | 6 | 8 | 9 |

[*] *πλ. αʹ* — *πλάγιος πρῶτος*, plagal first.  
[**] *βαρύς* — heavy [grave], designating the melodic character of the chant instead of a numerical designation.  

In this manner the melodies of the two Churches are far closer unto one another than their liturgical rites [^1574]. Yet chant is indeed the very depth and soul of divine worship…  
*(Orig. p. 336)*

## B. The Liturgical Typikon from the Appearance of Its Complete Manuscripts

### From the 9th Century

Now it remained for the liturgical typikon to define itself only in the minutest details and particulars, and its history from this era onward must assume the character of an explanatory (*tolkovy*) Typikon. By the 9th century our Typikon had already essentially formed in its fundamental conception. Now complete manuscript copies thereof could make their appearance, which, by virtue of the preceding foundational labor, might diverge from one another only in non-essential particulars. Soon, moreover, even such divergence between them disappeared, and a single liturgical typikon arose for virtually the entire Eastern Church.

### The Typikon of the Great Church of Constantinople and the Sung Office

Nevertheless, even now such unification was long hindered by the existence within the sphere of influence of this increasingly unified typikon—the persistence of an entirely distinct liturgical rite competing with, if not surpassing it in antiquity: an order long maintained in the principal temple of the imperial capital, Hagia Sophia of Constantinople, and in the cathedrals of other major cities. We have in mind the so-called Typikon of the Great Church of Constantinople and the order of the Sung Office (*ᾀσματικὴ ἀκολουθία* / *Asmatike Akolouthia*), which is closely related unto it, if not identical with it.

The daily cycle of divine worship at Hagia Sophia of Constantinople hath remained unto this day an enigma, notwithstanding the fact that there hath come down unto us—and that in more than one redaction—a complete Typikon of this church from the 9th century [^1575], alongside several other monuments of this rite. In this Typikon there are indicated only the proper characteristics *(Orig. p. 337)* of divine worship for each day, and those mostly ceremonial; nowhere is a complete order of service provided, and exceedingly few hints are given regarding its constituent elements.

In order to comprehend these sparse intimations, one must bear in mind that the Typikon of the Great Church—that is, of Hagia Sophia of Constantinople—presupposes the services subsequently denominated the 'Sung Office' (*ᾀσματικὴ ἀκολουθία*). Its order is set forth in detail by St. Symeon, Archbishop of Thessalonica († 1430), who terms it the 'Office of the Typikon of the Great Church', adopted in all cathedral churches, yet adds that since the capture of Constantinople by the Latins (from 1204) this order had ceased to be observed even in the 'imperial city' itself, much less in other churches, and that in his day this order was preserved solely in the Cathedral of Thessalonica.

The designation 'Sung' St. Symeon explains by the circumstance that in this office 'nothing was uttered without chant (*χωρὶς μέλους*) except the prayers of the priest and the petitions (litanies) of the deacon' [^1576]. Such an order of worship could naturally develop in the magnificent cathedral of Hagia Sophia, erected in 532–538 by Emperor Justinian, which was the principal palatine church and was endowed with an extensive staff of clergy and cantors. Divine worship here could not fail to be distinguished by extraordinary solemnity and to acquire certain peculiarities in comparison not only with monasteries, but likewise with parish churches. The presence of the Emperor at divine services demanded not only solemn receptions for him, but likewise a certain adaptation of the liturgy unto him, in which he at times took an active part (performing censing, participating in entrances). In such divine worship certain elements could receive special development and elaboration, while others were relegated unto the background or even disappeared. Under such conditions divine worship could not easily admit (as it did not permit of excessive length) any additions, particularly of a monastic (ascetic) character, such as the mandatory chanting of the entire Psalter within a fixed *(Orig. p. 338)* period (kathismata and biblical canticles, that is, the canon) [^1577]. All of this we observe in the Typikon of Hagia Sophia and in the Sung Office as set forth by St. Symeon of Thessalonica. Yet it must be remembered that the order of the Sung Office given by St. Symeon is separated from the surviving Typika of the Great Church by five centuries, during which Constantinople and Hagia Sophia experienced such convulsions as devastation by the Crusaders. Following the expulsion of the latter, Hagia Sophia ceased to be a palatine church, since the emperors took up residence in another palace and attended divine worship in the Church of Blachernae, traveling unto Hagia Sophia only on solemn occasions. This could not fail to affect its typikon in the direction of diminishing solemnity and approaching the ordinary monastic-parochial order of services. In any event, the chanted order of services provided by Symeon of Thessalonica cannot be transferred in its entirety unto the practice of Hagia Sophia of the 9th–10th centuries, nor may one fill in from it the frequent silences of its contemporary Typikon. The same must be said concerning other surviving monuments of the Sung Office and rites of the Great Church, which for the most part are no older than the 15th century, such as, for example: the 'Order (*τάξις* / *taxis*) observed at Vespers, Matins, the Divine Liturgy, and the Consecration of a Bishop' in a 15th-century canonical manuscript collection of the Russian Skete of St. Andrew on Mount Athos [^1578], which hath Hagia Sophia in view, yet dates from an era later than the surviving complete Typika (it, moreover, describes exclusively patriarchal and imperial processions and contains virtually no liturgical directions); the 'Order of Sung Vespers' in a 16th-century Typikon of the Jerusalem Library [^1579], and others. (These monuments are important solely in that they may supplement Symeon of Thessalonica). Nor can the same be said of the treatise *De Officiis Aulae Byzantinae* [*De Ceremoniis*], attributed unto Emperor Constantine VII Porphyrogenitus (912–959), yet definitively redacted, in all likelihood, in the 11th century [^1580]: the liturgical directions occasionally provided therein are close in date unto the practice of the surviving complete Typika of the Great Church and may be adduced for their elucidation and supplementation. Nonetheless, a portion of the fragmentary indications of these Typika finds explanation in Symeon of Thessalonica and in the monuments mentioned; and, in any event, these Typika confirm the testimony *(Orig. p. 339)* of St. Symeon that the Great Church possessed a distinctive liturgical order, justly denominated 'Sung', distinct from the contemporary practice of monasteries and perhaps of other churches, and partially coinciding with the 'Sung Office' of the era of the Hierarch of Thessalonica.

### Vespers and Matins according to the Typika of the Great Church of Constantinople of the 9th–11th Centuries

Apart from the Liturgy, the Great Church of the 9th–11th centuries possessed, apparently, among its services only Vespers and Matins, occasionally (on the eves of feasts) after Vespers a *pannychis* (*παννυχίς*, an all-night vigil distinct from Matins), and during Great Lent the office of *trithekte* (*тритекти*). The Hours are not mentioned. Of the constituent elements of Vespers there is indicated, at least at times, as its beginning: **"Incline Thine ear, O Lord"** (*"Prikloni Gospodi ukho Tvoye"*), that is, Ps. 85, with which the Vespers of the Sung Office began according unto Symeon of Thessalonica; after it a certain *τὸ τελευταῖον* (in all likelihood, the final antiphon of the opening antiphons of Vespers: see below) and **"Lord, I have cried"** (invariably); after **"Lord, I have cried"** there is indicated a troparion or '3 small antiphons' (at times these occur after the prokeimenon) or immediately the *synapte* prayer with petition (*εὐχὴ συναπτὴ μετὰ αἰτήсеως*), that is, litanies, in all probability the Great Synapte or Augmented Litany with the Litany of Supplication (at times this occurs after the prokeimenon and antiphons), then the Entrance (at times), the prokeimenon, and readings (paremias); in conclusion invariably—a troparion, at times thrice with the verses of the psalm and the *perisse* (*καὶ τὴν περισσήν*, that is, the troparion in conclusion; thus on the eve of Pentecost, followed by the deacon's exclamation: **"Wisdom!"**, whereupon the reading of the Apostle begins until the pannychis) [^1581]. Still fewer are the indications regarding the composition of Matins. At it there is customarily named the *amomos* (*ἄμωμος*, the "Blameless"), that is, indubitably, Ps. 118 [the 17th Kathisma], indicated in the 1st part of Matins of the Sung Office likewise by Symeon of Thessalonica; the Blameless [Amomos] was divided into 3 antiphons, and at the third a troparion was at times appointed and an entrance took place [^1582]. Apparently on more solemn Sundays (Cheesefare Sunday, Palm Sunday, Thomas Sunday [Antipascha], Myrrhbearers Sunday) and kindred days (Lazarus Saturday, Great Saturday, from Pascha through Wednesday inclusive, the Saturday of the 2nd Week after Pascha for the commemoration of James the Brother of the Lord, at Ascension, and at Pentecost) [^1583], after the Amomos there was appointed a certain *Eulogetos* (*Εὐλογητός*, "Blessed", perhaps the verse of Ps. 118: **"Blessed art Thou, O Lord"**, in an especially solemn execution or with certain refrains after the manner of our present troparia unto it [the Evlogitaria]). On immovable Great Feasts there is no mention at Matins either of the Amomos or of the *Eulogetos*; yet in place of both at the Nativity of Christ there stand 18 antiphons *σὺν τοῦ μεγάλου* ("with the Great"—in all likelihood the beginning of a certain hymn), one of two troparia, then another troparion at **"God is the Lord"**; consequently on all immovable feasts (and perhaps on certain Sundays as well, since the Matins of some of them likewise begins with the indication of a troparion at the 50th Psalm) the Amomos was not chanted and, in all probability, *(Orig. p. 340)* was replaced by another psalm. In a manuscript typikon of the Moscow Synodal Library, No. 333–391, of the 14th century (fol. 150v) there is an article under the heading: 'And these are the kathismata for feasts according to the typikon of the cathedral church', appointing one kathisma for each of the major feasts and ranks of saints (such kathismata are known likewise unto the most ancient Studite typika): for the Nativity of Christ—the 10th Kathisma; Theophany—the 16th; Transfiguration—the 12th; Exaltation—the 13th; Ascension—the 7th; Descent of the Holy Spirit—the 19th; Dormition—the 17th; Entry into the Temple—the 6th; for hierarchs and unmercenaries—the 5th; for martyrs—the 9th. It may be that these kathismata replaced the Amomos on feast days. All of this may be designated the first part of Matins according unto the ancient Sophia Typikon. From this type of Matins, provided by the Patmos manuscript of the Typikon (the earliest of the surviving copies), the first part of Matins in the Dresden manuscript (the latest, yet no later than the 10th–11th century) diverges considerably: for the Exaltation it is stated here concerning Matins: 'there is chanted *τὸ πρῶτον* (the first, the 1st antiphon?) of the day and 12 antiphons with the canon (*μετὰ καὶ τοῦ κανόνος*), and there is chanted likewise the Polyeleos and the *Benedicite* [*Благословите*]'. What is meant here by the canon, the polyeleos, and the *Benedicite* (the Canticle of the Three Holy Children?), it is difficult to say, yet scarcely do the first two terms bear their present significance. The subsequent constant, if not the most central, portion of Sophia Matins was constituted by Psalm 50; for all festal and many Sunday Matins there is invariably indicated a troparion *εἰς τὸν Ν* (that is, at Psalm 50), at times two troparia; the troparion was chanted, if not with every verse of the psalm, then at least with several; in the Dresden manuscript at the above-mentioned Matins a proper troparion is appointed for each of the first five verses of Psalm 50 and for the Doxology (*Glory...*) [^1584]. In addition unto Psalm 50, there is mentioned in this part of Matins **"Glory to God in the highest"** [^1585] (the Great Doxology). From these fragmentary and incomplete indications, naturally, it is impossible to construct an exhaustive conception of the order of Vespers and Matins at Hagia Sophia in the 9th century; nevertheless, scarcely is it accidental that no mention is made of such prayers as **"Vouchsafe, O Lord"** and **"Now lettest Thou Thy servant depart"** at Vespers, nor of the opening morning psalms (the Six Psalms), the biblical canticles, and the Gospel at Matins, the more so as several of these elements are not mentioned by Symeon of Thessalonica either. Their absence is all the more remarkable given that they entered into the composition of the services, at least in certain localities, as early as the 4th century, and some not only in the East but in the West as well. If silence concerning them is not accidental, is this not an abbreviation of the service for a palatine cathedral? Nevertheless, the rite in general bears the imprint of the most profound antiquity: a limitation of hymns (troparia) similar unto Western liturgical orders, and a predominant position of antiphons and prokeimena (= responsories).

### The Sung Vespers

The order of Vespers and Matins provided by St. Symeon already contains a series of accretions from other typika (monastic and, in all likelihood, parochial churches). We shall set it forth, supplementing and elucidating St. Symeon by the data of the two above-mentioned monuments (the 'Order' according unto the Athos manuscript and the Sung *(Orig. p. 341)* Vespers according unto the Jerusalem manuscript). Prior unto the beginning of Vespers the temple was filled with sweet fragrance (not by censing, but in all probability as is done among us at present before Paschal Matins). 'The priest, having taken his stand before the holy table', exclaimed: **"Blessed is the Kingdom…"**; not **"Blessed is our God…"**, observes St. Symeon, 'for this is not customary in the Sung Office, since such (the latter exclamation) hath reference solely unto Old Testament Scripture… thus the order of the Liturgy alone hath remained (with regard unto the opening exclamation) faithful unto the ancient rite'. Yet in the order of the 15th-century Athos manuscript the exclamation is: **"Blessed is our God"** or **"Blessed is the Kingdom"**. Following the petitions of the Great Synapte—which in the 'Order of Sung Vespers' of the Jerusalem manuscript possesses entirely our present composition—the chanting of 3 antiphons begins: specifically, after **"Help us, save us"** before **"Remembering our all-holy, immaculate…"** in the Great Synapte, according unto Symeon of Thessalonica the cantors (*οἱ ψάλται*) chant: **"Hear me. Glory to Thee, O God!"**, while according unto the Jerusalem manuscript the domestikos exclaims: **"And hear me"**; this is the second half of the 1st verse of Psalm 85, which constitutes the 1st Antiphon of Vespers; it was proclaimed prior unto the chanting of the entire psalm either as its theme or as a model for chanting the whole psalm according unto it [^1586]; characteristic is the introduction of this refrain into the interior of the litany before its conclusion, in all likelihood as a token of the close bond between psalm-praise and Christian prayer; in Symeon of Thessalonica unto this refrain are added several others: **"Incline Thine ear, O Lord, and hear me"**, **"Glory to God in the highest"**, **"Heaven and earth are full of Thy glory"**, **"Blessed is the glory of the Lord"** (all angelic hymns). Following the exclamation of the Great Synapte the entire 85th Psalm, **"Incline Thine ear, O Lord"**, is chanted by verses between both choirs with the refrain unto each verse: **"Glory to Thee, O God!"** According unto the Jerusalem manuscript, the domestikos chants the 1st verse of the psalm and for the final time the refrain unto it after *Glory... Now and ever...* After Psalm 85, according unto Symeon, the priest recites the Little Litany, and the chanter (*ψάλτης*), after **"Help us, save us"**, chants: **"The world (*τὴν οἰκουμένην*), Alleluia"**. Symeon of Thessalonica connects 'the world' grammatically with 'Help us, save us'; yet the analogy with the first antiphon compels us to perceive in this word a fragment of the psalm that constituted the 2nd Antiphon [^1587]. The Jerusalem manuscript makes no mention of this remnant of the 2nd Antiphon and indicates after the 1st Antiphon not the entire Little Litany, but only from **"Remembering our all-holy, immaculate…"** After the Little Litany, according unto Symeon, 'the chanter chants according unto the day the prokeimenon, which is called likewise the final (*τελευταῖον*) antiphon on account of the other antiphons read formerly, yet now omitted; on Saturday at Vespers (as such a prokeimenon) there is said: **"Let God arise"** (*ἀναστήτω ὁ Θεός*)'. In the Jerusalem manuscript in place of this 'prokeimenon' there is indicated: **"Unto the saints that are in His earth hath the Lord been wonderful"** (that is, Ps. 15:3 [16:3]), **"Alleluia, Glory..."** *(Orig. p. 342)* **"Now and ever..."**; perhaps this 'prokeimenon' is not for Sunday (although taken from a psalm containing a prophecy of the Resurrection of Christ, and the entire psalm might have been chanted with this refrain), but for ordinary Vespers and adapted unto the commemorations of diverse saints. All these antiphons constitute the introductory portion of Vespers, after which follows its principal part: Psalm 140, **"Lord, I have cried"**, with the refrain (*ὑπόψαλμα*) on one Sunday: **"Thy life-bearing Resurrection, O Lord, do we glorify"**, and on another: **"Thy saving Resurrection, O Lord, do we glorify"**; in the Jerusalem manuscript there is indicated the refrain: **"An evening sacrifice do we offer unto Thee, O Christ, which do Thou receive through Thy saints and save us"**—a refrain evidently adapted (like the preceding prokeimenon) not unto Sunday, but unto the commemoration of saints. At the verse of Psalm 140: **"For unto Thee, O Lord"**, the Entrance with lamps and censers took place (according unto St. Symeon), for which reason this verse according unto Symeon was pronounced by the chanter (according unto the Jerusalem manuscript, by the domestikos), turned toward the west, bowing unto the priest and 'as it were summoning him as one bearing the image of the Lord'; after the Entrance, accompanied by the prayer, as at present: **"Evening and morning and at noon"**, and by the exclamation: **"Wisdom! Stand upright!"**, according unto St. Symeon 'hymns of the Resurrection' are chanted upon the ambo, while according unto the Jerusalem manuscript from the verse: **"If Thou, Lord, shouldest mark iniquities…"**, stichera are chanted, first one set, and then another. During these hymns or stichera censing is performed, according unto Symeon by the priest or deacon, and according unto the Jerusalem manuscript by the deacon. The psalm concludes with *Glory... Now and ever...* According unto the 'Order' of the Athos manuscript, the Entrance takes place at *Glory...*, and the exclamation **"Wisdom! Stand upright!"** is made at the conclusion of the stichera (as at present). There follows the prokeimenon of the day (according unto Symeon: **"The Lord is King"**), the Litany: **"Let us all say…"** (according unto the Jerusalem manuscript; according unto Symeon: 'for all the faithful, emperors, and priests'), and the Little Litany with the exclamation, according unto Symeon: **"For Thine it is to have mercy…"**, and according unto the Jerusalem manuscript: **"For good art Thou…"** Then follow the Small Antiphons, so named because they consist not of entire psalms, but of 4 verses. The 1st Antiphon hath the refrain: **"By the prayers of the Theotokos…"**, with the verses of Psalm 114 [116:1–9]: **"I am well pleased, that the Lord hath heard…"** (in the Jerusalem manuscript: **"Because He hath inclined His ear…"**), **"Gracious is the Lord and righteous…"**, **"I will walk well-pleasing before the Lord…"** *Glory... Now and ever...* The Little Litany with the exclamation: **"For Thou art our God…"** The 2nd Antiphon hath the refrain: **"Save us, O Son of God, Who art risen from the dead…"** (on weekdays: **"Who art wonderful in the saints…"**), with the verses of Psalm 115 [116:10–19]: **"I believed, therefore I spoke: but I was humbled exceedingly"** [LXX Ps. 115:1], **"What shall I render unto the Lord…"**, **"I will take the cup of salvation…"** *Glory...* **"Only-Begotten Son..."** *Now and ever...* **"The all-glorious"** Mother of God. The Little Litany with the exclamation: **"For holy art Thou…"** The 3rd Antiphon hath the refrain: **"Holy God…"**, with the verses of Psalm 116 [117]: **"O praise the Lord, all ye nations…"**, **"The truth of the Lord endureth forever…"**, **"For His mercy is confirmed upon us…"** *Glory... Now and ever...* During the singing of the Trisagion all stand uncovered. The hierarch blesses the people thrice from his place. Then, according unto Symeon of Thessalonica, there follows the 'Great' (Augmented?) Litany and the petitions, that is, **"Let us complete our evening prayer"** (the Litany of Supplication). Following it, according unto the Jerusalem manuscript, there follow 'the dismissory troparion of the day and the dismissal'. In Symeon of Thessalonica the conclusion of Vespers is more complex. On Sunday after the Litany of Supplication 'there takes place a behind-the-ambo (not in the narthex!) litiya for the propitiation of God toward all the faithful; after the singing of the Sunday (stichera) on the verse (*τῶν ἀποστίχων* / aposticha) and *Glory... Now and ever...*, there is made by the priest a fervent prayer *(Orig. p. 343)* (*ἐκтеνὴς δέησις*) and **"Lord, have mercy"** according unto custom as it were before the tomb of Christ, and after **"Hear us, O God"**, the dismissory troparion and dismissal. If, however, it be an ordinary day, no litiya takes place, but the dismissory troparion is recited when the priest goes forth as it were for a litiya and stands behind the ambo, during the chanting of **"O Theotokos Virgin, rejoice"**. After this the priest exclaims: **"Let us pray to the Lord. For Thou art our enlightenment, O Christ our God, and unto Thee do we send up glory…"** The last of all prayers is the prayer of the bowing of heads and dismissal, thus both at Matins and at every service' [^1588]. The Jerusalem manuscript makes no mention of the prayers of the priest in the order of Vespers, evidently because this did not enter into its purpose. Symeon of Thessalonica indicates during the course of Vespers three prayers at appointed places: at the 1st psalm, at the Entrance, and the prayer of the bowing of heads and dismissal; while a fourth, **"O Lord, compassionate and merciful"**, he cites as an example that 'the remaining prayers of Vespers likewise possess thoughts adapted unto the psalms of the antiphons and borrow expressions therefrom'. Consequently, Symeon of Thessalonica did not set for himself the goal of indicating all the prayers of the priest at Vespers. A supplementation of him here may be found in ancient Euchologia, which, without providing the order of Vespers, as of Matins, cite only the prayers of the priest at either service, wherein in many of these Euchologia it is precisely the Sung Vespers and Matins that are had in view, as the titles of the prayers indicate. Although the majority of these prayers are identical with the present prayers of the lighting of lamps (Lucernarium prayers), read secretly by the priest during the Introductory Psalm, they are inscribed in certain Euchologia of the 9th–13th centuries very characteristically: 'Prayer of the 1st Antiphon' (our present 1st Lucernarium prayer), 'Prayer of the 2nd Antiphon' (our present 2nd), and so forth; our present Prayer of the Entrance is inscribed for the most part 'Prayer of the 8th Antiphon before **"Lord, I have cried"**'.
