Following these 8 prayers certain Euchologia possess yet a second series of prayers, at times with a new numbering of the antiphons, wherein explicit reference is made unto the so-called 'Small Antiphons' in St. Symeon of Thessalonica (as likewise in the copies of the Typikon of the Great Church of the 9th–10th centuries). Thus the Euchologion of the Barberini Library in Rome, No. 77 (8th–9th c.), the Cryptferratan [Grottaferrata] so-called Bessarion codex (9th c.), Sinai Library No. 958 (10th c.), Paris National Library No. 213 (11th c.), Barberini No. 88 (13th c.), and the Trebnik of the Moscow Synodal Library No. 675/371 (14th–15th c.) have 'after the prokeimenon and **"Lord, have mercy"**' the following prayers: 1) 'Prayer of the (1st) Antiphon, upon which is chanted **"By the prayers of the Theotokos"**': **"Blessed art Thou, O Lord our God, Who hast enlightened the day with the light of the sun…"** (identical with one of our present prayers of Pentecost), with the exclamation: **"For Thine it is to have mercy…"**; 2) 'Prayer of the (2nd) Antiphon, upon which is chanted **"Only-Begotten Son"**': **"O Lord, Who hast delivered us"** (identical with the prayer of Pentecost and of Great Compline), with the exclamation: **"By the favor and goodness…"**; 3) 'Prayer of the (3rd) Antiphon of the Trisagion': **"O God, great and eternal…"** (containing likewise a petition for the worthy chanting of the Trisagion), with the exclamation: **"For holy art Thou…"**; *(Orig. p. 344)* 4) 'Prayer of the Catechumens after the Trisagion': **"O God, Who knowest secret things…"**, with the exclamation: **"That they also with us [may glorify Thine all-honorable and majestic Name]…"**; 5) 'First Prayer of the Faithful': **"O Lord our God, even now…"**, with its central petition that He clothe us with the whole armor of the Holy Spirit against the spirits of wickedness, and with the exclamation: **"For unto Thee is due [all glory, honor, and worship]…"**; 6) 'Second Prayer of the Faithful': **"O Lord God, Who dwellest in light unapproachable…"**, with a petition for the enlightenment of the eyes of our souls, and with the exclamation: **"For Thine is the majesty…"**; 7) Prayer or Dismissal: **"O God, great and highest…"**, identical with our present 7th Lucernarium prayer, with the exclamation: **"For good art Thou and the Lover of mankind…"**; 8) our present Prayer of the Bowing of Heads, with the exclamation: **"Blessed and glorified be the majesty of Thy Kingdom…"** Unto this series of prayers certain monuments (the Ilitarion or Kondakarion of Sinai Library No. 956 of the 10th c., the aforementioned Euchologion of Paris National Library No. 213 of the 11th c., and the Trebnik of the Moscow Synodal Library No. 371/675 of the 14th–15th c.) append yet three more: a) 'Prayer said in the skeuophylakion of the vestry (*καταγύρων*, in the sacristy)', which is appointed to be pronounced after the exclamation **"Let us depart in peace"**, containing a petition to make us sacred vessels, with the exclamation: **"For holy art Thou…"**; b) 'Prayer said in the Great Baptistery after the conclusion of Vespers', containing thanksgiving unto God Who hath made us worthy of the lot of the saints, delivered us from the power of darkness, and translated us into the Kingdom of His love; after **"Peace be unto all"**, **"Bow your heads…"**; and furthermore c) a prayer containing thanksgiving for regeneration by water and the Spirit and a petition to preserve within us the grace of baptism, with the exclamation: **"For Thou art our God, a God Who hath mercy…"** [^1589] In this manner the faithful were accompanied by prayers upon departing from the church unto the very portico; remarkable it is that according unto the Ambrosian rite as well there are at Vespers and Matins special prayers and responsories *in baptisterio* (see above, p. 317). Concerning the prayer for the catechumens the Grottaferrata Euchologion observes: 'it must be known that the catechumens (that is, prayers for them) at Vespers do not always take place, but only on Thursday and Tuesday, and on these days not unconditionally, but when in the church there is no Liturgy or litiya'.

Consequently, in the 9th century, although the prayers for the catechumens and the distinct prayers for the faithful still existed at Vespers (and Matins, as we shall see), they were already near extinction. The silence concerning them in Symeon of Thessalonica indicates that by his time they had been abolished. — According unto the 'Order' (*Taxis*) of the Athos-St. Andrew manuscript, before the dismissal of Vespers 'all chant together: **"Establish, O God, our sovereigns; yea (*ναί*), O Lord, unto many years preserve their holy empire"**, as likewise: *Τὸν δεσπότην καὶ ἀρχιερέα ἡμῶν, Κύριε, φύλαττε* ["Preserve, O Lord, our master and hierarch"]'; upon the fulfillment of this, the patriarch glorifies (in all probability, he pronounces **"Glory to the Father…"**, **"Glory to Thee, O Christ God"**), and the dismissal is given by the priest; then, according unto custom, the clerics again chant aloud: **"Prolong (*πολυχρόνιον*)"** [^1590] **"O God, their holy empire unto many years"**, and *(Orig. p. 345)* **"The Master…"** (*Τὸν δεσπότην*); the patriarch blesses the people during the singing of *Εἰς πολλὰ ἔτη* ["Unto many years"]; they escort him with lamps unto his cell, where he blesses again during the singing of *Ispolla* [^1591].

### The Sung Matins

Matins in Hagia Sophia of Constantinople in the 12th century, according unto the testimony of a Russian traveler, 'is chanted first before the royal doors in the narthex; and going forth, they chant in the midst of the church; and they open the paradise doors, and chant thirdly at the altar' [^1592]. According unto the description of Symeon of Thessalonica, the Sung Matins began with the exclamation: **"Blessed is the Kingdom…"**, which was followed by *τὰ εἰρηνικά* (the 'peaceful' petitions), that is, the Great Synapte; during it the chanter (*ψάλτης*) begins, just as at Vespers, the singing of the 1st of the three opening psalms of Matins, Psalm 3: **"Lord, why are they multiplied that afflict me?"**, specifically after **"Help us, save us…"** The chanter sings a fragment of verse 6 of this psalm, expressing its theme, with the refrain of the psalm: **"And I slept. Glory to Thee, O God!"** Following the litany the psalm is chanted by verses, beginning with verse 6: **"I laid me down and slept"**, with the designated refrain; unto Psalm 3 are joined Psalm 62 [63]: **"O God, my God, unto Thee do I rise early…"**, and Psalm 133 [134]: **"Behold now, bless ye the Lord…"**, with the same refrain, which on feasts and on the Sundays of the Forefathers and Fathers is replaced by 'Trinitarian' refrains (*τὰ τριαδικά*): **"Glory to Thee, O Father; Glory to Thee, O Son; Glory to Thee, O Holy Spirit"**, and 'similar' hymns (*καὶ τὰ ὅμοια*). The refrain is repeated at *Glory...*, at *Now and ever...*, and in conclusion (*περισσήν*) with an elevated voice. During the singing of this Three-Psalm sequence, which replaces our present Six Psalms (Hexapsalmos), the priest reads the Morning Prayers. The Three-Psalm sequence concludes with the Little Litany, following which begins the singing of Psalm 118 [119]; it begins in the same manner as the other psalms, that is, with the proclamation by the chanter of its theme and refrain: **"Blessed are the undefiled in the way. Alleluia"** (it is noteworthy that this proclamation is not inserted into the preceding Little Litany). **"Alleluia"** serves as the refrain only for the 1st and 3rd staseis of the psalm, whereas for the 2nd stasis the refrain is: **"Give me understanding, O Lord"**, which is proclaimed at the Little Litany between the 1st and 2nd staseis; at the next Little Litany before the 3rd stasis there is proclaimed: **"The world [unto the ends of the world].

**Alleluia"**. The 2nd stasis begins with: **"Thy hands have made me"**, the 3rd with: **"Look upon me"** (as among us likewise). During the singing of Psalm 118 [119] the priest censes first the narthex, making a circuit along its walls (during the censing of which the people step back from them) from the place where he stands; on feasts, preceded by a lantern and under dimmed illumination of the narthex; upon the conclusion of the censing in the narthex the chanter proclaims: **"Blessed art Thou, O Lord"**, and the priest quietly says: **"Wisdom! Stand upright!"** After the narthex, the nave—which is still closed—is likewise censed, into which the priest enters through side doors, and then the altar is censed. Leaving the censer in *(Orig. p. 346)* the latter, the priest takes thence the cross from behind the holy table and, entering with it into the narthex through other side doors, sets the cross before the principal doors leading from the narthex into the nave. At the (170th) verse of Psalm 118 [119]: **"Let my supplication come before Thee, O Lord"**, the solemn Entrance is made from the narthex into the nave: the priest opens the doors, sings aloud the Entrance verse (*τὸ εἰσοδικόν*—in all probability, as at present, a psalm verse appropriate unto the feast) with **"Alleluia"**, and, holding the aforementioned cross upon which three lighted tapers are affixed (the embryonic form of our present Paschal rites), reciting the Prayer of the Entrance and blessing it with the words: **"Blessed is the entrance of Thy saints, O Lord"**, enters with the deacon and the hierarch, if they be present, into the nave through the main doors, while the people proceed through the side doors (the origin of the custom that laity do not enter through the Royal Doors); the priest passes unto (*πρός*) the altar, before which he sets the cross, and (naturally) takes his stand before it himself, while the hierarch proceeds unto his stasidion. The chanting of Psalm 118 [119] is brought to completion, after which is pronounced with melodic chanting (*ψάλλεται μετὰ ᾄσματος ἐμμελοῦς*) the Canticle of the Three Youths: **"Bless the Lord, all ye works of the Lord"**, with the refrain: **"Bless ye"**, and our present conclusion, that is, instead of *Glory...*: **"Let us bless [Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, the Lord]…"**; *Now and ever...*—the conclusion (*περισσή*): **"We praise, we bless [and we worship the Lord]…"**, and with the addition of the Theotokion: **"Thee, the invincible rampart and confirmation of salvation…"** (Thus of the biblical canticles, as in the Western rites at *Laudes*, only one was sung; compare concerning St. Auxentius on p. 356; this 'single-ode' developed into two-, three-, four-ode canons and the full canon). Following the Canticle of the Three Youths there was a reading from the Synaxarion or another reading, and there followed the most ancient and central portion of Matins—the 50th Psalm [51], sung antiphonally by verses by both choirs with the 'dismissory' (troparion) of the day, feast, or saint; at the verse: **"Cast me not away [from Thy presence]…"**, on ordinary days only, in all probability, there was sung: **"O Protection of Christians unashamed…"**; at *Glory...*: **"Only-Begotten Son…"**; at *Now and ever...*: **"The all-glorious [Mother of God]…"**; on feasts at *Glory...* and *Now and ever...*—the troparion of the feast. Following the 50th Psalm, in the time of Symeon of Thessalonica canons were chanted at 8, if there were two, at 6 for great saints, and at 4 on weekdays; this St. Symeon terms a beneficial innovation in the Sung Matins, which received its beginning, in all likelihood, only in his day. Following the canon and the exapostilarion followed the Praises (*Laudes* / *Хвалите*). The refrains unto these psalms, chanted by two choirs, were the following: for the first 6 verses: **"To Thee song is due, O God"** ('from this it is manifest', observes St. Symeon, 'that the Sung Matins provided occasion likewise for the monasteries to say at the beginning', that is, of the Psalms of Praise, **"To Thee song is due, O God"**); unto the next 6 verses: **"Give glory unto God"**; unto the next 4 verses: **"Unto Him praise is due"**; unto the next 2 verses: **"Glory to Thee, holy Father"**; unto the next 2: **"O Son of God, have mercy on us"**; unto the next 2: **"Spare us, O Lord, for the sake of Thy Holy Spirit"**; unto the next 4: **"O Son of God, have mercy on us"**; unto the final 2: **"Glory to Thee Who hast shown us the light"**. Then is sung the Canticle of Zechariah (intentionally—following all the Old Testament material of Matins) with the refrain unto each verse of the 1st verse; at *Glory...* aloud: **"Blessed is the Lord Jesus, for He hath visited [His people]…"**; at *Now and ever...*—the same, and the conclusion (*περισσήν*): **"Let us all hymn the Mother of God, through whom we have received the forgiveness of falls and the protection of our souls"**. *(Orig. p. 347)* The reader, taking the cross in hand and standing upon the ambo, begins the Great Doxology, which the cantors continue. 'On Sunday the Praises (*Ainoi*) are proclaimed in the tone with refrains (*ὑποψάλμων*, that is, the aforementioned ones?), and at the conclusion (*εἰς τὸ τέλος*) the stichera of the Resurrection, of the feast, or of the great saint; the Morning *Glory...* (the Doxasticon / Morning stichera), at which takes place the Entrance of the priests with the cross and the Holy Gospel'; the latter is elevated with the words: **"Wisdom! Stand upright!"**, then **"Now and ever... Most blessed art thou…"**; the reader with the cross begins the Great Doxology, the cantors sing it melodically, and from the words **"goodwill among men"** the priests in the altar join in. Next is sung the troparion **"Today is salvation come unto the world"** or **"Having risen from the tomb"** alternately 'thrice sweet-voicedly, both by the cantors without (the altar) and by the priests within. Then **"Arise, O Lord"** (the prokeimenon), the reading of the Gospel by the presbyter upon the ambo, 'the protracted supplication (*ἡ ἐκτενὴς δέησις*—the Augmented Litany), the great petitions (the Litany of Supplication), the bowing of heads, and the dismissal' [^1593].

Just as for Vespers, Symeon of Thessalonica scarcely indicates any priestly prayers for Matins (to such a degree had they already receded into the background), and here he must be supplemented by Euchologia of the 9th–14th centuries. Yet it is remarkable that whereas certain of the most ancient Euchologia designate the evening prayers by the number of the antiphons ('Prayer of the 1st Antiphon', '2nd', etc.), these same Euchologia—such as the Grottaferrata Bessarion Codex of the 9th century, Sinai Library No. 958 of the 10th century, and others—simply number the later morning prayers: *(Orig. p. 348)* 1st, 2nd (the latter codex designates the 4th prayer alone as the 'Prayer of the 4th Antiphon'); of the Euchologia investigated hitherto, apparently only No. 962 of the Sinai Library of the 7th [8th/9th] century designates evening and morning prayers alike by the number of antiphons. In consequence of this, the first 5–6 prayers, identical for the most part in ancient Euchologia with our present prayers at Matins, are difficult to assign unto definite moments of the Sung Matins. Yet the second half of the morning prayers, by their very rubrical headings, are assigned unto such moments. Thus our present 9th prayer is inscribed: 'Prayer of the Gospel', or '9th Prayer before the Gospel', or 'Prayer of the 50th (i.e. Psalm), 9th'; our present 10th prayer is inscribed in the majority of Euchologia as 'Prayer of the 50th', that is, Psalm; then there are prayers 'at the Praises' (*εἰς τοὺς αἴνους*), for the most part our present 11th; at **"Glory to God in the highest"**, otherwise designated 'Prayer of Dismissal', or simply 'Dismissal'—for the most part our present 12th; the final prayer is for the most part our present 'Prayer of the Bowing of Heads'. The Euchologia—the Grottaferrata Bessarion Codex of the 9th century, Paris National Library No. 213 of the 11th century, and the Slavonic Trebnik of the Moscow Synodal Library No. 371/675 of the 14th century—possess, besides these prayers at Matins, just as at Vespers, 1 prayer for the catechumens and 2 prayers for the faithful (before the prayers of dismissal and the bowing of heads); wherein the first Euchologion and the Trebnik make the observation concerning these prayers that they are read 'when there is an Entrance, and there are pronounced **"Glory to God in the highest"**, the Trisagion, and the prokeimenon'—more specifically: 'when there are chanted (certain) 12 prokeimena, specifically on Tuesday and Thursday of the two weeks before Meatfare (consequently from the Sunday of the Publican and Pharisee), on Meatfare and Cheesefare, provided that on these days there be no Liturgy or feast'; the prayer for the catechumens with the litany (*λιτανεύοντος*) of the deacon and the prayers for the faithful are pronounced following the Augmented Litany; while following these prayers comes the Litany of Supplication [^1594]. Beyond doubt, formerly these prayers were pronounced at every Matins and Vespers; by the 11th century they remained an adjunct of Matins, at least, only during the preparatory weeks for the Great Fast (during Great Lent they were not pronounced, in all probability because there Matins was not festive and daily the Presanctified Liturgy was celebrated). This was the final step toward their complete removal from these services.

### The Pannychis According unto the Typikon of the Great Church

In addition unto Vespers and Matins, the Constantinopolitan Sophia Typikon at times possessed yet another service: the *pannychis* (all-night vigil). It is unknown whether it ever fully corresponded unto its name (*pannychis* = 'all-night') in duration. The Patmos manuscript of the Typikon of the Great Church appoints the pannychis only on the 4th or 5th week of the Fast, and observes concerning its composition: 'the pannychis takes place in Blachernae thus: in the evening two weekly readers (from Hagia Sophia) go unto Blachernae; and one weekly reader executes (*ποιεῖ*) there Vespers and the kontakion; while the Triadikon (Troichen) and the Midnight Office are executed by the local (readers); and Matins is executed by the other weekly reader' [^1595]. Thus the constituent parts of the pannychis here are the kontakion, the Triadikon *(Orig. p. 349)* (which Symeon of Thessalonica cites), and some form of Midnight Office. — The Dresden manuscript of the Typikon of the Great Church indicates the pannychis on great feasts (thus on the eve of Pascha, on June 29, September 1), mentioning at it the troparion, the 50th Psalm [51], and the kontakion [^1596]. In greater detail its composition is unknown. — From this pannychis, in all probability, there differed significantly the pannychis of the 1st week of Great Lent and the first three days of Passion Week. Its order is provided by the Dresden manuscript of the Typikon of the Great Church, the Holy Sepulchre Typikon of 1122 according unto the manuscript of the Jerusalem Patriarchal Library No. 43, the manuscript of the Alexandria Patriarchal Library of the 14th century No. 144, and St. Symeon of Thessalonica, all with minor variants. Its prayers are supplied by the Euchologia of the Sinai Library Nos. 956, 958 of the 10th century, 962 of the 11th–12th century, and the aforementioned Trebnik.

The pannychis began following the prayer behind the ambo of the Presanctified Liturgy with the exclamation: **"Blessed is the Kingdom…"** (Dresden MS) and the singing by the chanter (Symeon) of Psalm 90 [91] with the conclusion: **"Thou hast made the Most High [thy refuge]"** thrice, *Glory... Now and ever...* (Dresden MS). During the singing of the psalm the priest, pronouncing a prayer, carries the sacred vessels into the skeuophylakion. Following the psalm comes the synapte litany (*συναπτή*—Symeon) of the first pannychis prayer: **"Who in the season…"** (Dresden MS), expressing with the words **"How magnified are Thy works, O Lord…"** [LXX Ps. 103:24] wonder at the goodness and wisdom of God in establishing day and night and imploring grace-filled illumination against sinful wrath; exclamation: **"For unto Thee is due…"** (This initial part of the pannychis is not indicated by the Alexandria MS and the Holy Sepulchre Typikon). Then were sung three antiphons, consisting of Psalm 119 [120]: **"Unto the Lord in mine affliction have I cried…"**, with the refrain (*ὑπόψαλμος*—Symeon), that is, the troparion (MSS): **"As Thou art compassionate"** (*Ὠς οἰκτίρμων*); Psalm 24 [25]: **"Unto Thee, O Lord, have I lifted up my soul…"** (according unto the Holy Sepulchre Typikon, Psalm 120 [121]: **"I have lifted up mine eyes…"**), with the troparion **"Open unto us the doors of compassion…"**; and Psalm 121 [122]: **"I was glad of them that said unto me…"**, with the troparion **"Have mercy on us, O Lord"** (according unto the Holy Sepulchre Typikon, unto the 2nd antiphon the troparion **"Have mercy on us…"**, and unto the 3rd **"The multitude of my transgressions…"**). The psalms are chanted (according unto St. Symeon) by both choirs by verses, but the Alexandria and Dresden manuscripts designate for singing only 4 verses from each psalm, with *Glory... Now and ever...* at the conclusion (*περισσήν*—Symeon); the psalm is begun by the chanter (Symeon) or the domestikos (MSS) of the choir on duty. At the antiphons 3 prayers were read; besides the aforementioned one, transferred by the time of Symeon of Thessalonica unto the beginning of the pannychis, but indicated by the manuscripts at the 1st antiphon, at the 2nd antiphon was read the prayer: **"Unto Thee, the invisible and unwaning Light…"**, imploring vigilance, alongside bodily eyes, for our thoughts likewise in contemplating the glory of God and in nocturnal singing; exclamation: **"For holy and glorified is [Thy Name]…"**; at the 3rd antiphon the prayer: **"Who receivest the unsleeping and ceaseless doxology…"**, imploring God to accept our nocturnal hymnody, offered after the pattern of the celestial intelligences; exclamation: **"For Thine is the dominion…"** Under St. Symeon the two latter prayers, together with the prayer of dismissal: **"O Sovereign Lord Almighty, incomprehensible…"**, imploring of God help to pass the entire night of our life in vigilance and to attain in virtue unto the Day of Christ, our God and Judge, and unto His joy, wherein *(Orig. p. 350)* there is neither sorrow nor sighing, with the exclamation: **"For good art Thou…"**—all these 3 prayers were read at the second antiphon. The antiphons were separated by Little Litanies, whose exclamations served, naturally, as the exclamations of the prayers as long as they were read in their respective places; yet under Symeon the exclamation of the 1st Little Litany was the exclamation of the 2nd prayer, and the exclamation of the 2nd litany was the exclamation of the 4th prayer (of dismissal). Following the 3rd antiphon there was no litany, but immediately the 50th Psalm [51] antiphonally by verses with the refrain (according unto Symeon): **"O Merciful Lord, have mercy on us…"** At the 1st antiphon (according unto the Dresden MS), or the 3rd (according unto Symeon), or following the 50th Psalm (according unto the Holy Sepulchre Typikon), the patriarch or priest, with a candle in hand or preceded by a candle, censes the altar and the church, reciting (according unto the Dresden MS): **"Glory to Thee, O Christ God, the Apostles' boast…"** Following the 50th Psalm comes the prokeimenon: **"The Lord will give strength unto His people…"**, verse: **"Bring unto the Lord…"** (according unto the Dresden MS), or Tone 4: **"Hear us, O God our Savior…"**, verse: **"To Thee song is due, O God, in Sion"** (according unto the Holy Sepulchre Typikon); **"Let us pray to the Lord…"**, **"For holy art Thou"**, **"Let every breath"**, and the Gospel (according unto the Dresden MS on the 1st week of the Fast—Luke: **"Take heed that ye be not deceived…"** [Lk. 21:8]; according unto the Holy Sepulchre—the daily Matins Gospel). There is sung the hymn: **"The Bodiless Nature…"** (at present at weekday Great Compline); according unto the Holy Sepulchre Typikon—the troparion of the day and Theotokion; **"Lord, have mercy"** 12 times according unto the Holy Sepulchre Typikon, 40 times according unto the Dresden MS, thrice by the chanter and 100 times by all according unto Symeon. During this the priest (according unto Symeon, secretly) recites the prayer of the bowing of heads: **"O Lord our God, incline our hearts unto obedience of Thy Divine commandments and turn away the eyes of our understanding that they bow not unto worldly vanity, but look upon the beauty of Thy glory"**; exclamation: **"For Thou art our God, a God Who hath mercy…"**; **"Lord, have mercy"** thrice; priest: **"Hear us, [O God our Savior]…"** [^1597]. — More complex and later (though represented likewise by 10th-century manuscripts) is another order of the pannychis, supplied by a manuscript formerly belonging unto the Lavra of St. Sabas, now in the Jerusalem Patriarchal Library No. 24 of the 10th century, the Triodia of the Vatopedi Library No. 316 of the 11th century, and the Sinai MS of 1206: the Six Psalms (10th-c. MS) or Psalm 142 [143] (13th-c. Triodion), **"Alleluia"** with verses, the Triadikon (Troichen) or troparia **"Have mercy on us…"**, the canon; following the 3rd ode at times a Little Litany (beginning from **"Help us…"**—13th-c. Triodion) and a sessional hymn; following the 6th ode—a similar litany and the kontakion (ibid.), prokeimenon, **"Let every breath"**, and the Gospel; following the canon, either only the Trisagion and dismissal (10th-c. MS), or 6 Theotokia troparia, the Trisagion, troparia **"Have mercy on us…"**, the litany **"Have mercy on us, O God…"** with a petition for the emperors and other persons at desire, the prayer: **"O Compassionate and Merciful One…"**, and the dismissal [^1598].

### Trithekte

On Cheesefare Wednesday and Friday, on all ordinary days (Monday through Friday) of Great Lent, and on Passion Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, and Friday, the Great *(Orig. p. 351)* Church of Constantinople and the churches following its Typikon possessed, in addition unto Vespers and Matins (and at times the pannychis), yet another special service: *Trithekte* (*τριτοέκτη* or *τριτέκτη* / the Third-Sixth Hour Office), celebrated at the 6th hour (= 12 noon) of the day. This service substituted for all the hours, which the Great Church did not possess, and for the full Liturgy (the Presanctified Liturgy was celebrated on those same days following Vespers), and, according unto the remark of Symeon of Thessalonica, 'followed the order of the great holy Liturgy up to the Great Entrance', or more precisely: 'possessed both the figure of the hours, whence its name, and the figure of the holy Liturgy'. The content of the service demonstrates [^1599] that it was intended originally for the catechumens, and subsequently for the faithful as well, who were regarded during Great Lent in the status of penitents and as it were only catechumens still (see above, p. 248). In contrast unto the three other services of the Great Church, Trithekte in all monuments of the Sophia Typikon (the Patmos and Dresden copies of the Typikon, in St. Symeon, in the Sinai Euchologion No. 958 of the 10th century, and others providing its prayers) possesses a very similar order. Following **"Blessed is the Kingdom…"** comes the Great Synapte (*τὰ εἰρηνικά*), 3 antiphons in Tone 7, Tone 3, and Tone 6 (Dresden MS) or **"Save us, O Son of God, who sing unto Thee Alleluia"**, Psalm 100 [101]: **"Of mercy and judgment [will I sing unto Thee, O Lord]…"**, with **"Only-Begotten Son…"** (Dresden MS) or **"Alleluia"** (Symeon). Following the 1st and 2nd antiphons comes the Little Litany; at each antiphon a prayer (according unto Symeon, secretly); the 1st: **"O God Who sittest upon the cherubim…"**, implores that God look upon us, arouse our mind unto the glorification of His goodness, deliver us from the snares of the evil one, and vouchsafe us the Heavenly Kingdom with all the elect; exclamation: **"For Thou art our God"** (Symeon: **"a God Who hath mercy"**) **"and unto Thee…"**; the 2nd prayer: **"We pray Thee, O Lord our God…"**, implores God to be longsuffering toward us and to spare us on account of our infirmity, to deliver us from temptations and the dominion of darkness, and to establish us in the Kingdom of the Only-Begotten; exclamation: **"For glorified is the all-honorable [Name]…"**; the 3rd prayer: **"O Lord our God, Whose glory is ineffable…"**, implores the Merciful God to look upon us and upon all His people, not to deliver us over unto sins, but to guide us unto His will and make us doers of commandments, that we be not put to shame in the day of judgment; conclusion: **"For good art Thou…"** At the verse of the final psalm: **"He that walketh in a blameless way [he served me]"**, the Entrance took place, 'without lantern or censer' (according unto Symeon, 'signifying the leading of the Lord unto death, which took place at the 6th hour, whence also the crimson vestments'); the deacon proclaims again *τὰ εἰρηνικά* (Symeon) or **"Let us all say…"** (Euchologia; Dresden: 'litany'; Patmos: *εὐχὴ συναπτὴ χωρὶς τῶν αἰτήσεων*—a synapte litany without the petitions of supplication; at the beginning of the service here no litany is indicated), during which is read the prayer: **"O Lord God of our fathers, Who givest prayer unto him that prayeth…"**, imploring the hearing of prayer, condescension toward sins, and guidance in virtue; exclamation: **"For good art Thou…"** (according unto the Euchologia; according unto Symeon: **"For unto Thee is due…"**). The cantors upon the ambo begin the Troparion of Prophecy (appointed at present at the Sixth Hour), which the readers upon the solea take up and sing thrice antiphonally by both choirs, the cantors singing the final *Glory...*; the prokeimenon *(Orig. p. 352)* (according unto the Dresden MS with 2 verses), the reading (*paroemia*) from Isaiah (in Cheesefare week—from Joel; in Passion Week—from Ezekiel), and the second prokeimenon (all appointed at present at the Sixth Hour). The Litany for the Catechumens and the prayer over them: **"O Lord Almighty…"**, of the usual content with our present exclamation; following the departure of the catechumens, 'from Wednesday of the 4th week of the Fast (Euchologion, Symeon) until Holy Friday' (Euchologion), the litany and prayer for those preparing for Holy Illumination— being our present ones; and the 2 prayers of the faithful: **"O Lord our God…"**, the first of which implores God, Who hath called us from polytheism, to preserve us in His Name, to sanctify us in truth, and to send down compassions (exclamation: **"For Thou art our God, a God Who hath mercy…"**), while the second implores Him to establish us in His fear and strengthen us in His service (exclamation: **"For blessed is [Thine all-honorable Name]…"**). The Litany of Supplication; and the lengthy ('great'—Symeon) '3rd Prayer or Dismissal': **"O Lord our God, Who alone art good…"**, with kneeling (Euchologia), in which, according unto the words of St. Symeon, 'mention is made of the crucifixion of the Savior, and of His rising, and of the ascension, and supplication is sent up that the grace of God may come upon us, strengthen and sanctify us, and in general all things necessary and beneficial are implored of God'; exclamation: **"For Thine is the dominion…"** (according unto the Euchologia before the exclamation: **"Help us, save us… A whole day, perfect…"**, that is, the Litany of Supplication); **"Peace be unto all"**. The bowing of heads and its prayer: **"O Lord our God, Who sittest upon the throne of glory and beholdest the abysses, looking down with compassionate eye upon our ministry, bless all of us who have bowed our heads unto Thee, and exalt our horn in Thy good will"**; exclamation: **"Blessed be the all-holy Name of Thy love for mankind…"**; **"Let us depart in peace"**, **"Let us pray to the Lord"**, and the 'Prayer Behind the Ambo' (Dresden MS): **"Blessed is the glory of the Lord from His holy place always, now and ever, and unto the ages of ages"**. (Concerning this final prayer St. Symeon remarks that with it likewise 'the litany begins'; perhaps it substituted here for the litany) [^1600]. On Great Friday at Trithekte at the litany for those preparing for illumination, following the exclamation: **"Ye who are for illumination, bow your heads…"**, the deacon proclaimed: **"As many as are for illumination, draw near for the imposition of hands and receive the blessing…"**, and the sponsors led forward the children preparing for baptism unto the patriarch, who, standing upon a carpet before the altar, blessed each of them individually and breathed upon him [^1601]. — In all probability throughout the entire Forty Days, as was the practice in the ancient Russian Church [^1602], baptism was not administered and was deferred until Great Saturday, by reason of which the Trithekte of Great Friday, the last during the Fast, was a solemn service for the children preparing for baptism (reminiscent of Western confirmation).

*(Orig. p. 353)*

### Litanies

A prominent feature of Constantinopolitan cathedral worship was constituted by litanies or processions (*αἱ λιταί*, in St. Symeon of Thessalonica *αἱ λιτανεῖαι*). Prior unto Constantinople they had received wide development in the Church of Jerusalem, where they were occasioned by the desire to visit at every festival service all the sites connected in any way with the commemorated event. Thus it was there, as we have seen, already in the 4th–5th centuries (see above, pp. 142, 251–257); similar litanies are known likewise unto the Holy Sepulchre Typikon of the 9th century according unto the 12th-century manuscript of the Jerusalem Patriarchal Library No. 43, where, for instance, at Matins of Palm Sunday there are appointed 6 litanies (unto Golgotha, Bethany, the Mount of Olives, Gethsemane, the Sheep Pool, and again unto Golgotha), at each of which a sticheron was chanted, and there were a prokeimenon, Gospel, the litany **"Have mercy on us, O God"** or **"Let us all say"** (not of our present composition, naturally), and a priestly prayer; at the Service of the Passion there were similar litanies at each Gospel, but already without litany and prayer [^1603]. In Constantinople litanies, in all probability, bore a different character: they were not so much of a festive character as of a propitiatory one on the occasion of diverse public calamities (as was already the case in the 4th century; see above, p. 151). Yet the most ancient Typikon of the Great Church knows litanies of the former (festive) character as well. Thus according unto the Dresden manuscript of this Typikon, on the Thursday following the Sunday of All Saints there was celebrated the 'Synaxis of the Theotokos in the Venerable House situated in ancient Petra', and from the Great Church a litany was directed unto seven quarters of the city, on the way unto each of which a troparion was sung once or twice, and three times there were litanies [^1604]. A complete and general order of the litany (for diverse occasions) in the Great Church is provided by the Euchologion of the Paris National Library No. 213, written in 1027, and the Trebnik of the Moscow Synodal Library No. 371/675. The prayers indicated here are identical with those provided by the Grottaferrata Bessarion Euchologion of the 9th century. The hierarch entered the sanctuary for the litany through side doors (in token of penitential humility); the service began without the customary festive exclamation at the beginning, directly with the Litany of Peace, following which the subdeacon with the cross that stands before the holy table takes his place unto the left of the hierarch, and the latter (as it were under the protection of this cross) reads the prayer: **"O Lord our God, remember us, Thy sinful and unprofitable servants…"**, of mournful-penitential content, with the exclamation: **"For good art Thou and the Lover of mankind…"** Following the imparting of peace and the bowing of heads, the priest read another prayer: **"Holy Lord, Who dwellest in the highest…"**, of similar content, adapted unto the bowing of heads, with the exclamation: **"For Thine it is to have mercy…"** The cantors begin the troparion of the litany; the hierarch takes the Gospel from the holy table; the deacon censes the holy table and the hierarch with the Gospel, which the latter, kissing it and the cross, hands unto the archdeacon. The procession begins: in front goes the deacon with the censer, then the cross, the archdeacon with the Gospel, and the hierarch, supported by no one. Upon stepping onto the third *potamion* (a band upon the temple floor), the hierarch halts, having unto his right *(Orig. p. 354)* the Gospel, and unto his left the cross; and upon the deacon proclaiming **"Let us pray to the Lord"**, he says: **"Blessed is the glory of the Lord from His holy place always, now and ever…"** The hierarch kisses the cross and the Gospel, a phelonion is cast upon the subdeacon carrying the cross, and the procession moves forward. At the royal doors of the narthex it halts again; the hierarch turns toward the east and prays, then, having covered his head, continues along the path. Upon the arrival of the litany at the Forum or other appointed place, the cantors glorify (*δοξάζουσι*, chanting the troparion, perhaps with *Glory... Now and ever...*); there is an Augmented Litany (*ἐκτενὴς δέησις*) with its prayer (our present one), at whose exclamation the hierarch seals with the sign of the cross (*σφραγίζει*) before him; following the imparting of peace and the bowing of heads, the prayer of the latter is the same as at the end of Trithekte (the penultimate prayer there), with the exclamation: **"Blessed be the all-honored Name of Thy love for mankind…"** The cantors begin the troparion and the litany moves forward [^1605]. Of somewhat different composition was the litany (according unto 11th-century and later manuscripts) on the New Year (Indiction) of September 1: at its beginning and along the way the Trisagion was sung; upon arrival at the Forum—three antiphons from Psalms 1, 2, and 64 [65] (**"To Thee praise is due, O God [in Sion]…"**), with the refrains: 1. **"Protect me, O Lord"**; 2. **"Alleluia"**; 3. Troparion, Tone 3: **"Refuge and strength"**, with the Theotokion, Tone 4: **"Thou Who art truly and genuinely the Theotokos"**; the hierarch pronounced three litany petitions: **"For the peace from above…"**, **"For our emperors…"**, and **"For the city and countryside"**, with a threefold **"Lord, have mercy"** and the exclamation: **"For holy art Thou…"**; the prokeimenon, Epistle, and Gospel are our present ones of the Indiction; the deacon recites the litany litany (*λιτανεύοντος*) with the 'great **"Lord, have mercy"**' and the exclamation: **"For a Merciful [God art Thou]…"**; at the exclamations the hierarch blesses; the prayer of the bowing of heads, and the troparion **"Creator of all creation…"** upon the return. (In general—the structure of Sung Vespers) [^1606].

*(Orig. p. 355)*

## Another Type of Divine Worship: The Holy Sepulchre Typikon

Alongside the described type of worship, which is justly termed the Sung Office, from the very beginning of the present period there existed and enjoyed no less, if not greater dissemination another type—that whose description has been preserved unto us in the account of the visit of Sophronius and John Moschus unto Abba Nilus of Sinai, and which, consequently, already in the 6th century had attained both a fairly complete development and no small degree of application. Differing in structure and composition—though in precision it is unknown in what respects—from the cathedral offices of that time, this type of divine worship continued its independent life alongside the latter; and at the very beginning of the 9th century we find it in a number of churches, moreover not only monastic, but cathedral as well; wherein the difference between the two types did not diminish with the course of time, but rather increased. Thus in the 9th century we find it, among cathedral churches, in the elder sister of the Great Church of Constantinople—in the Holy Sepulchre Church of Jerusalem. The fragment of the Holy Sepulchre Typikon that hath reached us from the 9th–10th century, containing the rubrics only of Passion and Paschal worship [^1607], provides for the daily offices entirely our present structure: at Vespers, Psalm 103 [104], the Kathisma, **"Lord, I have cried"** with stichera, the prokeimenon, the Gospel (at times; more frequently than among us at present), **"Vouchsafe, O Lord"**, the aposticha, **"Now lettest Thou Thy servant depart"**, and the dismissory 'sessional hymn' (troparion), at times a litiya; litanies are mentioned likewise, but their place is indicated indistinctly; at Matins: the Six Psalms (Hexapsalmos), **"God [is the Lord]"** **"is the Lord"** or **"Alleluia"**, kathismata and sessional hymns (*sedalny*); on Sunday the *Amomos* (Psalm 118 [119]) with the Resurrection Troparia (*Evlogetaria*), a sessional hymn, Psalm 50 [51] always with troparia, the canon, following the 3rd ode a sessional hymn, hypakoe, or kontakion, following the 6th ode the kontakion and ikos, at times the Gospel preceded by **"Let every breath"** and the prokeimenon, following the 9th ode—the exapostilarion, the Psalms of Praise (*Ainoi* / *Laudes*), and the Great Doxology. Following the Doxology the order is as at present, differing for festal and weekday Matins. For the former, for example, on Palm Sunday *(Orig. p. 356)*, following the Doxology the Gospel, not counting a series of litanies (a purely local peculiarity), the litanies, and the dismissal; on weekdays, for example, on Great Monday, **"Glory to God in the highest"** down unto **"Unto them that know Thee"**, the prokeimenon, readings (*paroemias*), and the Gospel (this, naturally, only in Passion Week), **"Vouchsafe, O Lord"**, the litany, the aposticha, and **"It is good to give praise"**. The Hours are three-psalm offices of the present composition, yet following the Trisagion the dismissal is immediately indicated (for example, on Great Monday). Consequently, the structure of the daily offices according unto the Holy Sepulchre Typikon is completely unlike the Sung Office. With the latter it shares in common here only the order of the pannychis (on Great Monday, Tuesday, and Wednesday), and furthermore, at the Ninth Hour (on those same days) there is appointed in a 'sung' manner only one of its psalms and a litany, with the remaining composition being ordinary.

## Monastic Divine Worship of the 9th and Subsequent Centuries

As regards the Eastern monasteries of the 9th and subsequent centuries, we do not exaggerate if we say that in the majority of them the daily office was of one and the same type, identical with the described worship of the Church of Jerusalem of the 9th–10th centuries and our present usage, and distinct from the Sung Office. This is evident from the preserved records concerning this worship, and chiefly from the ancient liturgical Typika of diverse monasteries that have reached us.

At the head of the monasteries of the 9th and immediately subsequent centuries stood now, at least for the western part of the Byzantine Empire, the Studion Monastery of Constantinople. A series of Typika of the 11th–12th centuries constantly either refer unto the Studite Typikon or even designate themselves as Studite; from the 12th century onward, Typika ever more frequently designate themselves as Jerusalemite and appeal unto the customs of the Lavra of St. Sabbas. Yet the daily worship of both groups of Typika, one may say, is completely identical in structure, with the exception of two or three not particularly significant peculiarities, which furthermore depended not so much upon the character of the Typika as upon their comparative antiquity (manuscripts of Studite Typika are for the most part older than Jerusalemite ones). The difference between the two groups of Typika concerns rather the liturgical year and the Menology. In order to demonstrate the scope of dissemination of the type of daily worship under consideration and to acquaint the reader with those peculiarities which diverse Typika possessed with respect unto the latter, it is necessary to provide here an historical survey of these Typika.

### The Studite Typikon

The Studion Monastery, founded perhaps as early as the 5th century (see above, pp. 233–234), received in the 9th century in liturgical respects from its hegumen, St. Theodore the Studite († 826) [^1608], so firm and definite an organization *(Orig. p. 357)* that it immediately became the model for monasteries throughout all Byzantium. This circumstance indicates that unto daily worship as well—which constitutes the central nerve of all monastic life—St. Theodore must have imparted, so to speak, a distinct character, differing from the practice of other contemporary monasteries and in some measure surpassing it. In that same practice throughout the Christian East of that time there was perhaps the same diversity that existed in the West, where, as we have seen, a whole succession of abbots of the 6th–8th centuries provided at times very diverse orders for the daily office. In the 9th century, as we have seen, there were two principal orders of daily worship in the East: the first might be termed Jerusalemite, the second Constantinopolitan. It is possible, and very probable, that Constantinopolitan and other monasteries, while following in their cloistered discipline one or another monastic rule (for example, of Pachomius the Great or Basil the Great), possessed a divine worship differing little from cathedral and parish usage. Only upon such a supposition can one explain why the liturgical reform of St. Theodore in the Studion Monastery so immediately brought the latter unto prominence and established it for whole centuries as the legislator of liturgical practice for the entire western half of the Greco-Byzantine Church. If now the liturgical order of St. Theodore presents a literal agreement with the Holy Sepulchre order of the same epoch, then the most natural, if not necessary, supposition is that St. Theodore the Studite borrowed this order thence (he did not invent it, which in general is not done by isolated individuals—and which is especially improbable given such agreement with another order). In favour of this speaks likewise the early adoption into the Studite Typikon—in all likelihood as early as St. Theodore himself—of the works of the Palestinian-Sabbaite hymnographers: Andrew of Crete, Cosmas of Maiuma, and John of Damascus. If the liturgical order of the Studion Monastery had been common in the epoch of St. Theodore unto neighboring monasteries, it would not have received the name of Studite. But in borrowing the order of the daily office from the Church of the Resurrection and from Palestinian monasteries, St. Theodore had to introduce into it certain modifications that entitled it unto a distinct designation. And it is understandable in what direction these modifications would tend. In Constantinople it was natural to adapt the Palestinian order of divine worship unto the Typikon of Hagia Sophia and cathedral churches. Such an adaptation we observe in the Studite Typika. Its traces in the daily office include the omission of the Hours on many days and of kathismata on certain days; in the church year, for example, the Presanctified Liturgy celebrated daily in Great Lent. These peculiarities, it is true, belong unto monuments of the Studite Typikon that arose later than St. Theodore; yet the significance that they possess therein, as well as their common presence in all these Typika, guarantees that they trace their origin back unto St. Theodore.

### Daily Worship in the Studion Monastery Under St. Theodore

In the absence of a manuscript copy of a church Typikon that might be attributed unto St. Theodore himself, on the question of the composition and form of the daily offices in the Studion Monastery of his time one is obliged to turn exclusively *(Orig. p. 358)* unto the writings of the holy father. The latter allow us to state that divine worship was celebrated in the monastery seven times in twenty-four hours, beginning from midnight [^1609]. The brethren were summoned unto the services by the sound of the semantron (*klepalo* / *bilo*). At the Hours the following psalms are mentioned: at the First Hour—Psalm 5; at the Sixth—Psalm 90 [91]; at the Ninth—Psalm 85 [86]; at Vespers—Psalm 103 [104]. At Matins there is mentioned the reading of the Life of the commemorated saint [^1610]; at Compline—a catechetical instruction (*oglashenie*) of the brethren by the superior or by one of the senior monks, thrice weekly [^1611]. The Liturgy, in all likelihood, was not always celebrated on weekdays; at the Sunday Liturgy, seemingly, not all the brethren received Holy Communion; yet certain ones communicated at every Liturgy [^1612].

### The Hypotyposis and Diatyposis and Daily Worship According unto Them

More information concerning daily worship in the Studion Monastery is provided by the *Hypotyposis* (*Ὑποτύπωσις καταστάσεως τῆς μονῆς τῶν Στουδίου* / "Outline of the Constitution of the Studion Monastery") attributed unto St. Theodore [^1613], and by the liturgically very similar testament of St. Athanasius of Athos († circa 1000), founder of the most ancient lavra on Athos [^1614]: the *Diatyposis* (*Διατύπωσις τοῦ *(Orig. p. 359)* ὁσίου πατρὸς ἡμῶν Ἀθανασίου*), which forms part of his *Typikon* (*Τυπικὸν ἤτοι Κανονικόν*, wherein, alongside the monastic-liturgical rule, there is also an account of the foundation of the Lavra of St. Athanasius) [^1615]. These monuments mention at Vespers the Prooemiac Psalm, **"Blessed is the man"** with three 'beginnings' (antiphons), and **"Lord, I have cried"** with stichera; at Matins: the Six Psalms (Hexapsalmos), **"The Lord is God"**, 'kathismata of the psalm' [psalter kathismata], on Saturday the *Amomos* (Psalm 118 [119]), 'troparia of the kathismata' (sessional hymns / *sedalny*), Psalm 50 [51], the canon, readings, the exapostilarion, and the Praises (*Ainoi* / *Laudes*).

### The Sinai Kanonarion

Approximately such a structure of the services is presupposed by the so-called Sinai Kanonarion (*κανονάριον*), that is, rubrical notes primarily concerning readings from Holy Scripture for the movable and immovable feasts (the Triodion and Menology), appended unto a liturgical Gospel Book. This Kanonarion has been preserved in two redactions closely related unto each other—one of the 9th–10th century, the other of the 10th–11th century [^1616]. In its Menology *(Orig. p. 360)* the Kanonarion in places coincides with the Typikon of the Great Church of Constantinople; yet as regards the daily office, although one can judge concerning it here only from the order of Paschal worship, there remains no doubt that in this instance we are dealing with the practice not of Hagia Sophia and the Sung Office, but either with the Holy Sepulchre-Studite usage, or, more accurately, with a combination of both practices with a predominance of the second: thus, at Matins there is a canon, preceded by the Litany of Peace (which is not mentioned at all at Matins in the Typika of the Great Church of the 9th–10th centuries), and the troparion **"Christ is risen"** (unknown unto those Typika) with verses, as in the Studite and Holy Sepulchre Typika.

### The Ktetorial Studite Typika

Finally, the most important daily offices—Vespers and Matins—are provided fully in the present type by a series of so-called complete ktetorial Typika, that is, Typika with a detailed order of service for every day of the ecclesiastical year, given unto diverse monasteries by their founders. The majority of these Typika designate themselves as Studite and are closest unto the customs of the Studion Monastery, in so far as one can judge concerning the latter from the aforementioned monuments; although in places they reflect also the practice of the Great Church, they do not do so with respect unto daily worship. The most ancient of such ktetorial Typika is 1) that given by Patriarch Alexis of Constantinople in 1034 unto the Monastery of the Dormition of the Mother of God founded by him near Constantinople. It has reached us only in Slavonic translations and manuscripts of the 11th–15th centuries (consequently nearly contemporary with its compilation). Since all the most ancient monuments of the ecclesiastical rule in Rus' transmit this Typikon alone, it is believed that it was precisely this rule that was introduced into the practice of the Kyiv Caves Monastery by one of its founders, St. Theodosius of the Caves [^1617]. In its disciplinary section it is entitled *(Orig. p. 361)*: 'The Ustavnik [Rule-Book] examining concerning the food and drink of monks and every other order, and concerning conduct both in church and everywhere, instituted not in writing in the Studite Monastery by our venerable father and confessor Theodore, formerly hegumen therein, but delivered in writing by Alexis, the holy and ecumenical patriarch, in the monastery established by him in the name of the Divine Mother' [^1618]. With this redaction *(Orig. p. 362)* of the Studite Typikon there coincides in the structure of the daily office a series of other more or less pure and unadulterated redactions of it, which in chronological order may be arranged in the following manner. 2) The Typikon of the Monastery of Grottaferrata (Cryptaferrata), 30 versts from Rome, founded by the monk Nilus († 1004), who gave it a rule; unto the latter frequent reference is made by the Typikon of this monastery preserved unto the present day, compiled by the second successor of Nilus, Bartholomew (who built in 1025 the principal church of the monastery which still stands), and significantly revised by the fourth hegumen, Blasius II († 1303), in the direction of rapprochement with the Roman rite; yet these revisions did not touch the structure of the daily office, and it bears the stamp of an antiquity and proximity unto the *Hypotyposis* only slightly less than the Studite-Alexis Typika [^1619]. 3) and 4) A series of Southern Italian and Sicilian Typika closely related unto this Typikon, falling into two redactions: at the foundation of the first lies the Typikon of the Monastery of San Nicola di Casole, founded upon the eastern extremity of Calabria (the peninsula 'by means whereof Italy, as it were, stretches forth its hand unto Greece') in 1099 by Greek emigrants with the assistance of Bohemond of Taranto (the monastery submitted unto the Pope only in the 14th century; now in ruins); its Typikon was compiled in 1174 by the third hegumen, Nicholas, 'according unto the tradition', as stated in the title, 'of the holy and God-bearing fathers Sabbas and the Studite, and most especially according unto the rule of the Holy Mountain, and partly upon the basis of the tradition of our venerable father Joseph', the first hegumen of the monastery († 1125), who governed it for 26 years. The Typikon refers in places unto the 'order of the Patriarchal Typikon' (of Hagia Sophia) and unto the 'Typikon of John the Faster' [^1620]. At the foundation *(Orig. p. 363)* of the second redaction lies the Typikon of the Monastery of the Mother of God upon the River Mili in Sicily, 7 miles south of Messina, which exists unto this day, founded in 1089 by Roger, Great Count of Calabria and Sicily, in commemoration of the victory over the Saracens and inhabited by emigrants from Byzantium headed by Hegumen Michael; this Typikon in certain manuscripts is inscribed: 'Typikon containing all the orders of the church office of Theodore the Studite and the rest', and observes concerning itself that it is 'collected from the Orientals'; in it there are references unto the Studite, Jerusalem, Constantinopolitan, Athonite, and a certain Olympian Typikon, and unto the replies of a certain 'Hierarch Anthony' (which were utilized also by the Evergetis Typikon) [^1621]. 5) The Evergetis Typikon, that is, of the Monastery of the Mother of God Evergetis ('the Benefactress') in the suburbs of Constantinople, founded in 1048 by the monk Paul († 1054); his successor Timothy expanded the monastery and gave it a Typikon, which in its synaxarion portion was revised and augmented circa 1150, and has reached us in that form, as is evident from the commemoration therein of Lazarus of Mount Galesios († 1053), which appears for the first time in Menologies from the 12th century (Coislin MS), and from the commemoration of the founders themselves, Paul and Timothy (their service on April 16 is combined both as venerable fathers and for the departed); in the Typikon there are frequent references unto the practice of the Great Church (which is natural for a Constantinopolitan monastery), yet in general the structure of the service is Studite with an inclination toward the Jerusalemite [^1622].

*(Orig. p. 364)*

### Vespers According unto the Ktetorial Studite Typika

Into the order of the daily office inherited from the Church of the Holy Sepulchre and Palestinian monasteries and transmitted unto them by the *Hypotyposis* and *Diatyposis*, all these Typika introduced certain peculiarities, although owing unto the incompleteness of the preceding monuments and the absence of Palestinian Typika contemporary with these rules, it is difficult to determine which of these peculiarities were received by them and shared in common with the contemporary Palestinian rule, and which belong exclusively unto them. As regards Vespers, these Typika appoint at it, following the *Diatyposis* [^1623], for Sundays and feasts the kathisma **"Blessed is the man"** in Tone 8, and for weekdays **"Unto the Lord in mine affliction"** (the 18th Kathisma) in the tone of the day [^1624], with this latter kathisma being omitted on Sunday and great feast days in the evening, during the Twelve Days (*Dodekaēmeron*, between the Nativity of Christ and Theophany), throughout Pentecostarion, on Cheesefare Sunday [^1625], and on Fridays of Great Lent [^1626] (in the Evergetis Typikon, on feasts of great saints likewise) [^1627]. At **"Lord, I have cried"**, following the *Hypotyposis*, the Studite-Alexis Typikon appoints for Sundays and Feasts of the Lord (of the Savior and the Mother of God) 9 stichera (3 stichera are tripled), and for great saints and weekdays—6 [^1628], while the Western Typika and the Evergetis appoint for Feasts of the Lord and Sundays—8, for great saints—6, and for weekdays (with one saint)—4 [^1629]. The troparion at the end of Vespers was chanted unto the saint not only on weekdays and feasts of saints, but on Sundays as well if the saint had a troparion; if not, then on weekdays there were chanted the troparia: **"O Theotokos and Virgin…"**, **"O Baptizer of Christ…"**, **"Beneath thy tender compassion…"** [^1630], and on Sunday either these same troparia [^1631], or the troparion was omitted [^1632], or else the Sunday troparion of the tone was chanted [^1633].

### Matins According unto the Ktetorial Studite Typika

At Matins on weekdays one kathisma was appointed from Antipascha until the Exaltation of the Cross, two from the Exaltation until Great Lent (except Cheesefare Week, when one was read), and three during Great Lent; on Saturday and Sunday according unto some Typika one kathisma was read (San Nicola di Casole), according unto others two (the *Hypotyposis*, Studite-Alexis, Evergetis), wherein on Saturday there was unfailingly read **"Blessed are the undefiled"** (the *Amomos* / Psalm 118 [119]), and on Sunday the 2nd, or the 2nd and 3rd Kathismata [^1634]; thus the Psalter was chanted through at times in less than *(Orig. p. 365)* a week, at times in more than a week (compare the Ambrosian rite, p. 317), for example being chanted through only once during the entire period from Antipascha until Mid-Pentecost [^1635]. The kathismata were always chanted in the appointed tone of the week, furthermore, at least according unto the Studite-Alexis Typikon, with certain 'alleluiaria'—it is unclear whether with special verses resembling current alleluiaria, or with a simple **"Alleluia"** set unto diverse melodies—the latter being more probable; of these alleluiaria St. Theodore the Studite 'instituted' 9 for each tone, 72 in total [^1636]. In this arrangement, the evening kathisma **"Unto the Lord in mine affliction"** was chanted with the first three alleluiaria of the presiding tone, while of the morning kathismata the first was chanted with the 3rd, 4th, and 5th alleluiaria, and the second with the 7th, 8th, and 9th (for this purpose there were 9 alleluiaria; three kathismata at Matins for some reason are not provided for). Yet certain kathismata—or rather, sections thereof—constituted an exception unto this rule by reason of the particular solemnity of their execution, for which purpose, in addition unto the aforementioned alleluiaria, there existed special alleluiaria: two in Tone 4, three in Tone 6, and one in Tone 8. Specifically, the first stasis (*slava*) of the 19th Kathisma, termed 'Many-Mercied' (*Polyeleos* / *Πολυέλεος*) because of the repeated refrain unto Psalm 135 [136]: **"For His mercy (*ἔλεος*) endureth forever"**, and consisting of Psalms 134, 135, and 136 [135, 136, 137], into whatever tone among the first four it fell, was always chanted in Tone 4 with the special alleluiaria of that tone (likewise termed 'Many-Mercied' or 'Polyeleos'), and into whatever tone among the remaining four tones it fell, was chanted in Tone 6 with the 1st alleluiarion among the special ones of that tone; wherein in the first case (when the *Polyeleos* was chanted in Tone 4), Psalm 135 [136] had two **"Alleluia"** refrains after each of its verses and one after the refrain **"For His mercy endureth forever"** (**"O give thanks unto the Lord, for He is good: Alleluia, alleluia; for His mercy endureth forever: Alleluia"**—as at present in the Kyiv Caves melody); in the second case, however, under Tone 6, **"Alleluia"** was sung once in both instances. (In all this lies the embryo of the later Polyeleos). The 2nd and 3rd staseis of the 19th Kathisma were chanted with the alleluiaria of the prevailing tone. If this kathisma occurred also at the Hours, it was chanted in the same manner, whereupon a transfer of this kathisma unto another Hour took place if the general tone of the Hour (that is, the tone of its troparion) did not correspond unto its chant. In addition unto the 'Polyeleos' psalms, there were distinguished from the ordinary chanting of the Psalter at Matins the 2nd stasis of the 7th Kathisma: **"God standeth in the congregation of gods…"** (Psalm 81 [82]), and the final (3rd) stasis of the last, 20th Kathisma: **"Praise the Lord from the heavens…"** (Psalms 148–150). The former was chanted with the 2nd of the special alleluiaria of Tone 6, the latter with the 3rd of them (yet the final Psalm 150, instead of **"Alleluia"**, had the refrain **"Glory to the Father…"**). Finally, a special alleluiarion of Tone 8 existed specifically for the festal **"Blessed is the man…"**, that is, for the 1st stasis of the 1st Kathisma; while its 2nd and 3rd staseis were chanted with the 2nd and 3rd alleluiaria of the prevailing tone [^1637]. With such solemn chanting of both ordinary and especially certain appointed *(Orig. p. 366)* kathismata (an influence of the Sung Office), the Studite-Alexis Typikon does not distinguish feasts with special kathismata, but distinguishes them, as also Sundays, only by the 'Hymns of Ascent' (*Stepenny* / *Anabathmoi*) [^1638], our present ones, yet chanted with the verses of the Gradual Psalms (Psalms 119–133 [120–134] = the 18th Kathisma) and alleluias with *nenenaiki* (melismatic vocables) [^1639]. Yet all other Typika of the Studite type appoint special kathismata for feasts. All Western Typika for every Feast of the Lord appoint before the Gradual Antiphons a three-antiphon, that is, three-psalm kathisma composed of psalms specially selected for the commemorated event, for example, for the Nativity of Christ: Psalms 134, 109, and 86 [135, 110, 87] (in the Grottaferrata Typikon; others have different ones), wherein unto certain verses of the final psalm appropriate unto the feast there was a refrain (*ekphōnēsis* or *hypakoē*), strongly reminiscent of our present Magnification (*velichanie* / megalynarion), for example, in the Grottaferrata Typikon for the Nativity of Christ unto verse 5 of Psalm 86 [87]: **"Mother Sion saith: A man, yea, a man was born in her"**, the refrain: **"We glorify the Nativity in the flesh of our Lord and God and Savior Jesus Christ, and faithfully we venerate His holy icon in the likeness of His holy countenance"** [^1640]; thus the 1st and 2nd time, and the 3rd time: **"We magnify thee, Mary Theotokos, and faithfully we venerate thy holy icon in the likeness of thy holy countenance"**; **"Glory..."**: **"We praise the Lord of glory and faithfully…"**; **"Now and ever..."**: **"We magnify thee, all-pure Virgin, and faithfully…"** Psalm 135 [136] in general is frequently placed in these Typika and other liturgical books of the same epoch and provenance (Southern Italian) as a festal antiphon at Matins, and for the most part is termed 'Polyeleos' (*πολυέлеος*) either alone (the Sicilian Typikon) or in combination with Psalm 134 [135] (San Nicola di Casole, December 25), wherein at times it is appointed for chanting in all 8 tones; in an Horologion unto verses 13–15 of this psalm there are appointed such refrains: **"All generations magnify thee, who art ever-blessed, and most blameless, and the Mother of our God"**; **"It is truly meet to magnify thee, the Theotokos, more honorable than the Cherubim, and beyond compare more glorious than the Seraphim, and the Mother of our God"**; **"Proclaiming thee to be the Theotokos, all generations magnify thee as the Mother of our God"** [^1641]. (An echo of the struggle against Nestorianism?). In the Evergetis Typikon the term *ho polyeleos* (*ὁ πολυέλεος*) = Polyeleos is already set down without further explanation and evidently in the sense of the current Typikon (perhaps composed, in addition unto Psalms 134 and 135 [135, 136], of Psalm 136 [137] as well, as in the Studite-Alexis Typikon); yet for Feasts of Christ and the Dormition, in addition unto one or two 'daily' kathismata with the sessional hymns of the feast, there is appointed also a special festal kathisma, with a sessional hymn or hypakoe following it, for example, for the Nativity of Christ and Theophany—Kathisma 16: **"The Lord said unto my Lord"** (Psalm 109 [110])—'slowly and with great alleluiaria' *(Orig. p. 367)*; on the Dormition—the *Amomos* (Psalm 118 [119]) with the alleluiaria of the tone (on other feasts alleluiaria are not mentioned) [^1642]. — Thus the execution of kathismata in the Studite Typika bears a clear resonance of the Sung Office. No mention is made in the Typika under consideration of any troparia or refrains unto Psalm 50 [51], which together with Psalm 50 [51] occupied a prominent place in the Sung Matins. — At the canon, concerning the number of troparia per ode of which the *Hypotyposis* is silent, and for which the *Diatyposis* appoints 8 troparia [^1643] for weekdays of Pentecostarion, 10 for its Sundays and feasts, and 10 or more for the remaining days of the year [^1644] (under Symeon of Thessalonica: 8, 6, or 4; see above, p. 346), the simplest practice is provided by the Grottaferrata Typikon, which does not indicate the number of troparia for the canon and only occasionally mentions the doubling of the heirmoi (for example, at the Nativity of Christ the second heirmoi **"He saved the people"** were doubled) [^1645]; the Typika of the Sicilian redaction likewise frequently omit the number of troparia (for example, for the Nativity of the Theotokos); they also provide for the canon the lowest number of troparia—8 (for example, for the Exaltation of the Cross) [^1646]; next in the number of troparia at the canon comes the Studite-Alexis Typikon, appointing them frequently at 10, maximum 12 (on great feasts, even the Nativity of Christ, and at concurrences) [^1647]; the Typika of the Calabrian redaction take a step further, appointing for great feasts, such as the Nativity of Christ, 14 troparia and regulating the number of troparia with particular precision [^1648]; finally, the Evergetis Typikon appoints for the most part 12 or 14 troparia, and for great feasts even 16 [^1649]. — At the Praises (*Ainoi* / *Laudes*), following the *Hypotyposis*, which requires for Sunday the doubling of the (four) Sunday stichera [^1650], the Western Typika and the Studite-Alexis Typikon appoint for Sundays stichera at 8, the Evergetis at 6; for feasts, among the Western Typika some appoint 4, others 6, the Studite-Alexis—6, the Evergetis—6, yet for saints the latter appoints 4, and for the Nativity of Christ—8 [^1651]. — As regards the Great Doxology and the conclusion of Matins, in the heart of the most ancient Studite Typika a significant transformation of this part of Matins took place, namely, that a different form was imparted unto it for weekdays and for feasts; clear traces of the gradual implementation of this reform have been preserved. The Studite-Alexis Typikon at festal and Sunday Matins, in addition unto the stichera at the Praises, indicates also stichera at the aposticha (*stikhovny*) [^1652]. If one adds unto this *(Orig. p. 368)* that the Great Doxology even in its current form, especially on weekdays, consists of two purely mechanically joined parts—the Doxology proper and the morning prayer **"Vouchsafe, O Lord, to keep us this day"**, corresponding unto the evening **"Vouchsafe, O Lord"**; if, further, one takes into consideration that our present Sunday stichera at the Praises represent an analogous mechanical combination of the stichera of the Praises proper (with the verses of the Psalms of Praise) and stichera with special Sunday verses, in other words 'aposticha' (*stikhovny*), then it becomes indubitable that the conclusion of every Matins in the most ancient Typika had the same form as the second part of festal Vespers at present from **"O Gladsome Light"**: following the stichera of the Praises (corresponding unto the stichera at **"Lord, I have cried"**) there followed the 1st tier of the Great Doxology (unto which the Latin *Gloria in excelsis* used at Mass is limited), corresponding unto **"O Gladsome Light"**; then followed the Augmented Litany (in the most ancient, in all likelihood, the Litany of Peace), **"Vouchsafe, O Lord, to keep us this day"**, the Litany of Supplication, the stichera at the aposticha, a verse corresponding unto **"Now lettest Thou Thy servant depart…"**—in all probability **"It is good to give praise unto the Lord…"**, the Trisagion, and the troparion. Thus according unto the Mili (Sicilian) Typikon during Great Lent (which preserves even now the greatest number of traces of ancient practice) Matins has the following conclusion: **"Glory to God in the highest"** without **"Vouchsafe, O Lord, to keep us this day"**, the Augmented Litany (*ektenē*), **"Vouchsafe, O Lord, to keep us this day"**, the Litany of Supplication (*tēn synaptēn tōn aitēseōn*), the stichera at the aposticha, **"It is good to give praise"**, the Trisagion through the **"Our Father"**, and the dismissory troparion of the day; Lenten Vespers has an identical conclusion: **"O Gladsome Light"**, the Augmented Litany, **"Vouchsafe, O Lord"**, the Litany of Supplication, **"Now lettest Thou Thy servant depart"**, the Trisagion, and the Lenten troparia [^1653]. Yet it is remarkable that already the Western Studite Typika, beginning with that of Grottaferrata, do not know such a type of Matins; thus on the Sunday of the Publican and Pharisee the Grottaferrata Typikon indicates only the stichera of the Praises, while the Calabrian and Sicilian redactions provide here the following detailed order for the conclusion of Matins: following the stichera of the Praises and **"Most blessed art thou"**: 'the *to Doxa megalōs* (**"Glory"**—greatly), the Trisagion, the Sunday troparion, then the litany, the petitions (the Litany of Supplication), and the rest, and the dismissal'. It is remarkable that according unto the Mili Typikon exactly the same order governs also the conclusion of festal Vespers: 'stichera at the aposticha, the Trisagion, the litany (that is, the Augmented Litany), the petitions (that is, the Litany of Supplication), and the rest, and the dismissal' [^1654]. The very term 'Great Doxology' is already employed by the Grottaferrata Typikon [^1655], not to speak of the Evergetis. Yet Nikon of the Black Mountain (11th century) considers the absence of the Great Doxology and the separation of the aposticha stichera from the stichera of the Praises at Matins on the greatest feasts to be a general peculiarity of all Studite Typika [^1656].

*(Orig. p. 369)*

### The Hours and Compline in the Studite Typika

Almost the most prominent peculiarity of the Typika under consideration is constituted, following the *Hypotyposis* and *Diatyposis* [^1657] and under the influence of the Typikon of Hagia Sophia, by the omission of the Hours on Sundays and feast days, even minor ones. The Studite-Alexis Typikon is interspersed with the remark *porozn' chasom* ('the Hours are omitted' / individual celebration of the Hours), for example, on September 1, 5, 6, 7, etc. [^1658]; the Western Typika and the Evergetis simply maintain silence concerning the Hours, yet the Grottaferrata Typikon takes a step toward Jerusalem practice when, for example, on the Nativity of the Theotokos, and consequently on other feasts likewise, it instructs to chant after Matins the 'dismissory' (troparion) thrice in place of the First Hour, and to celebrate the Hour itself individually (*katamonas*), while the Third and Sixth Hours with the Beatitudes of the feast the presbyters 'chant while vesting' for the procession before the Liturgy [^1659]. The Sicilian Typikon during Great Lent possesses single-psalm Sung Hours with a Great Litany following the psalm, three Little Litanies at the antiphons of the kathisma, and a Litany of Supplication following the troparion and reading—and with prayers of the priest [^1660]. — With respect unto Compline the Studite Typika exhibit the same diversity and vacillation as the Jerusalem Typika, and possess this service in general of an identical type with the latter (for which reason the history of this office is common unto both—see below, 'Compline'); yet the Evergetis Typikon, following the *Diatyposis* [^1661] and under the influence of the Typikon of the Great Church, in addition unto Compline—which it mentions only on the eves of Sundays, the Nativity of Christ, and Theophany—appoints during Great Lent a daily pannychis consisting of one or two canons with sessional hymns after the 3rd ode and a kontakion (for the most part **"O Protection of Christians…"**) after the 6th ode, preceded by Psalm 50 [51] and followed by the Trisagion, troparion, and litany (as among us on the eve of Pascha); during Great Lent, and perhaps in general on weekdays, this pannychis was joined unto Vespers; on the eves of feasts it preceded Matins and, having after itself also a reading, together with it and with Matins constituted a single 'vigil' (*agrypnia* / ἀγρυπνία) [^1662]; in this the Evergetis Typikon drew close unto the Jerusalem Typikon, toward which it inclines in other cases as well.

### The Jerusalem Typikon According unto Nikon of the Black Mountain

From the 11th century we possess the first report regarding the existence and dissemination in the East of more or less complete texts of Typika in the strict sense according unto the order of the Palestinian Lavra of St. Sabas (near Jerusalem). This report belongs unto Nikon of the Black Mountain, who was at first a certain official ('instructor' / *nastavnik*), and later hegumen in the monasteries of Rhaithou on *(Orig. p. 370)* Sinai and of St. Symeon the Wonderworker of the Admirable Mountain upon the Black Mountain near Antioch during the reign of Emperor Constantine Doukas (1059–1067), and who personally did much both in general for the development of the church Typikon and, in particular, for the replacement of the Studite Typikon by the Jerusalem Typikon [^1663]. Prompted by disorders in the monasteries of that era (disobedience toward superiors, striving toward idiorrhythmic / kellion living as granting greater freedom, discord among liturgical orders), Nikon resolved to provide a written manual for monastics, a consolidated typikon or *Taktikon*, through the collation of diverse typika. During the preliminary work for this composition, there was revealed unto Nikon not only the existence of a multitude of diverse typika—such as that of the Great Church, the Studite, the Jerusalem, the Hagiorite (Athonite), the typikon of the Patriarchate of Antioch, of the Monastery of St. Auxentius, and others (not to mention the ancient rules of St. Pachomius, Basil the Great, and Cassian)—but also a significant discrepancy among them, even between the different recensions of one and the same typikon: 'I read and collected diverse Typika, Studite and Jerusalem, and they did not agree one with another, neither a Studite with another Studite, nor a Jerusalem with another Jerusalem' (in all likelihood, Nikon had at hand ktetorial typika) [^1664]. For the resolution of his perplexities, Nikon turned unto the 'experienced fathers' in the monastery of St. Sabas, and upon their counsel 'took care concerning the ancient Jerusalem' Typikon [^1665]; the hegumen of this monastery directed him for an accurate manuscript of the Jerusalem Typikon unto Laodicea (evidently in the Lavra of St. Sabas they were guided, as in part at present upon Mount Athos, by an unwritten Typikon), and lo, 'at the Savior in Laodicea,' recounts Nikon, 'we found preserved in the library an ancient Jerusalem Typikon, which the blessed Nicodemus, former hegumen of St. Sabas (chronology unknown), set forth for the Metropolitan of Laodicea from the beginning; and that one I took, as thou knowest, and I have it here at St. Symeon the Wonderworker (upon the Black Mountain), so that those who wish copy from it. All the others, as we have said, were found incorrect and do not equate unto the ancient one. Likewise did I find the Studite typika diverse, and neither do they equate one with another; and on account of this inequality, and still more because they possessed not any testimonies from the Divine Scriptures, but merely spoke thus: that we perform this and that' [^1666].

*(Orig. p. 371)* Thus Nikon accords preference unto the Jerusalem Typikon over the Studite: (a) on account of the possibility of utilizing its ancient and complete manuscript; (b) because the Jerusalem Typikon substantiates its prescriptions upon the 'Divine Scriptures' and does not impart them, like the Studite, without motivation—an example of which Nikon points out further in the stricter rules of fasting according unto the Jerusalem Typikon, which are consonant with the canons of the holy Apostles, councils, and ancient ascetics (for example, regarding the non-mitigation of the fast on Wednesday and Friday on account of feasts, and regarding the hour of breaking the fast on Great Saturday).
