In view of such advantages of the Jerusalem Typikon, Nikon also labored for its dissemination, and composes his consolidated rule ('Typikon', *Taktikon*) in its spirit, noting nevertheless in places also the Studite practice, and occasionally borrowing prescriptions from the Hagiorite Typikon. (The disciplinary portion of this *Typikon* of Nikon was subsequently incorporated into the Slavonic manuscripts of the Jerusalem Typikon and exists in our present Typikon).

### The Domain and Recensions of the Jerusalem Typikon

Thus in the 11th century and earlier, the Jerusalem Typikon enjoyed dissemination not only in Palestine [^1667], but also in the Patriarchate of Antioch and Asia Minor. Around this time, if not earlier, the Jerusalem Typikon was adopted upon Sinai, as is evident from its manuscripts [^1668] and other liturgical books arranged according unto this Typikon in the Sinai Library, occasionally dating back unto the 10th century and earlier [^1669], although the Jerusalem Typikon that developed upon Sinai exhibits certain peculiarities in comparison with the genuine Jerusalem one [^1670]. Somewhat later (in the 12th century), in all probability, the Jerusalem Typikon was adopted in the Diocese of Constantinople, judging by the fact that Nikon says nothing regarding its dissemination there. Yet Patriarch Nicholas III Grammatikos of Constantinople (1084–1111), in his 'Epistle unto the Protos of the Holy Mountain' [^1671], resolves the perplexities of the Athonite monastics—arising upon the grounds of the conflict between the less strict Studite practice concerning fasts and the stricter Jerusalem practice—in the spirit of *(Orig. p. 372)* the latter. The ktetorial Typikon given by Empress Irene, consort of Emperor Alexios Komnenos († 1183), unto the Monastery of the Mother of God, Full of Grace (*Kecharitomene*), founded by her in Constantinople—which in its liturgical portion refers in general unto the 'Synaxarion' (generally accepted), presupposes Jerusalem practice: *agrypniai* (vigils) and inter-hours (*mesoria*) are mentioned [^1672]. Unto the Palestinian Typikon the Typikon of Neilos, Hegumen of the Monastery of the Mother of God of Machairas, likewise refers [^1673]. The Typikon of the Monastery of the Archangel Michael upon Mount St. Auxentius near Chalcedon, given unto it by its founder, Emperor Michael Palaiologos (1250–1282), requires that psalmody be celebrated according unto the ancient custom of the Palestinian monasteries 'or according unto the Jerusalem Typikon,' except for Sunday vigils, as being exceedingly burdensome [^1674]. The consolidation of the Jerusalem Typikon in Constantinople was, in all likelihood, facilitated by the devastation of the Studion Monastery by the Crusaders, from which it was restored only by Emperor Constantine Palaiologos in 1298. Around this same time, in the 12th century, the Jerusalem Typikon found dissemination upon Mount Athos. Even if at the beginning of this century the Jerusalem regimen of fasting still seemed strange unto the Athonites, in this very century there appear upon Mount Athos Menaia of Jerusalem liturgical structure, several copies of which were brought from there by Arseny Sukhanov unto Russia and are preserved at present in the Moscow Synodal (former Patriarchal) Library (MSS Nos. 446–451: Jan., Mar., June, Aug., Oct., Dec.). As upon Sinai, the Jerusalem Typikon upon Mount Athos acquired certain local peculiarities, retaining at times the Studite practice deeply rooted there (for example, regarding fasts) and forming a distinct form of the Hagiorite Typikon [^1675]. — From the 12th century is likewise known the first manuscript of the Jerusalem Typikon *(Orig. p. 373)* for Georgia, namely written for the monastery of St. Shio of Mghvime (near Tiflis) in 1172, in all probability from an original of the Wonderworking Mountain Monastery, and preserved in a 13th-century copy bearing the title: 'Typikon of the Church Office of the Well-Ordered Lavra of the Holy and God-Bearing Sabas; Such Also Occurs in All Other Monasteries of Palestine.' Among published manuscripts of the Jerusalem Typikon this is the most ancient (there is no Little Vespers; the Markian Chapters are without the name of Mark and are exceedingly brief; there are no commemorations of: the Holy Mandylion [*Ubrus*], established in 944; Athanasius of Athos, † 1000; Lazarus of Mount Galesios, † 1053; Michael Choniates, † 1266 [read 1222]; or even George the Chozebite of the 7th century) [^1676]. In the 13th–14th centuries the Jerusalem Typikon attains the widest dissemination throughout the entire East, as is evident from a series of its Greek manuscripts preserved from these centuries, such as, for example, its most ancient manuscript in Russia, yielding little unto the Shiomghvime manuscript, in the Moscow Public (Rumyantsev) Museum from the Sevastyanov Collection No. 35/491 (13th c.); the Typikon of the Moscow Synodal Library, Greek Department No. 381, written, judging by the names in the diptychs, under Patriarch Athanasius of Constantinople (1289–1332); the Typikon of the Moscow Synodal Library No. 456 with the dubious date 1298, more likely 14th century; and the Typikon of the Vatican Library No. 784, written in 1317 in *Tēphrei tēs chōras Rōsias* (in Russia, in Tver?) [^1677]. How *(Orig. p. 374)* widely disseminated in Greece the Jerusalem Typikon had become by the 14th century is attested by the so-called *Diataxis tēs hierodiakonias* (Order of the Holy Ministry / *Chin svyashchennosluzheniya*), attributed unto Patriarch Philotheus of Constantinople, the celebrated 14th-century liturgist, yet having appeared possibly even earlier [^1678]; appointed, evidently, for the widest universal application, it provides the Jerusalem order of the All-Night Vigil, striving to supply the omissions of ancient manuscripts of the Jerusalem Typikon concerning the liturgical actions of the priest and deacon during divine worship [^1679]. In Serbia, the first complete text of the Jerusalem Typikon was its translation in 1319, executed by Archbishop Nicodemus, former archimandrite of the Hilandar Monastery, from a Greek original obtained from the Patriarch of Constantinople (not from Mount Athos, where the Jerusalem Typikon existed not in its pure form), from the Monastery of the Forerunner (in all probability the Studion, where consequently the Jerusalem Typikon had already been introduced) [^1680]. Prior unto this time, Serbia was guided by the Hilandar Typikon, unto which there is an implicit reference in the preface unto Nicodemus's Typikon. In 1331, Nicodemus's Typikon was transcribed also for Hilandar by a certain Roman [^1681]. Following Nicodemus's Typikon, there appeared in Serbia a series of other Typika, for the most part close unto it [^1682]. — Unto the 14th century likewise belong the most ancient Slavonic translations of the Jerusalem Typikon made in Russia, such as Moscow Synodal Library MS No. 328/383 of the 14th century (their Russian origin is evident from the presence of several Russian saints and the absence of South Slavonic ones), exceedingly close both in contents and still more in the structure of the daily office unto ancient Greek and Serbian codices. The appearance in Russia of complete manuscripts of the Jerusalem Typikon was preceded by the gradual penetration of its practice from Greece, beginning from the 13th century. Unto the Synod of Vladimir in 1274 and that of Constantinople in 1276, Russian bishops already express perplexities concerning certain Studite customs (for example, regarding the Liturgy of the Presanctified Gifts on Cheesefare Wednesday and Friday and on Great Friday) and receive an answer in the spirit of the Jerusalem Typikon [^1683]. Yet even in the 15th century Studite practice persists in Russia, as shown by manuscripts of the Studite Typikon from that century and the queries of the Pskov clergy unto St. Metropolitan Photius (1410–1431) [^1684]. Unto the dissemination of the Jerusalem Typikon in Russia, *(Orig. p. 375)* St. Metropolitan Cyprian (1380–1406 with interruption) contributed greatly through his (manuscript) editions of the 'Horologion according unto the Typikon of the Lavra of our Venerable Father Sabas in Jerusalem' (the Sequenced Psalter / *Sledovannaya Psaltir*) and the *Sluzhebnik* of 1397, into which was incorporated the *Diataxis* of Patriarch Philotheus [^1685]. Under Cyprian as well, the first attempt at a Russian recension of the Jerusalem Typikon was made in the form of the *Tserkovne Oko* (*Oko Tserkovnoye*) by Hegumen Athanasius of Vysotsky, translated by him in the Peribleptos Monastery at Constantinople and furnished with additions—among others, disciplinary articles from Nikon of the Black Mountain [^1686]. This endeavor laid the foundation for an entire series of Russian recensions of the Jerusalem Typikon, concluding only with the appearance of its printed edition [^1687].

### The Character of the Daily Office According unto the Jerusalem Typikon

In contrast unto the Studite Typika, the Jerusalem Typika present a uniform structure of Vespers and Matins, identical with our present one. Although this is explained partly by the later date of these Typika, yet if one takes into consideration that this structure coincides also with that given by the Holy Sepulchre Typikon of the 9th century (the century unto which belong also the earliest monuments of the Studite Typikon) and at times remains truer than the Studite unto the ecclesiastical practice of the 4th–5th centuries (litiyas, as in Silvia/Egeria; vigils, which in the 4th–5th centuries occurred at least several times a year), then we may recognize as the first valuable characteristic in this domain—and one that contributed unto the ascendancy of the Jerusalem Typikon over the Studite—a greater stability, immutability, and fidelity unto antiquity in the daily office in comparison with the Studite Typikon. Another equally advantageous characteristic (from a Christian-ascetic perspective) of the Jerusalem Typikon was the greater duration of church services according unto it, which depended upon the greater proximity of this Typikon (both geographical and spiritual) and its fidelity unto the traditions of ancient asceticism (a characteristic manifested still more vividly in the comparatively greater strictness of this Typikon in its fasting regimen); most noticeably regarding the daily office, this characteristic revealed itself in the indispensable celebration of the Hours, which were not omitted for any feasts whatsoever. In relation unto the most important daily services—Vespers and Matins—this characteristic of the Jerusalem Typikon was manifested above all in a greater number of kathismata: at Matins there was always one kathisma more than according unto the Studite Typikon, except during Great Lent, Saturdays, Sundays, and feast days, when the number of kathismata according unto both Typika was identical. If one recalls that among Eastern monasticism there once existed a tendency *(Orig. p. 376)* to chant the entire Psalter every twenty-four hours (see above, pp. 294–295, the narrative of the visit unto Nilus of Sinai by John and Sophronius, and p. 299, 'Armenian Liturgy'), then in this characteristic of the Jerusalem Typikon as well one cannot fail to perceive its greater fidelity unto the traditions of asceticism, which attributed such paramount significance unto the Psalter (see above, pp. 189 ff.). Connected with this is likewise the greater number of stichera and troparia according unto the Jerusalem Typikon: the latter permits at **"Lord, I have cried"** (*Gospodi vozzvakh*) 10 stichera, and at the canon usually 14 and sometimes 16 verses, heirmoi, and troparia, whereas in the Studite Typika the maximum for the former was 9, and for the latter 14, usually 12. The same must be said regarding vigils: under the influence precisely of ascetic practice, with its customary all-night prayers, the Jerusalem Typikon, in place of the pre-dawn Matins customary in antiquity for Sundays and feast days, introduced all-night vigils (*agrypniai*) for both. Not unconnected with that same spirit of asceticism was the melodic simplification of divine worship in the Jerusalem Typikon: here drop away the requirements of the Studite Typikon, which constituted within it the heritage of the Sung Office (*asmatike akolouthia*), regarding the special, melodic execution of kathismata [^1688], hypakoai, and the like. — Other characteristics of the Jerusalem Typikon depended upon its place of origin: the Holy Land. From this perspective an explanation is provided for the litiyas which this Typikon requires, as was the case in Jerusalem practice as early as the 4th–5th centuries (see above, pp. 140 ff.), for every Vespers and Matins. The homeland of this Typikon, which compelled a more intense reliving of the celebrated sacred events, manifested itself also in the fact that the Jerusalem Typikon establishes a far sharper distinction between weekday and festal worship than does the Studite. This distinction is achieved—leaving aside vigils—on the one hand by the addition unto festal services of the Polyeleos (*Polyeleos*), whereas the Studite Typikon in such cases merely substituted certain (likewise chanted) kathismata for others; and on the other hand by the so-called 'Great Doxology,' which constitutes a technical term designating a completely different conclusion of Matins for feasts in comparison with weekdays: it signifies the transposition of the prayer **"Vouchsafe, O Lord"** (*Spodobi, Gospodi*) into direct conjunction with the Great Doxology, and the fusion of the aposticha stichera with the stichera at the Praises for feast days.

### Vespers and Matins of Mixed Type

All these, although characteristic, are not exceedingly significant peculiarities in the structure of the daily office, more specifically in the order of Vespers and Matins. In general, these two services in both Typika possess one and the same order and structure, diverging with almost equal *(Orig. p. 377)* sharpness from the so-called 'Sung Office' (*asmatikos typos*), or the court-cathedral Typikon of Constantinople. This latter order not only persisted intact in many churches until the 15th century, but also strove to assimilate unto itself the monastic, Studite-Jerusalem Vespers and Matins. The imprint of such a tendency is borne by the orders of Vespers and Matins in certain Euchologia of the 12th–16th centuries. Vespers in them exhibits the following peculiarities: According unto the Euchologia of the 12th century (1153) of the Sinai Library No. 973 and of the 13th century of the Patmos Library No. 105, Vespers begins with the exclamation **"Blessed is the Kingdom..."** (*Evlogēmenē hē basileia...* / *Blagoslovenno Tsarstvo...*). According unto the Euchologion in a 16th-century manuscript of the Tiflis Ecclesiastical-Archaeological Museum No. 450, at the beginning of Vespers the Introductory Psalm is not indicated; it begins with three 'antiphons' with Little Litanies and special prayers at each of them. Following **"Lord, I have cried"** (*Kyrie ekekraxa* / *Gospodi vozzvakh*), prior unto the stichera, there is again a Little Litany, yet of a distinctive type, similar unto the Second Litany of the Faithful at the Divine Liturgy ('In peace let us pray unto the Lord... For the peace from above... For the peace of the whole world... For this holy temple... Help us, save us... And for all who require aid from God. Calling to remembrance our all-holy, immaculate... For unto Thee is due...'). The Augmented Litany **"Let us all say"** (*Rtsem vsi*) is appointed in its present place—following the prokimenon and before **"Vouchsafe, O Lord"**—yet possesses a distinctive composition, identical, except for the first four petitions, with our present Great Litany; consequently it represents the Augmented Litany and the Great Litany still in the period of their union. According unto the aforementioned Patmos Euchologion of the 13th century, which provides fully our present order of Vespers in its festal form, after the exclamations of the Great Litany and the three Little Litanies there is appointed **"Peace be unto all,"** so that in the course of Vespers it is repeated six times (and before the prokimenon it is pronounced by the deacon) [^1689]; compare the Milanese (Ambrosian) and Mozarabic order of Vespers (see above, pp. 353 and 355). According unto the aforementioned Sinai Euchologion of the 12th century, the Litany of Supplication is appointed after **"Now lettest Thou Thy servant depart"** (*Nyně otpushchayeshi*) and the troparion; whereas according unto the Euchologion of the Tiflis Ecclesiastical-Archaeological Museum, in this place at festal Vespers there is indicated the litany **"Have mercy on us, O God..."** (*Pomiluy nas, Bozhe...*), and the Litany of Supplication before **"Now lettest Thou Thy servant depart"** (consequently, the conclusion of Vespers is as at present on weekdays). All the indicated Euchologia distribute the evening prayers throughout the entire course of Vespers at all its litanies. — No fewer variations in comparison with our present order are presented by the Euchologia of the same era for Matins. According unto the Sinai Euchologion of the 12th century, it begins with the exclamation **"Blessed is the Kingdom..."** Following the Hexapsalmos and the Great Litany, the Sinai and Patmos Euchologia indicate: the former prior unto the *kathisma* (sessional hymn) and Polyeleos, and the latter prior unto the Anabathmoi / Antiphons of the Degrees (*stepenny*—the Studite type of festal Matins) and the Gospel, the prayers of the 'three antiphons' with a Little Litany following the 2nd (Sinai) or 3rd (Patmos) among them, beginning **"Again and again"** (*Paki i paki*) or **"Help us, save us"** (*Zastupi, spasi*—Sinai, in accordance with the Sung Office), and with the exclamation **"Peace be unto all"** before it (Patmos) and after it (Patmos; Tiflis No. 450). In place of these 'antiphons,' the Tiflis Euchologion and the Georgian manuscript *(Orig. p. 378)* of the Imperial Public Library No. 208 of the 16th century indicate prayers and Little Litanies following each of the three 'psalms' of the kathisma (in all probability, there is presupposed a single sung-festal three-psalm kathisma, as in the Italo-Sicilian branch of the Studite Typika); after the kathisma there follow: the sessional hymn, reading (both Georgian monuments), Anabathmoi / Degrees (MS No. 208), the Blameless / Amomos (Psalm 118 [119]), the Evlogetaria / **"The Assembly of Angels"** (*Angelskiy Sobor* / *Ton angelōn ho dēmos*—No. 450), the Gospel, and Psalm 50 [51]. The most ancient of the aforementioned Euchologia, the Sinai manuscript, indicates Psalm 50 [51] after the 'kontakion,' that is, after the 6th ode of the canon (or a triodion with the kontakion at the beginning is presupposed—see below), and the Gospel after the Great Doxology (in accordance with the Sung Office). This same Euchologion indicates after the 'kathisma' the 'Prayers of the Sunday Polyeleos in Holy Lent' (a hint at the original use of the Polyeleos exclusively in Lent), wherein it further apparently cites these prayers: the first having no heading whatsoever, and the subsequent ones designated: 'Prayer of the 5th Antiphon' (consequently the preceding was of the 4th), 'of the 6th Antiphon,' '7th Prayer'—four in all; after the last (8th) follows the rubric: 'Then the kontakion, the 50th (Psalm), and immediately the deacon: **"In peace let us pray unto the Lord,"** the 9th prayer..., **"Help us, save us..."** **"The morning and..."** (*tēn orthrinēn kai tēn...*), **"An angel of peace..."** **"Pardon..."** and immediately the odes, and after the 9th ode: **"Again and again..."** with the prayer.' Thus, after the antiphons of the Polyeleos or of some festal kathisma, this Euchologion indicates immediately the kontakion, Psalm 50 [51], the Litany of Supplication with an opening taken from the Litany of Peace and the Little Litany, and only then the canon ('the odes'), yet a canon evidently of exceedingly brief composition (since there is no mention of the customary inter-ode hymnody), perhaps a diodion or triodion; moreover, earlier in this Euchologion, prior unto the discussion of the Polyeleos prayers, occurs the rubric: 'after the 6th ode the kontakion'; perhaps at weekday Matins, in place of the Polyeleos, there was a full canon (precious vestiges of the ancient structure of Matins at the transition from the kontakion-based system unto the canon-based system). All other aforementioned Euchologia, after Psalm 50 [51], presuppose the customary full canon; yet the Georgian manuscripts place before it, after Psalm 50 [51], a Litany of Peace of a distinctive composition differing in both manuscripts (one of 6 petitions, the other of 9), and with our present exclamation (which precedes the canon). The Georgian monuments appoint a litany with prayer also at the 7th ode of the canon, and a prayer at the 8th ode. (It is possible that litanies formerly occurred at every ode, and here we have a survival of this practice, as at present at Paschal Matins and in the Cryptaferrata / Grottaferrata Typikon at Nativity Matins [^1690]). The order of litanies at the conclusion of Matins is in all of them of our present festal type, yet in the Patmos codex it is of our present weekday type (although Matins is presupposed to be festal). The Georgian codices do not name the Augmented Litany, but indicate only its prayer, the first with a ninefold **"Lord, have mercy"** [^1691].

If the Studite and Jerusalem Typika possessed so much in common in the structure of the most important services of the daily cycle—Vespers and Matins—then in the secondary services, such as the Hours, Compline, Midnight Office, and Typika (*Izobrazitelnye*), *(Orig. p. 379)* they were rendered completely uniform. These services possessed their own distinct history, taking no account of the peculiarities of the one or the other Typikon.

### The Hours

As regards the Hours, we have seen that already in the 9th century their order had developed up unto the Trisagion, where the order of the Hour concludes both according unto the Holy Sepulchre Typikon and according unto the Sinai Horologion of the 8th–9th century according unto the order of the Lavra of St. Sabas (see above, p. 298), which represent in general a complete coincidence in the order of the Hours. The latter Horologion provides likewise all our present psalms of the Hours, and both monuments provide our present troparia of the Hours (their first series following the psalms) and the 'verses' of the Hours (**"Order my steps..."** / *Stopy moya...* and the like). If in this Horologion and certain subsequent ones (for example, Sinai No. 864 of the 9th century), other psalms are joined unto our present three psalms of the Hours, this is because these Horologia, evidently, were intended for cell use rather than for church celebration. For this reason, one must suppose, these Horologia do not contain the priestly element in the service of the Hours. A supplement unto them may be found in the ancient Euchologia, which provide—as, for example, the Greek Sinai MS No. 958 of the 10th century, Paris National Library MS No. 213 of the 11th century (1027), and the Slavonic *Trebnik* of the Moscow Synodal Library MS No. 371/675—the priestly prayers of the Hours. Of such prayers at each Hour there are indicated here six: 'Prayer of the 1st Antiphon,' 'of the 2nd Antiphon,' 'of the 3rd Antiphon,' 'Prayer of the Dismissal,' 'of the Bowing of Heads,' and a special concluding prayer without title; each with an exclamation (it is not everywhere marked: 'exclamation'); before the 5th, **"Peace be unto all,"** **"Bow your heads..."**; before the concluding prayer, the deacon: **"Wisdom."** In their contents the prayers are adapted unto the time of day and the sacred commemorations of the Hour, frequently containing expressions from our present psalms and verses of the Hours; in the prayer of the Third Hour commemoration is made of the Descent of the Holy Spirit; of the Sixth Hour, of the Crucifixion; of the Ninth Hour, of the going up unto prayer at that hour of the Apostles Peter and John [^1692]. Judging by the fact that these prayers are located in Euchologia that presuppose the Sung Office structure of Vespers and Matins, they were intended, in all probability, for Sung Hours. Such Hours are appointed for Lent by the Western ktetorial Typika of the Sicilian recension (see above, p. 402). Their order was as follows: a single psalm of the Hour was chanted, followed by the Great Litany; the priest recited the prayer lying prostrate before the altar; then the 'stichology' (*stichologia* / στιχολογία), that is, a kathisma, at each antiphon of which a Little Litany was said (prayers are not mentioned); then the troparion of the Hour (Lenten) with its Theotokion;

a reading; the Litany of Supplication; the verse of the Hour (**"Order my steps..."** and the like); the Trisagion through the **"Our Father"**; **"Lord, have mercy"** 12 times on each choir; **"Glory to the Father..."**; **"In the Name of the Lord, bless, father"**; the priest: **"O Lord Jesus Christ, our God, have mercy on us"**; three great prostrations; the prayer **"Unto all who lie prostrate"**; and the dismissal [^1693] (in this same manner, as we have seen, the Ninth Hour was chanted according unto the Holy Sepulchre Typikon during Passion Week). *(Orig. p. 380)* It is possible that in churches where the Sung Office was maintained, such Hours—arising, in all probability, under the influence of the *trithekte*—were chanted outside of Great Lent as well, or at least that ordinary Hours there possessed priestly prayers in such or a smaller number.

In addition unto the indicated series of prayers, the Paris Euchologion in separate rubrics provides yet another prayer, rather lengthy, for each Hour—perhaps precisely for the occasion when the Hours were celebrated with less solemnity. This latter practice—of only a single priestly prayer at each Hour—prevailed; yet this priestly prayer of the Hour was gradually abbreviated unto the brief exclamation **"God be bountiful unto us..."**, borrowed from Psalm 66:1 [67:1] and recalling the Old Testament priestly blessing, or unto the exclamation **"O Lord Jesus Christ, our God, have mercy on us"** (see above), later augmented by the addition at the beginning of **"Through the prayers of our holy fathers."** That these exclamations replaced the former (lengthy) prayer of the priest at the Hours is evident from the fact that in ancient Typika they are customarily accompanied by the note: 'and the priest prays' (*euchetai* / εὔχεται), and at times are even directly replaced by this note or designated the 'prayer of the Hours' or 'of Compline' [^1694]. Yet the memory of the former practice prompted the introduction, in place of the priestly prayers that had disappeared from the Hours, of prayers recited by the reader—originally one for each Hour and brief, in the manner of a troparion [^1695], and later several (two or three), among which appears the prayer **"Thou Who at all times"** (*Hō en panti kairō* / *Izhe na vsyakoye vremya*) [^1696]. The latter, on account of its universal contents, was in the course of time appropriated unto each Hour, which received in addition unto it another specialized prayer as well [^1697]. Beside the transformation of the prayer element in the Hours, the present era brought unto the service of the Hour certain additions as well. Such above all was the repeated **"Lord, have mercy,"** which was an echo of ascetic practice (see above, p. 190) [^1698]. *(Orig. p. 381)* Later than other parts, there entered into the composition of the service of the Hours the troparia after the Trisagion, concerning which ancient Horologia and Typika not only exhibit, but also expressly state [^1699], a great vacillation.

### The Inter-Hours (Mesoria)

Besides the Hours, the Jerusalem Typikon from its most ancient manuscripts (at least among those published) possessed also the inter-hours (*mesoria*) or intermediate hours (*pochasiya*). Them is indicated already by the Shio-Mgvime Typikon (which possesses no Little Vespers), wherein their order is literally identical with the present one—only the concluding prayer is lacking; even the selection of psalms and troparia coincides almost entirely with the present one (the sole difference in psalms being that at the Inter-Hour of the Ninth Hour there is a superfluous psalm: Psalm 50 [51]). Yet Horologia from the 12th century, in which the order of the Inter-Hours first appears, although likewise presenting their present structure, exhibit great vacillation in the selection of psalms and prayers for the Inter-Hours; moreover, it is remarkable that in the most ancient Horologia there are more coincidences with the present order: thus, the Horologion of the Sinai Library MS No. 865 of the 12th century contains all the present psalms (only at the First and Third Hours with the additional Psalm 50 [51]); in the Sinai Horologion MS No. 870 of the 13th century, only two psalms coincide with the present ones; while in the Horologia of the Athos-Vatopaidi Library MS No. 350/984 of the 13th century, the Sinai MS No. 868 [printed: 8686] of the 13th–14th centuries, and the Novgorod-Sophia Library (at the St. Petersburg Theological Academy) MS No. 1052 of the 13th–14th centuries, not a single psalm coincides with the present cursus; evidently these Horologia, being manuals of the kellion-skete rule (see below), do not take into account the generally accepted and ancient order of the Inter-Hours; according unto some of them, certain Hours even possess more than one inter-hour: thus, in the Sinai Horologion MS No. 870 of the 13th century, the First Hour has one inter-hour, the Third and Sixth have two each, and the Ninth has three inter-hours [^1700] (corresponding, in all probability, unto the importance of the commemorated events).

### Compline

Subject unto no fewer modifications than the Hours was the order of Compline (*apodeipnon* / повечерие), and in like manner the particularities of the diverse Typika exercised no influence upon the development of this office: in both the Studite and Jerusalem Typika it shared a common history. The earliest notices concerning this office lead us to understand that in both branches of the Typikon it possessed a very similar, if not identical, composition. Thus the *Hypotyposis* and *Diatyposis*, distinguishing two forms of Compline (*ta apodeipna* / τὰ ἀπόδειπνα)—complete (*holoklēra* / ὁλόκληρα) and abbreviated for festal days—direct that the second be commenced from **“God is with us”** (*Hypotyposis*) or from **“He that dwelleth in the help of the Most High”**, that is, Psalm 90 [91] (*Diatyposis*) [^1701]. If one compares with these rubrics the order of Compline in the most ancient Horologion according unto the rule of the Lavra of St. Sabas, Sinai Library *(Orig. p. 382)* MS No. 863 of the 8th–9th centuries, one cannot fail to notice that in both instances approximately one and the same office is intended. And in this Horologion, Compline, as we have seen (see above, p. 298), not yet possessing even this title, but designated “Prayer at the 1st Hour of the Night,” has a structure very close unto our present Great Compline in its first part, namely: Psalms 4, 12 [13], 26 [27], **“Glory,”** Psalms 30 [31], 90 [91], 6 (at present: 4, 6, 12 [13], 24 [25], 30 [31], 90 [91]), **“God is with us,”** Alleluia with the verses **“Look down and hear me, O Lord...”** and **“In peace in the selfsame...”** (the present verses unto the troparia **“Mine unseen enemies”**), then the troparia **“Mine unseen enemies...”** or others according unto the day, **“Lord, have mercy”** thrice, **“Deliver not unto beasts the soul that confesseth Thee...”** (a verse or a prayer?)—thereafter the manuscript breaks off. A similar composition, yet somewhat more complex and closer unto the present one, is exhibited by Compline in the Studite-Alexis Typikon:
“Having chanted the 6 psalms, then **‘God is with us’** and **‘The Bodiless Nature’** and the Creed (**‘I believe’**) and **‘All-Holy Sovereign Lady’** and **‘Our Father’** and **‘Lord, have mercy’** 30 times, then they make 3 prostrations... and likewise again at the 3rd prostration to say: **‘Come, let us worship,’** then Psalm 7, **‘O Lord, rebuke me not in Thine anger,’** and the Trisagion and **‘Our Father’** and **‘Lord, have mercy’** 12 times, and a prayer having been said by the priest, they depart unto their cells” [^1702].

Such a Compline (*pavechernitsa*) is termed *ispoln* (complete, full) and, among other times, is chanted from the Monday of Thomas Week (Antipascha) until Ascension. Yet it is remarkable that even for the Apostles’ (St. Peter’s) Fast a shorter Compline is indicated: “The 6 psalms and **‘God is with us’** and **‘The Bodiless Nature’** and the Creed (**‘I believe’**) and **‘All-Holy Sovereign Lady’** and the Trisagion and **‘Our Father’** and **‘Lord, have mercy’** 12 times, and they finish” [^1703]. In the first Compline there are clearly two parts; the second is not divided into parts. Since it is improbable that during a fast Compline would be shorter than during the semi-festal period of Pentecost, especially in view of the fact that the Studite-Alexis Typikon requires an abbreviated Compline not only for Sundays and feast days, but also, for instance, for the afterfeast of Ascension, it must be that in both places one and the same order of Compline is intended, and its second form is a representative of its most ancient type, accidentally left uncorrected on the pages of the Typikon after its complication with new insertions. This daily-furious/lenten order of Compline according unto the Studite-Alexis Typikon was abbreviated for feasts and other alleviated days by means of curtailing its initial psalms; namely: “on Saturday evening and on a Feast of the Lord, Compline from **‘God is with us’** and the rest and **‘Lord, have mercy’** 15 times; and from the Ascension of the Lord until All Saints, from **‘He that dwelleth in the help’** and the rest.” In the first case, consequently, all initial psalms were omitted and their place was taken by the canticle of Isaiah; in the second case, a series of psalms up unto Psalm 90 [91] was omitted, concerning which it is unknown what place it occupied among them—whether the last, as at present, or penultimate, as in the Sinai Horologion of the 8th–9th centuries. The first kind, that is, the more abbreviated Compline, was appointed, besides Sunday and feast days, on Great Friday, on Ascension evening, and in all probability in other analogous cases; the second, besides the afterfeast of Ascension, on the eve of the 1st Saturday of Lent “for the sake of the feast of St. Theodore,” on the eve of Lazarus Saturday (Palm Saturday), on the first three days of Mid-Pentecost, and in all probability on similar semi-festal *(Orig. p. 383)* days [^1704]. It is unknown whether, besides these three forms of Compline, there existed also a special form of it for Great Lent; the data for resolving this question consist solely in the following remark concerning the service of Great Monday: “and the great *methimon* [great compline / μεθέορτον/меθύμνον] is chanted even as in the fast” [^1705]; judging from the fact that “Great Compline” (*Velikaya pavechernitsa*) was appointed in Great Lent and on the eves of Saturdays [^1706], when “there is no fasting,” it is to be supposed that Lenten Compline did not differ from the daily office (*ispoln*), even as at present the Compline of the lesser fasts does not differ from that of Great Lent.

### The Nocturnal Hours and the Rule of the 12 Psalms

The further development of Compline, wherein it received—in addition unto the two parts already delineated here—a third part as well, and enriched its concluding section, was conditioned on the one hand by its fusion with the Sung Office rite of the Great Pannychis, but especially by the inclusion into it of the office of the so-called “Nocturnal Hours” [^1707], an order which stood in turn in connection with the ancient “Rule of the 12 Psalms” mentioned already by St. John Cassian (see above, p. 216) and included in Horologia and Followed Psalters (*Sledovannye Psaltiri*) as an independent service. A reference unto both rites (the Nocturnal Hours and the 12 Psalms) is found also in the *Diatyposis*:
“It is needful to know that after the feast of Thomas Week (Antipascha), immediately after Compline, we begin the *pannychis*; and until All Saints we perform only the canon (such a composition was possessed by one form of the sung pannychis) and after it the Blameless (the *Amomos* / Psalm 118 [119]); from that time until Ascension we append 6 psalms, at which there are 3 prostrations and standings (*staseis* / στάσεις); after the Exaltation (of the Holy Cross), however, we perform 12 psalms and the other offices until the Great Forty Days; for then at every Trisagion we perform bows (*metanoiai*) with standings” [^1708].

The most ancient complete order of the 12 Psalms and Nocturnal Hours is provided in the Sinai Horologion MS No. 864 of the 9th century. The manuscript, preserved in a fragment, commences with the psalms of the Ninth Hour, wherein the sequence of psalms is interrupted by a special division sign, after which follow 12 psalms, divided by three **“Glories”** into 4 parts, three psalms in each. There follow next two Theotokia, two “nocturnal canons” with special penitential refrains and troparia adapted in their contents unto the midnight hour; and then is set forth a special “office of the Midnight Office.” The psalms here are the following: 83 [84], 84 [85], 85 [86], 68 [69], 112 [113], 110 [111], 120 [121], the division sign, 74 [75], 20 [21], 54 [55] + 5, 7, 40 [41] + 31 [32], 80 [81], 81 [82] + 93 [94], 104 [105], 56 [57]. All these psalms, with slight variations in composition, enter into the *kanones nykterinōn psalmōn* (κανόνες νυκτερινῶν ψαλμῶν / canons of nocturnal psalms) of the 10th-century Psalter of the Athos University Library MS No. 7/67, where such an order of psalmody is set forth: *Kanones hēmerinōn* *(Orig. p. 384)* *psalmōn* (Κανόνες ἡμερινῶν ψαλμῶν / canons of diurnal psalms). Morning, three: 60 [61], 141 [142], 61 [62]. Hours: I, 8; II, 29 [30]; III, 30 [31]; IV, 41 [42]; V, 50 [51]; VI, 6; VII, 65 [66], 69 [70]; VIII, 84 [85], 81 [82]; IX, 114 [115], 111 [112]; X, 150; XI, 110 [111]; XII, 120 [121]. *Kanones nykterinōn psalmōn* (Κανόνες νυκτερινῶν ψαλμῶν / canons of nocturnal psalms). Evening (“lucernarium”) three: 120 [121], 140 [141], 112 [113]. Hours: I, 74 [75], 14 [15]; II, 29 [30]; III, 54 [55]; IV, 5; V, 7; VI, 40 [41]; VII, 31 [32]; VIII, 8; IX, 97 [98]; X, 95 [96]; XI, 104 [105]; XII, 55 [56] (fol. 11). The italicized psalms are common unto the preceding monument. Even the sequence of psalms remains invariable [^1709]. Consequently, here we have homogeneous offices of the Nocturnal Hours. The Horologion of the Sinai Library MS No. 868 of the 13th–14th centuries contains the same system of 12 single-psalm Nocturnal Hours (under the title *akolouthia tēs nyktos* / ἀκολουθία τῆς νυκτὸς), after which it has the Midnight Office; each of the first 6 Hours consists of a psalm, a troparion with its Theotokion, and a prayer, while the last six Hours consist solely of a psalm and a prayer (the 12th having two prayers). Psalms: 74 [75], 26 [27], 55 [56], 101 [102], 7, 40 [41], 31 [32], 80 [81], 91 [92], 6, 95 [96], 56 [57] with 69 [70]. The troparia are all our present sessional hymns (*sedalny* / kathismata) of the Octoechos at Matins, and the Theotokia are our present dismissal Theotokia. Of the prayers, remarkable are the 1st: **“O Lord our God, Father of True Light, Who hast enlightened the day with heavenly light and illumined the night with fiery beams...”** (at present at Pentecost Vespers) and the 6th: **“Thou Who at all times”** [^1710]. Other monuments make attempts toward the concentration of this excessively copious liturgical material. The Athos-Iviron Synaxarion in the manuscript of the Tiflis Ecclesiastical-Archaeological Museum MS No. 222 of the 12th century appoints the Nocturnal Hours in Great Lent, wherein they are inserted into Compline, which in its turn is inserted between 2 parts of the Midnight Office [^1711]. These Hours consist of 12 unnamed psalms with the Trisagion and **“Lord, have mercy”** after every two [^1712]. Here, consequently, there are 6 Nocturnal Hours. The Athos-Vatopaidi Horologion MS No. 350/984 of the 12th century, between Compline (already three-part) and the Midnight Office, contains only two two-part prayers of the night (*hai litai tēs euphronēs* / αἱ λιταὶ τῆς εὐφρόνης), that is, properly four Nocturnal Hours, yet preserves the same number of psalms for them: 12. Each Hour here has three psalms (in the last, two), three troparia, and a prayer. Psalms: 55 [56], 139 [140], 140 [141],—40 [41], 101 [102], 138 [139],—6, 31 [32], 76 [77],—86 [87], 41 [42]. The troparia are all penitential—the greater part at present serves as sessional hymns of the Octoechos at Matins. Of the troparia at the second service, two are Theotokia: **“All-Holy Lady Theotokos, during the time of my life...”** and **“A multitude of my transgressions, O Theotokos...”**—troparia in the final part of our present Compline [^1713]. The Horologia of the Imperial Public Library MS Q. I. 57 of the 12th–13th centuries and of the Sophia Library at the St. Petersburg Theological Academy MS No. 1052 of the 13th–14th centuries (with which the Slavonic Sinai MS No. 12 of the 12th–13th centuries is cognate), in their “Order of how it behooveth to chant the Nocturnal Hours,” likewise provide only 4 Hours, with three psalms, three troparia, and one prayer in each. Psalms: 26 [27], 31 [32], 56 [57],—37 [38], 38 [39],—69 [70], 70 [71], 76 [77],—101 [102], the Prayer of Manasseh, and Psalm 50 [51]. At the Fourth Hour, after the prayer, follows: **“Glory to God in the highest,”**—then **“Lord, Thou hast been our refuge,”**—and **“Vouchsafe, O Lord, to keep us this night without sin,”**—*(Orig. p. 385)* then penitential troparia (*pokayanna*) of the occurring Tone with the verses: **“Behold now, bless ye the Lord”** and **“In the nights lift up your hands,”** (in the first monument also a verse and troparion for the departed), and with **“Glory... Both now...”** After the “penitential” troparia, in the first monument follows the prayer of St. Eustratius: **“Magnifying, I magnify Thee, O Lord”** (at present at Saturday Midnight Office), a threefold prayerful invocation: **“Lord, have mercy on my soul defiled by the passions of life,”** **“Glory... Both now...,”** the Trisagion, and 20 troparia: (**“Save, O Lord,”** **“Thou wast transfigured,”** **“Thou didst ascend”** [temple troparia?], unto the Archangel, the Forerunner, apostles, prophets, etc., common according unto ranks and unto individual saints: St. Theodore, Nicholas, Basil, Clement, Hilarion), **“Glory,”** troparion for the departed, **“Both now,”** Theotokion; a prayer for compunction of soul (**“My soul, why complainest thou against the Lord”**), a dismissal prayer “before going to sleep”: **“And grant unto us, O Master”** (at present at Compline), a prayer unto the Guardian Angel, and an exorcism against the devil [^1714]. In the second and third monuments, after the penitential troparia follow the Trisagion, troparia unto the Saviour, the Theotokos, the Archangel, John the Baptist, and all saints; 15 troparia in total; after the troparia follow prayers: **“And grant unto us, O Master,”** **“Magnifying, I magnify Thee,”** the threefold prayerful invocation: **“Lord, have mercy on my soul defiled by passions,”** and a prayer “for all Christians” [^1715]. The psalms indicated in all three monuments are identical, with the exception of one in the sixth place: instead of Psalm 40 [41], the first monument has Psalm 31 [32]; and they coincide with the “Rule of the 12 Psalms,” excluding Psalm 37 [38] (in the “Rule,” 33 [34]) and Psalm 50 [51] (which is absent in the “Rule,” having in its stead as the 12th psalm the Great Doxology).

### The Three-Part Compline

Thus the “Rule of the 12 Nocturnal Psalms” increased the number of Compline psalms from the original 6 unto 12, and introduced into it the morning hymn **“Glory to God in the highest,”** since, by virtue of the fusion of this rule with Compline, the latter was in principle intended to continue until morning; while the influence of the *pannychis* inserted into Compline its middle part with Psalm 50 [51] and a canon. In such a complicated, three-part, and already almost entirely modern form do we find Compline in the Western Studite Typika. Furthermore, in the Calabrian recension of these Typika it is simpler in composition. In its full composition (for fasts), according unto its fragmentary description in the Typikon of the Monastery of San Nicola di Casole (ch. 25), in its first part it contained the Six Psalms and **“God is with us”**; in the 2nd, a canon or triodion; in the 3rd, the Blameless (the *Amomos* / Psalm 118 [119]), **“Glory to God in the highest,”** and **“O Lord Almighty”** (prayer); on non-fasting days this Compline was celebrated only up unto **“Glory to God in the highest”**; in Pentecost, up unto the Blameless; on Sundays, feasts, and the Twelve Days (Dodekaēmeron), the first two parts were celebrated, with **“Glory to God in the highest”** and the Trisagion [^1716]. In the Western Studite Typika of the Sicilian recension, Compline is longer. According unto the Typikon of San Salvatore di Messina (the Melite/Mili Typikon), in the Forty Days it has likewise a three-part composition: the 1st part *(Orig. p. 386)* coincides entirely with the 1st part of our Compline (only the concluding prayer **“O Lord, Lord, Who hast delivered us”** is lacking); the 2nd part consists of **“Come, let us worship”** twice, Psalm 50 [51], the canon of the saint of the day, after the 6th ode of which follow his sessional hymn with its Theotokion and the Synaxarion, after the 9th ode the “customary heirmioi of the Theotokos in the Tone of the canon” (?), the Trisagion, the dismissal troparion of the day, **“Lord, have mercy”** 12 times by the chanters and the people, the priest recites the prayer **“O Lord Almighty...”** with all lying prostrate; at the 3rd part, after **“Come, let us worship”** twice, “I begin to recite the 12 psalms”: 26 [27], 30 [31], 31 [32], 34 [35], 39 [40], 40 [41], 43 [44], 60 [61], 69 [70], 70 [71], 76 [77], 139 [140] (in italics: psalms common with the “Rule of the 12”). This sequence of 12 psalms is divided into two Six-Psalm groupings by an intercalary Trisagion and **“Come, let us worship”** twice, and each Six-Psalm grouping is subdivided again into three-psalm sections by an intercalary **“Glory... Both now...”** and **“Alleluia”** thrice; after the 12th psalm follow **“Glory to God in the highest,”** the Trisagion, the troparion **“O God of our fathers,”** with the Theotokion **“We shall never cease,”** **“Lord, have mercy”** 12 times by the chanters and the people, the prayer **“O Lord Almighty...”** by the chanters, and **“Blessed is He that is”** (*He On eulogētos* / *Sy blagosloven*) [^1717]. Close unto these is the Evergetis Compline; it has three forms: non-fasting, for the lesser fasts, and Great Lenten. The composition of the first, termed “Little,” is not indicated in the Typikon. During the lesser fasts, Compline was distinguished by the chanting at it of a special office, *hē pannychis* (ἡ παννυχὶς) or canon, which on non-fasting days was detached from Compline and joined unto Vespers, having then the following order: “after the dismissal of Vespers, **‘Come, let us worship’** thrice, and upon proceeding into the narthex, Psalm 50 [51], the canon of the pannychis; after the 3rd ode, a litany and sessional hymn; after the 6th ode, the Kontakion of the Theotokos; upon completion of the canon, **‘Glory to God in the highest,’** the Trisagion, 3 quick bows, the prayer of Vespers, and the dismissal.” The order of Great Lenten Compline according unto the Evergetis Typikon is: the Trisagion, the Six Psalms, “with voice” (sung) **“God is with us,”** the troparia: **“Mine unseen enemies,”** **“Glory,”**—**“How fearful is Thy judgment,”** **“Both now,”**—**“An unashamed hope, O Theotokos”** (likewise sung), **“Lord, have mercy”** 45 times, **“Thou Who at all times,”** the customary 15 prostrations, the prayer **“O Lord, Lord, Who hast delivered us”**; Psalm 50 [51], the customary canon of the pannychis of the Tone, after the 3rd ode the compunctious sessional hymn of the Tone, after the 6th ode the Kontakion of the Theotokos from among the customary ones, at the end of the canon **“Glory to God in the highest”** “more slowly and more attentively,” the Trisagion and litany, **“O Lord Almighty,”** and together a prayer for kinsmen (*homogenōn* / ὁμογενῶν), “the Trisagion for our deceased holy fathers and brethren,” a prayer for them, and the dismissal, “and there takes place the customary bow and mutual forgiveness, and the remainder of the office we chant in our cells” [^1718].

*(Orig. p. 387)*
### Little Compline

It now remained for Compline to develop its second part into its modern form and, upon its foundation, to form a special kind of Little Compline. This is observed in the Horologia of the Sinai Library MS No. 868 of the 13th–14th centuries and of the Athos-Vatopaidi Library MS No. 350 of the 12th century. In the first, Compline, in the composition of the 1st part of our present Great Compline, possesses the following supplementary part: Psalms 50 [51], 66 [67] and 69 [70], the troparia **“Have mercy on us, O Lord...”** and **“Open unto us the door of compassion...”**; prayers: **“O God of our fathers...”** (at present a troparion at Little Compline), **“Magnifying, I magnify Thee...”** (at present at the Midnight Office), and **“O Lord, Lord, Who hast delivered us...”** (at present at the first part of Great Compline). The second Horologion, without using the title “Compline,” headlines the corresponding office: “Customary prayers of pre-nocturnal chants” (*tōn pronyktiōn hymnōn* / τῶν προνυκτίων ὕμνων). It consists of three parts. The first part corresponds unto the first part of our present Compline in a somewhat abbreviated form. The troparia missing therein: **“Enlighten mine eyes,”** **“Defender of my soul,”** and—in place of **“Since we have no bold trust”**—**“Most glorious Ever-Virgin,”** as well as the prayer **“O Lord, Lord, Who hast delivered us,”** having been detached from the composition of the first part, in conjunction with the psalms of the preceding (Sinai MS No. 868) “inter-hour of Compline” (50 [51], 66 [67], 69 [70]), form the second part. The third part is formed of the Great Doxology, the prayers of Kings Hezekiah (Book of Isaiah 38:9–20) and Manasseh, three special troparia (Tone 2: **“Commanders of the Host of God,”** **“The memory of the righteous,”** **“Apostles, martyrs, and prophets”**) with their Theotokion (**“Being a fount of tender mercy”**), and three prayers: two present ones (**“Thou Who at all times”** and **“And grant unto us, O Master”**) and one distinctive prayer: **“O Lord God of heaven and earth, forgive me whatsoever I have sinned.”** In the Sinai Horologion MS No. 806 of the 13th century, Little Compline first appears in its present composition, yet not as an independent service with its modern title, but as the third part of Compline, wherein during the Forty Days this part is replaced by another, fully corresponding unto the third part of our present Great Compline with the prayer **“O Master Great in Mercy”** [^1719]. As an independent office, Little Compline appears for the first time in Slavonic Jerusalem Typika of the 14th century.

### Great and Daily Compline

The Typikon of the Shio-Mgvime Monastery of the 13th century provides an order for Great Compline (Little Compline is not mentioned) almost literally identical with the present one; the difference in the 1st part being: **“Lord, have mercy”** 40 times, and the priest says: **“O Lord Jesus Christ, our God, have mercy on us.”** Before the troparia **“Mine unseen enemies”** it is remarked: “there are, however, also other troparia of Compline”; before the second part it is remarked: “and we begin the nocturnal service of Great Compline” [^1720]. Alongside our present two forms of Compline, the Slavonic Jerusalem Typika of the 14th–16th centuries and the first printed Horologia (Cracow *(Orig. p. 388)* 1491, Moscow 1652) possessed also a 3rd form, intermediary between Great and Little, under the name of “Ordinary Compline” (*obychnaya pavechernitsa*). Its composition was: the first part of our present Great Compline from Psalm 90 [91] and the whole of our present Little Compline without the Symbol of Faith (the Creed); at the first, a troparion from the Menaion with its Theotokion; at the second, weekly troparia and our present **“O God of our fathers,”** and in place of **“Thou Who at all times”** in the 2nd part, the prayer **“O Spotless, Undefiled, Incorrupt...”** (*Neskvernaya, neblaznaya*). Herewith Great Compline was appointed for all fasts when Alleluia is chanted, the ordinary for weekdays, and Little Compline for Saturdays, Sundays, and Polyeleos feasts [^1721].

### The Midnight Office

The most ancient purely Studite Typika did not acknowledge the Midnight Office (*mesonyktikon* / полунощница), judging by the fact that it is not mentioned by the *Hypotyposis* and the Studite-Alexis Typikon [^1722]. The latter possesses an office corresponding unto the Midnight Office solely for Great Lent. The Studite-Alexis Typikon during Great Lent appended unto Great Compline an unnamed office, in its composition recalling partly our present Midnight Office and partly the 3rd part of Great Compline:
“Concerning Compline in Great Lent. It is to be known that throughout the entire fast, when Great Compline is chanted, upon its completion and after 6 (?) psalms and after the Holy God, they immediately begin the Blameless (*Amomos* / Psalm 118 [119]), not dividing them by tone nor into verses, but all reciting them with one accord; thereafter is chanted the Holy God, then **‘Glory to God in the highest,’** and the troparion **‘With a merciful eye,’** and the other troparion: **‘My life is drawing to a close,’** and the Theotokion: **‘Thou Who wast born for our sake’**; thereafter he reciteth the Prayer of Manasseh, whose beginning is: **‘O Lord Almighty,’** and this other prayer: **‘Grant unto us, O Master,’** the prayer of St. Eustratius: **‘Magnifying, I magnify Thee,’** thereafter **‘Lord, have mercy’** thrice, and **‘Defiled by passions,’** and **‘Lord, have mercy’** 50 times, and a prayer having been said by the priest, the dismissal taketh place” [^1723].

In the representative of the Western ktetorial Typika of the Sicilian recension, in the Typikon of San Salvatore di Messina (the Mili Typikon), the Midnight Office both receives already its proper title and is liberated from elements of Compline. This Typikon likewise speaketh solely of the Great Lenten Midnight Office and provideth for it an order cognate unto the Studite-Alexis: after the customary beginning (from the Trisagion), “the Blameless (*Amomos*) with 2 **‘Glories,’** the Trisagion, and troparia: **‘Have mercy on us...,’** **‘Lord, have mercy...,’** **‘Open unto us the door of compassion,’** **‘A multitude of my transgressions...,’** and nothing more, **‘Lord, have mercy’** 50 times, the prayer from the priest **‘Thou Who at all times,’** and the dismissal” [^1724]. In both places we find the simplest type of the Midnight Office. The Athonite Typika complicate it considerably, and that beginning with their most ancient representative—the *Diatyposis*, which, although like the Studite-Alexis Typikon merging the Midnight Office with Compline and not assigning unto it this appellation, nevertheless possesses it daily and provideth the most significant of its later elements, appointing for its *pannychis*, as we have seen (see above, *(Orig. p. 389)* p. 383), in Pentecost only “the canon and the Blameless; in summer 6 more psalms; and in winter and in the Forty Days 12 psalms and yet certain “offices” with several Trisagia. The Athos-Iviron Synaxarion in the manuscript of the Tiflis Museum MS No. 222 of the 12th century, while providing only the order of the Great Lenten Midnight Office, likewise merges it with Compline and the Nocturnal Hours, precisely in such a way that both are inserted between the first and second parts of the Midnight Office, which possesses a structure very close unto the present one:
“At the beginning of the 10th hour they ring for Compline and celebrate first the Midnight Office without the Blameless (*Amomos*); after the Holy God, **‘Our Father,’** **‘The unseen, unsleeping...’** **‘Glory,’**—**‘How fearful...’** **‘Both now,’**—**‘Unashamed hope,’** **‘Lord, have mercy’** 40 times. The priest: **‘O Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on us,’** the people: **‘Amen’** (Midnight Office); **‘Come, let us worship,’** **‘Have mercy on me, O God...’** (Psalm 50 [51]) and the canon of the Mother of God and of the saint from the Menaion, the Holy God, **‘Our Father,’** **‘Lord, have mercy’** 40 times (the *pannychis* or Compline); **‘Come, let us worship’** and they read through 12 psalms, wherein after every 2 psalms: Holy God, **‘Our Father,’** **‘Lord, have mercy’** 40 times (Nocturnal Hours); the Beatitudes, **‘Glory to God in the highest,’** Holy God, **‘O Lord of Hosts, be with us,’** **‘Lord, have mercy’** 40 times, **‘O Holy Lord Almighty,’** **‘Lord, have mercy’** 40 times (Compline); **‘Come, let us worship...’** **‘I have lifted up mine eyes...’** (Psalm 120 [121]) **‘Behold now, bless ye...’** (Psalm 133 [134]), Holy God, **‘Lord, have mercy’** 12 times” (the second part of the Midnight Office).
This office is designated “the Nocturnal Hours” [^1725].

A still greater development is attained by the Midnight Office in the Jerusalem Typika. And so ancient a Horologion of the Jerusalem type as that of the Sinai Library MS No. 864 of the 9th century (in Sinai MS No. 863 of the 8th–9th centuries there is no Midnight Office, perhaps torn out) possesses 2 Midnight Offices. After the aforementioned 12 nocturnal psalms, appended here unto the Ninth Hour, and 2 Theotokia following them, there follow here two nocturnal canons with corresponding troparia and refrains, and after them similar stichera concluding with a supplication for tranquil sleep. Then follows a special Midnight Office; it begins with the prayers of Kings Hezekiah and Manasseh and with Psalm 90 [91] (at present in the order of Compline); then: Alleluia with our present morning verses from Isaiah (26:9, 11, 15 [printed: 29, 9, 11, 15]), and the “triadic hymn” **“Behold, the Bridegroom cometh”**; then Psalm 118 [119] (the 17th Kathisma), and after it special sessional hymns and Theotokia, with troparia of penitential content. The Sinai Horologion MS No. 865 of the 12th century contains already two Midnight Offices: a daily one with the 17th Kathisma, and a Saturday-Sunday one with the 9th. Both are of identical structure and fall into four parts, with three troparia and two prayers in each part for the daily, and an equal number of troparia and one prayer for the Saturday-Sunday; besides this, at the beginning of the service are three introductory troparia. The greater part of these troparia serve at present as penitential sessional hymns and dismissal Theotokia at daily services. The prayers are likewise all of a penitential character, wherein among them are found all 4 prayers of our present daily and Saturday Midnight Office. Thus the Midnight Office according unto this monument does not alter for Saturday and Sunday its *(Orig. p. 390)* penitential character, but merely receives additional troparia for the departed (further heightening its sorrowful character). Besides the Midnight Office, the monument possesses also an “inter-hour of the night, chanted at the 3rd hour of the night,” consisting of Psalms 74 [75], 26 [27], and 55 [56] with penitential troparia **“Have mercy on me, O God”** and a prayer. Finally, the Horologion of the Novgorod-Sophia Library at the St. Petersburg Theological Academy MS No. 1052 of the 13th–14th centuries (unto which the Slavonic Sinai MS No. 12 is very close) provides already a Midnight Office of a completely modern type, differing solely in its troparia and prayers. The Horologion has, like the present one, three forms of the Midnight Office: daily, Saturday, and Sunday; yet the latter is of an identical type with the first two. In the daily, the 1st part has the present troparia, while the 2nd part has a different first troparion: **“I am enfeebled by the sleep of despondency...,”** **“With profundity of wisdom...,”** and **“All generations call thee blessed...”** (the troparion **“With the saints give rest”** is absent). The Saturday Midnight Office—troparia: I: **“With vigilant mind let us look up unto God,”** **“Let us shake off slothful sleep, the Bridegroom draweth nigh,”** **“Present our prayers unto the Mother of God”**; II: **“Since the Judge is come, take heed, O my soul,”** **“With profundity of wisdom,”** **“Thee, a city and haven”** (= wall and haven). The Sunday Midnight Office—I: **“The Life of all hath risen from the dead,”** **“That fearful day,”** **“Thee, an impregnable city”** (= an indestructible wall); II: **“The tomb being opened and hades lamenting,”** **“Grant me the vigilance of the wise virgins,”** **“Our prayers, O Mother of God.”** The prayers common unto all three Midnight Offices are: 1) “The prayer of St. John Chrysostom unto the Holy Lady Theotokos”: **“Having enjoyed many and great gifts from God Who created me”**; 2) **“Thou Who at all times”**; and 3) the concluding prayer: **“Remember, O Lord, the whole world; have mercy on all, defend all; sail with them that sail upon the sea.”** In addition, at each of the three Midnight Offices, after **“Thou Who at all times,”** a single proper prayer is appointed: at the daily—**“O Master, Lord Jesus Christ, Father of compassions and God of all consolation, have mercy also upon me, Thine unworthy servant”**; at the Saturday—**“O Almighty God, Creator of creation above and beneath, Who hast appointed the sun for the enlightenment of the day, and the moon and the stars for the illumination of the night, Who didst command, O Lord, light to shine forth out of darkness”**; at the Sunday—**“O Lord our God, True Radiance of the Father”** [^1726]. In comparison with the preceding monument, there is here a significant differentiation, especially in relation unto the Sunday order of the Midnight Office. Yet in comparison with our present orders, in the 2nd part of the Midnight Office its mortuary character is not so strictly maintained, while the Sunday office has many penitential motifs. In any case, from here, from this last monument, there remained but one step unto the present Typikon. In the most ancient Slavonic copies of the Jerusalem Typikon (Greek manuscripts do not provide the order) there already appears the present order of the daily and Saturday Midnight Office, with the sole difference that in the second part, in place of the concluding prayer for the departed, **“Remember, O Lord, in the hope of the resurrection”** (*“Помяни, Господи, в надежди воскресения”*), and the prayerful invocations **“Most glorious, Ever-Virgin...”** (*“Преславная Приснодево...”*) and **“My hope is the Father...”** (*“Упование мое Отец...”*), there is prescribed a prayer-litany, **“Let us pray for all and for everything...”** (*“Помолимся о всех и за вся...”*), consisting of 12 petitions beginning **“Remember, O Lord...”** (*“Помяни, Господи...”*), resemb*(Orig. p. 391)*ling the present **“Let us pray for our most pious...”** (*“Помолимся о благочестивейшем...”*), during the recitation of which by the priest “the brethren say **‘Lord, have mercy,’** while the priest makes commemoration,” and at the conclusion of which is a brief prayer, **“Those gathered by Thee in this holy precinct”** (*“Собранные тобою во св. сию ограду”*), for forgiveness of sins and non-condemnation at the Dread Judgment (cf. **“Behold, the Bridegroom cometh”** [*“Се Жених грядет...”*]), concluding: “For Thine it is to have mercy”; after the prayer follow the dismissal and the litany **“Let us pray”** (*“Помолимся”*) [^1727]. As regards the Sunday Midnight Office, the Greek Jerusalem Typika are completely silent concerning it, since they presuppose an All-Night Vigil before Sunday; only the most ancient Slavic witnesses in the Moscow Synodal Library, after setting forth Vespers at the Vigil, remark that in view of “the poverty and inability of artful chant” (*“скудоты и неумения хитрогласного пения”*), by reason of which the Vigil cannot be prolonged throughout the entire night, in autumn and winter after Vespers “we chant Small Compline, which begins from **‘Have mercy on me, O God,’** after this we chant a supplicatory canon for those who show us alms or for whomsoever we wish, then we chant the Sunday Midnight Office, and if it is not late we read a reading, and after this we chant Matins” [^1728]; yet the composition of the Sunday Midnight Office is not specified in these Typika. In the *Followed Psalter* of the 15th century (Moscow Synodal Library MS No. 350/406, fol. 166), after the Daily and Saturday Midnight Office, there is placed: “Canon unto the Holy and Life-Originating Trinity, chanted on Sunday before Matins in place of the Midnight Office,” and after it the refrains for **“It is truly meet”** and the prayer — identical unto the present ones (canon of Tone 1); in the Psalter of the same library of the 16th century (MS No. 709/409, fol. 233v), this same office is already entitled: “The Midnight Office for all Sundays.”

### The Order of the Typika

The Order of the Typika (*chin izobrazitel’nykh*), in comparison with the form that it had acquired by the 9th century — that is, the form it exhibits in the Palestinian-Sabbaite Horologion of the Sinai Library MS No. 863 of the 8th–9th century (see above, p. 298) — underwent insignificant development. Compared unto its present form, this monument still lacks Psalms 102 [103] and 145 [146], **“Only-Begotten Son,”** **“Pardon, remit,”** and almost the entire subsequent office (with the exception of **“Lord, have mercy”** thrice, the opening words of Psalm 133 [134], and **“Blessed be the name of the Lord”**); in substitution for the present conclusion, it contained prayers adapted for the reception of the Holy Mysteries (inasmuch as the office itself was designated for this purpose, as is evident from its inscription: *eis tēn metalēpsin*, εἰς τὴν μετάληψιν), namely: **“One is Holy...”**, **“O taste and see that Christ is the Lord,”** and the prayers of Holy Communion. Now it, first of all, gradually loses this last element of its composition — its adaptation unto Communion, evidently because the former custom of self-communion by monks (anchorites) disappears (although it is still defended by the anonymous author of the Life of St. Luke the Younger of Steiris, who provides an order of self-communion, attested by Euthymius, Patriarch of Trnovo, 1375–1393 [^1729], and justified by St. Symeon of Thessalonica in the 15th century [^1730]). Thus Horologia from the 9th century no longer inscribe the Order of the Typika “unto Communion” and contain within it neither the prayers of Communion *(Orig. p. 392)* nor the verse **“O taste and see.”** The verse **“One is Holy”** as an independent element, without the prayer preceding it **“All-Holy Trinity,”** is still found in the Horologia of the Sinai Library MS No. 868 and MS No. 12, Sophia MS No. 1052 (13th–14th centuries), and even in our present Paschal Order of the Typika. The Psalms at the beginning and **“Only-Begotten Son”** are already contained in the Horologia of the Sinai Library MS No. 866 and MS No. 867 (13th century) and all subsequent ones; Sinai MS No. 868 has the Trisagion before the **“Our Father.”** The prayer **“Pardon, remit”** after the **“Our Father”** appears from approximately the same period: it is contained in the two aforementioned latter Horologia and later ones, but the Studite-Alexis Typikon does not prescribe it, while Sinai MS No. 12 and Sophia MS No. 1052 have another in its stead: “O Lord our God, Who didst reveal Thy most glorious Mother as more honorable than the Heavenly Hosts...” **“Lord, have mercy”** is still prescribed 3 times, similar unto Sinai MS No. 863, in Sinai MS No. 866 and MS No. 868. Other Horologia, for example Sinai MS No. 12 and Sophia MS No. 1052, have **“Lord, have mercy”** 12, 30, or 50 times. Later than the other constituent parts, the Order of the Typika acquires its kondakia: it lacks them entirely in the Studite Typikon, Sophia MS No. 1052, Sinai MS No. 868, etc.; in Sinai MS No. 876, among the kondakia is that of St. John Chrysostom or Basil the Great (a close affinity unto Communion); in Sinai MS No. 866 the kondakia are **“As first-fruits...”** (unto the martyrs and all saints), **“With the saints give rest...,”** **“Protection of Christians...”** [^1731]. According unto the Shio-Mgvime Typikon: the kontakion of Chrysostom, **“Glory...,”** **“With the saints...,”** **“Both now...,”** **“Hope of Christians...”** [^1732]; according unto the most ancient Greek witnesses of the Jerusalem Typikon: the kontakion of the temple saint, **“With the saints...,”** and **“Awesome protection...”** or **“Protection of Christians...”**; according unto later Greek witnesses of the Jerusalem Typikon: also (after that of the temple) the kontakion of the “daily” (weekly?) saint, and the first Theotokion is omitted [^1733]; according unto the most ancient Slavic witnesses of the Jerusalem Typikon: also the kontakion of the Menaion, if there is one (before the weekly and temple kondakia), and on Saturday, in place of **“Protection...,”** **“As first-fruits...”** [^1734]; according unto later witnesses, before all others, the kontakion of the Transfiguration. Finer variants of the rite: before the second psalm, **“Glory... Both now...”**; before **“Only-Begotten Son,”** again (Sophia MS No. 1052) or only before **“Only-Begotten Son”** (Slavic MSS of the Jerusalem Typikon); **“Lord, have mercy”** thrice also before the Beatitudes (Sinai MS No. 12, etc.); before Psalm 33 [34] and before the dismissal: “Bless, ye holy ones; bless, father” (Sophia MS No. 1052). If the Typika replace the Liturgy appointed for that day (according unto the Typikon of Empress Irene, for example, they were chanted instead of the Liturgy on Monday, Tuesday, and Thursday) [^1735], then according unto the Jerusalem Typikon there were read at them the Epistle and Gospel of the day (with prokeimenon and Alleluia); according unto Greek witnesses of the Jerusalem Typikon, they were read immediately after the Typika Psalms and **“Only-Begotten Son,”** while according unto Slavic manuscripts, after the Beatitudes before **“Remember us, O Lord...”** (an adaptation unto the order of the Divine Liturgy); certain Horologia prescribe even at every Typika *(Orig. p. 393)* permanent readings of the Epistle and Gospel, namely: 2 Cor. 6:16–7:1 [printed: 3 Cor.] and Matt. 25:31–46, and on Saturdays readings for the departed [^1736]. Characteristic is the position in which the Typika were placed within the cycle of daily services: the most ancient Horologia place them after the Ninth Hour (cf. among the Armenians, where the Liturgy is likewise always after the Ninth Hour); the *Hypotyposis* indicates to celebrate them immediately after the Liturgy [^1737]; the most ancient manuscripts of the Studite-Alexis Typikon likewise prescribe them immediately after the Liturgy, followed at once by the Ninth Hour (such, at least, is the rule during the Apostles’ Fast) [^1738]; its later manuscripts (likewise during the Apostles’ Fast) place them after the Ninth Hour [^1739]; and so likewise do the Jerusalem Typika during fasts [^1740]; on non-fasting days, however, in place of the Liturgy (yet not after it), after the Sixth Hour.

### Skete Typika and Rules

Apart from those types of divine worship provided by the various Typika and performed in churches, there existed perpetually, from the very inception of monastic asceticism in the 4th century, a distinct form of private, solitary, skete worship within monastic practice. This possessed its own developmental trajectory and acquired during the period under review a highly intricate structure, not failing, of course, to exert an influence upon the general church cursus. Represented in Nikon of the Black Mountain (11th century) and by a series of Greek and Slavic Typika and Horologia, this type of worship traces its lineage unto St. Pachomius the Great, specifically unto the “Rule given him by an Angel” — that is, unto the primitive rule of Pachomian monasteries set forth above (see pp. 207–209). This rule was somewhat modified and elaborated by later ascetics. Thus Abba Isaiah (an anchorite of Scetis in the 5th century), as reported by Nikon, transmits it in this form: “By day 12 prayers, and for the Ninth Hour 3 prayers, and before each prayer a psalm”; the remainder of St. Isaiah’s daily distribution of time: “At night I sleep 4 hours, 4 hours I stand in chanting, and 4 hours I work; by day I work until the sixth hour, read until the ninth, and from the ninth I attend unto food and unto everything necessary for the cell” [^1741]. According unto the rule of St. Barsanuphius (at first Bishop of Damascus and thereafter an anchorite in Nitria in the mid-5th century): “The Scetiotes have neither hours nor do they chant hymns,” but spend their time in manual labor, meditation, and prayer; during manual labor one must meditate (“study”) or recite psalms, but at the end of each psalm one must say, “O God, have mercy upon me, a wretch,” or another prayer “for deliverance from the old man”; if thoughts assail: “Lord, Thou seest my affliction, help me”; having completed three rows of weaving, one may alternate with reading the lives of the saints for 5 to 8 leaves; at the evening chanting the Scetiotes, according unto Barsanuphius, recite 12 psalms and *(Orig. p. 394)* at night 12, and at the end of each psalm, in place of the doxology, they say Alleluia and a single prayer: the **“Our Father”** or “Lord Jesus Christ, have mercy on me” [^1742]. As one of the skete rules, Nikon of the Black Mountain cites also the well-known narrative concerning the liturgical service of St. Nilus of Sinai (see above, p. 294).

### The Order of the 12 Psalms and the Chanting of the Psalter

Upon the basis of these rules there emerges in monuments of the 9th and subsequent centuries the distinct “Order of the 12 Psalms,” mentioned above in connection with Compline (see pp. 383–384), which was specifically designed for solitary and cell usage. On the other hand, upon the foundation of these rules there developed in monasticism the custom of reciting the entire Psalter in one's cell daily. This custom even received a specific typikal formulation that adapted the Psalter unto cell execution through the addition unto the kathismata of special prayers, doxologies, and troparia. Such an order is set forth in a 14th-century Slavic manuscript of the Synodal Library under the title: *“Typikon of the Skete Chanting, That Is, Concerning the Cell Rule: An Explanation Concerning the Psalter, How It Is Meet to Chant Individually”* [^1743]. The Typikon requires the recitation of the entire Psalter over the course of a day and night (*“день и нощь”*), dividing it among the Midnight Office, Hours, Vespers, and Matins; unto each service there are assigned 3 kathismata (*“по тристатии”*), and at each kathisma a Trisagion with prostrations, troparia, and a prayer; this order of “skete chanting” even had its own manner of reciting the Psalter — drawn out (troparic): “not hastening, but chanting with stillness, as is the custom of the Scetiotes, in Tone 4 or Tone 8.” He who accomplished such a rule was no longer obliged to attend church services. In the same manuscript there is set forth also the “Order of the 12 Psalms” [^1744], which is recommended unto those who “are unable to complete the whole Psalter”; this order is given in the following form: introductory prayers with Psalm 50 [51], 12 psalms (26, 31, 56, 33, 38, 40, 69, 70, 76, 101, 50, and the Great Doxology) [LXX] with a Trisagion after every three psalms; the troparia and prayers at the end are penitential [^1745]; the illiterate, in lieu of the 12 psalms, must make 300 prostrations with the prayer: “Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me, a sinner” [^1746]. For the infirm, this relaxation is granted:

“Begin the Psalter as much as thou art able, and having rested a little, begin the Midnight Office, and after the Midnight Office chant 6 kathismata with prostrations and with prayers; having made the dismissal and thanked God, and having taken rest lawfully, rising again before Matins, chant 6 kathismata with prostrations and with prayers; then begin Matins according unto cus*(Orig. p. 395)*tom; whatever remains for thee in the Psalter, chant it during the day; or if thou hast some manual labor and wishest to rest at night, chant 10 kathismata at night and 11 by day (the 21st kathisma being the Biblical Odes); but do not venture to abandon this rule, but day and night chant through the Psalter; and if thou art able to finish reciting the whole Psalter before the arrival of light or before the conclusion of the day, begin again from the beginning, for the Psalter never cometh to an end.”

### The Karyes Typikon and the Horologion of Theokaras

Mount Athos accomplished especially much for the development of the Skete Typikon. Among the skete rules that arose here, the most notable are the Karyes Typikon of St. Sava of Serbia of the 13th century and the cell rule set forth in the so-called Horologion of Theokaras (*Chasoslov Fikary*). The first typikon (“The Typikon for the Cell of Karyes in the Name of St. Sabbas”), intended for two hermits (one elder and one disciple), mandates the daily performance of all church services, at which the entire Psalter is chanted (in summertime daily: the 1st, 2nd, and 3rd staseis, that is, kathismata, at Matins; the 4th and 5th at the Hours; the 6th at the Typika; the 7th at Vespers; the remaining in the cells), the canon unto the Mother of God is performed (at Compline), and a prescribed number of prostrations is executed (in Great Lent — 300 per day). On Saturday and Sunday “the entire church office” is chanted (Vigil with Liturgy). A solemn vow is laid upon the hermit-brother: never to abandon the cell of Karyes (“as long as he liveth let him have no liberty to go forth from this cell... save on account of some great calamity”), “that the Protos [the governor of Mount Athos] have authority in nothing” over this cell; and to partake of meals three times a week (on fasting days) solely of bread and water [^1747]. — An even more elaborate form is exhibited by the rule in the “Horologion” compiled in the 14th century by a certain Athonite monk, Thomas Theokaras (*Phikaras*, a Greek who had visited Rus’), the *Askētikē* (or *hiera*) *akolouthia* (Ἀσκητικὴ [or ἱερὰ] ἀκολουθία), an order of cell rule for Scetiotes adopted on Athos and in Russia [^1748]. This order constitutes a reworking of the corporate church services, adapting the latter for cell usage through the addition of new psalms and especially prayers and devotional formularies.
