Matins according unto this typikon begins with troparia and a prayer invoking the Holy Spirit (cf. the Roman Catholic Tierce); the Six Psalms are divided by a Trisagion into two halves, each half concluding with a prayer; the hymn **“God is the Lord”** is replaced by verses of the Psalter with the refrain “Alleluia,” prefaced by a special prayer with a petition for the acceptance of our chanting (cf. the *praefatio* in the Roman Catholic Mass); before the canon a special prayer is prescribed; at the ninth ode the additions unto the Biblical Odes take on a Eucharistic/thanksgiving character; after the sixth ode follows the “kontakion of the day, and if there be a gathering (*druzhina*), the canonarch reads the canon of the day or from the Oktoechos, but the solitary reads it upon the completion of the odes and their chanting”; at the ninth ode, before other additions, the Prayer of Manasseh is recited, followed by a special prayer; further at Matins follows the “customary office,” and again a prayer. At Vespers, after the customary beginning, a prayer is indicated and 3 staseis with preface, chanting, and *diadochai* (as at Matins and at the canon); at the end of the third stasis there is also an “apostrophe” (a laudatory address unto God), then a prayer; on feasts a special “chanting,” two apostrophes, *(Orig. p. 396)* and after the appointed kathisma (namely the 7th, since at the Hours and Typika the first 6 kathismata are chanted, and at Matins presumably 8 to 10, while the remaining kathismata may be distributed between services or all across 48 hours) the Trisagion and 3 stichera of penitential character, including a Theotokion. At the Third, Sixth, and Ninth Hours an introductory prayer is indicated (at the Third Hour two prayers, and after them the exclamation **“Glory to the Holy...”**, **“Glory to God in the highest”** thrice, and **“O Lord, open Thou my lips”** twice), 3 staseis of the same composition as at Matins (at the Sixth Hour with an apostrophe), the appointed kathisma (at the Third Hour — the 3rd, at the Sixth — the 4th, at the Ninth — the 5th), after each **“Glory...”** of which follow the Trisagion through the **“Our Father,”** 3 penitential troparia, **“Lord, have mercy”** 20 times, and a prayer; in conclusion of each Hour the prayer **“Master, God, Father Almighty...”**, the dismissal, and a reading. The First Hour is of a unique structure (cf. Sinai Horologion MS No. 863, Roman Catholic and Ethiopian Hours): after the customary beginning, a special “Hymn in honor of the Holy Trinity” consisting of 9 verses beginning with the word “Glory,” a prayer, a “preface,” and Kathismata 1 and 2 with additions as at the other Hours. At the Typika (*obednitsa*, following the Ninth Hour), a similar 9 verses unto the Holy Trinity and the 6th kathisma with identical additions. Compline is of customary composition; but after **“Glory to God in the highest,”** the Trisagion, and troparia, follow a prayer, a “preface,” and 3 staseis as at Matins. The Midnight Office is likewise of customary composition, but at the beginning are 9 verses unto the Holy Trinity, as at the First Hour and Typika, with a prayer, and after Psalm 50 [51], in place of the Blameless (*Amomos*), a prayer-preface, on Tuesday a prayer for the departed.

### The Russian Skete Typikon

Transferred, principally from Mount Athos, unto Russia, the Skete Typikon received here, presumably, further development and complications, concerning the extent of which one cannot judge owing unto the non-existence of Greek originals for the Slavo-Russian witnesses of the Skete Typikon. The most ancient of such witnesses is the “Rule of the Holy Mountain” of the Caves Hegumen Dositheus of the 13th century [^1749]; according unto this rule there is daily prescribed half of the Psalter, 600 Jesus Prayers with 300 or 500 prostrations; for the illiterate, however (in lieu of the Psalter), 7,000 prayers. More intricate and later is the Skete Typikon entitled: *“Tradition According unto the Rule for Monks Dwelling in the Skete Life: The Rule Concerning Cell Sobriety and Daily Chanting (katadnevnom, ‘daily’ with the Greek preposition kata, κατὰ), Which We Also Received from Our Fathers,”* found in manuscripts from the 15th century onward [^1750]. Before Sunday and Thursday (if there be no feast), according unto this typikon there is celebrated first Vespers, apparently ordinary, which is followed by the refectory, spiritual conversations, and reading (after which sleep is also permitted); the Vigil from 1–2 hours after midnight, in place of Vespers, has a special introductory part consisting of 3 staseis; in the 1st stasis are 3 kathismata, a canon unto the Most Holy Theotokos or another with censing at the 8th ode; then a reading with conversation and confession unto the superior for the duration of 2–3 hours; in the 2nd stasis are 3 kathismata and a canon unto Jesus; the 3rd stasis consists of 3 kathismata likewise and a Triadicon canon on Sunday, but on feasts of litiya stichera; then Matins of customary composition, but with only a single kathisma — the Blameless (*Amomos*). If only 2 or 3 brethren gather for the service *(Orig. p. 397)*, then in place of this Vigil there are chanted 10 or all 20 kathismata of the Psalter, divided into staseis of 5 kathismata each. On weekdays Matins begins at dawn directly from Psalm 50 [51] (cf. Matins according unto Basil the Great, above, p. 147). The Hours, Typika, Vespers, and Compline are celebrated according unto the general typikon. In addition, daily there are appointed in the winter half of the year, from September unto April (cf. Western monastic rules above, pp. 309ff.), 10 kathismata, 600–1,000 Jesus Prayers, and 300–600 prostrations, and in summer 7 kathismata and prayer according unto devotion [^1751].

### The Influence of the Skete Typikon

The Skete Typikon exerted a profound influence upon the general church cursus, or at least upon the monastic Typikon. Under its influence the generally accepted order of services received additions, especially at the beginning and conclusion of the offices. Thus, presumably under this influence, the Studite-Alexis Matins in later recensions of this Typikon received at the beginning Psalm 6 [^1752]. In Slavic Horologia of the 13th–14th centuries these accretions are exceedingly intricate. Thus in Sophia MS No. 1052 Vespers and Matins receive the following stratifications: after the customary beginning, Psalm 6, Trisagion, a prayer for the blessing of the service, and **“Lord, have mercy”** 12 times; and at Matins, moreover, at the very beginning a brief “prayer that beginneth all chanting,” preceded by an elaborate order of morning prayers with penitential troparia and Psalms 107 [108], 126 [127], 127 [128], and 121 [122] [LXX] [^1753]. Unto the cell-skete rule of the nocturnal and diurnal hours, as we have observed, the Mesoria (inter-hours), Midnight Office, and elaboration of Compline owe their genesis. From this same typikon, presumably, there infiltrated on fasting services the addition of the Trisagion and 12-fold **“Lord, have mercy”** before the concluding prayer, by virtue of which the conclusion of the service is transformed into what is effectively a separate brief office (*“pochasie”*).

### Menologia: The Constantinopolitan Menologion

By the 9th century the Menologion, as we have seen (see above, pp. 320ff.), had attained less development in the Orthodox East than in the West: there, calendars of the 6th–7th centuries already possess commemorations for all days of the year, whereas Eastern Menologia — for instance, the Constantinopolitan — even in the 8th century have them for no more than half of all days in the year. Furthermore, the East has left far fewer monuments permitting us to judge concerning its most archaic calendar. The greatest number of such monuments dating from the 9th century and periods proximate unto it has survived from the Church of Constantinople, whence one may conclude that the local Constantinopolitan calendar achieved broad dissemination throughout the East, displacing local calendars everywhere, wherever such had existed. Thus, the Menologion appended unto the 10th-century Gospel written in Jerusalem, and unto the 11th-century Syriac Gospel from Antioch [^1754], is of the exact type *(Orig. p. 398)* that had already emerged in the 8th-century Constantinopolitan Menologion (described above, pp. 322–323) and is represented by a multitude of Greek manuscripts and recensions of the 9th–11th centuries [^1755].

### Local Menologia: Georgian, Antiochene, Neapolitan, and Sicilian

Gradually the Menologion acquires commemorations for all days of the year [^1756], initially a single commemoration per day [^1757], and subsequently ever more [^1758]. Yet it was not swiftly that this almost uniform Constantinopolitan type of Menologion (differences across varying recensions affect for the most part the dates of only 5 or 6 commemorations in the year) secured universal acceptance across the Orthodox East: alongside it there persisted in certain places Menologia of a distinctive, local type, sometimes revealing kinship and a quasi-succession with the Syriac Menologion of the 4th century (see above, p. 277), and sometimes endeavoring to impart unto themselves a more ecumenical character through the incorporation of Western and other commemorations. Of the first kind is the Menologion provided by the Georgian Festal Menaion with Triodion interpolations in the manuscript of the St. Petersburg Imperial Public Library MS No. 11 (from the collection of Bishop Porphyrius Uspensky) of the 9th century, which has on December 28 the Apostles Peter and Paul; on December 29 John the Evangelist; on January 1 Hierarchs (all of them); on January 29 Venerable Fathers; on January 29 the Apparition of the Cross unto Emperor Constantine; on June 25 the “Nativity of John”; on September 27 the “Dumbness of Zacharias” [^1759]. Such is the most ancient *(Orig. p. 399)* Antiochene Menologion, insofar as it can be reconstructed by aid of the works of St. John Chrysostom and Patriarch Severus of Antioch, and from two Syro-Phoenician Festal Menaia of the 9th century (in the manuscripts of the Sinai Library MSS Nos. 233 and 234): December 24 commemoration of all the Forefathers and Prophets; 25 the Nativity of Christ; 26 commemoration of the Mother of God; 27 St. Stephen; 28 the Apostles Peter and Paul; 29 John the Evangelist and James his brother; 30 the Apostles Thomas and James the Brother of the Lord; 31 all the Apostles; January 1 Basil the Great; 7 John the Forerunner; 15 or 20 the Egyptian Fathers; 24 Paul the Simple (disciple of Antony the Great); 25 Babylas of Antioch; 27 commemorations of (all) the Martyrs; 28 the Apparition of the Cross unto Constantine; 29 St. Ignatius the God-Bearer [^1760]. Among the Menologia converging with Western calendars, the most remarkable is the so-called “Neapolitan Marble Calendar,” presumably of the 9th century, with the latest commemorations from the 7th century, discovered on the reverse side of marble door-frames in the Neapolitan church of St. John the Baptist (6th century). It possesses commemorations for all days save 3: all consisting of a single commemoration, and approximately 25 days with 2; 30 commemorations are exclusively Western; 25 are of Neapolitan bishops and unknown saints; the remainder are common unto Constantinopolitan Menologia and, with the exception of 20, also unto Slavic ones, though frequently on Western dates; there is no small number of Old Testament saints (Abraham, Isaac, etc.), but there is, for example, no Isaiah; there are few Constantinopolitan bishops; Emperor Constantine appears without Helena; Theodosius the Great (October 10); there are duplications of commemorations (found also in ancient Constantinopolitan witnesses), for instance, Mark the Evangelist, the Apostle Philip, and Pope Sylvester [^1761]. Such also is the Menologion of the Sinai Canonaria of the 9th–10th centuries described above (p. 359), which generally follows the typikon of the Great Church of Constantinople (see below), but contains commemorations of Sicilian and Calabrian saints unique unto itself and partly unto the Neapolitan calendar, as well as, for instance, purely Western ones: May 3 the Invention of the Cross; May 8 Archangels Michael and Gabriel (in memory of the apparition of Michael on Mount Gargano in Italy in 493) [^1762].

*(Orig. p. 400)*
### Recensions of the Constantinopolitan Menologion: The Menologion of the Great Church

Nevertheless, the Constantinopolitan type of Menologion acquires everywhere a predominant importance, and this principally because, with its further development, it strives increasingly to smooth away its local coloration and become universal throughout the whole Church. This is as yet little observed in so ancient a representative of the Constantinopolitan Menologion as the Typikon of the Great Church (see above, pp. 336–337). Its foundation is some ancient Menologion containing martyrs alone, like the Syriac of the 4th century; Old Testament saints, apostles, hierarchs, and venerables are placed sometimes after the martyrs, but more often between the martyrs of a given day;

this latter circumstance being a sign that these commemorations — martyrs following non-martyrs — were interpolated later. In general, the Menologion was visibly composed with great gradualness and was not edited rigorously by any single individual: duplications of commemorations occur even on the same day with a slight variant of the name. There are from 5 to 7 commemorations per day, many with historical notices. Among Old Testament saints, Ezekiel and Haggai are absent, and an office is provided only for Elisha; among the Apostles, there is no commemoration of James the son of Alphaeus and no offices for Simon, Jude, and Matthew; there is no Synaxis of the Seventy Apostles, though commemorations of certain among them are present; there are no Syrian venerables. Of 130 commemorations with offices, 18 are Constantinopolitan.

### The Menologion of Emperor Basil

The next monument of the Constantinopolitan Menologion in terms of chronology and importance is the “Menologion of Emperor Basil” (not Basil I the Macedonian [† 889], but Basil II the Bulgar-Slayer [† 1025], since there are commemorations from the close of the 10th century), preserved for September through February in a parchment manuscript, presumably the original, adorned with gold and precious stones, in the Vatican Library. Half of this manuscript is occupied by highly artistic miniatures depicting the feats and deaths of the saints, which often take the place of the narratives concerning the saints themselves; the Menologion was transcribed at the behest of the designated emperor (in the prologue it is stated that the Emperor himself “composed” it). The supply of the missing months is found in the Menologion provided by the *Eulogadion* in an 11th-century manuscript and by Menaia in manuscripts of the 11th–13th centuries in the Cryptaferrata (Grottaferrata) Library, where the narratives for the first half of the year coincide literally with the Vatican manuscript (save for the absence of miniatures), while in the second half of the year all the methods of description, style, and length of the biographical notices (the customary length being 70 words, excluding particles) remain identical. The total number of commemorations in the Menologion is approximately 800; of our present commemorations, up to 350 are still absent; many venerables are lacking (of Syrian ones only 6), as well as saints of the 8th–10th centuries, Western saints (e.g., Cassian, Hilary), and Sicilian and Cretan saints; the Holy Mandylion (*Ubrus*) on August 16 is absent, as are the Procession of the Cross on August 1 and the Synaxis of the Seventy Apostles; there are approximately 50 commemorations superabundant *(Orig. p. 401)* in comparison with the present calendar (for instance, Empress Irene on August 7). The compiler evidently had before him the Typikon of the Great Church, repeating its commemorations for many days even in identical order (martyrs frequently standing even ahead of apostles), but he visibly desired to soften the local coloration of the Menologion: of the Constantinopolitan Patriarchs, none of those who were in previous calendars are present (for instance, Nectarius, Gennadius [5th century], Paul II [7th century]), the only additions being Patriarchs Germanus, Tarasius, and Antony II († 896); the first 4 Ecumenical Councils each have a separate day, whereas the Constantinopolitan Councils have a collective day; he endeavors to avoid repetition of commemorations, outstripping in this regard even our present calendar: Great Martyr Euphemia appears solely on July 11, with no commemoration on September 16; St. Maximus solely on August 17, with no commemoration on January 21 [^1763].

### The Prologues

Among subsequent recensions of the Greek Menologion, one must note the verse (metrical) *Prologue of Christopher of Mytilene* of the 11th century, which is very close unto the Studite-Jerusalem Menologion; next, the *Prologue of a certain Peter* containing commemorations down unto the 10th century, in a manuscript probably of the 13th century (St. Petersburg Public Library, from the collection of Bishop Porphyrius). The latter has 70 commemorations more than the Menologion of Basil, lacks 70, and includes 140 new ones: several are transposed unto other days in accordance with the Jerusalem Typikon; all the Syrian ascetics from the *Historia Religiosa* (*Philotheos Historia*) of Blessed Theodoret are incorporated and in the same sequence; many of the Seventy Apostles are missing (by comparison with the Menologion of Basil) as is their Synaxis. Close unto it is the *Sirmondian* (named after its owner, Fr. Sirmond) or *Claromontane* (named after the Parisian college) Synaxarion, or Prologue, compiled in the 11th–12th centuries. According unto the Menologion of Basil or the latter two Prologues, the *Verse Prologue* in the 1295 manuscript of the Moscow Synodal Library MS No. 390 and others was compiled; it is closer than they are unto the Jerusalem Typikon, yet it still lacks the Three Hierarchs, George Chozebite and Emilian on January 8, Theoktistos on January 4, Leo of Catania on February 20, Basil the Decapolite on February 28, the Great-Martyr George on November 3; on other dates Cosmas of Maiuma, Andrew of Crete, Paul of Thebes, Venerable Malachi, the Apostle Archippus; and in a different sequence the saints of September 21, January 4, and February 27. A redaction of the Menologion of Basil is likewise represented by the most ancient Slavic *Prologues* in manuscripts of the 12th–14th centuries; here the daily saints are already arranged according unto the dignity of their choirs—prophets and apostles coming first [^1764].

### The Evergetis Menologion

Among subsequent recensions of the Greek Menologion, one must note that provided by the *Evergetis Typikon* (see above, p. 363). It wavers between the Studite and the Jerusalem (see below), not infrequently departing from both; of present-day commemorations, it lacks those specifically of Jerusalem: September 1, the Dedication (*Enkaínia*), *(Orig. p. 402)* October 11, Theophanes the Confessor; October 28, Stephen the Sabbaite; November 3, the Great-Martyr George; January 8, George Chozebite; May 7, the Apparition of the Cross; it lacks the following Constantinopolitan saints and feasts: August 30, the Three Patriarchs; June 14, Patriarch Methodius; July 19, Venerable Dius; December 30, Venerable Zoticus; October 17, Andrew of Crete; December 29, Marcellus; November 9, Matrona; April 4, Joseph; August 1, the Procession of the Cross; October 28, the Earthquake (*seismos*); it contains not a single Athonite saint; it lacks the Synaxis of the Seventy Apostles, Cassian on February 29, Benedict on March 14, Ezekiel on July 21; on other dates it assigns John of Damascus unto December 2, Jonah the Prophet and Jonah the Presbyter unto September 21, and the Apostle Philemon unto November 23.

### The Studite Menologion

*The Studite Menologion was the penultimate step toward the establishment of the present one.* Yet it exhibits considerable variety across its various witnesses—in the Menaia and Typika. The most ancient of the Greek Studite Menaia—those of Grottaferrata of the 11th–12th centuries—contain, for example, on November 16, besides the Apostle Matthew, the Martyr Barlaam; they lack Paul of Thebes on January 15;

on January 20, rather than the 26th, Xenophon; they lack Venerable Benedict on March 14; contrary unto the Studite Typikon, they contain on September 13 the office of the Dedication (*Enkaínia*). Still closer unto the Jerusalem Typikon are the Greek Studite Menaia from the collection of Bishop Porphyrius in the St. Petersburg Imperial Public Library of the 12th century; its most significant differences from the latter are only on January 4, Martyr Phostirios rather than the Seventy Apostles; on January 5, Paul of Thebes; it lacks the Dedication, Cassian, and Benedict; and it contains three Italo-Sicilian saints. The Menologion of the Greek Studite Menaia often diverges from that of the Western Studite Typika, which, with the exception of that of Grottaferrata, are closer than they unto the Jerusalem Typikon. In the Menologion of the *San Nicola di Casole Typikon* (see above, p. 402), which does not indicate commemorations for every day, the Dedication is found on September 13; Western commemorations occur; and local peculiarities appear, such as December 7, the Apodosis of St. Nicholas, and December 8, the forefeast of the Conception of St. Anna. The *Mili* (*San Salvatore di Messina / Mili*) Menologion wavers among the Studite, Evergetis, and Jerusalem types; it contains commemorations found in no other Menologia, including several ancient Western ones. The Menologion in the *Studite-Alexis Typikon* is still closer unto the Jerusalem. It is not identical across the different copies of the Typikon (see above, p. 361). In the most ancient witness of the Studite-Alexis Typikon of the Moscow Typography Library MS No. 285/142/1206 of the 11th–12th centuries, there is no Menologion section proper, but it is replaced by a Kondakarion, wherein, evidently, only those saints who possess kontakia are listed; 105 days in all; all commemorations fall on their present dates, yet of Russian and Slavic saints there is not a single one. The Menologion in the Studite-Alexis Typikon of the Moscow Synodal Library MS No. 330/380 of the 12th century is likewise incomplete: approximately 160 days; all commemorations are the present ones with the addition of several Studite fathers, but it lacks 12 commemorations found in the Kondakarion as well as such customary ones as the saints of December 21–24 (doubtless because of the forefeast), Theodore the General (*Stratelates*) on February 8, Mary of Egypt on April 1, Isaiah on May 9, Nicephorus of Constantinople on June 2, Florus and Laurus on August 18, and the Apostle Bartholomew on August 25; of Slavic and Russian saints it has only Boris and Gleb on July 24. More than these redactions, the Typikon of the Moscow Synodal Library MS No. 333/382 of the year 1398 bears the imprint of Constantinopolitan provenance: thus on October 20 it assigns saints found *(Orig. p. 403)* only in the Typikon of the Great Church; on June 5 and August 7, commemorations of deliverance from enemies; on August 14, the Dedication of the temple entirely according unto the order of the Great Church; it has commemorations for all days; there are 3–4 commemorations unknown unto any other Menologia: of Russian saints, Vladimir, Olga, Boris, Gleb, Venerable Theodosius, and Leontius of Rostov; it also has Methodius, Bishop of Moravia, on June 20, and the Martyr Wenceslaus (*Vyacheslav*) on October 28. Close unto it is the Typikon of the Moscow Synodal Library MS No. 383/905 of the 15th century; mostly with one commemoration per day; June 15, Venerable Isaiah; June 23, the restoration of the narthex of St. John the Forerunner, as also on August 14 of the Church of the Theotokos; 5–6 commemorations fall on unusual dates. Richer in commemorations than it is the Typikon of the Moscow Typography Library MS No. 1444/1236 of the 14th century; it likewise contains several commemorations on unusual dates; there are repetitions of commemorations side by side on two consecutive days, and even on the same day. The Menologion of the *Slavic Studite Menaia* in the Moscow Typography and Synodal Libraries of the 12th–14th centuries coincides in its dates with the Menaia, excepting Venerable Joannicius on November 3; Cyril and Methodius are present on February 14 and April 6, and four other Moravian saints (indicating Moravian provenance?); of Russian saints: the Translation of the Relics of St. Nicholas, the Great-Martyr George on November 26, Boris and Gleb on July 25, and Leontius and Ignatius of Rostov.

### The Jerusalem Menologion

*The Menologion in the witnesses of the Jerusalem Typikon—both Typika and Menaia—is more uniform than that of the Studite.* The most ancient *Greek* Typika of the Moscow Rumiantsev Museum, Sevastyanov Collection MS No. 35/491 of the 13th century and the Moscow Synodal Library MSS Nos. 456 of the 13th century and 381 of the 13th–14th centuries, contain for the first time on January 8 George Chozebite; on October 14 (not the 12th, as at present) Cosmas of Maiuma; on November 3 the Dedication of the Church of the Great-Martyr George in Lydda; supernumerary commemorations compared with the present Typikon include: September 1, the Great Fire (in Constantinople in 468 AD); September 4, additionally Martyr Babylas of Nicomedia and 84 children (4th century), Hermione and Eutychia, sisters (in others—daughters) of Deacon Philip; July 4, Michael Choniates, Archbishop of Athens (13th century); while they lack the present-day: September 6, the Apostle Archippus; September 22, Jonah the Prophet and Jonah the Presbyter; October 15, Euthymius the New; November 29, Acacius of the Ladder; December 13, Martyr Lucia; May 31, the Apostle Hermas; June 12, Peter of Athos; on July 5 Athanasius of Athos was added by a later hand. The *Slavic* Jerusalem Typika repeat the Menologion of the Greek ones almost in its entirety, sometimes revealing traces of even greater antiquity; for instance, the Typikon of the Moscow Synodal Library MS No. 328/383 of the 14th century contains on September 6 Venerable Eudoxius, on December 23 Venerable Niphon, and on February 28 Patriarch Proterius. In varying quantities, different copies of the Typikon introduce specifically Russian and Slavic commemorations; thus in MS No. 328/383 of the 14th century there are the Protection (*Pokrov*), St. Nicholas on May 9, Venerable Theodosius, St. Vladimir, Boris and Gleb twice, Ignatius of Rostov, and St. Cyril on February 14; in MS No. 329/384 of the 14th century the days of the repose of Metropolitans Peter and Alexis of Moscow are also noted (by a later hand), but in MS No. 678/386 of the 15th century there are already fewer Russian commemorations: Venerable Theodosius, St. Vladimir, Boris and Gleb, Venerable Sergius, Metropolitan Peter, and Bishop Ignatius of Rostov (the last three appended later); on the contrary, MS No. 336/388 of the 16th century contains not only more Slavic and Russian *(Orig. p. 404)* saints than the present Typikon, but also more Greek commemorations than the Greek Typikon, for instance on November 3 and 14 Gregory Palamas, and on January 28 Isaac the Syrian. Manuscript Slavic *Menaia* of the Jerusalem type present even greater variations: the majority have Martyr Conon on March 4, and Venerable Gerasimus on March 5; in one manuscript Hypatius of Gangra is on November 16 rather than March 31; in 16th-century Menaia there appear offices for Stephen of Surozh on December 15, Venerable Parasceve on October 14 (from South Slavic Menaia of the 14th century), the Great-Martyr Parasceve on October 28, and Venerable Andrew on October 2. For the first time among Athonite saints, besides Athanasius and Peter, there appear in 14th–15th century Menaia Michael Maleinos on July 12 and Euthymius the New on October 15. In Slavic and Russian saints the Menaia are poorer than the Typika; offices for them were customarily written at the end of the book, and prior unto the 15th century they are scarcely present; the first to appear are the commemorations of Venerable Sava on January 14 and Arsenius of Serbia on October 28, and later those of the Bulgarians: John of Rila on October 19 and Hilarion of Moglena on October 21; Cyril and Methodius are absent. Of Russian saints in 14th–15th century Menaia there are occasionally offices for the Protection (*Pokrov*), St. Vladimir, the Sign (*Znamenie*) on November 27, and Barlaam of Novgorod on November 6.

### The Roman Catholic Liturgical Year

*The present Roman Catholic calendar was the outcome of the above-described gradual abbreviation and adaptation of the Pseudo-Hieronymian martyrology.* It acquired its present form under Pope Gregory XIII, who entrusted its reform unto Cardinal Guglielmo Sirleto; the latter accomplished this by 1584 with the assistance of the renowned historian Baronius and the astronomer Lilius, adopting the Martyrology of Usuard as its foundation [^1765]. Although the calendar contains commemorations for every day, approximately 70 days of the year lack proper offices, for which reason the *Missale* and *Breviarium* display no commemorations in the calendar for those days. What it shares in common with our calendar: all the Twelve Great Feasts and those akin unto them: the Nativity of John the Forerunner, the Beheading, and the Apostles Peter and Paul on the identical dates (the Conception on December 8). Of the commemorations of saints shared in common with ours on the identical dates: Paul of Thebes, Antony the Great, Agnes, Agatha, Gregory the Great, Cyril of Jerusalem, the Great-Martyr George, Mark the Evangelist, Athanasius the Great, the Apostle Barnabas, the Maccabees, Laurence, Eustathius (Placidus), Luke the Evangelist, Gregory the Wonderworker of Neocaesarea, the Apostle Andrew, Sabbas, Nicholas, and Ambrose; on other dates: Timothy on January 24, Polycarp on January 26, Ignatius the God-Bearer on February 1, Cyril of Alexandria on February 9, the Twenty-Five [Forty] Martyrs on March 10, Joseph the Betrothed on March 19, John of Damascus on March 27, Leo the Great on April 11, Justin the Martyr on April 14, the Apostles Philip and James the Brother of the Lord on May 1, Gregory the Theologian on May 9, Basil the Great on June 14, the Apostle James the Son of Zebedee on July 25, Anna on July 26, Nazarius and Celsus on July 29, the Chains of St. Peter on April 1 [August 1], the Finding of the Relics of St. Stephen on August 3, Helena on August 18, *(Orig. p. 405)* the Apostle Bartholomew on August 24, Cyprian and Justina on September 26, Matthew the Evangelist on September 21, Cosmas and Damian on September 27, Chrysanthus and Daria on October 25, Pope Martin on November 12, Catherine on November 25, the Apostle Thomas on December 21, Stephen on December 26, John the Evangelist on December 27, the Holy Innocents on December 28 [printed: 2], and Pope Sylvester on December 31. Specifically Roman Catholic commemorations, aside from Western saints, include: (a) in honour of the Saviour: (1) the Feast of Corpus Christi (*Corpus Domini*) on Thursday (as the day of the institution of the Eucharist) after the octave (on the 8th day) of Pentecost, instituted in the 13th century to counter doubts concerning transubstantiation; (2) the Feast of the Holy Name of Jesus on the second Sunday after Epiphany, detached from the Feast of the Circumcision and authorized by the Pope only in the 18th century; (3) a series of commemorations of individual events and instruments of the Passion of Christ on certain days of Lent and its preparatory period, such as: the Prayer in Gethsemane, the Crown of Thorns, the Spear and Nails, the Holy Winding-Sheet (*Plashchanytsia* / *Sindone*), the Five Wounds, the Precious Blood of Jesus, or the Sacred Heart of Jesus (the latter on the first Sunday of July); (b) in honour of the Mother of God: (1) 'Her Holy Name' on the 1st Sunday after the Nativity of the Theotokos (from the 16th century); (2) 'Her Espousals with Joseph' on January 23 (from the 16th century); (3) 'Her Visitation (*Visitatio*) unto Righteous Elizabeth' on July 2 (from the 13th century, cf. our feast on July 2); (4) [printed: omitted numeral 4] 'The Rosary', that is, beads, in honour of the prayer rule among Roman Catholics (which attained wide diffusion in the 12th–13th centuries), consisting in the frequent repetition of the *Ave Maria* (**'Rejoice, O Virgin Theotokos'** / *Bogoroditse Devo, raduisia*) joined with the *Pater Noster* (*Our Father*) counted upon beads; authorized after the victory over the Turks on October 7, 1571 (cf. our feast on October 1); (5) 'The Seven Sorrows of the Blessed Virgin Mary' (these sorrows: the Circumcision of Christ, the Flight into Egypt, the Loss of the Child Jesus in the Temple, the Carrying of the Cross, the Crucifixion, the Deposition from the Cross, and the Burial) on Friday of the 6th week of Great Lent (universally from the 15th century, but the hymn for it, *Stabat Mater*, originates in the 13th century); (6) 'The Seven Joys of the Virgin Mary' (these joys: the Annunciation, the Visitation, the Nativity of Jesus, the Adoration of the Magi, the Resurrection, the Descent of the Holy Spirit, and Her Coronation by God the Father and the Son) on the 3rd Sunday of September, established in the 18th century as a parallel unto the preceding feast and assigned unto the day on which the military Order of St. Mary (Mercedarians), founded for the redemption of captives, celebrated the liberation of captives from the Saracens in 1198; (7) 'Our Lady of the Snows' on August 5, that is, the Dedication of the Basilica on the Esquiline Hill in Rome, erected in the 4th century by direction of a miraculous vision upon the site where snow had wonderfully fallen; (8) 'Our Lady of Mount Carmel' on July 16—the feast of the Carmelites, an Order founded upon that mount, from the 13th century; (9) 'The Translation of the Holy House of Mary unto Loreto' on December 10—by angels from Nazareth, where it had been exposed unto peril from the infidels; there are also 13 less significant feasts of the Mother of God that are not entered into liturgical calendars. Of the feasts of saints not identical with the Eastern Church, the most significant are: 'All Saints' on November 1 (instituted prior unto the 8th century); All Souls' Day on November 2 (subsequent unto the 8th century); the Apparition of the Archangel Michael upon Mount Gargano (in Apulia) on May 8; the Dedication of the Church in Castel Sant'Angelo in honour of a similar apparition of the Archangel Michael there on September 20 (from the 5th century); the 'Holy Guardian Angels' on the 1st Sunday of September (from the 17th century); the 'Chair' (that is, in honour of the episcopate of the Apostle Peter in Antioch) on February 22; *(Orig. p. 406)* 'His Chair in Rome' on January 18 (from the 5th century); the 'Conversion of St. Paul' on January 25 (from the 13th century); and the Dedication of famous basilicas, such as that of Saints Peter and Paul in Rome on November 18 [^1766].

### The Classification of Feasts

Only in the present period was the current division of feasts according unto their degree of solemnity definitively established. Already in the preceding period, feasts in honour of the Saviour and the Mother of God occupied the most honourable position among others, and even the current number of these feasts—twelve—was approximately adumbrated. Yet it may be stated that prior unto the 11th century, the number of the foremost feasts was not measured with such precision and symbolic intent as now, that is, it was not subsumed under the number twelve. The Grottaferrata Typikon (11th–12th centuries) enumerates 14 'Dominical feasts (*despotikaì heortaí / δεσποτικαὶ ἑορταί*)': the Annunciation, the Nativity of Christ, the Circumcision, the Meeting (*Hypapante*), the Theophany (*Baptism*), the Raising of Lazarus, Palm Sunday, the Transfiguration, the Mystical Supper, the Crucifixion, the Resurrection, New Sunday (*Thomas Sunday*), the Ascension, and Pentecost [^1767]. Theodore Prodromus in the 12th century omits from this catalog the Mystical Supper and New Sunday, thereby arriving at 12 feasts; Nicephorus Callistus in the 14th century replaces the Circumcision with the Dormition, and thus likewise obtains the number twelve [^1768]. Consequently, Marian feasts—among which the Annunciation (= the Conception of Christ) was not included—were not entered into the rank of the Twelve Great Feasts. In the Typikon of the Great Church of Constantinople, the Entry is merely named under November 21, but regarding its service no rubrical directions are provided, nor are Epistle and Gospel readings even indicated, which is done there for numerous saints. Yet all other Typika, beginning with the most ancient Studite witnesses, assign for all feasts of the Mother of God services of equal solemnity with Dominical feasts, with those exceptions that are likewise made in this regard by the present Typikon (the absence of antiphons at the Liturgy—which ancient Typika permitted even for certain Dominical feasts—and a shorter afterfeast) [^1769]. With almost the same solemnity as the Twelve Great Feasts, the ancient Studite Typika prescribed the celebration of only two feasts of the Forerunner—June 24 and August 29—both because of the elevated dignity of this saint and, doubtless, because of his close association with the Studion Monastery: these feasts had an afterfeast, the Oktoechos was cancelled for them (though not unconditionally: on Wednesday and Friday the 1st apostichon sticheron was from the Oktoechos); they had stepennas (*gradual psalms*, which in the Studite-Alexis Typikon served in place of the present Polyeleos), and the like; yet all other feasts (excepting, naturally, the commemoration of Theodore the Studite, which constituted a great feast), even June 29, were celebrated according unto *(Orig. p. 407)* these Typika with significantly less solemnity: the Oktoechos was sung alongside the festal office (at the aposticha, the 1st sticheron was from the Oktoechos), and there were no stepennas. The Jerusalem (and Evergetis) Typikon advanced further in this regard: it imparted the same festal structure of service, with the absolute exclusion of the Oktoechos, unto an entire series of feasts in honour of saints: not only June 29, but also September 26 and December 6; moreover, with each subsequent redaction of this Typikon, the compass of such feasts—which acquired the designation of *Polyeleos* feasts—expanded: gradually there were included here the commemorations of all the Apostles in the order of their veneration (the earliest being November 30; yet all commemorations of the Apostles were made Polyeleos feasts only in the printed editions of the Typikon, though upon the authority of certain ancient recensions of the Jerusalem Typikon, for instance in Nikon of the Black Mountain), as well as certain martyrs and venerable monastics. Of the remaining saints, the more venerated were distinguished in both types of Typika—Studite and Jerusalem—by joining unto the aposticha stichera a sticheron unto the saint, and by an increased number of troparia at the canon (in the Studite the troparia of the canon were sung twice, in the Jerusalem the canon was at 6), occasionally by special Praises (*Ainoi*) stichera at Matins and Epistle and Gospel readings at the Liturgy; while in the Studite Typika they were marked beyond this by exemption from the Hours and from manual labor until midday (sometimes **'Blessed is the man'** at Vespers, for example on September 26 and November 8 according unto the Studite-Alexis Typikon). A service of this type is prescribed by the Studite Typika for all the Apostles (excepting John the Evangelist) and for the majority of present-day Polyeleos and certain six-troparion (*shesterik*) saints; for these same saints the Jerusalem Typikon prescribes the like, with the aforementioned exceptions (Polyeleos saints). The Jerusalem Typikon, by virtue of its practice of the Great Doxology, was able to detach several commemorations from this compass of middle feasts into the rank of 'Doxology' feasts, that is, with the Great Doxology but without the Polyeleos: in the most ancient copies of the Jerusalem Typikon, September 23 and November 30 appear as such feasts. With respect unto the remaining saints, in both types of Typika (and in the Evergetis) some of them (those more venerated) possessed a troparion; for such was sung at Matins **'God is the Lord'** (*Theos Kyrios*); while others possessed none, and then there was sung at Matins *Alleluia* with the Triadica; the number of this latter class of saints was reduced in each subsequent recension of the Jerusalem Typikon (remaining almost constant in the Studite), until (already in the printed editions of the Typikon) *Alleluia* remained exclusively for the multi-day fasts. Thus, in both types of Typika there existed from of old three principal ranks of feasts: great, middle, and minor; their composition and ceremonial varied, yet the fundamental distinction among them has remained unto this day such as Nikon of the Black Mountain indicated:

> Great feasts 'have assemblies of the people according unto the rule (a service obligatory for all), and prophecies at Vespers, and readings (festal homilies) at Matins, and **"Let every breath"** and the Gospel... at minor feasts in church prostrations do not take place during the fast (public fasting?), but privately (in the cells) both take place (prostrations and fasting); at middle feasts in church prostrations in no wise take place, but privately as each one chooses; while at great feasts prostrations do not take place, neither fasting, neither in *(Orig. p. 408)* church nor in the cells' [^1770].

Nikon provides in a table these three ranks of feasts from various Typika (the Studite, the Jerusalem, and the Holy Mountain / Athonite), designating great feasts with a cross in a circle, middle feasts with a cross, and minor feasts with three dots. Yet since full consensus did not exist among the Typika in the distribution of feasts across these ranks, Nikon provides another table of them with certain variations from the first; moreover, different manuscripts of Nikon's work do not always agree in assigning a given feast unto a specific rank. In any event, this represents the earliest known attempt at a complete classification of feasts, and a comparison thereof with the present-day Typikon demonstrates what development the church year has undergone in this regard since the 10th–11th centuries. Great feasts in Nikon, besides the Twelve Great Feasts and the movable feasts, are: January 1, or the entire Twelve Days (*Dodekahemeron*), June 24 and 29, August 29; in certain manuscripts of Nikon also November 13, April 23, and May 8. Middle feasts: September 26; October 6, 9, 18, 23, 26; November 8, 13, 14, 16, and 30; December 20; January 7, 20, and 25; April 25 and 30 [printed: 39]; May 8 and 10; June 11 and 19; July 8, 20, and 27; August 9; in certain manuscripts also September 1, 6, 9, 13, 16, 20, 23; November 6, 12, 25; December 4, 5, 9, 21; January 16, 17, 18, and 27; February 3 and 24; March 9; May 21; June 8 and 30; July 2, 13, and 25; August 1 and 31; according unto another table also December 26 (in certain manuscripts even a great feast), December 27, and May 25. Minor feasts, besides those just enumerated—which in some manuscripts are middle, and in others minor—in all manuscripts also include: September 2, 3, 5, 7, 15, 24, 28, and 30; October 1, 2, 3, 21, and 24; November 1, 11, and 22; December 13 and 17; January 14, 22, 23, 28, 29, 31; February 1; May 2, 15, and 24; June 14; July 1, 11, 15, and 22; August 2, 5, 7, 14, and 24; according unto another table also September 4 and 29; October 11 and 12; November 2, 3, 9, 17, 24, 27, and 27; December 31; January 19 and 21; May 1 and 12; August 28.

### The Roman Catholic Table of Feasts

*In the Roman Catholic Church, feasts are divided according unto their degree of solemnity into six ranks.* Feasts of the first four ranks, since each encompasses approximately two days (some have an eve or vigil, others continue through certain offices of the following day), are termed doubles (*duplicia*). Unto *duplicia primae classis* (first class doubles) belong feasts that possess an eight-day afterfeast (*octava*), which is especially solemn not on its final day—the Apodosis, as with us—but upon the Sunday falling within that eight-day period. Among the feasts with an eight-day octave are the Nativity of Christ, Epiphany, Easter (*Pascha*), Ascension, Pentecost, Corpus Christi, the Assumption (*Dormition*), the Immaculate Conception, the Nativity of John the Baptist, the Apostles Peter and Paul, All Saints on November 1, and the Dedication of a Church; unto this same first class are likewise assigned the following feasts that lack an octave: Joseph the Betrothed on March 19, the patronal *(Orig. p. 409)* saint and protector (*patronus*) of the country or locality (the locally venerated saint); secondary feast (*secundaria*, in distinction from those enumerated, which are *primaria*): the Sacred Heart of Jesus. Unto the second rank (*duplicia II classis*) belong: Circumcision, the Most Holy Trinity (on the 1st Sunday after Pentecost), Purification (*Meeting / Hypapante*), Visitation (July 2), Dedication of the Basilica of St. Michael the Archangel (September 29), commemorations of the Apostles, the Evangelists, Stephen, the Holy Innocents, and Laurence (the last three possessing an octave), Anna, Joachim (March 20); secondary: the Holy Name and Most Precious Blood of Jesus, the Finding of the Holy Cross, the Rosary, and the Patronage of St. Joseph. Unto the third class, *duplicia majora* (greater doubles), belong: the Transfiguration, the Exaltation of the Holy Cross, the Presentation (*Entry*), the Beheading, and others, besides those enumerated above, the feasts of the Mother of God, the Forerunner, the Apostles, and the foremost saints: Benedict, Dominic, Francis. Unto the fourth rank (*alia duplicia*, other doubles) belong feasts of other foremost saints. Unto the fifth and sixth ranks, *semiduplicia* (semidoubles) and *simplicia* (simple), belong the remaining days. Sundays (*Dominicae*) are divided into three classes: I: 1st of Advent, 1st of Lent, Passion Sunday (5th of Lent), Palm Sunday, Easter, Low Sunday (*in Albis*), Pentecost, Trinity Sunday; II: 2nd, 3rd, and 4th of Advent, 3rd and 4th of Lent; III: the remainder. This classification is essential for determining which office is to be celebrated upon the confluence of movable feasts with immovable ones: thus upon the concurrence of feasts of the first three classes with a Sunday of the 1st class, the feast is transferred (*translatio*); upon the concurrence of other feasts with Sundays, for the most part only a commemoration of the former is made at the prayer (*commemoratio*) or a short reading (*capitulum*) is assigned for them [^1771].

### The Nativity Fast

In the present period, the *Nativity Fast* received universal recognition in the East, having arisen and spread, as we have seen, earlier in the West in the 6th century (see above, p. 327). In the treatise *On the Three Quadragesimas*, attributed unto Anastasius of Sinai, Patriarch of Antioch (561–600 AD), but having made its appearance scarcely prior unto the 9th century (as is evident from the fact that mention is made therein of the Dormition Fast, which was unknown prior unto the 9th century), it is stated that the obligatory nature of the Nativity Fast was still contested, that it was regarded as a monastic rather than an apostolic ordinance, that its duration was shortened unto 19, 12, 6, or 4 days, and that during its course it was deemed permissible to partake of everything except meat, save for a single day; the author defends the apostolic origin and universal obligation of the fast by appealing unto the tradition concerning the Apostle Philip, according unto which tradition it was revealed unto the Apostle, because before his death he had prayed for heavenly punishment upon his persecutors, that for 40 days he would not be admitted into Paradise, for which reason Philip entreated the Apostles to fast on his behalf during those days [^1772]. *(Orig. p. 410)* In the *Hypotyposis* and *Diatyposis* (9th century) detailed instructions are already given concerning food during the Quadragesima of St. Philip. The Council of Constantinople under Patriarch Luke Chrysoberges and Emperor Manuel Comnenus (1143–1180 AD) requires this fast to begin on November 14; Balsamon (12th century), in his commentary upon the canons of this Council, regards the fast in its full scope as obligatory for monks, but for laity considers a reduction thereof unto 7 days permissible [^1773]. According unto the testimony of Codinus (14th century), at the Constantinopolitan court the Nativity Fast was observed for 40 days, and on the day of the Nativity of Christ, upon the occasion of the dispensation from the fast, the protopapas (the first archpriest) came unto the palace to bless the imperial table [^1774].

### The Dormition Fast

In the 9th century we encounter the earliest mentions also of the *Dormition Fast*. The *Hypotyposis* and *Diatyposis* do not yet mention it, even in manuscripts of the 14th century. Only in a 16th-century manuscript of the second of these Typika, in the margin opposite the chapter on fasts, is there an annotation: 'noteworthy (*semeiosai / σημείωσαι*), that nothing is said concerning the Fast of the Dormition' [^1775]. There is likewise no mention of it in the Evergetis Typikon (11th century) or that of the Pantokrator Monastery of Constantinople of 1136. Among Typika, the first indication of the Dormition Fast is encountered in the Typikon of the San Nicola di Casole Monastery (12th century). Here under August 1 there is the following observation:

> 'Of Nicholas, Most Holy Patriarch of Constantinople, New Rome (Nicholas I Mystikos, 895–925 with interruption, or Nicholas II Chrysoberges, 983–996 AD), concerning the Quadragesima of the Dormition of the Most Holy Theotokos: We have another fast, called that of the Most Holy Theotokos, commencing from the 1st day of the month of August, which is mentioned by the Holy Council of Union (*henoseos / ἑνώσεως*—in another manuscript: "and by the Seventh Council at Nicaea"). Yet on the first day of August we do not fast because of the feast of the Holy Maccabees, but from the 2nd day of August [we begin] the established fast, and the office of the Transfiguration, that is, for 8 days, we sing entirely in full' (that is, despite the fast, the service of the Transfiguration is sung in church with its forefeast for 8 days).

Yet the same Typikon in its 'canon' on food does not name the Dormition Fast [^1776]. This Typikon furnishes us with the guiding thread for tracing the origin of the Dormition Fast. According unto it, the earliest mention of the fast must be sought in the acts of the so-called 'Council of Union' (*Synodus Unionis*) held in 920 AD. This Council, regarding the question of the admissibility of a fourth marriage, decreed that even trigamists are subject unto special ecclesiastical penance: they must 'receive communion three times a year: at Pascha, on the feast of the Dormition of the Mother of God, and at the Nativity of our Lord Jesus Christ, forasmuch as fasts precede these feasts' [^1777].
*(Orig. p. 411)*
A putative earlier mention of the Dormition Fast in the letter of Pope Nicholas I (859–867 AD) unto the Bulgarians is doubtful: 'the Holy Roman Church received from antiquity and observes the following fasts: 40 days before Pascha, after Pentecost, before the Dormition of Mary the Mother of God, as well as before the feast of the Nativity of the Lord.' The Roman Church never knew the Dormition Fast, and it never lasted 40 days. In the aforementioned treatise *On the Three Quadragesimas*, attributed unto Anastasius of Sinai, the Dormition Fast is represented as having detached itself from the Fast of the Holy Apostles: the latter originally extended from the first Sunday after Pentecost until the Dormition, but subsequently, on account of human infirmity, the month of July was excluded therefrom. The Athonite monks around 1085 AD inquired of Nicholas Grammatikos, Patriarch of Constantinople, concerning the fasts, among which the Dormition Fast especially perplexed them. Concerning it they wrote unto the Patriarch: 'Concerning the fast which is in the month of August until the fifteenth day, we find [mention] in the union at the Council held in the city of Constantine concerning marriages, and being at a loss to commemorate it, we entreat: resolve us from contention.' The Patriarch, after deliberating with the Synod, replied: 'The fast was at that time transferred (that is, the fast was transposed from this time unto another) for this reason, lest they fall into the pagan fasts occurring at that time; nevertheless, many persons even yet fast for the sake of cleansing from illness' [^1778].

The nascent fast aroused such interest in society that around that same period—in the 11th–12th centuries—there appeared also a specialized treatise by a certain Anastasius of Caesarea. The antiquity of the fast is therein demonstrated by appeals unto the testimonies of the Patriarchs of Antioch and the Council of Union, and the author arrives at the conclusion that the fast was observed even prior unto Emperor Leo the Wise (886–911 AD) [^1779]. Finally, around that same period the question of the Dormition Fast, as well as the Nativity Fast, was once again examined at the Council of Constantinople under Patriarch Luke and Emperor Manuel Comnenus (12th century). According unto the account of Balsamon, certain persons at this Council asserted that in the decree of the preceding (above-mentioned) Council under Patriarch Nicholas mention had been made of transferring the Dormition Fast unto another time, and therefore the fast could have no place during the first half of August; but since that Council had not specified unto what time the fast had been transferred, while from the mention of the Council it was clear that the fast had been observed of old in August, this Council confirmed the observance of the fast in this month. During his patriarchate Balsamon wrote encyclical and private epistles exhorting the observance of this fast [^1780]. Nikon of the Black Mountain (11th century) states concerning the Dormition Fast that those who do not observe it have no foundation in antiquity for themselves, yet those who observe it are likewise established not upon apostolic tradition, but upon the custom of subsequent times, which is, however, exceedingly ancient [^1781].

*(Orig. p. 412)*

### Byzantine Hymnographers of the Ninth to Eleventh Centuries

As in the 6th–8th centuries, parallel with the development of the church year proceeded the activity of church hymnographers. It had three directions, aiming at the enrichment of: a) the Octoechos, b) the Triodion, and c) the Menaion. At the head of the hymnographers of this period must be placed, in significance and talent, St. Theodore the Studite († 826 AD). In the Octoechos unto him belong the Degrees (*Anabathmoi / Stepenny*) [^1782]; in the Triodion—the triodia for all the ordinary weekdays (Monday through Friday) of the Great Fast and the tetraodia for the ordinary (2nd through 5th) Saturdays of the Great Fast, amounting in all to 39 canons, which presently occupy the second place at the services (the first being the triodia of his brother Joseph); furthermore, one sticheron at *Lord, I have cried* and one sessional hymn (*sedalen*) for all ordinary weekdays of the Great Fast—likewise occupying at present the second place in the service after Joseph's stichera and sessional hymns; canons on Meatfare Sunday, Cheese-fare Saturday, and the Sunday of the Veneration of the Precious Cross; in the Menaion—probably only stichera. Unto his brother, St. Joseph the Studite, fellow confessor for the holy icons and Archbishop of Thessalonica († before Theodore), belong in the Triodion the first triodia, the stichera at *Lord, I have cried*, and sessional hymns for those same weekdays of the Great Fast, triodia for Cheese-fare Sunday, and the canon for the Sunday of the Prodigal Son. Other monks of the Studite Monastery likewise composed hymns, frequently concealing their names (whence the inscription 'Of the Studite' [*Studitovo*]); from acrostics two of the immediate successors of St. Theodore in the hegumenate are known: St. Nicholas—by a canon unto St. Theodore the General (*Stratelates*) on February 8, and Clement the Studite—by canons unto the Prophet Moses on September 4, the Archangels on November 8, the Sunday before the Nativity of Christ, and the Holy Martyrs of Ephesus on August 4 (it is noteworthy that his canons bear the acrostic *Κήμεντος*, with the omission of *λ*—a sign of the subsequent removal of the second ode from the canons); a contemporary of Clement, Cyprian the Studite, wrote only a few stichera—for November 8, December 17 and 27, the Forefeast of the Nativity of Christ, January 28, February 1, and March 9. Less in this era—as is natural—was contributed unto hymnography by the Lavra of St. Sabbas. It produced only a single prolific hymnographer, St. Theophanes the Branded (*Graptos*, † 843 AD), a confessor for the holy icons, who died as Bishop of Nicaea. He wrote for the Octoechos canons in the eight tones unto the angels, the apostles, and the reposed, and probably certain Theotokia canons at Small Compline; for the Triodion, canons for the 1st Sunday of Lent—unto the prophets (presently sung at Compline, formerly probably at Matins) and unto Orthodoxy, for Mid-Lent Wednesday, and for Palm Saturday, completing the tetraodia of Cosmas and the Damascene, the first troparia of the Paschal Theotokion canon (the second troparia being by Joseph the Hymnographer), canons for Mid-Pentecost and unto the Holy Spirit at Compline of Pentecost; for the Menaion—the canon for the Annunciation, for John the Forerunner on January 7, for his brother Theodore the Branded on December 27, and for the greater part of the days of the year over 180 canons, not all of which are in use today; together with Joseph the Hymnographer (see below), he is the most prolific author of canons. George, at first chartophylax of St. Sophia, later Metropolitan of Nicomedia, a friend of Patriarch Photius, and a re*(Orig. p. 413)*nowned preacher of the 9th century, wrote for the Triodion a canon for the Sunday of the Publican and the Pharisee, and for the Menaion canons for the Entry (*Presentation*), the Conception of St. Anna, the Forefeast of the Meeting and the Annunciation, the Deposition of the Cincture (*Sash*) of the Mother of God on August 31, the Holy Cross on July 31, and unto several saints. Metrophanes, Bishop of Smyrna, a supporter of Patriarch Ignatius in his controversy with Photius, wrote for the Octoechos Triadica canons and probably certain Theotokia. Joseph the Hymnographer († 883 AD), a Sicilian who suffered greatly during a prolonged life for the holy icons, replenished the Octoechos unto its present form (after John of Damascus, Theophanes, and Metrophanes) with penitential canons on Monday and Tuesday, canons unto the Forerunner, the Cross, St. Nicholas, and All Saints; he likewise replenished the Triodion unto its present form with the canon for the Samaritan Woman and probably others, as well as triodia for all the days of the Pentecostarion; he performed the same work also for the Menaion, composing canons principally for days omitted by Theophanes—approximately 180 canons, including canons for the majority of the forefeasts. Less prolific, but for the most part equally talented hymnographers were: Theosteriktos at the beginning of the 9th century, a Bithynian monk and disciple of St. Nicetas of Medicium, author of the Paraklesis Theotokion canon: **"Held by many temptations"** (*"Многими содержим напастьми"*); Sergius, a monk of Jerusalem, termed therefore Hagiopolites or the Holy-City Dweller (*Svyatogradets*), a confessor for the holy icons under Emperor Theophilus (829–842 AD), an historian, author of stichera for September 8 and November 21; Kassia or Ikasia, who narrowly missed becoming the consort of that same emperor, foundress of a monastery in Constantinople, who completed Cosmas' tetraodion for Great and Holy Saturday, and was author also of other canons not presently in use, as well as stichera for the Nativity of Christ, June 25, November 15, December 13, and probably for Great and Holy Wednesday and other occasions; Ignatius, at first hierodeacon and skevophylax of St. Sophia, subsequently Metropolitan of Nicaea (9th century), author of the canon unto the Hodegetria (presently October 22, July 8 and 28), unto the 42 Martyrs on March 6, the Martyr Tatiana on January 12, the Martyr Xenia on January 24, and St. Nicephorus on March 12; Arsenius, Archbishop of Corfu, a contemporary of Photius who conducted correspondence with him, author of the canon for holy unction (*Euchelaion*) and of several stichera for September 6, November 8, June 29, and July 20; Ephraim, Bishop of Caria, likewise a contemporary of Photius and author of several stichera for September 3, 9, and 20, November 1 and 8, June 20, and August 8; Anatolius, Bishop of Thessalonica (9th century), author of stichera unto the Great Martyr Demetrius of Thessalonica, and probably for many twelve great feasts, their forefeasts, and the foremost saints of various orders; Mark, monk of the Lavra of St. Sabbas, later oikonomos of St. Sophia and Bishop of Otranto (*Hydrous / Idruite*) in Calabria, an ascetic and clairvoyant elder (9th–10th centuries), who supplemented Cosmas' tetraodion for Great and Holy Saturday (in the present canon his troparia remain up unto the 6th Ode, and the heirmoi are thought to be Kassia's), and wrote perhaps the prayer unto the Most Holy Trinity at the Sunday Midnight Office; unto him are ascribed the rubrical directions for cases of concurrence between movable and immovable feasts—the 'Markian Chapters' (*Markovy glavy*), which in ancient Typika are not inscribed with his name and in general, evidently, were formed gradually; Emperor Leo VI the Wise († 911 AD)—author of the eleven Resurrectional Gospel Stichera, stichera unto righteous Lazarus (and of a canon unto him, no longer in use), unto the Most Holy Trinity, and for August 16; unto him are likewise attributed stichera bearing the inscription 'Byzantios' (that is, of Byzantium): September 1, 2, 16, 23, 25, November 8, 11, 14, December 4, *(Orig. p. 414)* 6, 17, January 1, March 25, June 11, 24, 29, July 20, 26, and August 6; Emperor Constantine VII Porphyrogenitus, son of Leo VI († 959 AD), author of the Sunday Exapostilaria. Symeon Metaphrastes (that is, the paraphraser of the lives of the saints), in rank Logothete of the Byzantine Court, a secret ascetic († 940 AD), author of the canon on the Lamentation of the Theotokos at Compline of Great and Holy Friday, stichera of the Great Canon, perhaps triodia for the forefeasts of the Nativity of Christ and Theophany [^1783], the canon unto St. Mary of Egypt on April 1, and various prayers; Basil, surnamed Pagariotes, Archbishop of Caesarea (10th century), author of stichera for January 1, and probably of the canons for the Entry and St. Nicholas—the second of those presently used; George Skylitzes (11th century), formerly master of the school in Constantinople, a preacher (surnamed *Mauropous*), author of many penitential canons unto the Lord Jesus (25 canons, of which one is presently appended unto the Akathist), unto the Most Holy Theotokos (60–70 canons, of which certain ones—no fewer than four—are used at Compline, as well as in the services of the 1st Saturday of Lent, January 27 and 30), canons unto John the Forerunner (11 canons, of which one is for August 29), and the canon unto the Guardian Angel—the present one (**"Thou sleepless guardian..."** / *"Неусыпаемаго хранителя..."*); he composed the offices newly instituted in his time unto the Three Hierarchs on January 30 and unto the Holy Great Martyr Theodore the Recruit (*Tyro*) on the 1st Saturday of the Great Fast; Paul of Evergetis (*Ammoraios*), founder of the Evergetis Monastery (11th century), author of stichera unto the Theotokos at *Lord, I have cried* at Sunday Vespers (where there is no Menaion) and litany stichera for the dedication of a church; Christopher, patrician and proconsul of Mytilene (11th century), author of the Verse Prologue (see above, p. 401) and the canon of Cheese-fare Sunday; Nicephorus Blemmydes, a learned exegete (13th century), unto whom is attributed the compilation of the 'selected psalms' (for the Megalynaria) [^1784]; Gregory of Sinai (13th–14th centuries), that is, an ascetic first at Sinai, subsequently on Mount Athos, founder of his own monastery in Macedonia, author of the Triadica Megalynaria at the Sunday Midnight Office, canons unto the Cross, the Holy Fathers, and the Lord Jesus, which are not in use today; Germanus, Patriarch of Constantinople, 'the New' (1226–1239 AD), author of stichera and the second canon for the Sunday of the Holy Fathers nearest to July 16, and the office for the Fathers on the Sunday nearest to October 11; Nicephorus Callistus Xanthopoulos, church historian of the 14th century, author of the synaxaria of the Triodion and the service for the Life-Giving Spring; Philotheus [Kokkinos], Patriarch of Constantinople (1354–1376 AD with interruption), formerly Abbot on Mount Athos and Archbishop of Heraclea, probably the author of the renowned *Diataxis* (see above, p. 374), author of several canons unto saints, penitential canons, litany prayers (not in use today), as well as refrains unto selected psalms similar unto our Megalynaria and having probably served as models for them (see below); Nicholas Malaxos, priest of Nauplia (15th century), supplemented liturgical books with his hymns and services: for example, he composed the 'office of the Great Hours on the eve of *(Orig. p. 415)* Pentecost', triodia for every day of the Dormition Fast, and services for certain days of the months; these additions were included in certain printed editions (for example, the aforementioned Hours in the Venetian edition of the Pentecostarion of 1579), but were subsequently excised; there remained only a few stichera of his in the Menaion: November 30, December 17, and at Small Vespers of the Sunday of Orthodoxy. Not all of the designated hymnographers can be recognized with equal certainty as the authors of the hymns attributed unto them; one is obliged to trust the testimony of ancient manuscripts, which are nevertheless later than the authors by two or three centuries. Moreover, for a significant quantity of liturgical chants, especially stichera, troparia, and sessional hymns, their authors are entirely unknown, and one can only surmise approximately concerning the place and time of their origin. Such is the case even with the most important chants. Thus, nothing is known concerning the author of the Sunday kontakia; judging from the fact that Typika prior unto the 15th century do not know them, they appeared around that century. Nothing is known concerning the author of the present-day Megalynaria (*velichaniya*) and the analogous 'Lamentations' (*encomia / pokhvaly*) of Great and Holy Saturday: the Megalynaria are not mentioned at all by Typika, whether Greek or Slavic; they were and are found only in the Sequenced Psalters (*Sledovannye Psaltiri*), and their present-day form appears in 15th-century manuscripts [^1785]; while the 'Lamentations' of Great and Holy Saturday *(Orig. p. 416)* are not yet mentioned in Greek Typika even of the 14th century (for example, Moscow Synodal Library MS No. 381), but Slavic ones of that century (for example, Moscow Synodal Library MS No. 328/383) speak already of the 'Lamentation' (*Pokhvala*); Sequenced Psalters even in the 15th century contain only one stanza of praise for each stasis (the first of those presently used); and only in Triodia of the 16th century and early-printed Greek editions do they appear in their complete present-day form.

The compositions of the enumerated church hymnographers, which are used unto this day in divine services, did not, of course, rapidly gain universal dissemination and acceptance, nor have they reached us in an immutable form and composition. As previously, there appeared alongside them other hymnographers, and in certain churches (for example, the Georgian Church) native national hymns, which were admitted into the liturgical corpus and only in the course of time were supplanted by Greek ones. Thus in a Georgian Festal Menaion with Triodion interpolations and Octoechos according unto MS No. 425 of the 10th century from the Tiflis 'Society for the Propagation of Literacy', for the Nativity of Christ and Theophany there are canons by a Georgian hymnographer, whereas the canons for these feasts by John of Damascus and Cosmas are appointed: the former on the Sunday before the feasts and the latter at the Paramon (*eve*) [^1786]. In the Slavic Floral Triodion (*Pentecostarion*) of the Moscow Synodal Library MS No. 896/428 of 1311 AD, for Antipascha there is not the same canon as presently (consequently not that of John of Damascus), just as for the Ascension the second canon is not the present one. We do not speak of less important services and feasts: on ordinary weekdays of the Triodion, as also on its less significant Sundays (such as the 2nd and 4th), and on weekdays of the Octoechos, the canons in manuscript Triodia and Octoechoi are frequently not those of today, or if they are the same, they have extra or different troparia, or fewer troparia; while stichera and sessional hymns are distinguished by even less stability, even for the Twelve Great Feasts [^1787].
*(Orig. p. 417)*

### Russian and Slavic Hymnographers

When the commemorations of Slavic and Russian saints were entered into the calendar, services were likewise composed for them. The names of Serbian and Bulgarian hymnographers are unknown. Among the Russians, however, the following are known: Gregory, a monk of the Caves Monastery (11th century), called by his contemporaries 'the Creator of Canons', author probably of the service unto St. Vladimir and St. Theodosius of the Caves (the author of this latter service is also considered to be James the Monk, an 11th-century monk of the Caves); a certain Cyril the Monk, author of the canon unto St. Olga (the service unto her is also attributed unto 'Pachomius of the Holy Mountain', perhaps the author also of the service unto St. Michael of Chernihiv); Pachomius the Logothete, a Serbian scholar summoned by Prince Basil II († 1462 AD) [erroneously styled Basil III], author of canons unto St. Alexis, St. Sergius, St. Nicon, St. Jonah, and St. Stephen of Perm, and of the service for the translation of the relics of St. Peter; Michael Tuchkov (in monasticism Elias) and the monk Macarius, by commission of Metropolitan Macarius (1542–1564 AD), wrote services: the former unto St. Alexander Nevsky, and the latter unto St. Macarius of Kalyazin († 1483 AD) on March 17; Herodion, disciple of St. Alexander of Svir († 1553 AD) and hegumen of his monastery, wrote the service unto him for August 30; Tsarevich John, son of Tsar Ivan IV, wrote the service unto St. Anthony of Siya († 1557 AD) for December 7 [^1788]; Cyprian, Metropolitan of Krutitsy († 1635 AD), wrote the service for the Placement of the Honorable Robe of the Lord on July 10; Epiphanius Slavinetsky († 1675 AD), summoned from the Kyiv Academy to Moscow under Patriarch Nikon for the correction and translation of books, wrote the canon unto St. Alexis on February 12; St. Demetrius, Metropolitan of Rostov († 1709 AD), wrote the service unto St. Gurius on October 4 [^1789]; Theophan Prokopovych, Archbishop of Novgorod († 1736 AD), probably wrote, by commission of Emperor Peter I, the service in commemoration of the Poltava Victory on June 27 and for the translation of the relics of St. Alexander and the conclusion of peace with the Swedes on August 30 (the former perhaps by Theophylact Lopatinsky, † 1741 AD).

### Western Hymnography

The 9th–14th centuries contributed much also unto Latin hymnography, which revived after currents unfavorable unto it in the 6th–8th centuries (see above, pp. 304, 334) in the person of the Venerable Bede († 735 AD; his *Liber hymnorum* is lost) and, following the Greek, replaced the ancient classical metrical quantity with accentual-syllabic meter (see above, p. 333). The foremost hymnographers were: Paul Warnefrid, surnamed the Deacon, a monk of Monte Cassino (in Italy, † c. 790 AD), who wrote three hymns for the feasts of the Forerunner; Alcuin, Abbot of Tours, court scholar of Charlemagne († 807 AD), who wrote a sequence (*sequentia*, a hymn between the reading of the Epistle and the Gospel at Mass, a refrain unto the Alleluia) unto the Archangel Michael; Paulinus of Aquileia († 802 AD)—author of several hymns unto the Apostles Peter and Paul; Rabanus Maurus, Abbot of Fulda, later Archbishop of Mainz († 856 AD), who wrote hymns unto the Archangels Michael and Raphael, unto All Saints, and probably for Pentecost *(Orig. p. 418)* (attributed unto Emperor Charlemagne); Pope Innocent III († 1216 AD)—a hymn for Pentecost; the celebrated theologian Thomas Aquinas († 1274 AD)—hymns for Pascha and for the feast of Corpus Christi; Jacopone da Todi († 1306 AD), author of the *Stabat Mater*. There likewise entered into liturgical use several hymns of the 15th and even 14th centuries [^1790].

### The Disciplinary Portion of the Typika

From the very emergence of eremitism and monasticism, the divine services came to be regarded merely as one of the constituent parts of spiritual ascetic labor (*podvig*) in general. The entire day of the monk, and indeed of every Christian, ought to be a divine service, and church prayer serves merely as the supreme moment of this latter. Therefore in the primitive monastic rules, such as those of St. Pachomius and St. Sabbas, exceedingly little attention is accorded unto the divine services. Not so from the 9th century. The Rule of St. Theodore the Studite, insofar as it can be reconstructed from his writings, as well as the earliest recording of this rule in the so-called *Hypotyposis*, together with the *Diatyposis* of St. Athanasius of Athos, devote approximately one-fourth of their content unto the divine services. Yet even here it constitutes only a small constituent part of the common ascetic labor. The ktetorial Studite Typika of the 11th and subsequent centuries are already predominantly monuments of a liturgical character, and the disciplinary portion occupies little space within them. Still less space does it occupy in the Jerusalem Typika, at times almost disappearing entirely. Nevertheless, by the very idea of Orthodox liturgical worship and by the historical circumstances of its development, in which monasticism played so vast a role, the liturgical Typikon unto this day deservedly does not dispense with the disciplinary element, however small it may be in the present-day Typikon in comparison with its archetypes of the 4th–6th centuries. This element within it—its disciplinary portion—continued its evolution during the present period in the history of the Typikon. This development was directed both toward the curtailment of the disciplinary portion within the Typikon, and toward the mitigation of its requirements.

### Monastic Discipline under St. Theodore, in the Hypotyposis and Diatyposis

The decline of monasticism and the relaxation of strictness of life within it, by which the iconoclast emperors at times justified their persecution thereof, compelled St. Theodore to attend unto the firm organization of his monastery, which numbered up to 1,000 monks [misprinted 100]. In his admonitions unto the monks he frequently insists upon the undeviating observance of the order established by him, attributing in general great importance unto the will of the superior (*hegumen*) and obedience thereunto:

> 'Let each of you watch with attention how and whither he directs his steps, whether they are in accordance with my humble commandment, with the cenobitic rule, with the requirement of cutting off one's own will' [^1791].

Of the hegumen he demands:

> 'Without extreme necessity do not alter the outline and *(Orig. p. 419)* rule which you have received from our humility in all things' [^1792].

Fidelity unto the monastic rule is maintained under St. Theodore, on the one hand, by a system of monastic hierarchy, and on the other, by a penal code for infractions thereof—epitimias (*penances*). In the monastic administration, after the hegumen, the second rank was occupied by the *deuterarios* (cf. in the Pachomian monasteries, above, p. 211), *ho ta deutera pheron* (*ὁ τὰ δεύτερα φέρων*), *ho deutereuon* (*ὁ δевτερεύων*) [^1793], his closest assistant and deputy—almost identical with the ecclesiarch of subsequent Typika. The third rank was occupied by the oikonomos (*steward*) [^1794]. Next followed the epistemonarchs—who examined offenses and assigned penances; according unto the *Hypotyposis*, 'unto them lesser transgressions are reported, and they apply measures of correction' [^1795]; taxiarchs assigned places unto all in assemblies; according unto the *Hypotyposis*, they reminded the brethren to stand decorously in the choirs; under St. Theodore there were four of them, while the *Hypotyposis* appoints two for the two choirs [^1796]; overseers (*epiteretai / ἐπιτηρηταί*)—supervised the fulfillment of the monastic rule [^1797]; according unto the *Hypotyposis*, two are appointed every evening; 'after the striking of the wooden semantron (*bilo*), they urge the slothful to go to Vespers and Compline, and upon the conclusion of the latter they inspect the hidden places in the monastery, and with due severity disperse those who gather for unseasonable assemblies' [^1798]; the awakener (*aphypnistes / ἀφυпνιστής*), according unto St. Theodore, awakens the brethren for Matins [^1799]; according unto the *Hypotyposis*, during the readings at Matins, quietly making the rounds of the brethren, he awakens those who have fallen asleep [^1800]. There are likewise mentioned in St. Theodore the *kellarites* (*κελαρίτης*)—the cellarer, in charge of provisions, and the *aristetarios* (*ἀριστητάριος*), literally the supervisor of morning collation, the refectorian [^1801].
