56. In Rome, already under Pope Gregory I the Great, there existed a calendar with commemorations for each day of the year, as is evident from the response of this Pope in 598 to the request of Patriarch Eulogius of Alexandria to send him the "Acts of All the Martyrs" collected by Eusebius of Caesarea; replying to the Patriarch that no such collection was found in the Roman archives, the Pope writes: "But we have collected in a single codex the names of almost all the martyrs, with the designation of their passions for all days, and each day celebrate masses in their honor; however, in this volume it is not shown how each one suffered, but only the name, place, and day of passion are designated... We think that you also possess this, most blessed brethren" (Gregory the Great, *Registrum*, VIII, 29). The compiler of the most ancient Roman calendar that has reached us is considered to be Blessed Jerome, on the basis of the testimonies of Cassiodorus († 563): "Read the passions of the martyrs, which you will find, among other places, in the letter of Jerome to Chromatius and Heliodorus" (*De Institutio Divinarum Litterarum*, 32; Migne, *Patrologia Latina*, vol. 70, col. 1147) and of the Venerable Bede († 735 [printed: 753]): "...the martyrology which by name and preface is ascribed to Blessed Jerome, although Jerome was not its author, but its translator, while the author, they say, was Eusebius" (*Liber Retractationis in Actus Apostolorum*, c. 1; Migne, *Patrologia Latina*, vol. 92, col. 997). The correspondence of Blessed Jerome with Bishops Heliodorus and Chromatius is appended to copies of the Hieronymian Calendar; these bishops asked that the calendar (*feriales*) of Eusebius be sent to them from Caesarea for the greater honoring of the martyrs, wherein Bishop Gregory of Cordova had especially distinguished himself, as became known at a certain Council of Milan, who celebrated "on every non-fast day morning masses, and during fasts evening masses, and commemorated at them many names of martyrs"; Blessed Jerome, instead of the calendar of Eusebius, sends the bishops his own, wherein, according to his epistle, he "wrote the festivals for each month and for each day; but since for each day there occurred the names of martyrs from various regions numbering more than 800–900, and for no single day, except January 1, fewer than 500, he writes only the more renowned." The authenticity of this correspondence is doubtful, as the style here is non-Hieronymian; and apart from it, the compilation of the calendar by Blessed Jerome is confirmed by nothing else: neither he himself, nor Gennadius of Marseilles († after 495) in his work *On Illustrious Men* (*De Scriptoribus Ecclesiasticis*), nor Gregory the Great speaks of such a compilation; furthermore, there are commemorations in the calendar later than Blessed Jerome. It was published from a tenth-century manuscript in Migne, *Patrologia Latina*, vol. 39, and by the Bollandists, *Acta Sanctorum*, Novemb., vol. II, 1894, from an eighth-century manuscript (by De Rossi and Duchesne).

57. If in the second century mass slaughter of Christians was expressed by a figure of no more than 40 (Lyons, 177), then in the third century, and especially under Diocletian, the martyrs numbered in the thousands; the magnitude of the figure therefore arouses no doubt, as does also the frequent repetition of certain names (Felix 118 times, Saturninus 87, etc.), as well as the strangeness of other names (Manira, Jtercola, Barbalabia); one must keep in mind the custom of the Romans not to be constrained in giving nicknames to slaves.

### Notes to the Chapter: Divine Worship in the VI–VIII Centuries

58. Archbishop Sergius, *Complete Menology of the East*, I, 58–61.

59. Now in the Paris National Library. Described by Kellner, *Heortologie*, 213–215, after Morin, *Anecdota Maredsolana* [printed: *Amecdota Maredsolana*], Paris, 1893, I. Not mentioned in Archbishop Sergius.

60. Among other menologies in the West in this period, the following are known: 1) that published by Allatius (*De Ecclesiae Occidentalis atque Orientalis Perpetua Consensione* [printed: *De eccl. lccident фейгу lrient. perpetua consensione*], Rome, 1648, p. 1487) from a Breviary [printed: *Braviary*] of the Vatican Library of the eighth century; of the 84 commemorations, half are present among us; certain commemorations fall on the same dates as among us, and not as at present among Roman Catholics; the Transfiguration and the Entry [of the Theotokos into the Temple] are absent; not all Apostles are included; from March 12 to April 14 there are no saints. 2) The Calendar in the Sacramentary ascribed to Gregory the Great, of the seventh–eighth century; similar to the preceding, but certain commemorations are lacking and certain new ones appear; all Apostles are present. 3) The Gallican: the latest commemoration is that of St. Gregory the Great († 604); commemorations are for all days, but August 16–December is defective. 4) That of Protasius [printed: *Protisius*], Bishop of Besançon († 625); similar to the Sacramentary of Gregory; in March [printed: *in Marta*] there are only 5 commemorations; by another hand later commemorations have been entered, for example of Charlemagne [Karl the Great].—In addition, there appeared a whole series of abridgments of the Hieronymian Menology. Such an abridgment was first of all the martyrology of Bede († 735), the renowned English monk-writer, "who sought diligently to note by what manner of martyrdom and under which judge the martyrs overcame the world," and for this reason left for each day from the Hieronymian Martyrology one or two saints, and certain days without commemorations at all. However, the martyrology of Bede has reached us only in a form augmented circa 830 by Florus Drepanius, a canon of the diocese of Lyons; in this latter form, commemorations likewise do not occur on all days. This last martyrology was reworked (commemorations rearranged) and slightly augmented: in the diocese of Trier by Wandalbert circa 848; in Mainz by Archbishop Rabanus Maurus in the middle of the ninth century (commemorations for all days); in Lyons circa 858 by Ado, subsequently Archbishop of Vienne (containing very extensive narratives concerning the saints, beginning December 25); by Usuard, a Benedictine near Paris circa 858 [printed: 8585]; and by Notker in Switzerland circa 894 (Archbishop Sergius, *Complete Menology of the East*, I, 62–73).

The kontakia and ikoi for the Annunciation, which now constitute the Akathist to the Mother of God, but which in ancient menaia (for example, Moscow Synodal Typography, fourteenth century, no. 68) were placed under March 25 after Ode 6 of the canon, are ascribed to George Pisida as the author of the account of that very war with the Avars, upon whose auspicious conclusion "the people began annually to chant a thanksgiving hymn, naming the day itself the Akathist" (*Synaxarion of the Saturday of the Akathist*, Triodion). That the akathist kontakia and ikoi could have been originally composed for the Annunciation and subsequently adapted to the commemoration of the war is evident, apart from their content, from the textual variants in the First Kontakion: "Thy servants," "Thy servant," "city." Archimandrite Amphilochius, *The Kondakarion in Greek Originals of the XII–XIII Centuries*, Moscow, 1879, 15 [printed: *Kodakarion*].

82. Metrical poetic verse in Greek church hymnody was discovered quite recently by Cardinal Pitra, *Hymnographie de l'Église grecque* [printed: *Об hymnographie de l'églisr grecque*], Rome, 1867 (the book is reviewed by A. Vasiliev, "On Greek Ecclesiastical Hymns," in *Vizantiyskiy Vremennik*, St. Petersburg, 1896, III, 582 ff.). Prior to this, it was thought that Greek church hymnody followed the rhythm of biblical poetry, concerning whose nature scholars still dispute, though the majority reduce it to parallelism of members (*parallelismus membrorum*). Nevertheless, seventeenth-century scholars [printed: *учение*, erratum for *ученые*] also vaguely presaged Pitra's discovery. Thus Baronius observed that in manuscripts of canons there is a punctuation that sometimes runs counter to the sense and serves, apparently, to preserve a certain meter (Baronius, *Annales Ecclesiastici*, Mainz, 1601 [printed: 1501], p. 1054). S. Vagnereck (*Pietas Mariana*, Munich, 1647, p. 32) remarks that when reading the Menaia he seemed to hear the voice of an unknown muse.

85. The difference here is introduced by organs. But in Roman Catholic worship they appeared very late. Although the *Liber Pontificalis* attributes to Pope Vitalian († 671) the introduction of the organ into Italian churches, and a number of historians repeat the account of the dispatch of an organ by Constantine Copronymus to Pepin in 757 AD and by Emperor Michael I to Charlemagne, yet even in the ninth–twelfth centuries the organ encountered opponents in the West: among them were the renowned liturgist Amalarius (ninth century), the Scottish abbot Aelred [Ealred] (twelfth century), the most celebrated theologian Thomas Aquinas, and later Erasmus (Luft, *Liturgik*, II, 258; Binterim, *Die vorzüglichsten Denkwürdigkeiten*, IV, 1, 55; Archbishop Philaret, *Historical Review of Hymnographers*, 264).

### Notes to the Chapter: The Liturgical Typikon from the Appearance of Its Complete Manuscripts

1. [Absent]

2. Published for the first time in full by Prof. A. A. Dmitrievsky according to a tenth-century manuscript of the Patmos Library, no. 266, in *Description of Liturgical Manuscripts*, I, *Τυπικά*, Kyiv, 1890, pp. 1–153. Besides this manuscript of the Sophia Typikon, two others are known at present: in the Jerusalem Patriarchal Library, no. 40, tenth–eleventh century (reported by Papadopoulos-Kerameus in *Ἰεροσολυμιτικὴ Βιβλιοθήκη*, St. Petersburg, 1897, 80), and in the Dresden Royal Library, no. 140 [printed: *no. 104*] (described in detail for the first time by A. Dmitrievsky, *The Most Ancient Patriarchal Typika of the Holy Sepulchre of Jerusalem and of the Great Church of Constantinople*, Kyiv, 1907, 214 ff.). The most ancient is the Patmos redaction; the latest commemorations in it are Ignatius, Archbishop of Constantinople († 877), and the consecration of the Church of All Saints in Boule, built by Leo VI in memory of his consort Theophano († 894) during her lifetime; there is "the commemoration of the Martyr Bacchus, who suffered in our days under Irene (797–802) and Constantine (VI, 780–797)"; the feast of the Image Not Made by Hands on August 16, instituted in 944, is absent. The Jerusalem manuscript was copied by command of Constantine VII Porphyrogenitus (912–959 [printed: 953]): the latest commemoration is Tryphon, Patriarch of Constantinople († 933). In the Dresden manuscript the Image Not Made by Hands is already present, as is also on January 25 the translation of the relics of Gregory the Theologian from Arianzus to Constantinople, which occurred in 950, but the commemoration of the Three Hierarchs on January 30, instituted in 1084, is absent.

3. St. Symeon of Thessalonica, *On Divine Prayer*, ch. 345; Migne, *Patrologia Graeca*, vol. 155, col. 624.

4. The Typikon of St. Sophia is placed not only in connection with, but also in genetic dependence upon the Jerusalem Typikon of the Holy Sepulchre (the Church of the Resurrection). The grounds for this are the agreement of later (ninth–tenth century) redactions of the two in certain minor particulars (for example, the distribution of the so-called *rouga*—stipends, gifts—by the Patriarch on great feasts, the chanting of certain hymns by cantors upon the ambo and others by monastics, *spoudaioi*, etc.) and in a few rites: both have the trithekte and the pannychis (A. Dmitrievsky, *The Most Ancient Patriarchal Typika*, 144, 147, 206, 208, 298). But the structure of the daily cycle according to each Typikon is different: in the Jerusalem Typikon of the ninth century, at least, this structure is much closer to our present order than to the contemporary Constantinopolitan order, and of earlier divine worship in either church we know nothing (not counting the description of Silvia).

The "Order" (*Ordo*) of the Athonite St. Andrew Skete fifteenth-century manuscript and the musical manuscript *Παπαδικὴ τέχνη* [printed: *Паладикὴ τέχνη*] of the fourteenth century in the library of Vatopedi Monastery, no. 297 (931), describe more fully the entrance, the chanting of the Doxology, and the reading of the Gospel. The cantors chant **"Most blessed art thou"** (*Preblagoslovenna jesi*) only up to the words **"Blessed is Christ our God."** At the entrance the domestikos intones in a higher voice these words of the Theotokion (musical MS); at the entrance, between the preceding candle-bearers, walks a reader in a (short) phelonion bearing a large cross (mentioned above); upon the entry of the priests into the sanctuary, he ascends two steps of the ambo and here intones melodically the beginning of the Doxology: **"Glory to God in the highest"** (*Slava v vyshnikh Bogu*) (*Ordo*). "And the domestikos begins the sweet-sounding hymn (*ᾀσματικὸν ὕμνον*), that is, the Doxology, while the priests recite the remainder. (After the Doxology) the domestikos: **"Having risen from the tomb and burst the bonds..."** and the priests speak the remainder. Then the domestikos: **"Glory to the Father and to the Son..."** and again the priests: **"Having risen from the tomb"**; the domestikos in a high voice: **"Risen. A psalm of David"**; and immediately the reader says: **"Arise, O Lord"** (musical MS). According to the *Ordo*, the reader after the Great Doxology "chants melodically: 'A Psalm of David' and the remaining verses. The reader departs, and the domestikos or laosynaktis ascends to the third step of the ambo and chants the prokeimenon with the remaining readers; the domestikos also chants the initial melodic model (*ἤχημα*) at the cadences." The verses to the prokeimenon are indicated by the musical MS: **"I will confess Thee, O Lord..."**; **"I will be glad..."**; and then the rubric: "*Θεσσαλονικαῖον* (according to the Thessalonian order?): 'O Lord my God, let Thy hand be lifted up'; *ἡ μεγάλη δοχή* (the great feast, the banquet of love): 'Arise, O Lord God, let Thy hand be lifted up, forget not Thy poor unto the end.'" Further according to the *Ordo*, the priest in full priestly vestments carries the Gospel preceded by readers with two candlesticks and two deacons, ascends the ambo, and sits with the deacons until the conclusion of the prokeimenon, after which there is chanted **"Prolong the holy reign of our rulers"** [printed: *царство из*, error for *царство их*] and *Τὸν δεσπότην*; at these hymns the clergy stand; after the reading of the Gospel upon the ambo by the priest, it is presented by the deacon for kissing to the hierarch and by him is carried into the sanctuary preceded by the reader with the cross and accompanied by the priest (Dmitrievsky, *Τυπικά*, 164).

33. Euchologion of the Paris National Library of the year 1027, no. 213, fol. 81v; Dmitrievsky, *Εὐχολόγια*, 1110, *Τυπικά*, 152.—Similar litai (*litaniae*) existed and exist in the Western Church. Such are the *litania major* on April 25 on the feast of the Apostle Mark, and the *litania minor* or *rogationes* (supplications) on the three days before the Ascension. The designations "greater" and "lesser" do not correspond to the comparative solemnity of these litanies, but are explained historically: the former was instituted earlier (probably by Pope Liberius in the fourth century) in place of the very solemn pagan procession *ambarvale* (from *arva*, field—a procession into the fields, as distinguished from the *amburbale*, a city procession) to propitiate the goddess Robigo, upon whom depended the rust (*robigo*) on grain crops (for which reason April 25 was called the *Robigalia*); Pope Gregory the Great regulated the Christian litany that replaced this pagan procession, directing seven distinct corporations of Rome (clergy, men, monks, handmaids, women, widows, and the poor with children) to set forth in litany from different churches (hence the name *litania septiformis*; *Epistle* II, 2). The *litania minor* was first instituted circa 470 by Bishop Mamertus of Vienne on account of an earthquake and other calamities, was enacted for Gaul by the Council of Orléans in 511 (canon 27), received wide dissemination in the sixth century, but in Rome was adopted only under Pope Leo III (795–816). On the days of these litanies, especially the second, services were especially prolonged; in the ninth century in certain churches heads were sprinkled with blessed ashes, sprinkled with holy water (as even now according to the Ambrosian/Milanese rite), and all walked barefoot (according to canon 33 of the Council of Mainz [*Concilium Moguntinum*], 813). A series of rites for the lesser litany has been preserved: according to them, after a series of antiphons and psalms there was a supplication very similar to our Litany of Fervent Supplication **"Let us all say"** (*Rtsem vsi*) (indeed it begins: *Dicamus omnes, Domine miserere*); after a series of other antiphons, resembling in general content our penitential troparia, there was the litany in the proper sense, called *statio* (station, as it was performed at the stations of the procession) or *oratio* (from the frequent chanting of *ora*—"pray"), consisting of a long series of petitions (sometimes more than 100) addressed for the most part in order to all the most renowned saints and performed antiphonally (by clergy and choir), for example: *Sancta Maria—ora pro nobis* [printed: *pra pro nobis*], *Sancte Michael—ora*, *Sancte Gabriel—ora* or *intercede* (intercede); for the more venerated and intimate saints "pray for us," and for the remainder simply "pray" (Martène, *De Antiquis Ecclesiae Ritibus*, II, 514 sq.; Kellner, *Heortologie*, 127).

34. Preserved in a manuscript of the year 1122 in the Jerusalem Patriarchal Library. It may be assigned to the tenth century, because in the litany there is the name of Patriarch Nicholas (857–887 with interruption), and the topography of the holy places corresponds to their state following the restoration after the Persian conquest under Patriarch Modestus (610–637) down to the destruction under Caliph Al-Hakim in 1010. Published in full by A. Papadopoulos-Kerameus, *Ἀνάλεκта Ἱεροσολυμιτικῆς Σταχυολογίας*, St. Petersburg, 1894, II; in abridgment (the opening words of hymns) with translation and extensive notes by A. Dmitrievsky, *Divine Worship of Passion and Paschal Weeks in Holy Jerusalem in the IX–X Centuries*, Kazan [printed: *Koz.*], 1894 (here also the chronology of the monument is established, p. XIII).

35. A courtier by origin, having embraced monasticism together with his parents—persons of wealth—and his wife at the onset of Iconoclasm, Venerable Theodore labored greatly for the defense of the Church and the Faith against the encroachments of the heretical emperors, for which he endured imprisonment and exile. He was also a gifted hymnographer.

40. The monument represents, as stated in the preface, a record of "the tradition which we received from our great father and confessor Theodore, and not we alone, but also many of the best monasteries have chosen." The record was made by one of the monks no later than the middle of the ninth century, since this record served as the foundation for the *Diatyposis* of Venerable Athanasius of Athos and the *Typikon* of Patriarch Alexis (see concerning them below). Published from a very ancient manuscript by Cardinal Mai, *Nova Patrum Bibliotheca*, Rome, 1849, vol. V, whence it was reprinted in Migne, *Patrologia Graeca*, vol. 99; according to a later manuscript with significant variants of Vatopedi Monastery, no. 322 (956), thirteenth–fourteenth century, published by Prof. Dmitrievsky, *Description of Liturgical Manuscripts*, I: *Τυπικά*; Russian translation from the first edition in E. Golubinsky, *History of the Russian Church*, I, 2, 671.

41. Concerning the origin of monasticism on Athos there is no reliable information; Athonite traditions trace the appearance of monasteries here back to pagan times (the Emperor Caracalla, 211–217 [printed: 219]) or at least to the flourishing of Egyptian-Palestinian asceticism; the Arab devastations of Athos circa 670 and then circa 830 do not permit anything reliable to be affirmed concerning Athos prior to the ninth century, although the foundation of almost all present-day Athonite monasteries ascends to this most ancient period. The first historically known Athonite solitary ("hesychast") was Venerable Peter (who lived on Athos 681–734); in the era of Iconoclasm many monks sought refuge here; Venerable Euthymius (circa 840) restored monasticism on Athos after the second Arab devastation; his disciples established the first cenobium on Athos—Vatopedi; and John Kolobos built the first stone monastery on the isthmus at Ierissos and obtained from Emperor Basil the Macedonian in 872 a chrysobull by which Athos was granted into the exclusive possession of monks. But at this point enmity began between cenobites and anchorites; the latter separated and established their own administration in Karyes (the "Protaton") with a protos at its head. After a new Saracen devastation circa the middle of the tenth century, monasticism on Athos was restored by Venerable Athanasius, who founded the Great Lavra on Athos through the donations of his friend, Emperor Nicephorus Phocas. Upon the complaint of the anchorites concerning the dominance of cenobitic life—foreign to ancient Athos—Emperor John Tzimiskes by the typikon (*τυπικόν* or *τράγος*) of 971 recognized equal rights for both modes of ascetic life on Athos. To this period belong the first authentic testimonies concerning the majority of present-day Athonite monasteries, such as Iviron (founded by Georgians), Docheiariou or Daphne, Panteleimon or Thessalonian, Esphigmenou (founded by inhabitants of the Thessalian village of Sphigi), Hilandar (named after the family of the ktetor), Zographou, founded by the Greek George the Iconographer (in Greek *ζωγράφος*), Koutloumousiou (after the surname of the ktetor), Xiropotamou [printed: *Skiropotamos*] ("dry torrent"), Dionysiou, founded by Alexios Komnenos [printed: *1118*, recte Alexios III Komnenos] at the request of Dionysius who labored there. Emperor Constantine Monomakhos by the Typikon of 1046 prohibited Athos from commercial intercourse with the laity. From this time onward the present strict order was established on Athos (the unconditional exclusion of women). Alexios I Komnenos in 1090 recognized Athos as independent of the Metropolitan of Thessalonica and subordinated it solely to its own protos. In the eleventh century Bulgarian monks appeared on Athos, settling the Zographou Monastery; in the twelfth century Serbian monks (headed by Prince Stephen-Symeon Nemanja [printed: *Vimeon*] and his son Venerable Sava), to whom Hilandar was granted; and Russians, to whom there was given at first the Monastery of Xylourgou, and in 1169 also St. Panteleimon ("Rossikon"). The majority of Athonite monasteries are dedicated to the Most Holy Theotokos [printed: *прп. Богородице*]; there are churches of the Forerunner, Chrysostom, Nicholas. There was on Athos (in the tenth century) also a Latin monastery with the Rule of St. Benedict—Karakallou (after the surname of the ktetor) [or the Amalfitans]. (Bishop Porphyrius [Uspensky], *History of Athos*, Kyiv, 1876, *passim*; I. Sokolov, *The State of Monasticism in the Byzantine Church from the Middle of the IX Century to the Beginning of the XIII Century*, Kazan, 1894, pp. 214 ff.).

42. The *Diatyposis* of St. Athanasius was published by Ph. Meyer, *Die Haupturkunden für die Geschichte der Athosklöster*, Leipzig, 1894, pp. 17 ff., and by A. Dmitrievsky, *Description of Liturgical Manuscripts*, I: *Τυπικά*, 238, from sixteenth-century manuscripts (Athos-Iviron Library, no. 754) and even nineteenth-century ones, which nevertheless represent copies from eleventh-century codices—perhaps even from the autographs of Venerable Athanasius (preserved in the skeuophylakion of the Lavra of St. Athanasius and shown to no one), with which they were collated in Meyer's edition (Dmitrievsky, *ibid.*, XXXIII).

43. The first, most ancient manuscript is preserved in the Sinai Library in a separate quire torn from a Gospel lectionary, lacking the beginning (the Triodion begins from Ascension) and the end (terminating on August 6); the second, in that same library attached to Gospel MS no. 150, is complete, but only for the most important days. The difference in the Synaxarion from the Typikon of the Great Church, besides the order (the Triodion comes first): Patriarchal celebrating is not presupposed; commemorations of the consecration of churches and of earthquakes (except October 26) are absent. It must have been used in a diocese subject to the Patriarch of Constantinople. Judging by the mention of the Church of Elijah, whither a litany was made on the Second Sunday after Pascha (according to the Constantinopolitan Typikon on that day the litany went to Chalkoprateia), one might think that it was used on Sinai, where there was a Church of Elijah. But it is more probable that the Canonarion is of South Italian or Sicilian provenance, because there are Western and Eastern commemorations placed on the dates of Western calendars (May 8, Archangels Michael and Gabriel—"the apparition on Mount Gargano"). In the older manuscript the latest commemoration is Theodore the Studite; in the later, Paul the New († 784) (Archbishop Sergius, *Complete Menology of the East*, I, 145). Published in Russian translation by Archimandrite Antonin, *The Ancient Canonarion of the Sinai Library*, Kyiv, 1874; in the original Greek by A. Dmitrievsky, *Description of Liturgical Manuscripts*, I: *Τυπικά*, 172.

44. The Chronicle states sub anno 1051 that Venerable Theodosius, upon the multiplication of the brethren in his monastery, "began to seek a monastic rule; and there was found then Michael, a monk of the Studite Monastery, who had come from the Greeks with Metropolitan George; and he began to seek from him the rule of the Studite monks; and having found it from him, he copied it out, and established in his monastery how to chant the monastic chants, and how to make bows, and to read the readings, and the standing in church and the whole ecclesiastical order, the seating at the refectory, and what to eat on which days, all according to the ordinance"; and from the Caves Monastery "all monasteries received the rule" (*Chronicle according to the Laurentian Manuscript*, published by the Archaeographic Commission, St. Petersburg, 1872, p. 156). But according to the *Life of Venerable Theodosius* composed by Nestor, Theodosius "sent one of the brethren to the city of Constantine unto Ephrem the Eunuch, that he might copy out and send him the entire rule of the Studite Monastery," which took place circa 1062 (*Life*, ed. Bodyansky in *Readings of the Imperial Society of Russian History and Antiquities*, 1858, fol. 111v). These conflicting accounts are reconciled by the supposition that the monk Michael possessed an incomplete copy of the rule, perhaps the *Hypotyposis*, for which reason ten years later Venerable Theodosius felt the need for the complete ("entire") rule.—Prior to the appearance of the Studite Typikon and afterward, until the Tatar invasion, in cathedral and parish churches, it is thought, people in Russia were guided by the Typikon of the Great Church of Constantinople. The Council of Vladimir in 1274 and that of Constantinople in 1276 establish the existence in the Russian Church of certain customs of the Great Church, such as the performance of the proskomedia ("proskomisanie") by a deacon (apparently such may have been the most ancient custom generally), the Liturgy of the Presanctified Gifts on Cheese-fare Wednesday and Friday and on Great Friday, the reading of the Gospel by the hierarch four times a year (the first Passion Gospel, at the Paschal Liturgy and Vespers, and at the Litiya on September 1), the Exaltation of the Cross with features of the Great Church: some of these customs are confirmed by councils, while others are abolished (A. Pavlov, *Russian Historical Library*, St. Petersburg, 1880, VI, nos. 6, 12), yet in places all were maintained down to the fifteenth and even seventeenth centuries, especially in the Novgorod territory, which occupied the entire north of Russia. In addition, in relatively late manuscripts of the fourteenth–fifteenth centuries there has survived the translation of whole rites of the Great Church into Church Slavonic, for example, the Rite of Washing the Altar Table on Great Thursday, the Rite of the New Year on September 1, and the litany according to the Typikon of the Great Church. The same is attested by Church Slavonic manuscripts of asmatika (refrains to the psalms in the Sung Office, for example, *Tin ikoumenin* = **"The universe"** [Greek: *Τὴν οἰκουμένην*]), the expression in ancient typika "chanting at the trithekte" indicating the existence of this office, and finally even a fragment of the Typikon of the Great Church in the Slavonic translation of Archbishop Clement of Novgorod († 1299) in the Moscow Khludov Library (A. Popov, *Supplement to the Description of Manuscripts of the Khludov Library*, Moscow, 1875, p. 117), etc. See concerning this in more detail and with citations in the work now in press by Archpriest M. Lisitsyn [printed: *A. Lisitsyn*], *The Original Slavonic-Russian Typikon*, St. Petersburg, 1910, where the author also points out another fragment of the Slavonic translation of the Typikon of the Great Church in Popov's description, p. 117, designated a Triodion.

45. The most ancient manuscripts of the Studite-Alexis Typikon: 1) in the manuscript of the Moscow Synodal Typography Library, no. 285/142/1206, eleventh–twelfth century, lacking the beginning (Meat-fare Sunday) and the end, containing only the Triodion Typikon, and instead of a Menology (which may, however, have been torn away), a Kondakarion, with musical notation in places, for the entire year; 2) almost whole (from the Sunday of the Prodigal Son) and complete (with the entire Menology and an extensive disciplinary section) in the manuscript of the Moscow Synodal Library, no. 330/380, twelfth–thirteenth century, of a more extensive redaction than the first; closer to the Typikon of the Great Church than the first (commemorations of the Sundays of Great Lent), consequently no less ancient, although it has more commemorations (by 12); then 3) former Sophia-Novgorod Library (now preserved in the St. Petersburg Theological Academy), no. 1136, probably of the thirteenth century—only the Triodion from ...Vespers of Meat-fare [Sunday] and the Menology through January 17; 4) Moscow Synodal Typography Library, no. 144/1236; 5) Moscow Synodal Library, no. 333/381, written in 1398 AD without the disciplinary section; 6) no. 905/382 of the fifteenth century. All these manuscripts, beginning with no. 330, are almost literally identical with one another, clearly copied from a single archetype, but the later ones occasionally present slight alterations of specifically Studite practice (for example, there is no mention of the fasting Liturgy on all days of the Fast; the commemoration of St. Theodore on November 11 is observed with less solemnity; he is spoken of as "father", and not "our father"). There are also several fragments of the Studite-Alexis Typikon (for example in a miscellany of the former Kirillo-Belozersky Library [in the St. Petersburg Theological Academy], no. 275, etc.).

46. The Grottaferrata Monastery and its Typikon long defended their independence from their mighty neighbor. Friends could not persuade its first hegumen, Nilus, even to visit Rome and its holy places. Hegumen Bartholomew, although in friendly relations with Popes John XIX and Benedict IX and even participating in the Lateran Council of 1044 AD, nevertheless the Menaia copied under him strictly observe Eastern traditions and diverge from the later Cryptoferratan Typikon. Only Hegumen Blasius is styled by Pope Martin IV as his vassal; in view of such new relations with Rome, an updating (*ἀνακαινίσθη*) of the Cryptoferratan Typikon was undertaken by this hegumen; it is immediately evident in what this consisted: on November 1 it is proposed to celebrate All Saints; on great feasts a Latin litany is prescribed, and at the Liturgy a "combined Greek and Latin order"; during Great Lent a daily Presanctified Liturgy is recommended in view of the custom of the Roman Church to celebrate a full Liturgy daily; on the Exaltation [of the Holy Cross] and during the Nativity Fast [Philip Fast] cheese and eggs are permitted; in the ectenias the Pope is commemorated with the title "our most honorable and most holy father *ὁ δεῖνα*" [N.], Latin terminology is employed, and the like. The Typikon has survived in a manuscript contemporary with Blasius bearing the date 1200 AD in the monastery library, no. A. II. 7. Described by Th. Toscani, *Ad Typica Graecorum*, Rome, 1864; supplementary to this description in Dmitrievsky, *Τυπικὰ*, pp. 899 ff.

D. 61 of the thirteenth century; 4) of the Laurentian Library in Florence, no. 15 of 1336 AD; 5) of the Barberini Library, no. III, 102 (236) of 1583 AD, displaying literal agreement (excluding the end) with the Turin manuscript.

48. The primary manuscript: 1) of the Vatican Library, no. 1877, prepared for this monastery in 1292 AD; close to it are: 2) the manuscript of the Vienna Imperial Library, no. 1126/326/144 of the thirteenth century; 3) of the Barberini Library, no. 67, written in 1552 AD for the cathedral of the city of Bova in Calabria; 4) of the Vatican Library, no. 1609 of the sixteenth century, presented in 1585 AD to Pope Sixtus V by the chorepiscopus of Rhodes (in the form of a separate appendix there is a Latin menology here). Preserved in a manuscript of the Athens University Library, no. 788 of the twelfth century, whence it was first published by Dmitrievsky, *Description of Liturgical Manuscripts*, I: *Τυπικὰ*, pp. 256–656.—From the same era several more ktetorial typika have come down to us, but of disciplinary content only, referring for liturgical practice to the typika listed above or to the Studite rule generally, or finally to the common-use typikon ("synaxarion"), without designating it specifically. Such are: the Typikon of 1130 AD of the Pantokrator Monastery in Constantinople (in honor of the Almighty), founded by Emperor John Komnenos (in an eighteenth-century manuscript of the Halki School in Constantinople, no. 85), prescribing divine worship "according to the model of the great church in the palace", and occasionally referring also to the "office of the Hagiopolite" (as the title shows—Jerusalemite; according to Dmitrievsky, *Τυπικὰ*, p. LXIV—the "court typikon"); the Typikon of the suburban Constantinopolitan Monastery of St. Mamas of 1159 AD, the prologue of which is signed by several hegumens, among others by the Studite hegumen, and which indicates that divine worship is to be guided by the Evergetis Typikon "as already accepted and established by custom" (ch. 8, etc.; original manuscript in the Paris National Library); the Typikon of the Asia Minor Monastery of the Theotokos *τῶν Ἡλίου Βωμῶν ἤτοι Ἐλεгмῶν* ("of the Altars of the Sun, that is, of Convictions") of 1162 AD, referring to the Studite Synaxarion (ch. 8, etc.; original in the Patmos Library); all published by Dmitrievsky, *Τυπικὰ*, pp. 656–715.

90. A native of Constantinople, Nikon was compelled to remove from the Rhaithu Monastery, where he had embraced monasticism, on account of the discontent of the brethren, to the Black Mountain Monastery; following the devastation of the latter, first by the Turks in 1085 AD and then by the Crusaders in 1098 AD, he returned to Rhaithu. He is known as the author of the *Pandects* ("Collection"), a work of canonical content, and of the *Taktikon* ("Rule"), of liturgical and monastic-disciplinary character, as well as of other writings. His works in Greek have not yet been published (preserved in manuscripts of the Sinai Library), with the exception of excerpts (in Pitra, etc.); the *Pandects* and the *Taktikon* enjoyed great veneration in ancient Russia and provided much material for the *Kormchaya Kniga*. They were printed in Church Slavonic in Ostrog in 1645 AD, in Pochaiv in 1795 AD, and in Moscow at the Edinoverie Typography in 1889 AD. Mansvetov, *The Ecclesiastical Typikon*, pp. 187 ff.; Golubinsky, *History of the Russian Church*, I, 1, p. 748.

102. The most ancient representative of the Holy Mountain Typikon after the *Diatyposis* of St. Athanasius (excerpts from which are repeatedly cited also by Nikon of the Black Mountain), still in its purely Studite form, may be recognized in the Georgian *Great Synaxarion*, translated for the Iviron Lavra by its decan (deputy hegumen, *καθηγούμενος*) George the Hagiorite [Mtatsmindeli] in 1038–1042 AD, which was employed, as is evident from its contents, also in other Athonite monasteries and, presumably, in the Lavra of St. Athanasius, upon which Iviron was dependent; this Synaxarion is close to the *Hypotyposis*, the *Diatyposis*, and the excerpts from the Holy Mountain Typikon in Nikon (who likewise calls this rule a Synaxarion); it is a ktetorial typikon of Studite type (no all-night vigils, the number of kathismata is the same, festal antiphons at Matins), but with local peculiarities (fasting regimen, Georgian commemorations). (The Synaxarion in Russian translation from manuscripts contemporary with St. George—Tiflis Ecclesiastical Museum, nos. 193 and 222—is published in Archpriest Kekelidze, *Liturgical Georgian Monuments*, pp. 228–272). From the thirteenth century onward complete Jerusalem typika also appear on Athos. The Typikon given by St. Sava of Serbia († 1237 AD) to Hilandar Monastery on Athos refers for divine worship to a certain "Synaxarion"—perhaps the one whose fourteenth-century manuscript is now in the Hilandar Library (no. 66/70)—of purely Jerusalem type (Dmitrievsky, "The Most Ancient Hilandar Synaxarion according to the Jerusalem Typikon", *Works of the Kyiv Theological Academy*, 1905, II, p. 473), just as it itself represents a mixture of Jerusalem observances (vigils) with local ones (fasting regimen). (The Hilandar Typikon from a manuscript contemporary with Sava was published by Bishop Demetrius, *The Hilandar Typikon*, Belgrade, 1898). Even after the introduction of the Jerusalem Typikon in the Athonite monasteries, earlier and local observances continued to be maintained, for which reason this introduction did not destroy the distinct Holy Mountain Typikon, but merely imparted to it a Jerusalem coloring, as is evident already from the very titles of its surviving manuscripts (none of which has been published). Thus the Greek manuscript of the Vatican Library, *cod. Palat.* no. 101 of 1474 AD, is titled "Typikon of the Lavra of St. Sabas and of the Lavra of St. Athanasius the Athonite"; of that same library, no. 38 of 1423 AD: "Typikon of the Holy and Great Monastery of St. Athanasius on Mount Athos"; in the Typikon of 1336 AD of the Florentine Laurentian Library, no. 15, there are "chapters of the most renowned ecclesiastical ordering of the Holy Mountain". The most important Athonite monasteries now possess written records of their typikon (of Jerusalem type); thus the Lavra of St. Athanasius in a fifteenth–sixteenth century manuscript, the Pantokrator Monastery in a fifteenth-century manuscript. The observances of the Dionysiou Monastery were recorded in 1624 AD by its hieromonk Ignatius, and this record enjoyed great authority—copies of it exist in many Athonite monasteries; thus for St. Panteleimon Monastery a revised copy was made (an eighteenth-century manuscript exists) from the Dionysiou Typikon under the title: "Exact Typikon of the Ecclesiastical Office, Compiled from St. Sabas and Other Diverse [Fathers]"; here there are references, besides the Typikon of Athanasius, to the Athonite typika of the "right choir", "left choir", and the "Great Typikon of the Adrianopolitan". From this same Dionysiou Typikon a copy was made in 1875 AD for Iviron Monastery under the title: "Abridged Typikon Combined with the Local [Customs]" (all remain unpublished and unexamined). But even down to the present day, as always, the Holy Mountain follows in divine worship unwritten traditions rather; consequently the services here are guided not so much by the Typikon as by the typikaris (the most honorable person in the monastery), and in difficult cases—by a council of typikarioi (Dmitrievsky, A., "The Holy Mountain [Athonite] Typikon", *Guide for Village Pastors*, 1897, nos. 1, 3, 4, 5).

The multiple **"Lord, have mercy"** was originally, apparently, repeated 3, then 12 times—a trace of which remains at present at the conclusion of fasting services and in Typika of the Studite redaction; later it could be increased to 30, and then to 40 times (in non-Chalcedonian Eastern churches even to 60 and 100; so among the Armenians, see above, p. 333); a trace of all these types of practice is provided by the Horologion of the Moscow Synodal Typography Library, no. 77/150/1223 of the fifteenth century, where at the First Hour **"Lord, have mercy"** is appointed 30 times, at the Third 40, and at the Ninth 12 times (fols. 20 and 38); in Studite typika for ordinary hours 40 times, and for the Royal Hours 30 times (Typikon of the Moscow Synodal Typography Library, no. 185/142/1206, fols. 20v and 7v); occasionally such a distinction is made: in Great Lent 50 times, in the Nativity and Apostles' Fasts 40 times, on ordinary days 30 times (Horologion of the Imperial Public Library, Q I no. 67 of the fifteenth–sixteenth century, fol. 154v); at the Mesoria in the majority of manuscripts 30 times (see below). Distinctive in the fourteenth-century Ethiopic Horologion—41 or 51 times (Turaev, *Horologion of the Ethiopian Church*, pp. 39, 49, etc.).

144. On the Fridays of all fasts according to this Typikon, in place of Compline a special office was appointed: *ἡ πρεσβεία* (intercession, supplication; cf. the *preces* in Western offices), in two parts: the first, after the exclamation "Blessed is the Kingdom" and the Great Ectenia, consisted of three pairs of Theotokia (with an intercalary **"Glory... both now..."** pronounced by the deacon in each pair), separated by Little Ectenias; the second part represented our present Molēben, consisting of Psalm 112 [LXX], **"God is the Lord"**, the troparion, the canon to the Mother of God with the customary inter-ode refrains, after which the Trisagion, after the **"Our Father"** the troparion, and the Ectenia (of Fervent Supplication). The service was performed in white vestments. Dmitrievsky, *Τυπικὰ*, pp. 874–877.

182. Such are, for example, appended to the Gospel of the Jerusalem Library of the ninth century; appended to the Apostolos of the St. Petersburg Imperial Public Library, no. 57 of the ninth–tenth century; appended to the Gospel of the Florentine Laurentian Library of the tenth century; a manuscript of the Odessa Museum of the tenth century; of the Museum of the Kyiv Theological Academy, no. 708 of the tenth century (from the Nizhyn church); of the Paris Coislin Library, no. 205 of the tenth–eleventh century. All of them, like the Constantinopolitan of the eighth century, have commemorations not for all days of the year, and contain few venerables (the Odessa MS); among them especially ancient—perhaps from a seventh–eighth century archetype—is the Coislin: the Entry [of the Theotokos into the Temple], the Synaxis of the Theotokos on December 26, the Veneration of the Chains [of the Apostle Peter], St. Mark, Venerable Jeremiah, Martyr Procopius, and others are absent.

183. Thus for all days commemorations are present in the aforementioned Jerusalem MS of the tenth century; appended to the Gallipoli Gospel in the Paris National Library, no. 79 of the tenth century; Moscow Synodal Library, no. 43 of 1055 AD; the Cryptoferratan Monastery MS termed the "Eklogadion" of the eleventh century. But the majority of eleventh-century menologies, and some of the twelfth, even thirteenth centuries, still do not contain commemorations for all days of the year—among others, for example, the Menology appended to the renowned Ostromir Gospel of the eleventh century; appended to the Greek New Testament of the Florentine Laurentian Library, no. 27 of the twelfth century; appended to the Slavonic Apostolos of the Slepče Monastery (near Prilep) of the twelfth century; appended to the Glagolitic Gospel of the Zographou Monastery of the twelfth–thirteenth century; appended to the Slavonic Gospel of the Reims Library of the thirteenth century.

212. In the most ancient Psalters (for example, one from the library of the Xeropotamou Monastery on Athos), the "refrains" to the selected psalms—inscribed here as "the creation of Kyr Philotheus" and replacing the present-day megalynaria (*velichaniya*)—have the following form: for the Nativity of the Most Holy Theotokos, the Entry [into the Temple], and the Annunciation: **"Rejoice, O Virgin Mary, full of grace, the Lord is with thee, alleluia"** (*Raduysya obradovannaya Mariye, Gospod' s Toboyu, alliluiya*); for the Exaltation: **"Thou hast given a sign to them that fear Thee, to flee from the face of the bow, Thy Cross, O Christ God"** (*Dal yesi znameniye boyashchimsya Tebe yezhe ubezhati ot litsa luka krest Tvoy Khriste Bozhe*) [cf. Ps. 59:6 LXX]; to the Apostle John the Theologian: **"Come, let us all praise the son of thunder, John the virgin, Christ's bosom-friend"** (*Priidite vsi syna gromova voskhvalim Ioanna, devstvennika, Khristova napersnika*); to the Great-martyr Demetrius: **"Come, ye lovers of the martyrs, let us praise Demetrius the myrrh-gusher, zealot of the Savior"** (*Priidite muchenikolyubtsy, voskhvalim mirotorchnogo Dimitriya, revnitelya Spasova*); to St. Chrysostom: **"Come, let us all with one accord praise John Chrysostom, the universal teacher"** (*Priidite vsi soglasno voskhvalim Ioanna Zlatousta, obshchago uchitelya*); to the Apostle Andrew: **"Come, let us all with one accord praise Andrew the first-called, Peter's kinsman"** (*Priidite vse soglasno voskhvalim Andreya pervozvannogo, Petrova srodnika*); to Venerable Sabbas: **"Come, let us all with one accord praise Sabbas the all-consecrated, praise of the Cappadocians"** (*Priidite vsi soglasno voskhvalim Savvu vseosvyashchennogo, Kappadokov pokhvalu*); to St. Nicholas: **"Come, all ye earthborn, let us praise the hierarch Nicholas, instructor of the laity"** (*Priidite vsi zemnorodnii voskhvalim iyerarkha Nikolaya, miryanom nastavnika*); to Martyr Eustratius and his companions:

**"Come, let us praise Eustratius and Auxentius, Eugene and Mardarius, and glorious Orestes"** (*Priidite Yevstratiya, Avksentiya voskhvalim, Yevgeniya i Mardariya i Oresta slavnogo*); for the Nativity of Christ: **"Come, let us cry out with angelic choirs: Glory to God in the highest, born in a cave"** (*Priidite s angel'skimi liki vozglasim: slava v vyshnikh Bogu, rozhdennomu v vertepe*); to Basil the Great: **"Come, all ye earthborn, let us praise Basil the Great, praise of Caesarea"** (*Priidite vse zemlenorodnii [v] voskhvalim Vasiliya Velikogo kesareom pokhvalu*); for Theophany: **"My Jesus is baptized by a servant in the Jordan River, enlightening the whole creation"** (*Kreshchayetsya Iisus moy ot raba v Iordanstey retse prosveshchaya vsyu tvar'*); to Venerable Theodosius (likewise to Venerable Euthymius and Sabbas of Serbia): **"Come, let us all with one accord praise Theodosius the cenobiarch, instructor of monks"** (*Priidite vsi soglasno voskhvalim Feodosiya obshchezhitelya, inokom nastavnika*); to Athanasius of Alexandria: **"Come, let us all with one accord praise great Athanasius, glory of the Alexandrians"** (*Priidite vsi soglasno voskhvalim velikago Afanasiya, aleksandrom slavu*); to Gregory the Theologian: **"Come, let us praise the depth of wisdom, the second bosom-friend"** (*Priidite, premudrosti glubinu vozkhvalim, vtorogo napersnika*); to the Three Hierarchs: **"Come, let us praise Basil, Gregory, and John Chrysostom, champions of the Trinity"** (*Priidite Vasiliya, Grigoriya voskhvalim i Ioanna Zlatoustago, Troitsy poborniki*); on Meat-fare Sunday: **"Turn again, O Lord, the captivity of our souls, and plant Thy fear in our hearts, O Planter of good things, alleluia"** (*Vozvrati, Gospodi, ploneniye dush nashikh i strakh Tvoy vsadi v serdtsa nasha, Nasaditelyu blagikh, alliluiya*); on the Sunday of the Veneration of the Cross: **"Before Thy Cross we bow down, O Master..."** (*Krestu Tvoyemu poklanyayemsya Vladyko...*); for Palm Sunday: **"Come, let us also, as the children, offer faith as palm-branches to God, and love as boughs"** (*Priidite i my yako otrotsy prinesem veru yako vaya Bogu, lyubov' zhe yako vetvi*); to St. George: **"Come, ye lovers of the martyrs, let us praise George the victorious, praise of the Cappadocians"** (*Priidite muchenikolyubtsy, voskhvalim pobedonostsa Georgiya, kappadokom pokhvalu*); for Ascension: **"God is gone up with a shout, the Lord with the sound of a horn, to save the image of Adam"** (*Vzyde Bog v voskliknovenii Gospod' vo glase trubne, yezhe spasti obraz adamov*); for the Nativity of John the Forerunner: **"Let us all with one accord praise John the Baptist, the Bridegroom's friend"** (*Vsi soglasno voskhvalim Ioanna Krestitelya, druga Zhenikhova*); to the Apostles Peter and Paul: **"Let us praise Peter and Paul, disciples of Christ, citizens of the heavenly Jerusalem"** (*Vyshnyago Iyerusalima grazhdany voskhvalim Petra i Pavla, ucheniki Khristovy*); to Venerable Athanasius of Athos: **"Come, let us all with one accord praise Athanasius of Athos, glory of monastics"** (*Priidite vse soglasno voskhvalim afonskago Afanasiya, inokuyushchim slavu*); for the Transfiguration: **"My Jesus and Lord is transfigured on Mount Tabor, having shown His glory"** (*Preobrazuyetsya Iisus moy i Gospod' na gore Favorstey, pokazav slavu svoyu*); for the Dormition: **"A song of departure is offered unto thee, O Virgin Mary, for thou hast passed over from earthly things to eternal mansions"** (*Pesn' ti iskhodnuyu prinoshayet Mariye, pristavibosya ot zemlenykh k vechnym obitelem*); for the Beheading: **"Come, let us all praise the Bridegroom's friend, the rebuker of Herod, John the Forerunner"** (*Priidite vsi Zhenikhova druga voskhvalim, Irodova oblichitelya, Predtechu Ioanna*); after the megalynaria: **"Glory to the Father... Glory to Thee, O Holy Trinity; glory to Thee, O Father, and Son, and with the Holy Spirit; O Holy Trinity, glory to Thee"** (*Slava Ottsu... Slava Ti Troitse Svyataya, slava Ti Ottse i Syne i [so] Svyatym Dukhom, Troitse Svyataya, slava Tebe*), **"Both now and ever... Rejoice, O Virgin Mary, full of grace, the Lord is with thee, and for thy sake with us. Alleluia [thrice], glory to Thee, O God"** (*I nyne i prisno... Raduysya, obradovannaya Mariye, Gospod' s Toboyu, i Tebe radi s nami. Alliluiya 3, slava Tebe Bozhe*). These refrains are important also because they show which feasts were regarded as the most significant. In the printed Serbian Menaion of 1536 AD, to these refrains are added refrains for Pentecost: **"Glory to Thee, O Trinity, Father, and [Word], and Holy Spirit, glory to Thee, O God"** (*Slava Ti Troitse, Otche i [S]love i Dushe Svyaty, slava Tebe Bozhe*), 6 refrains to the Theotokos at the Polyeleos, appended alternately to the verses of Psalm 134 [LXX], and refrains at the 9th Ode (Archimandrite Antonin, *Notes of a Pilgrim to the Holy Mountain*, Kyiv, 1864, p. 252). In the Horologion of the Kraków edition of 1491 AD, there are cited in one place two megalynaria for each feast—one distinct from the present one, the other the present one (fols. 270v ff.); in another place (fol. 163v) only the present ones.

233. The extent to which this rule was implemented in the Athonite Iviron Lavra even before the appearance there of a complete copy of it, under St. Euthymius, its second hegumen († 1012 AD), is evident from the latter's Life compiled by his successor and translator of the described "Synaxarion", George the Hagiorite (Mtatsmindeli). According to the biographer, Euthymius stood in church without leaning on a staff and without leaning against a wall. The brethren who stood by the wall were likewise forbidden to lean against it. The younger brethren stood in the middle of the church in two or three rows, reverently, with their hands lowered; when prescribed, they sat upon their benches, which likewise stood in the middle of the church in two or three rows. Euthymius appointed two God-fearing epitropoi-overseers: one senior, and the other junior, subordinate to the first. The junior epitropos was dispatched to the cells and brought to the church any brother remaining in his cell. A brother who did not arrive by the Six Psalms Euthymius judged according to the rules of Father [Theodore] in the following manner: one who labored much by day and had no time to sleep he did not punish—his daytime labors were credited to him as a prayerful ascetic struggle. But those having leisure or performing petty tasks, as well as priests, deacons, and readers, he subjected to such punishment: the young he compelled to make 100 prostrations before the altar, while the old and infirm he deprived of wine and food for that day. During divine service the senior epitropos stood at the doors and inquired of any departing brother concerning the reason for his leaving: if no essential need appeared, he did not permit him to leave; but in the event of genuine necessity he permitted him to leave, only on condition of returning immediately. In the event that one who went out was tardy, he was subjected to a reprimand; if he was tardy a second time, on that day he was not admitted to the refectory, but was kept on dry bread or sentenced to 100 prostrations. To those laboring tirelessly the holy father permitted leaving the church after the Six Psalms and resting, but with the strict obligation to return at the second bell. To the weak among the brethren he allowed standing in the narthex and leaning upon a staff, and to the sick even sitting. Younger brethren who talked, laughed, or took each other by the hand were immediately reproved; if they were caught a second time, they were reported to the holy father, who judged them strictly. One guilty of a quarrel or fight was brought to the cell of the holy father, who commanded him to lie upon the ground; the guilty one, having bowed, lay down; one of the brethren held him by the head, another by the feet, while a third administered to him over his cassock 30, 40, or 60 blows with a belt. If anyone interceded for the one being punished, he was subjected to the very same punishment. The punished, kneeling, bowed to the holy father and with tears in their eyes begged him for forgiveness. After this they lay upon the ground and remained in such a posture for two or three weeks (?). From time to time the holy father came to them and consoled them by word and deed; to the same he also urged other monastery officers. The executor of the punishment likewise consoled the punished one and presented him with a cassock or a shoulder-cloak, or some other necessary item. The punished regarded the chastisement borne by them as if they had endured it from the hands of Christ Himself. Above all, the holy father took care that no one should give false testimony or witness in any matter without knowing its circumstances; one convicted of this he expelled from the monastery. The blessed father provided the brethren with everything, down to needle and thread, and thereby deprived everyone of occasion to sell or acquire anything without his command; a brother could not transfer his property to another without the consent of the holy father. If anyone transgressed the will of the holy father and acquired clothing or anything valuable, he strictly rebuked him. More than once we saw how he burned a shoulder-cloak, a garment, or a cowl in the monastery precinct. Often he said to the brethren: "The saints denied themselves even water. Is it not enough for us to take food twice a day, and that in abundance—with wine and varied dishes?" Therefore if anyone purchased wine and oil, the entire purchase was poured into the refuse pit. Kekelidze, *Liturgical Georgian Monuments*, pp. 305 ff., 478 ff.

237. The extent to which Venerable Theodosius himself followed this requirement of the Studite-Alexis Typikon introduced by him into his monastery is witnessed by the incident recounted in his Life: when the cellarer came to him requesting to send some unoccupied monk for the chopping of firewood, the venerable father, with the words "I am not occupied," took up this work himself, which impelled the entire brotherhood to take up axes as well. Venerable Sergius, founder of the Holy Trinity Lavra, was likewise not ashamed of any labor, neither cooking nor shoemaking, and worked for two; his special tasks were the preparation of flour for prosphora and their baking, the rolling of candles, and the boiling of kolyvo (Golubinsky, E., *Venerable Sergius of Radonezh and the Trinity Lavra Founded by Him*, Sergiyev Posad, 1892, p. 26).

238. According to the Triodion portion of the typikon, fol. 456v, in agreement with the most ancient MS of the Typography Library, no. 285/174/206, fol. 13v, Matins from Antipascha until the Exaltation [of the Cross] is at the 7th hour. A customary mitigation of a severe regimen accompanied by apprehension of altering the text of the ancient typikon to eliminate contradiction.

239. It is noteworthy that the hegumen is permitted, as a special reward for his labors, to have a better table except during fasts. At this, the hegumen invites to his table 8 more brethren, including the priest who served, fol. 205v.

240. Here is seen the influence of the typikon of the Great Church of Constantinople, according to which the Patriarch on Great Saturday distributed the stipend (*ruga*, salary) of the clerics; the Patriarch of Jerusalem did the same on Great Thursday (Dmitrievsky, *Ancient Patriarchal Typika*, p. 144).

241. By this custom Venerable Theodosius explained to the Grand Prince who visited him the exquisite flavor of monastic dishes.

244. Dmitrievsky, *Τυπικὰ*, pp. 671, 678. In the Typikon of Empress Irene this order of election is developed into a very elaborate rite. Upon three identical parchment strips was written the prayer: "O our Master Jesus Christ, through the prayers of our all-immaculate Lady, the Theotokos, full of grace, reveal to us sinners whether Thou dost deem our sister N. worthy of superior authority over us"; the parchment strips, sealed by the patroness of the monastery, were placed upon the holy table for the duration of the Vigil and Liturgy; immediately after the Liturgy the Trisagion and the troparia are chanted: **"Have mercy on us, O Lord..."** (*Pomiluy nas Gospodi...*); **"Glory: O Lord, look down from heaven and behold..."** (*Slava: Gospodi prizri s nebese i vizhd'...*); **"Both now: Only-begotten, consubstantial..."** (*I nyne: Yedinorodne, Yedinosushchne...*). The priest (in full vestments) recites the Augmented Litany (*suhubaya yekteniya*), to which he adds also the petition: "Again we pray that the Lord may show us her who is worthy of superior authority among us"; the sisters chant **"Lord, have mercy"** 30 times with 15 prostrations, uplifting their hands and praying: "O God, knower of hearts, reveal to us sinners her who is worthy of superior authority among us." The priest, having made 3 prostrations before the holy table with the same prayer, takes one of the parchment strips, and after verification of the seal, the one who sealed it opens it; the elected one, after 3 prostrations, takes from a special place before the altar the Typikon and the staff, stands at the hegumenal place, greeting is offered to her, glory is sent up to God, and the customary dismissal is made by the priest. (Typikon of Empress Irene, ch. 11; Migne, *Patrologia Graeca*, vol. 127).

257. This office, which replaced the rite of kneading dough of the Studite-Alexis Typikon (see above, p. 426) and was retained by certain Slavic MSS, consisted in the following: after Matins and the 1st Hour, if the leavening of bread occurs in the bakery, the priest on duty proceeds thither in epitrachelion with the censer and preceded by a candle, as for a litiya, to the singing of the temple sticheron of the litiya with its Theotokion, accompanied by the brethren; in the bakery the Little Litany (*malaya yekteniya*) and the prayer for the blessing of bread as at the Vigil are said (only instead of "these loaves"—"this kneaded dough"); holy water (*hagiasma*) is poured into the leaven, and there follows the dismissal: **"May Christ our true God, through the prayers of His most pure Mother and of all the saints, grant heavenly reward to our fathers and brethren laboring in this monastery, and have mercy on us..."** (*Khristos istinny Bog nash molitvami Prechistyya Svoyeya Matere i vsekh svv. truzhdayushchimsya vo obiteli sey ottsam i bratiyam nashim podast mzdu nebesnuyu i nas pomiluyet...*) (MS of the Moscow Synodal Library of the sixteenth century, no. 379, fol. 290; no. 380, fol. 22; Slavic no. 678/386, fol. 233, and other MSS).

259. The invariable reading of the Resurrection Gospel at Sunday Matins was a peculiarity of the Typikon of the Holy Sepulchre, preserved in the Church of the Resurrection from the 4th century (Dmitrievsky, *Divine Services of Passion and Paschal Weeks*, pp. 9, 225) and passed into the Russian Church, presumably through the mediation of the Typikon of the Great Church of Constantinople.

261. It is characteristic, however, that even in the Palestinian Lavra of St. Sabbas, whence our present Typikon derived, they are now guided by this Constantinopolitan edition of the Typikon.

### Editorial Annotation

The text of the *Explanatory Typikon* contains Greek citations with full diacritics and requires a full-Unicode font containing this range of Unicode (such as Arial Unicode MS, Palatino Linotype). In curly brackets of the form `{p. NN}` is the page numbering of the original, marked at the beginning of each page according to the edition: *Explanatory Typikon: An Expository Account of the Typikon, with a Historical Introduction*, Publishing House of Sretensky Monastery, Moscow, 2004.

The text represents the second part of the *Explanatory Typikon*, comprising the second and third chapters of the work of M. Skaballanovich.

[^8]: Sacred trumpets also took the place of our bells among the Hebrews: by them the people were summoned to the Tabernacle, and later, presumably, to the Temple; for this purpose there were two silver trumpets at the Tabernacle; when both were sounded together, it was a summons to the whole congregation; the sound of a single trumpet summoned the leaders alone; to strike camp an alarm was sounded (Num. 10:1–7). This passage from the Book of Numbers is read in our Church and in the Roman Catholic Church at the blessing of bells. At the Temple the number of trumpets reached up to 100 (1 Chron. 15:24; 2 Chron. 5:12; cf. Flavius Josephus, *Antiquitates Judaicae* III, 12, 6). The trumpets had an exclusively sacred use. They resembled the horns with which muezzins currently summon Muslims to prayer. A. Olesnitsky, "Ancient Hebrew Music and Singing" [*Drevneevreyskaya muzyka i penie*], in *Trudy Kievskoy Dukhovnoy Akademii* (1871), no. 11, p. 117.

[^11]: Perhaps the places in the Psalms where such a raising of pitch and trumpet accompaniment occurred are designated by the enigmatic term *selah*. This term appears in 39 Psalms (e.g., 7, 21 [22], 22 [23]) and the Canticle of Habakkuk; 16 Psalms have it once, 15 have it twice, 7 Psalms and the Canticle of Habakkuk have it three times, and one Psalm (88 [89]) has it four times. The Septuagint translates this term as *διάψαλμα* (*diapsalma*); the Slavonic Bible omits it. The term, as well as its translation in the Septuagint, has been explained in various ways (the most ancient explanation being "unto eternity" / "forever"), but the majority of scholars incline to the opinion that it indicates the beginning of strophes or a change of voice and musical pitch, most probably an upward elevation of the pitch. (J. Sommer, *Biblische Abhandlungen*, vol. 1, Bonn, 1844, I: "Erklärung des Sela", pp. 1–84). It is also thought that *selah* signifies the place in the canticle where one choir paused and the other repeated what was sung by the first, and that the word forms an acronym of the words: *sor lemahla hashar* ("return, singer, to the beginning"). (A. Olesnitsky, "Ancient Hebrew Music and Singing", *TKDA* [1871], no. 12, p. 371).

"Blessings" (*berakhot*) are the customary name for prayer and the most commonly used prayer formula among the Hebrews. It is prescribed by the Talmud for all occasions: "During rains and upon hearing good news, they pronounce: 'Blessed is the All-Good Benefactor'; upon hearing evil tidings: 'Blessed is the righteous Judge'; upon seeing a rainbow, they pronounce: 'Blessed is He Who is faithful to His covenant'; upon seeing a Black man, a red man, an albino, a giant, or a dwarf, they pronounce: 'Blessed is He... Who maketh varied His creatures'; upon seeing a handsome person or a beautiful tree, they say: 'Blessed is He... Who hath created beautiful creatures in His world'; upon seeing an idol, they pronounce: 'Blessed is the Long-Suffering One'" (*Berakhot* IX, 1).

[^81]: To such chanting in ancient Temple practice reference is made perhaps in Psalm 146:7 [147:7]: "Sing alternately" (Heb. *'anu*, "respond," yet in Greek *ἐξάρξατε*, Slavonic *начните* ["begin"]); the expression can be understood also of the two other genres of singing: epiphonic and hypophonic. The musical term *Selah* is likewise interpreted as indicating antiphonal chanting. It is thought that antiphonal singing was borrowed by the Hebrews from Egypt, where choral songs were divided between priests and people, between men and women, between children and adults. Such singing accompanied the worship of the golden calf: descending the mountain and hearing the tumult, Moses says: "It is not the voice of them that shout for mastery, neither is it the voice of them that cry for being overcome, but the noise of them that sing do I hear" (Exodus 32:18); more literally from the Hebrew: "It is not the alternating voice [*'anot*—answering] of victors, nor the alternating voice of the vanquished, but alternating voices do I hear." Philo perceives the first instance of antiphonal chanting in the Canticle of Moses upon the crossing of the Red Sea. How accurate is this? The execution of this canticle is thus described in Exodus: "Then sang Moses and the children of Israel this song unto the Lord, and spake, saying: I will sing unto the Lord, for He hath triumphed gloriously..."; after the exposition of the canticle it is added: "And Miriam the prophetess, the sister of Aaron, took a timbrel [tambourine, drum, a dance musical instrument] in her hand, and all the women went out after her with timbrels and with dances [Heb. *mecholot*, choral dances, Greek *χορῶν*]; and Miriam answered them: Sing ye to the Lord, for He hath triumphed gloriously; the horse and his rider hath He thrown into the sea" (Exodus 14:31; 15:1, 20–21). Commentators interpret this description diversely (and not merely in the sense of antiphonal chanting): according to some, the men repeated directly after Moses and according to his melodic pattern every verse of the song, and then the same verse was sung by the women (as in our rite the prokeimenon, troparion, or exapostilarion is chanted thrice); according to others, the women sang one verse, the men another, and so on alternately; yet far more directly from the context of the discourse emerges the understanding that after Moses the verse intoned by him was repeated by the men, while the women constantly repeated the single first verse, changing the first person "I will sing" into the imperative "Sing ye," as if thereby inviting their husbands to sing more harmoniously the hymn to the Lord—all the more so since only those standing closest to Moses could distinctly hear the words of the canticle. A. A. Olesnitsky, *Drevneevreyskaya muzyka i penie* [Ancient Hebrew Music and Singing], in *Trudy Kievskoy Dukhovnoy Akademii* (1871), no. 11, pp. 115–116. Our liturgical order for the execution of this canticle on Holy and Great Saturday is founded upon this latter understanding. (Cf. also C. F. Keil, *Manual of Biblical Archaeology*, Russian trans., Kyiv, 1879, vol. II, § 136).

[^222]: The gift of tongues is represented in the New Testament as such a miraculous, sublime, and reverently awe-inspiring phenomenon that it can in no wise be acknowledged as a phenomenon of the same order as the glossolalia of Russian and foreign sectarians (Khlysts, Malevantsy, Irvingites, Mormons), consisting of entirely nonsensical combinations of syllables and words (for example: *rentre fente rente fintrifunt—trrr, tlim, tlim, dze*; D. Konovalov, "Religiozny ekstaz v russkom misticheskom sektantstve" [Religious Ecstasy in Russian Mystical Sectarianism], in *Bogoslovsky Vestnik* (1908), no. 4, pp. 738, 744), representing a purely nervous phenomenon accompanied by convulsions (*ibid.*, no. 10, p. 200; no. 4, p. 754), whirling (no. 3, pp. 734, 755), nervous laughter, and weeping (no. 4, p. 753). On a purely neuropathic basis there may also appear in certain individuals speech in a foreign tongue previously heard by them and unconsciously retained. Both phenomena were known also to early Christians, yet were sharply distinguished by them from the gift of tongues imparted by the Holy Spirit; they were explained as the influence upon man by evil spirits. Eusebius cites the narrative of an ancient historian concerning the glossolalia of the Montanists: "A certain one named Montanus, it is related, from among the recent converts, through an inordinate desire for preeminence, fell under the influence of the adversary, and suddenly, falling into a state of possession and ecstasy, began to speak and utter strange sounds (*lalein kai xenophōnein*), that is, he prophesied contrary to the custom transmitted from of old and preserved by succession in the Church... He [the devil] even raised up two women and filled them with a lying spirit, so that they also, like the aforementioned Montanus, spoke senselessly, inappropriately, and strangely" (Eusebius, *Historia Ecclesiastica*, V, 16). According to the account of Bl. Jerome, a certain Frankish official, having fallen under demonic possession from childhood, in the presence of St. Hilarion began to speak, scarcely touching the ground with his feet and turning exceedingly red, in Syriac and Greek—languages completely unknown to him—with entirely correct pronunciation (*Life of St. Hilarion*, ch. 22). Among Russian and foreign sectarians, however, speaking in unknown foreign languages has not been observed, but solely the utterance of unintelligible sounds.

[^231]: 1 Corinthians 14:16. "He that occupieth the room of the unlearned" [literally "simple man / commoner"], Slavonic *nevezhdy*, Greek *idiōtou*. *Idiōtēs*—a person who does not hold an official or leading position, or a non-specialist, for example ordinary citizens as distinguished from the king (Herodotus II, 81, et al.), the general public as distinguished from the scholars of a school (Plutarch, *Quaestiones Convivales* I, 1); non-ecstatics and non-mantics as distinguished from the visionary (Pausanias, *Corinthiaca* 13). In the LXX in Proverbs 6:8, as in Herodotus. In the Talmud—an ordinary man as distinguished from a rabbi, craftsman, magistrate, and the like. In agreement with all these meanings, the word here clearly signifies each member of the liturgical assembly as distinguished from him who cometh forward with some revelation, in this particular case with speaking in tongues. Consequently, the word stands not in the sense of a casual visitor to the assembly, for example an unbeliever, as in verse 24, where the very same word is used, nor in the general sense of an ignorant or uneducated person, still less in the modern sense of this word, which some also admitted, rendering it, for example, in German as *Idiot* (A. J. Binterim, *Die vorzüglichsten Denkwürdigkeiten der Christ-Katholischen Kirche*, IV, 1, Mainz, 1827, p. 319). "He that occupieth the room" indicates that the status of the *idiōtēs* is not permanent, but occasional: all, except him who actively ministereth during divine worship, are *idiōtai*, and each becometh such at a given moment when he hath no revelation (Th. Zahn & Ph. Bachmann, *Der erste Brief des Paulus an die Korinther*, Leipzig, 1904, pp. 420–421). Here, consequently, is already given a rather sharp (more so than in the synagogue) division of worshippers into clergy [those who minister sacred rites] and laity, although this demarcation is not yet rigid, but fluid.

[^339]: Recently in Russian scholarship the opinion was advanced that the ancient veneration of martyrs in the 2nd–4th centuries also included religious dancing (D. Konovalov, "Religiozny ekstaz v russkom misticheskom sektantstve" [*Religious Ecstasy in Russian Mystical Sectarianism*], in *Bogoslovskiy Vestnik*, 1907, no. 10, p. 351; 1908, no. 4, pp. 707–728). In the acts of the martyrs, which frequently conclude with descriptions of liturgical assemblies in honor of the martyrs, there is no mention of dancing in their honor: to interpret the phrase in the *Martyrdom of Polycarp* concerning celebrating his commemoration "with jubilation and joy" (*agalliasei kai charai* [ἀγαλλιάσει καὶ χαρᾷ]) as referring unto dancing (Konovalov, p. 707) is arbitrary. Only a few monuments of the 3rd and 4th centuries speak of such dances as a local and tolerated phenomenon. Thus, according to the testimony of St. Gregory of Nyssa, St. Gregory the Wonderworker (3rd cent.), yielding unto the inclinations of his flock in order to divert them from pagan festivals, permitted a little leaping/dancing (*ti mikron hypokirtan* [τὶ μικρὸν ὑποκιρτᾷν]) in honor of the martyrs (*Hom. in Eccl.* 6). A 4th-century homily on the commemoration of the martyr Polyeuktos († 259 in Armenia) invites: "according to the established custom let us exult/dance (*choreusōmen* [χορεύσωμεν]) in honor of the martyr" (B. Aubé, *Polyeucte dans l'histoire*, Paris, 1882, p. 79). There is also cited an expression of St. Basil the Great: "we dance with sacred dances (*entheois choreiais* [ἐνθέοις χορείαις]) at the tombs of the saints" (cited in F. C. Conybeare, *Philo: About the Contemplative Life*, Oxford, 1895, p. 154: *Bas.*, t. 1, p. 512 B). In Abyssinian worship to this day dancing has been preserved at molebens and processions of the cross, in which the priests also take some part (B. Turayev, "Abissiniya," in *Pravoslavnaya bogoslovskaya entsiklopediya*, vol. I, St. Petersburg, 1899, col. 71). Orthodox Arabs in Jerusalem also permit it around holy shrines (A. N. Muravyov, *Puteshestviye ko svyatym mestam* [*Journey to the Holy Places*], part 2, St. Petersburg, 1849, p. 124). Thus all these were religious excesses, occurring only in such enthusiastic localities as Asia Minor and Armenia, and never approved by the Church. St. John Chrysostom regards dancing as a demonic enterprise (*Hom. in Matt.* 48). St. Gregory the Theologian advises dancing as David did, understanding David's dance in an allegorical sense (*Oration* 5). Bl. Augustine expresses indignation at the former dances in the martyrium of St. Cyprian and directly before the basilicas of the saints (*Sermon on the Feast of St. Cyprian*; *Sermon* 215 [265]). The Council of Carthage (397), Canon 71, prohibited "abominable dances (*orcheseis mysaras* [ὀρχήσεις μυσαράς]) performed in sacred places, even on the days of commemoration of the blessed martyrs." The Council of Laodicea (late 4th cent.), Canon 53, forbids even at weddings to leap or dance (*ballizein ē orchesthai* [βαλλίζειν ἢ ὀρχεῖσθαι]). In view of such an attitude toward religious dancing in the Church and such rarity of it among ancient Christians, one can hardly see a ritual survival of it in the circular procession during Baptism, Marriage, and Chirotony (Konovalov, p. 723).

[^462]: *Ibid.*, ch. 18. This rite even under the apostles had very wide application during divine worship, judging from 1 Pet. 5:14, 2 Cor. 13:12, and others. Under Tertullian they still kissed at prayer without distinction of sex: "what pagan will permit his wife to approach one or another of the brethren for a kiss?" (*Ad Uxorem*, II, 4). Yet in the *Apostolic Constitutions* men kiss men, and women women (VIII, 15). The intermediate link between both practices is found in St. Ambrose: the deacon kisseth the deaconess, and she the women (*Epistle* 6 *Ad mulieres*).

Of this form St. John Chrysostom likewise maketh mention (*Homily on Christ Being God*); yet unto him the sign of the cross upon the lips and breast is already known (*Homilies on Matthew*, Hom. 87 [88]), as likewise unto Blessed Jerome (*Funeral Oration on Paula*, Ep. 108 [27]). The formula "In the name of the Father..." is found first in St. Ephrem the Syrian (*On the Whole Armor*); it arose from the commandment concerning baptism (Matt. 28:19). Cf. X. Schmid, *Der christkatholische Kultus*, Passau, 1840, vol. I, p. 245.

[^514]: It is commonly thought that by "stations" (*stationes*) in Tertullian and writers of that era is meant the fast of Wednesday and Friday. But Tertullian calls "station" also the three-week fast of the Montanists (*De Jejuniis*, ch. 19), and neither he nor other writers apply this term exclusively unto either fast, but unto fasts in general. Hermas, unto the Shepherd's question: "Why hast thou come hither (unto the mountain) so early?" answers: "Because, sir, I am keeping a station..." "And what is a station?" he asked. "That is, I am fasting, sir, said I" (*Shepherd of Hermas*, Similitude 5). Only the following passages from Tertullian might speak in favor of such a narrow meaning of the term "station": "we dedicate unto stations the fourth and sixth day of the week" (*De Jejuniis*, 19); and concerning a Christian carried away by military service: "and stations doth he perform, either rather unto someone else than unto Christ, or on the Lord's day, when (they are performed) in any case not unto Christ" (*De Corona Militis*, 11).
