[^527]: One cannot therefore, with certain Western scholars, suspect the authenticity of all mentions of the Forty-Day Fast (Четыредесятница / Lent) found in 3rd-century monuments solely on the ground that other monuments of that century do not yet know such a prolonged fast. Thus Achelis in his edition of the Canons of Hippolytus regards the word "40" in the aforementioned passage of this monument as a later insertion (Achelis, *Die Canones Hippolyti*, p. 102). The testimonies of Origen are suspected on the ground that Origen's commentary on the Book of Leviticus, where it is found, hath reached us in the translation of Rufinus († 410). Now Rufinus was a very free translator, which he not only admits, but repeatedly warns the reader of—for example, in the preface unto the translation of Origen's work *De Principiis* [printed: *«Περιὶ ἀοχῶν»*, i.e. *Περὶ ἀρχῶν*]. In the postscript unto the translation of Origen's commentary on the Epistle to the Romans, he remarks concerning his labor: "we supply that which was stated by Origen for the Church of his time not so much for the purpose of explanation as for the purpose of edification, as we did also in the homilies or discourses upon Genesis and Exodus; and especially in the homilies upon the Book of Leviticus, what was spoken by him for beauty of style we render in direct language for clarity; this labor of supplying what was lacking we undertook that the Latin reader might not encounter difficulties from questions raised and left unresolved, as Origen is accustomed to do according unto the requirements of homiletic art." Once such principles were laid at the foundation of the translation, then, as the editor of Origen in Migne's Patrology remarks, the reader can never be certain whether he is reading Origen or Rufinus. True, even so broad a freedom of translation ought not to extend unto such purely factual data in Origen as the indication of the existence in his time of the fast of the Forty Days (Lent). But here they recall Rufinus' translation of Irenaeus' words concerning 40 hours of fasting... Furthermore, in Origen's expression concerning the Forty Days—"the days of the Forty-Day Fast consecrated unto fasting"—attention is drawn unto the inappropriate floral verbosity of the phrase, which doth not answer unto the simplicity of that which followeth it: "we fast both on Wednesday and on Friday." Funk thinks that Origen here was speaking of the forty-day fast of the Savior (F. X. Funk, *Kirchengeschichtliche Abhandlungen und Untersuchungen*, vol. 1, Paderborn, 1897, p. 254).

In the era of the monument, consequently, the phenomenon of "demonic possession" had no small dissemination, unless prayers for the "possessed" were then such a relic of antiquity as prayers for the catechumens serve today. Characteristic is the place occupied by this class of worshipers: between the catechumens and those being illuminated; the catechumens prior to exorcism were likewise considered to be under the influence of unclean spirits, like all pagans.

[^613]: The monument was discovered by the Italian archaeologist Gian Francesco Gamurrini in 1884 in a Latin manuscript of c. the 12th century of the Confraternity of St. Mary in Arezzo. The opening leaves of the work are lost, for which reason neither the title of the work nor the name of the author has been preserved. In the margins of the manuscript in two places in the corner stand the letters *PE*, which are considered an abbreviation of the title. Indirect evidence in the work points unto the end of the 4th century as the time of the origin of the *Peregrinatio*: the Jerusalem edifices are described in such a manner that Constantine's structures can be recognized in them; mention is made of a recently built church in Edessa, which occurred in 372 under the Emperor Valens; of the Persian possession of the left bank of the Tigris, which was ceded unto them by the Emperor Jovian in 363; of the Thebaid ascetics (among them St. Anthony the Great, † 356, and St. Pachomius, † 340); on the other hand, the traveler is unacquainted with Jerome's translation of the Holy Scriptures, or the decree of Pope Gelasius of 494 against the reading of apocrypha—the Letter of Abgar, the Acts of the Holy Apostle Thomas, and of the Holy Martyr Thecla; Justinian's buildings in Sinai and Constantinople are not mentioned. The pilgrim came unto the Holy Land *de extremis porro terris* (from the distant ends of the earth); judging by the fact that she compares the Euphrates with the Rhône (*Rhodanus*), she was presumably a native of Gaul; she was an educated and well-read woman; she travels as a noble personage—with a retinue; she is provided with a military escort; bishops receive and accompany her. In Palestine she remained three years, dwelling in Jerusalem and making excursions from thence. Having returned unto Constantinople, she described her pilgrimage unto the "sisters" (fleshly sisters or nuns?). The identification of the pilgrim by some with Galla Placidia, daughter of Theodosius the Great, and by others with Sylvia, sister of the Prefect of Constantinople Rufinus (an Aquitanian), is rather arbitrary. The monument is, of course, of invaluable liturgical importance, yet one cannot but regret that it belongs unto a foreigner and a woman: the pilgrim observes only ceremonies, litanies, how they approach the bishop's hand, and the like, while concerning the content of divine worship she restricts herself unto the remarks: "psalms and hymns were sung," "prayers were read." Nevertheless the order of divine worship is presented rather distinctly. The monument was published in the *Pravoslavny Palestinsky Sbornik*, fascicle 20, 1889, from a transcript made directly from the manuscript itself, and provided with a Russian translation and preface (by I. V. Pomialovsky), whence the present data concerning it are also drawn (pp. I–IX).

[^619]: It is unknown whether *missa* signifies the dismissal or the Liturgy, which is designated by the pilgrim at times as *oblatio*, *offertur*, and rarely *sacramentum*. The name *missa* was adopted for the Liturgy in the West either from the solemn formula of dismissal therein: "*Ite, missa est*", or from the fact that it is celebrated after the dismissal of the catechumens and constitutes the conclusion of lengthy church services. If in the pilgrim *missa* signifies the Liturgy, then daily in the Church of Jerusalem two Liturgies were celebrated—one after Matins, and another after Vespers (on Great Thursday and Holy Saturday two Liturgies—*oblatio*—morning and evening, are clearly indicated by the pilgrim, yet in different churches: *Peregrinatio*, §§ 35, 38), inasmuch as the description of Vespers in the pilgrim also concludes with the words *missa fit* (the opinion concerning two Liturgies was expressed by G. F. Gamurrini, *S. Hilarii tractatus de mysteriis et hymni et S. Silviae Aquitanae peregrinatio*, Rome, 1887, pp. 77–78). If, however, *missa* here signifies the dismissal, then on weekdays there was no Liturgy (so thinks A. de Waal, "Die Feste des Kirchenjahres zu Jerusalem gegen Ende des IV. Jahrhunderts," *Römische Quartalschrift für christliche Alterthumskunde und für Kirchengeschichte*, 1887, no. 4, p. 313; N. F. Krasnoseltsev, "The Divine Services of the Church of Jerusalem at the End of the 4th Century," *Pravoslavny Sobesednik*, 1888, II, pp. 351, 359).

[^816]: Concerning the acclamation "Glory to Thee, O Lord" before the reading of the Gospel from the 4th and 5th centuries there are no reliable testimonies. In a homily on the circus or hippodrome, formerly attributed unto St. John Chrysostom, it is stated: "When the deacon beginneth the course (*dromou*) of the readings, we immediately arise, proclaiming: 'Glory to Thee, O Lord'." In the Mozarabic Liturgy (the order of which has been preserved more or less unchanged from the 6th–7th centuries), unto the naming of the prophecy and the epistle the people respond: "Thanks be to God" (*Deo gratias*). Thus originally and in certain localities the acclamation "Glory to Thee, O Lord" or the like accompanied the reading of other scriptures as well, besides the Gospel. In the Mozarabic Liturgy and in the Rule of St. Benedict of the 6th century (ch. 11), after the reading of the Gospel the people pronounce "Amen," which, according unto the explanation of other commentators, possesses here the sense: "May God grant us firmly to abide in the evangelical teaching." [^914]: Palladius, *Historia Lausiaca*, ch. 128 (145), and many others. St. Isidore († 491) said: "it is not so harmful for a man to eat meat as to become proud and puffed up" (*Apophthegmata Patrum*, Isidore, § 4). In other Christian lands abstinence from meat among monastics was not so unconditional as in Egypt: according unto the words of St. Epiphanius, "some of them (monks) abstain from all meats, both of quadrupeds and of birds, and from fish, and from eggs, and from cheese; others only from quadrupeds, permitting the use of birds and the rest; others abstain also from birds, using only cheese and fish; others taste not even fish, but only cheese; while others eat not even cheese" (*Expositio fidei*, § 23).
[^915]: "It happened that certain fathers came unto the house of a Christ-loving man, among whom was also Abba Poemen. At table meat was set before them. All began to eat except Abba Poemen (5th c.). The elders, knowing his discernment, marveled why he did not eat. When they arose from the table, they said unto him: 'Thou art Poemen, yet what hast thou done?' The elder answered them: 'Forgive me, fathers. You ate, and no one was scandalized; but if I should eat, many brethren coming unto me would be scandalized and say: Poemen ate meat; why then should not we also eat?' And the elders marveled at his discernment" (*Apophthegmata Patrum*, Poemen, § 170). The "fathers" who visited Theophilus, Archbishop of Alexandria, ate calf meat offered unto them; but when Theophilus, handing a piece of meat unto the elder next to him, said: "here is a good piece, eat, abba," the elders said: "until now we thought we were eating vegetables; if this be meat, we will not eat"; and not one of them ate any more (*Ancient Patericon Arranged by Chapters*, IV, 75 (63). This collection, closely related unto the *Sayings of the Holy Fathers* but somewhat younger than it, is described by Patriarch Photius in his *Bibliotheca*, codex 198, under the title Ἀνδρῶν ἁγίων βίβλος. It was translated into Latin in the 6th century by Pelagius and John, Roman deacons; the translation was published by H. Rosweyde, *De vitis et verbis seniorum*, Antwerp 1628, and in Migne, *PL*, t. 73, and is preserved in Greek in an 11th–12th century manuscript of the Moscow Synodal Library, No. 782, etc. The Greek text in places differs from the Latin; from it was made the Russian translation published by the Athonite St. Panteleimon Monastery, Moscow 1891; the numeral in parentheses indicates the section according unto the Latin edition).
[^916]: "Clerics forewarned Abba Simon (presumably of the 5th c., of Sinai): 'Abba, prepare thyself, for a certain magistrate, having heard concerning thee, is coming to receive a blessing from thee.'—'Well, I will prepare myself,' said Simon. Putting on a *kenton* (a garment fashioned of multicolored rags) and taking into his hands bread and cheese, the abba sat at the door and ate. The magistrate came with his retinue; beholding the elder, those who had come looked upon him with disdain, saying: 'Is this the hermit concerning whom we heard?' And they immediately departed" (*Apophthegmata Patrum*, Simon, § 2).
[^917]: Palladius, *Historia Lausiaca*, ch. 128 (145), on St. Candida. St. Hor († c. 390) and Aphre tested each other's obedience with fish: at the wish of the latter, the former praised a spoiled fish stew and declared poorly cooked a well-prepared fish (*Apophthegmata Patrum*, Pistus, § 1).
[^918]: "A brother asked Abba Xoi: 'If I drink three cups (*poteria*) of wine, is it not too much?' The abba answered: 'If there is no devil, it is not too much'" (*Apophthegmata Patrum*, Xoi, § 1). "Unto Abba Xanthias on account of his arduous labor they brought a little wine. A possessed person was brought unto him. The demon began to revile the elder: 'Unto this wine-bibber have you brought me!' The elder did not wish to cast out the demon, but because of his reviling said unto him: 'I trust in Christ that before I finish drinking this cup, thou shalt depart.' And as soon as the elder began to drink, the demon cried out: 'Thou burnest me, thou burnest me!' And before the elder had finished the cup, the demon went out through the operation of the grace of Christ" (*Apophthegmata Patrum*, Xanthias, § 2). Even St. Sisoes did not refuse wine; but when a third cup was offered him, "the abba accepted it not, saying: 'Desist, brother; knowest thou not that there is a Satan?'" (*Apophthegmata Patrum*, Sisoes, § 8).
[^919]: St. Hyperechius equates wine with meat: "it is better to eat meat and drink wine than to devour the flesh of a brother through slander" (*Apophthegmata Patrum*, Hyperechius, § 4; *Ancient Patericon*, IV, 59 (51)). When unto a certain elder at a festal meal a cup of wine was offered, he said: "take away from me this death" (*Ancient Patericon*, IV, 63 (53)). Peter Pionita, a Sinaitic ascetic of the 5th century, would not allow himself in old age even a slight mingling of wine with water (*Ancient Patericon*, IV, 33 (35)). St. Paphnutius (4th–5th c.), who drank no wine his entire life, when he drank it at the demand of a brigand chieftain, thereby converted him unto repentance along with his whole band (*Apophthegmata Patrum*, Paphnutius, § 2). "Certain persons recounted unto Abba Poemen (5th c.) concerning a monk that he drank no wine; the elder answered: 'Wine is not a thing for monks at all'" (*Apophthegmata Patrum*, Poemen, § 10). St. Athanasius the Great, reproaching the monks, said: "we see bishops who drink no wine, and monks who drink" (*Epistle to Dracontius*).
[^920]: Palladius, *Historia Lausiaca*, ch. 73 (86), etc. Water at times had to be gathered from dew, as in the case of St. Onuphrius: *Veterum patrum analecta nova*, Venice 1781, pp. 122–127.
[^921]: Abba Agathon († 435) had two disciples who lived separately in the desert. One day he asked one of them: "How livest thou in thy cell?" He answered: "I fast until evening, and then I eat two rusks (*paxamatia*)." The elder said unto him: "Thy manner of life is good and not overly arduous" (*Apophthegmata Patrum*, Agathon, § 20). St. Megethius of Sinai, a disciple of Saints Sisoes and Poemen of Egypt, ate one loaf of bread every two days (*Apophthegmata Patrum*, Megethius, § 2). The bread used was for the most part barley rusk (*paxamos*), which can keep for half a year and was commonly used by the poor population of Egypt (St. Athanasius the Great, *Vita Antonii*, § 12); they ate it soaked in water (*Ancient Patericon*, IV, 68 (56)). Freshly baked bread, which could be had only by hermits living near villages or monasteries, was considered a luxury, and unto it, as unto a treat, neighbors were invited (*Ancient Patericon*, IV, 76 (64)). Cooked food, for the most part in the form of lentil porridge, was prepared only for guests (*Ancient Patericon*, IV, 68 (56), 69 (57)). A certain elder refused to eat porridge made from sebesten tree plums/buds (*myxaria*) even during severe hemorrhaging (*Ancient Patericon*, IV, 77 (59)). Another "elder during illness was visited by a brother, who prepared a cooked meal for him from his own provisions and offered him to eat. The elder said unto him: 'In truth, brother, I had forgotten that men have such consolation'" (*Ancient Patericon*, IV, 78 (66)). Concerning St. Isaac it was recounted that he ate his bread with ashes from the liturgical censer (*Apophthegmata Patrum*, Isaac, § 6). St. Macarius of Alexandria († 394), "hearing that a certain monk ate only one litra (12 ounces) of bread, resolved to imitate him: he broke up all his rusks into pieces and dropped them into a jar with a narrow neck, establishing a rule to eat no more than his hand could draw out. Cheerfully he recounted this unto us (saith the author of the *Lausiac History*): 'I would seize a larger handful, but the narrow neck would not permit me to draw it out; my jar would not let me eat at all.' For three full years he labored in such abstinence, eating only four or five ounces of bread and drinking a proportionate quantity of water" (Palladius, *Historia Lausiaca*, ch. 19).
[^922]: Concerning St. Evagrius Ponticus, deacon († 399), it is recounted in the *Lausiac History*: "This blessed man said: 'From the time that I came into the (Egyptian) desert, I have eaten neither lettuce, nor greens, nor any fresh herbs, nor tree fruit, nor grapes; I have not washed my body; I have eaten neither meat, nor bread, nor wine, nor in general anything prepared over fire, except for certain raw herbs and a small quantity of water.' At length, after he had lived in this manner sixteen years without taking cooked food, and when his body was weakened and his stomach disordered, he felt the need of food prepared over fire and began to eat bread; but even during the last two years he ate no cooked vegetables, save only cabbage and pulse" (Palladius, *Historia Lausiaca*, ch. 73 (86)). "St. Macarius of Alexandria resolved for seven years to eat nothing prepared over fire, but nourished himself solely upon raw vegetables, or when it happened, soaked pulse; nothing else did he taste during those seven years; having fulfilled his vow, he nevertheless laid aside such a manner of life" (*Historia Lausiaca*, ch. 19). Heron, a young Egyptian ascetic (a younger contemporary of Evagrius), who soon fell into delusion and repented only before death, "often took food only once in three months, being content with the reception of the Holy Mysteries alone, and if perchance he came upon some wild herb" (*Historia Lausiaca*, ch. 32 (30)).
[^923]: St. Candida "did not eat the flesh of animals; she ate only fish, oil, and vegetables, and this only on feast days; at all other times she was content with water mingled with vinegar, and dry bread" (Palladius, *Historia Lausiaca*, ch. 128 (145)). The aforementioned St. Evagrius, prior to settling in the deep desert, lived for fourteen years in the monastery of the Cells (*Kellia*), and throughout all this time consumed a litra of bread daily, and in three months expended a sextarius (ξέστης—one-sixth of a congius) of oil (*Historia Lausiaca*, ch. 86 (73)). St. Macarius also during his three-year fast upon bread alone expended one-sixth of a congius of oil (*Historia Lausiaca*, ch. 19). St. Dorotheus ate six ounces of bread daily and a bundle of greens, and drank a little water (*Historia Lausiaca*, ch. 2). St. Elias of Thebes in old age ate three ounces of bread and three olives daily (*Historia Lausiaca*, ch. 51 (46)). A certain virgin, after sixty years of enclosure, at the bidding of the local martyr Colluthus who appeared unto her, came in the morning on the day of her death unto the meal in his church, having taken in a basket bread and a few greens; and having waited until the ninth hour, the customary time for taking food, when no one was in the church, she partook of these provisions there, returned home after prayer unto the martyr, and died that night (*Historia Lausiaca*, ch. 123 (139)).
[^924]: Palladius, *Historia Lausiaca*, ch. 123 (139) (see above); *Apophthegmata Patrum*, Macarius of Egypt, § 32: two hermit brethren offer a meal unto St. Macarius of Egypt visiting them only at the ninth hour; Silvanus, § 5: a visitor unto St. Silvanus of Sinai expecteth at the ninth hour to be invited unto the table; cf. Zeno, § 8. Among hermits this was a general rule equally for fasting and non-fasting days. "A brother asked Abba Matoës: 'What should I do if on a fast day, or at dawn, a brother cometh unto me? This troubleth me.' The elder answered him: 'If without qualm of conscience thou eatest with thy brother, thou doest well; but if thou expectest no one, yet eatest, in this is already thine own will'" (*Apophthegmata Patrum*, Matoës, § 6). But in monasteries, especially in later coenobia, the taking of food no earlier than the ninth hour was made a rule only for fasting days: *Apophthegmata Patrum*, Matoës, § 5; *Ancient Patericon*, IX, 16, 12; X, 37 (30). The following passage from the *Ancient Patericon* scarcely testifieth unto an earlier taking of food: "A certain brother hungered one morning and wrestled with his thought not to eat until the third hour; when the third hour arrived, he resolved to endure until the sixth hour; when the sixth hour arrived, he soaked his bread, and sitting down to eat, arose again and said: 'I will endure until the ninth hour'; the ninth hour arrived, and the elder, having made prayer, saw the power of the devil departing like smoke from his bosom; and thus his hunger passed away" (IV, 70 (58)). Nor does the following incident concerning St. Sisoes testify unto taking food on non-fasting days in the morning: he persuaded Adelphius, Bishop of Nicopolis, visiting him with companions, to take food for the road in the morning, and this was during a fast. When the table was set, lo, brethren knocked at the door; Abba Sisoes said unto his disciple: "Give them a little porridge, for they are weary." "Leave it," Abba Adelphius said unto him, "lest they say that Abba Sisoes eateth in the morning" (in general, and all the more so during a fast). It turned out that the brethren who knocked begged that Sisoes not be compelled to eat, lest on that account he subsequently afflict himself with several days of total fasting (*Apophthegmata Patrum*, Sisoes, § 13).

"Once Abba Macarius the Citizen (of Alexandria) went out to cut palm leaves. The brethren said unto him on the first day: 'Come and eat with us.' The elder went and ate with them. [^934]: "Abba Joseph asked Abba Poemen (5th c.): 'How ought one to fast?' Abba Poemen answered him: 'In mine opinion, one ought to eat every day, but eat little, not unto satiety.'—'How then, abba, didst thou in thy youth fast for two days together?' said Abba Joseph. 'In truth I fasted for three days, and for four, and even for a week,' answered the elder; 'but the fathers tested all these things, as being mighty in virtue, and found that it is better to eat every day a little, and they showed us the royal road, for it is more manageable for us'" (*Apophthegmata Patrum*, Poemen, § 186; also in *Ancient Patericon*, IX, 59 (44)). Unto Megethius, a contemporary of Poemen, who ate one loaf every two days, a "holy man" who visited him advised him to eat half a loaf every day: "and doing thus, Megethius found peace" (*Apophthegmata Patrum*, Megethius, § 2).

[^938]: St. Arsenius († 450) "passed the entire night in vigil, and when toward morning nature urged him to sleep, he would say unto sleep: 'Come hither, evil servant'; and having slept a little while sitting, he would immediately arise" (*Apophthegmata Patrum*, Arsenius, § 14). He said that for a monk, if he be an ascetic, it is sufficient to sleep for one hour (*ibid.*, § 15). St. Bessarion († 466) "for forty years did not lie down upon his side, but slept sitting or standing" (*Apophthegmata Patrum*, Bessarion, § 8). "God is my witness," recounteth Palladius concerning St. Dorotheus of Thebes, "I never saw him stretch out his legs, or lie down to sleep upon a mat or upon a bed; throughout the entire night he would sit and plait ropes. And from youth for sixty years he lived thus; he never lay down to sleep, but only perchance during work or at table would close his eyes for a few minutes, so that even a morsel of food would sometimes fall from his mouth during his slumber" (Palladius, *Historia Lausiaca*, ch. 2).

[^977]: Under the name of St. Anthony, however, written rules have also come down unto us. They are cited by Benedict of Aniane (9th c.) in his *Codex regularum*; in a somewhat different recension they were discovered in an Arabic manuscript in the 17th century (both recensions published in Migne, *PG*, t. 40; Russian translation in *Khristianskoye Chteniye*, 1880, part 37). Yet the authenticity of these rules is doubtful, because St. Athanasius and Blessed Jerome make no mention of them, and because written rules for monks would conflict with St. Anthony's general outlook upon asceticism; the rules, moreover, are wholly devoid of the spirit of St. Anthony; they do not reflect the theological views of St. Anthony (demonology, polemics against the Arians); and they presuppose a monastic order far too complex for the era of Anthony: subordination unto a hegumen, a church building, assemblies of the brethren, monastic lands, monastic habit with symbolic significance, and the like. These "Rules" represent a compilation of the monastic typika of Saints Pachomius, Isaiah, and others, interwoven with thoughts of St. Anthony. Lobachevsky, *St. Anthony*, pp. 168ff.

[^1007]: Under such a way of life, complete poverty in the monastery is not surprising: "A certain nobleman from a certain land brought with him much gold and entreated the presbyter of Scete to distribute it unto the brethren. The presbyter said: 'The brethren have no need.' But since he pressed the presbyter earnestly, the latter set a basket by the church doors and said: 'Whosoever hath need, let him take.' Yet none approached it, and others paid no heed whatever. Then the presbyter said: 'God hath accepted thine alms; go and distribute it unto the poor'" (*Ancient Patericon*, VI, 23 [19]).
[^1008]: Concerning the agape in Scete, in *Apophthegmata Patrum*, Isaiah (5th c.), § 4: "When at the agape meal the brethren were eating in church and conversing with one another, a presbyter from Pelusium, rebuking them, said: 'Keep silence, brethren! for I saw a brother eating with you and drinking with you the same cups, and his prayer ascendeth unto heaven like fire.'"
[^1009]: A brother asked Abba Sisoes (who had begun his ascetic labors in Scete): "'What shall I do? When I come unto church, an agape meal often taketh place, and they detain me at it.' The elder said unto him: 'It is a hard matter!' Abraham, his disciple, likewise said unto him: 'If it happen that there is an agape on Saturday or Sunday and a brother drinketh three cups (*potēria*, that is, of wine), would that be too much?' The elder replied: 'Were there no Satan, it would not be much'" (*Ancient Patericon*, IV, 45 [37]).
[^1010]: Cassian and Germanus were thus entertained (ca. 390–400) in Scete by Abba Serenus after the Sunday service: "Instead of brine (*muria*, probably water with salt, from *mare*—sea), which was served daily with the addition of a drop of oil, he prepared a little broth (*liquamen*), pouring into it a little more oil than usual; for this trifle of oil each one poureth in daily (a mitigation of the former regime?) not in order to afford thereby any sweetness unto the throat, because they pour in so little of it that it is scarcely enough, I say not to lubricate, but even to reach the gullet, but in order by this consumption to subdue vainglory of heart. Then he served three olives each, seasoned with salt. Afterwards he brought a basket with roasted chickpeas (*cicer frictum*), which they call dessert (*trogalia*), from which we took only six grains (*grana*) each, two plums (*sebesten*, *mixaria*), and one dried fig (*carica*); to take more than this number is accounted blameworthy in that desert." John Cassian, *Conferences*, VIII, 1.

[^1014]: P. Kazansky, *History of Orthodox Monasticism in the East* (*Istoriya pravoslavnogo monashestva na Vostoke*), part 2, Moscow, 1865, p. 152. The order of life in these three principal monasteries of ancient Christian Egypt was so simple that it could not be defined by a written typikon. For this reason and by internal evidence one must recognize as spurious the rules for monks allegedly established by an assembly of four Nitrian and Scetic fathers (Serapion, the two Macarii, and Paphnutius) (Migne, *PG*, t. 34, cols. 971–978), the collection of which is divided into four parts, each part being ascribed unto one of these fathers. The most characteristic of these rules are: "Let there be one superior over all the brethren; let none depart from his counsel and command, but let everyone obey him with joy, as God Himself. In the church assembly let none begin the singing of the psalms without the command of the superior; if the superior delay, let him be notified and proceed according unto his instruction. Let those entering the monastery lie before the gates for an entire week. From the 1st hour until the 3rd, time is dedicated unto God; from the 3rd until the 9th, unto work. Everything in the monastery—vessels, tools, and the like—is sacred. A visiting cleric, even of the lowest rank, begins the prayers at divine service."

Amélineau in *Annales du Musée Guimet*, t. XVII, Paris, 1889, pp. 366–369.
[^1043]: Sozomen: "The rules permitted each to eat and drink, to work and to fast or not to fast, as much as each was able, and commanded that upon those who ate more the more difficult labors be laid, while upon the ascetics, lighter ones." Dionysius: "Permit each to eat and drink according unto his strength, and in proportion unto nourishment constrain him to labor; forbid neither moderate eating nor fasting; give the stronger and those who eat heavier labors, and the weaker and abstinent lighter ones." Arabic: "Permit each to eat and drink what shall be needful for him; hinder them not from fasting, but leave this unto their free choice, and give unto those strong in body heavy and burdensome labors, and unto those weak and pious, light and unburdensome ones." In the Arabic this rule standeth in the second place, while in the first place is that concerning cells (which followeth in the Greek *Lausiac History*).
[^1044]: Sozomen: "to build many small dwellings." Dionysius: "make diverse cells." Arabic: "build many cells in thy monastery."
[^1045]: Sozomen: "house." Arabic: "unite them at a single table for food."
[^1046]: Sozomen: "enclosed on both sides." Arabic simply: "low seats." In Dionysius this entire rule is absent.
[^1047]: Sozomen: "a leather garment." Arabic: "tanned skin, of sheep or goat."
[^1048]: Arabic: "if they desire on Saturday or Sunday to receive the Holy Mysteries"; in Dionysius "on Saturday or Sunday" is absent.
[^1049]: Absent in the Arabic.
[^1050]: Sozomen: "woolen caps." Dionysius simply: "cowls (*cuculli*)." Arabic: "cowls resembling those worn by children who have done no evil"; according unto the Arabic they are put on seemingly only for the reception of the Eucharist.
[^1051]: Absent in Dionysius and in the Arabic; in Sozomen: "to make upon the caps marks of purple color (*kentron*)."
[^1052]: In Sozomen such practical application is not indicated, whereas in the Arabic another application is given: "that by means of the form of the letter assigned unto them they might examine their deeds, know their conduct, guard themselves against evil habits, and transfer themselves into the rank designated by the letter *iota*, with the assistance of their zeal and emulation in conduct."
[^1053]: In Dionysius the letters *alpha*, *zeta*, *lambda*, *rho*, *sigma* are additionally adduced as examples, yet without indication of their significance. In the Arabic recension: "and as for the letter *rho*, beware of it and act in accordance with the sign that it representeth."
[^1054]: Arabic: "The Angel instructed Pachomius how best to familiarize the spiritual fathers also with these signs."
[^1055]: Sozomen: "Permit not a stranger to eat together with them, unless some traveler be received." Dionysius: "If a stranger should come from another monastery, having a different habit (*habitum*), let none eat with him, except one who, being on a journey, could not observe this (*observare*)." Arabic: "Receive not a brother coming from another monastery if he hath in general acquired habits not identical with thine; but receive strangers, comfort them, and show mercy unto the poor in a special place of thy monastery, so as not to eat or drink with them."
[^1056]: Arabic adds: "tonsure the hair of his head."
[^1057]: Dionysius: "*studiis sacratioribus*" ("unto more sacred pursuits").
[^1058]: Dionysius: "let him perform only his labors." Arabic: "employ him in the affairs of the monastery."
[^1059]: Sozomen: "to sit at table with covered faces, so as not to see one another or anything else except the table and the foods set before them."
[^1060]: Sozomen: "to pray every day 12 times, and as many in the evening and as many at night, and at the ninth hour 3 times; moreover, prior unto taking food to preface prayer by the chanting of a psalm." Dionysius: "there shall be 12 day prayers (*diurnae orationes*), 12 evening prayers, and 12 night prayers." Arabic: "let each of the brethren make 12 prayers in the course of the day; and at the evening hour, when they assemble to take food, let each of them make three prayers before eating, and six before sleep, and with every prayer a psalm. Let them sleep half the night, and let them spend the other half keeping vigil, for the sake of unceasing prayer and the glorification of God."
[^1061]: Arabic: "these prayers are not few for those who have spent but a little time in such a life, lest prayer become wearisome unto them."
[^1062]: Dionysius: "remaining in their cells, they pray without ceasing." Arabic: "and I know that their days and nights shall be employed in accordance with the laws of God."
[^1063]: Let us recall this practice depicted on pp. 202–210 and we shall become convinced that each rule as it were lowereth its individual requirements by several degrees. From such a point of view the rule concerning sleep will likewise not appear petty (see I. Troitsky, *Review of Sources for the Primary History of Egyptian Monasticism* [*Obozrenie istochnikov nachal'noy istorii egipetskogo monashestva*], p. 62); in place of sleep in a standing or sitting posture, sleep in a semi-reclining posture is permitted. Most strange appeareth the rule concerning the division of the monks into classes according unto the number of the letters of the Greek alphabet. One may regard this rule as a distinctive poetic (with mystical coloring) representation of the pastoral care of the superior of the monastery for the brethren.
[^1064]: See above, p. 139.
[^1065]: The Arabic recension of the typikon defineth the number of prayers only in place of the Liturgy with its Hours ("day prayers"), the 9th Hour ("before food"), and Vespers ("before sleep"), appointing for each service a number of prayers proportional unto its importance: 12, 6, 3; whereas the night office it defineth not by the quantity of prayers, but by their duration: half the night.

[^1067]: See above, pp. 189 ff.
[^1068]: The not entirely clear expression concerning this latter "prayer" hath, probably, such a meaning: if the meal on a given day is not common, but separate for each "order" or class of monks, for each house of the monastery, then prior unto it there is chanted one psalm with prayer; whereas if it is common, for several orders (houses), then as many psalms with prayer are chanted as there are of these "orders" participating in the meal. Thus the meal was prefaced by an office in composition not different from other offices; cf. among us the Order of the Panagia; see the explanation of Chapter 2 of the Typikon, end.

St. Eusebius placed an iron chain upon his neck and connected it unto a similar girdle, so that, "being thus bent double, he was continually constrained to look upon the ground" (*ibid.*, ch. 4; *PG*, t. 82, col. 1345).

In confirmation of this Bingham citeth the following narratives of Sozomen and Eusebius: Unto St. Spyridon of Trimythous "a certain traveler entered from his journey during the Forty-Day Fast, when the saint fasted with his household and partook of food only on a designated day, remaining without food on the others. Seeing that the stranger was exceedingly weary, he said unto his daughter: 'Wash this man's feet and set food before him.' When the maiden answered that there was neither bread nor flour—for a store thereof by reason of the fast would have been superfluous—he first prayed and asked forgiveness, and then commanded his daughter to roast some salted pork that happened to be in the house. And when it was roasted, Spyridon, seating the stranger beside him, began to eat the meat set before them and urged the man to imitate him. When the latter, calling himself a Christian, refused, the saint added: 'All the less oughtest thou to refuse, for the word of God (Titus 1:15) hath declared: unto the pure all things are pure'" (Sozomen, *Historia Ecclesiastica*, lib. I, cap. 11). Unto the martyr Attalus there was a revelation concerning his fellow-martyr Alcibiades, who ate nothing save bread and water, that the latter "did not do well in refusing to make use of the creatures of God, and thereby leaving an example of stumbling unto others" (Eusebius, *Historia Ecclesiastica*, lib. V, cap. 3).

[^1338]: Since the lunar year is shorter than the solar year by 11 and 1/4 days, among those who use lunar reckoning (the Semites) an addition of an intercalary month unto the year is made from time to time; to equalize both reckonings it is necessary in 8 lunar years to make 3 intercalary months. The supplementary month among the Jews was added unto the last month of the year, Adar (corresponding unto February), and was called "Veadar," "another Adar." Yet in that epoch such intercalations were not regulated and depended upon the arbitrary discretion of influential rabbis. And if an intercalation was not made in timely fashion, Pascha fell before spring. In the Talmud there is preserved an epistle of Rabbi Gamaliel (the teacher of the Apostle Paul) unto Babylon and Media: "We inform you that since the pigeons (for sacrifice) are still too tender and the lambs too young, and the season of Aviv (= Nisan, the first spring month) hath not yet arrived, we, in agreement with our colleagues, have deemed it necessary to add 30 days unto the year" (Kellner, *Heortologie*, S. 34). For this reason in every year a special announcement was required concerning the advent of Pascha. When the Sanhedrin existed, it dispatched annually throughout all Palestine special messengers with an announcement as to from which day the beginning of the month of Nisan was to be counted and upon which day Pascha would fall; and in order to make this known unto the Euphrates Jews as well, at the Nisan new moon fires were kindled upon the Mount of Olives and following it upon other mountains as far as Babylonia itself (V. Rybinsky, *On Pilgrimage unto Jerusalem in Biblical Times* [*O palomnichestve v Ierusalim v bibleyskoye vremya*], *Trudy Kievskoy Dukhovnoy Akademii* [1909], no. 11, p. 499).

[^1377]: For the feast upon the 40th day after Pascha there is no mention of such a Gospel or in general of any commemoration of the Ascension. It may be that the Ascension and the Descent of the Holy Spirit were celebrated together at Pentecost. In general these two festivals were not yet everywhere segregated. Thus the Council of Elvira (ca. 305 AD) decrees: 'It behooveth to correct the erroneous practice according unto the testimony of the Scriptures and for all to celebrate the day of Pentecost; otherwise whoever acteth not thus shall declare himself the introducer of a new heresy' (Canon 43). An ancient *epitome* (abbreviated collection) of this Council renders this canon thus: 'Following Pascha let the 50th day be observed, and not the 40th' (J. D. Mansi, *Sacrorum Conciliorum Nova et Amplissima Collectio*, t. II, col. 13). It may be that the Montanists, who believed that only in Montanus did the Holy Spirit first appear upon earth, were opposed unto the celebration of Pentecost (K. J. von Hefele, *Conciliengeschichte*, Bd. I, Freiburg im Breisgau, 1855, S. 145).

[^1400]: The latest and most complete edition in *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, *Auctores antiquissimi*, t. IX, vol. 1, fasc. 1, Berlin, 1891. The principal sections of the collection are: *Natales Caesarum* (the birthdays of the Caesars), *Fasti consulares* (official calendar) for the year 354, a Paschal Cycle for 312–358 AD, extended by a later hand unto 410 AD, a list of Roman urban prefects unto 354 AD, the *Depositio episcoporum* (the days of the demise of Roman bishops from 255 unto 352 AD), the *Depositio martyrum* (the burial days of Roman martyrs), and a calendar of pagan festivals, inscribed and artistically illuminated by Furius Dionysius Filocalus (known from catacomb inscriptions as the calligrapher of Pope Damasus). The collection, embellished also with numerous illustrations (portraits of Caesars, views of cities), doubtless constituted a reference manual for a high dignitary; it has been preserved in a VII–VIII century manuscript. K. A. H. Kellner, *Heortologie*, S. 92.

[^1403]: Otherwise K. A. H. Kellner, *Heortologie*, S. 99. Scholars determine variously that which gave occasion unto the separation of the festival of the Nativity of Christ from Theophany. It is thought that the cessation of martyrdom exerted a partial influence here, enabling Christians to value more highly earthly life and the nativity thereof; perhaps they desired to establish a Christian festival in opposition unto the pagan feasts celebrating the December solstice. In Rome from December 18 to 23 the Saturnalia were celebrated; in correspondence unto the grim character of the god Saturn or Cronus (who devoured his own children), this was a mournful festival with gladiatorial combats (St. Cyril of Alexandria, *Contra Julianum*, lib. IV); following upon it came the joyful feast of the 'Unconquered Sun' (*Sol Invictus*), celebrated with particular splendor by Emperor Julian in honor of the rising sun and on the threshold of the new year, falling at the season when the turning of the sun had already become noticeable unto all (Emperor Julian, *Oratio IV* [*In Solem Regem*]). In the aforementioned Roman Calendar of Philocalus under December 25 there is noted: '*N(atalis) Invicti*'—'the birthday of the Unconquered': 'Unconquered' was a customary epithet of the gods, especially appropriate with respect unto the nascent sun (it is possible, however, that the birthday of the reigning emperor was so styled in this calendar, since in other months the calendar designates the birthdays of the emperors—Bishop Christopher [F. Smirnov], *The Origin and Significance of the Feast of the Nativity of Christ* [*Proiskhozhdeniye i znacheniye prazdnika Rozhdestva Khristova*], Kyiv, 1883 [al. 1893], pp. 92 et seq.). In Alexandria on December 25 there was the pagan festival of Kikellia; there were festivals in such a season in other countries as well. The supposition hath also been voiced that the Jewish feast of the Dedication of the Temple on the 25th day of the month of Kislev [al. Tebeth] (= December), unto which indications are found in the Prophets Haggai (2:15–18) and Zechariah (8:19; compare John 10:22), and that moreover in connection with Messianic predictions, could likewise have exerted an influence upon the establishment of the festival upon December 25 (F. Smirnov, *ibid.*, pp. 59 et seq.). — When the festival of the Nativity of Christ was assigned unto December 25, that day came to be accounted the day of the historical event itself. Prior unto that time the question concerning the day of the Saviour's birth was disputed. We have seen that Clement of Alexandria indicates, apparently, three opinions existing in his day regarding the day of the Saviour's birth; some assigned it unto Pachon 25 (an Egyptian month, = May 20), others unto Tybi 15 or 11 (January 10 or 6). Compare above the opinion of St. Epiphanius of Cyprus. In the III–IV century treatise *De pascha computus*, attributed unto St. Cyprian of Carthage, March 28 is accounted the day of Christ's Nativity, whereas in the inscription upon the statue of St. Hippolytus of Rome it is March 25. In the portion of St. Hippolytus's *Commentary on the Book of the Prophet Daniel* newly discovered by Georgiades (in Chalki) there is the observation: 'The first manifestation of our Lord in the flesh, wherein He was born in Bethlehem, occurred on December 25 in the 42nd year of Augustus, 5500 years from Adam; and He suffered on March 25 on a Friday, in the 18th year of Tiberius, in the consulate of Rufus and Rubellius'; but in other fragments of the same commentary (for example, in the ancient manuscript of the Chigi Library) and in the quotation of this passage by the Armenian Bishop George from 714 AD, the day of the month is not indicated here, nor is it required by the context of the commentary (K. A. H. Kellner, *Heortologie*, S. 98). Only in the IV and V centuries did fathers begin resolutely to defend the date of December 25 for the Nativity of Christ—St. John Chrysostom (see below) and Blessed Augustine (*Sermones* 190, § 1; 192, § 3; 196, § 1).

[^1442]: On the grounds that it containeth a commemoration of 'Arius, presbyter of Alexandria' and Eusebius of Caesarea, and containeth no commemorations of the Fathers of the Nicene Council, and that the martyrology was compiled during the era and in the region of Arian dominance, Western scholars almost unanimously acknowledge it to be Arian (Duchesne, Egli, Kellner). Against this it is objected (Bickell, Bolotov) that Arius here is a martyr, and such a martyr and presbyter indeed existed in Alexandria; that there is no commemoration of Eusebius of Nicomedia (an uncompromising Arian, whereas Eusebius of Caesarea was a semi-Arian); and that there is a commemoration of St. James of Nisibis, a participant in the Nicene Council (V. V. Bolotov, "Traces of the Ancient Menologia of Local Churches," *Khristianskoe Chtenie*, 1893, vol. I, pp. 177 ff.). In the martyrology, evidently, certain martyrs are entered several times; there are corruptions in the names of saints (for instance, *Axitos* instead of *Sixtus*), and especially in the names of cities; the most substantial discrepancy—if indeed it be an error—is that in comparison with the Pseudo-Hieronymian Martyrology the commemorations of June 8–30 are shifted unto the corresponding dates of July (K. A. H. Kellner, *Heortologie*, S. 196 f.).

(For Christian antiquity, fasting and feasting were almost synonymous, which is why the term *feriae* came to signify in the Roman Church initially a fast-day, and subsequently an ordinary weekday; in the Jerusalem Church the Forty Days' Fast was denominated *heortae*—festivals; cf. *Peregrinatio*, attributed to Sylvia [Egeria], § 27.)

[^1540]: With the psalms "the lesser antiphons with their alleluiatics (*allelujaticis*)..." "After Pascha until Pentecost on Fridays they take refreshment (*reficiendum*) once, and after the 12th (hour) there are six *missae*, that is, 18 readings must be pronounced from memory and then 18 psalms, 3 antiphons; after the nocturn there must be 3 *missae* from the book until daybreak." This obscure passage of Caesarius presumably prescribes throughout the entire period of Pentecost on Friday evenings before Saturday especially long vigils from 6 p.m. Friday without supper until the very dawn of Saturday (cf. in Cassian, above p. 162), whereby the customary vigil of 18 psalms was preceded by 18 readings and followed by yet 3 readings. All this is in the *Regula ad virgines*, § 66. Caesarius describes the night service more briefly in the *Regula ad monachos*: "The vigils from October until Pascha comprise two nocturns and three *missae* (readings): at one *missa* a brother reads three folios and they pray; he reads another three folios and arises, say an antiphon, a responsory, and another antiphon; the antiphons being according unto the order of the Psalter; at the 1st *missa* the reading is concerning the resurrection and at it all stand" (canon 21).

[^1545]: In Rome already under Pope Gregory I the Great there existed a martyrology with commemorations for each day of the year, as is evident from the reply of this pope in 598 unto the request of Eulogius, Patriarch of Alexandria, to send him the *Acts of All the Martyrs* collected by Eusebius of Caesarea; replying unto the patriarch that no such collection was found in the Roman archives, the Pope writes: 'But we possess a collection in one codex of the names of almost all the martyrs, with an indication of their passions for all days, and daily we celebrate masses in their honor; however, in this volume it is not shown how each suffered, but only the name, place, and day of the passion are indicated... We think that you also possess this, most blessed brother' (Gregory the Great, *Registrum epistolarum* VIII, 29). Blessed Jerome is considered the compiler of the most ancient Roman martyrology that has come down unto us, on the basis of the testimonies of Cassiodorus († 563): 'Read the passions of the martyrs, which you will find, among other places, in the letter of Jerome unto Chromatius and Heliodorus' (*De institutione divinarum litterarum*, c. 32; Migne, *Patrologia Latina*, Vol. 70, col. 1147), and of Bede († 735): '...a martyrology which by name and preface is attributed unto Blessed Jerome, although Jerome was not its author, but its translator, while the author, they say, was Eusebius' (*Liber retractationis in Acta Apostolorum*, c. 1; Migne, *PL*, Vol. 92, col. 997). The correspondence of Blessed Jerome with Bishops Heliodorus and Chromatius is appended unto the copies of the Hieronymian Martyrology; these bishops requested that he send them from Caesarea the calendar (*feriales*) of Eusebius for the greater veneration of the martyrs—in which Gregory, Bishop of Cordova, was especially renowned, as was revealed at a certain Council of Milan, celebrating 'on every non-fasting day morning masses, and during fasts evening masses, and commemorating therein many names of martyrs'; Blessed Jerome, in place of the calendar of Eusebius, sends unto the bishops his own, wherein, according unto his epistle, he 'inscribed the feasts for each month and for each day; but since for each day there occurred more than 800–900 names of martyrs of diverse regions, and for no single day, except January 1, fewer than 500, he records only the more renowned.' The authenticity of this correspondence is doubtful, since the style here is not Jerome's; and apart from it, the compilation of the martyrology by Blessed Jerome is corroborated by nothing else: neither he himself, nor Gennadius of Marseilles († after 495) in his work *De scriptoribus ecclesiasticis*, nor Gregory the Great speaks of such a compilation; furthermore, the martyrology contains commemorations later than Blessed Jerome. It was published according unto a 10th-century MS in Migne, *Patrologia Latina*, Vol. 30, and by the Bollandists, *Acta Sanctorum*, Novembris tomus II, Brussels, 1894, according unto 8th-century MSS (edited by Giovanni Battista de Rossi and Louis Duchesne).
[^1546]: If in the second century mass slaughters of Christians were represented by a figure of no more than 40 (Lyons, 177), then in the third century and especially under Diocletian the martyrs were numbered in the thousands; the magnitude of the figure here therefore excites no suspicion, nor does the frequent repetition of certain names (Felix 118 times, Saturninus 87, etc.), as well as the strangeness of other names (*Manira*, *Jtercola*, *Barbalabia*); one must bear in mind the Roman custom of showing no restraint in assigning nicknames unto slaves.

[^1549]: Of other menologia in the West during this period are known: 1) that published by Leo Allatius (*De Ecclesiae Occidentalis atque Orientalis perpetua consensione*, Rome, 1648, p. 1487) from an 8th-century Breviary of the Vatican Library; of its 84 commemorations, half are present among us; certain commemorations fall on the same dates as among us, and not as at present among Roman Catholics; there is no Transfiguration nor Entry into the Temple; not all Apostles are present; from March 12 to April 14 there are no saints. 2) The calendar in the Sacramentary attributed unto Gregory the Great, 7th–8th century; similar unto the preceding, yet certain commemorations are lacking, while certain ones are new; all the Apostles are present. 3) The Gallican: the latest commemoration is that of St. Gregory the Great († 604); commemorations occur for all days, yet August 16 to December is defective. 4) That of Protasius, Bishop of Besançon († 625); similar unto the Sacramentary of Gregory; in March there are only 5 commemorations; later commemorations, such as Charlemagne, were inserted by another hand.—In addition, there appeared a whole series of abbreviations of the Hieronymian Martyrology. Such an abbreviation was first of all the martyrology of Bede († 735), the renowned English monk and writer, 'who strove carefully to note by what manner of torment and under which judge the martyrs conquered the world,' for which reason he retained for each day from the Hieronymian Martyrology only one or two saints, and left certain days without any commemorations at all. Nevertheless, the martyrology of Bede hath come down unto us only in the redaction expanded c. 830 by Florus Drepanius, canon of the diocese of Lyons; in this latter redaction, likewise, commemorations do not occur for all days. This last martyrology was reworked (with rearranged commemorations) and slightly augmented: in the diocese of Trier by Wandalbert c. 848; in Mainz by Archbishop Rabanus Maurus in the mid-9th century (commemorations for all days); in Lyons c. 858 by Ado, subsequently Archbishop of Vienne (containing very extensive narratives concerning the saints, beginning on December 25); by Usuard, a Benedictine near Paris, c. 858; and by Notker in Switzerland c. 894. (Archbishop Sergius, *Polnyi mesiatseslov Vostoka*, Vol. I, pp. 62–73.)

That the akathist kontakia and ikoi could originally have been composed for the Annunciation and only later adapted unto the commemoration of the war, apart from their content, is evident from variants in the 1st kontakion: 'Thy servants' (*rabi tvoi*), 'Thy servant' (*rab tvoi*), 'the city' (*grad*). [^1571]: Poetic meter in Greek ecclesiastical hymnography was discovered very recently by Cardinal Pitra (*Hymnographie de l'église grecque*, Rome, 1867; the book was reviewed by A. Vasiliev, 'O grecheskikh tserkovnykh pesnopeniiakh' [On Greek Church Hymns], in *Vizantiiskii Vremennik*, St. Petersburg, 1896, Vol. III, pp. 582 ff.). Prior unto this, it was believed that Greek ecclesiastical hymnody followed the rhythm of biblical poetry, concerning whose nature scholars still dispute, though the majority reduce it unto parallelism of members. Moreover, 17th-century scholars vaguely presaged Pitra's discovery. Thus Baronius observed that in manuscripts of canons there is punctuation that at times runs counter unto the sense and serves, apparently, to preserve a certain meter (Baronius, *Annales ecclesiastici*, Mainz, 1601, p. 1054 [Skaballanovich prints Moguntiae 1501, an obvious typographical error for 1601]). Vagnereck (*Pietas Mariana*, Munich, 1647, p. 32) states that upon reading the Menaia he seemed to hear as it were the voice of an unknown muse.

[^1574]: A difference here is introduced by organs. Yet they appeared in Roman Catholic worship very late. Although the *Liber Pontificalis* attributes unto Pope Vitalian († 671) the introduction of the organ into Italian churches, and a number of historians repeat the report concerning the sending of an organ by Constantine Copronymus unto Pepin in 757 and by Emperor Michael I unto Charlemagne, nevertheless even in the 9th–12th centuries the organ encountered opponents in the West: among these were the renowned liturgist Amalarius (9th c.), the Scottish [English Cistercian] Abbot Aelred (12th c.), the most eminent theologian Thomas Aquinas, and later Erasmus (Luft, *Liturgik*, Vol. II, p. 258; Binterim, *Die vorzüglichsten Denkwürdigkeiten*, Vol. IV, Part 1, p. 55; Archbishop Philaret [Gumilevsky], *Istoricheskii obzor pesnopentsev*, p. 264).

Dmitrievsky from a 10th-century manuscript of the Patmos Library, No. 266, in *Opisanie liturgicheskikh rukopisei* [Description of Liturgical Manuscripts], Vol. I: *Τυπικά*, Kyiv, 1890, pp. 1–153. In addition unto this copy of the Sophia Typikon, two others are known at present: one in the Jerusalem Patriarchal Library, No. 40, of the 10th–11th century (reported by A. Papadopoulos-Kerameus in *Ἰεροσολυμιτικὴ βιβλιοθήκη*, St. Petersburg, 1897, p. 80); and another in the Dresden Royal Library, No. 104 (described in detail for the first time by A. Dmitrievsky, *Drevneishie patriarshie Tipikony Sviotogr. Ierus. i Velik. Konstantinopol'sk. tserkvi* [The Most Ancient Patriarchal Typika of the Holy Sepulchre of Jerusalem and of the Great Church of Constantinople], Kyiv, 1907, pp. 214 ff.). The most ancient is the Patmos redaction: the latest commemorations therein are Ignatius, Archbishop of Constantinople († 877), and the dedication of the Church of All Saints in the Boule, built by Leo VI in memory of his consort Theophano († 894) during her lifetime; there is also the 'commemoration of the Holy Martyr Bacchus, who suffered in our days under Irene (797–802) and Constantine (VI, 780–797)'; the feast of the Image Not Made with Hands on August 16, established in 944, is absent. The Jerusalem manuscript was written by order of Constantine VII Porphyrogenitus (912–959): the latest commemoration is Tryphon, Patriarch of Constantinople († 933). In the Dresden manuscript the Image Not Made with Hands is already present, as is likewise on January 25 the translation of the relics of Gregory the Theologian from Arianzus unto Constantinople, which occurred in 950; yet the commemoration of the Three Hierarchs on January 30, established in 1084, is absent.

The grounds for this are the coincidence of later (9th–10th c.) redactions of both in certain minor details (for example, the distribution of the so-called *roga*—stipends or gifts—by the patriarch on great feasts, the chanting of certain hymns by cantors upon the ambo and others by monks, spoudaioi, etc.) and in a few rites: both possess *trithekte* and the *pannychis* (A. Dmitrievsky, *Drevneishie patriarshie Tipikony*, pp. 144, 147, 206, 208, 298). Yet the structure of the daily office according unto both Typika is entirely different: in the Jerusalem Typikon of the 9th century, at least, this structure is far closer unto our present order than unto that of Constantinople at that time, and concerning earlier worship in either church we know nothing (leaving aside the description of Sylvia [Egeria]).

The 'Order' (*Taxis*) of the Athos-St. Andrew 15th-century manuscript and the musical manuscript *Papadike Techne* (*Παπαδικὴ τέχνη* [printed *Παλαδικὴ*]) of the 14th century of the Vatopedi Monastery Library No. 297 (931) depict in greater detail the Entrance, the singing of the Doxology, and the reading of the Gospel. The cantors chant **"Most blessed art thou"** only up unto the words: **"Blessed is Christ our God"**. At the Entrance the domestikos pronounces in an elevated voice these words of the Theotokion (musical MS); at the Entrance between the preceding candlebearers walks the reader in a (short) phelonion with the large cross (aforementioned); upon the entrance of the priests into the altar, he ascends two steps of the ambo and here pronounces in chant the beginning of the Doxology: **"Glory to God in the highest"** ('Order'). 'And the domestikos begins the sweet-sounding hymn (*ᾀσματικὸν ὕμνον*), that is, the Doxology, while the priests pronounce the remainder. (Following the Doxology) the domestikos: **"Having risen from the tomb and burst the bonds…"**, and the priests say the remainder. Then the domestikos: **"Glory to the Father, and to the Son…"**, and again the priests: **"Having risen from the tomb"**; the domestikos with a high voice: **"Having risen. A Psalm of David"**, and immediately the reader says: **"Arise, O Lord"** (musical MS). According unto the 'Order', the reader, following the Great Doxology, 'chants melodically: **"A Psalm of David"** and the remaining verses. The reader departs, and the domestikos or laosynaktes (*λαοσυνάκτης*) ascends unto the 3rd step of the ambo and chants the prokeimenon with the remaining readers; the domestikos likewise chants the musical intonation (*ἤχημα* / *ἤχισμα*) at the endings'. The verses unto the prokeimenon are indicated by the musical manuscript: **"I will confess Thee, O Lord…"**; **"I will be glad…"**; and further the rubric: *Θεσσαλονικαῖον* (according unto the Thessalonian order?): **"O Lord my God, let Thy hand be lifted up"**; *ἡ μεγάλη δοχή* (the great feast / agape feast): **"Arise, O Lord [my God, let Thy hand be lifted up,] forget not Thy poor unto the end"** [LXX Ps. 9:33 / 10:12]. Further according unto the 'Order', the priest in full sacerdotal vestments carries the Gospel, preceded by readers with two candlesticks and two deacons, ascends the ambo and sits with the deacons until the conclusion of the prokeimenon, after which is sung: **"Prolong the holy empire of our sovereigns"** and **"The Master…"** (*Τὸν δεσπότην*); at these hymns the sacred ministers stand up; upon the reading of the Gospel upon the ambo by the presbyter, it is borne by the deacon unto the hierarch to be kissed, and is carried into the altar by the deacon, preceded by the reader with the cross and accompanied by the presbyter (Dmitrievsky, *Τυπικά*, p. 164).

A., *Opisanie liturgicheskikh rukopisei*, Vol. II: *Εὐχολόγια*, p. 1110; Vol. I: *Τυπικά*, p. 152. — Similar litanies existed and still exist in the Western Church: such are the *litania major* on April 25 on the feast of the Apostle Mark, and the *litania minor* or *rogationes* (petitions) on the three days before Ascension. The designations 'major' and 'minor' do not correspond unto the comparative solemnity of these litanies, but are explained historically: the former was instituted earlier (in all probability by Pope Liberius in the 4th century) in place of the very solemn pagan procession *ambarvale* (from *arva*, field—a procession into the fields, in contrast unto *amburbale*, a city procession, to propitiate the goddess Robigo, upon whom depended mildew [*robigo*] upon crops; for which reason April 25 was termed *Robigalia*); Pope Gregory the Great regulated the Christian litany that replaced this pagan procession, appointing seven distinct corporations of Rome (clergy, men, monks, handmaids, married women, widows, and the poor with children) to go forth with the litany from different churches (whence the name *litania septiformis*; *Epistolae*, II, 2). The *litania minor* was first instituted circa 470 by Bishop Mamertus of Vienne on account of earthquakes and other calamities; it was legalized for Gaul by the Council of Orléans in 511 (Canon 27); in the 6th century it received wide dissemination, yet in Rome it was adopted only under Pope Leo III (795–816). On the days of these litanies, especially the second, services were exceptionally lengthy; in the 9th century in certain churches heads were sprinkled with blessed ashes, sprinkled with holy water (as is still done at present according unto the Ambrosian rite), and all walked barefoot (according unto Canon 33 of the Council of Mainz [*Concilium Moguntinum*] of 813). A number of orders have been preserved for the minor litany: according unto them, following a series of antiphons and psalms there was a supplication very similar unto our litany **"Let us all say"** (it begins indeed: *Dicamus omnes, Domine miserere*); following a series of other antiphons reminiscent in general content of our penitential troparia, there followed a litany in the proper sense, termed *statio* (station, since it was performed at the stopping-places of the procession) or *oratio* (from the frequent singing of *ora*—'pray'), consisting of a long series of petitions (at times exceeding 100), addressed for the most part in order unto all the most renowned saints and executed antiphonally (by clergy and choir), for example: *Sancta Maria, ora pro nobis*; *Sancte Michael, ora*; *Sancte Gabriel, ora* or *intercede* ('intercede'); for the more venerated and intimate saints 'pray for us' (*ora pro nobis*), and for the others simply 'pray' (*ora*) (Martène, *De antiquis ecclesiae ritibus*, Vol. II, pp. 514 ff.; Kellner, *Heortologie*, p. 127).
[^1607]: Preserved in a manuscript of the year 1122 in the Jerusalem Patriarchal Library. It may be assigned unto the 10th century because on the litany occurs the name of Patriarch Nicholas (857–887 with an interruption), and the topography of the holy places corresponds unto their condition following the restoration from the Persian conquest under Patriarch Modestus (610–637) down to the devastation under Caliph al-Hakim in 1010. Published in full by A. Papadopoulos-Kerameus, *Ἀνάλεκτα Ἱεροσολυμιτικῆς σταχυολογίας*, St. Petersburg, 1894, Vol. II; in abridgment (the initial words of the hymns) with translation and extensive notes by A. A. Dmitrievsky, *Bogosluzhenie strastnoi i paskhal'noi sedmits vo sviatom Ierusalime IX–X v.* [Divine Worship of Passion and Paschal Weeks in Holy Jerusalem in the 9th–10th Centuries], Kazan, 1894 (where the chronology of the monument is established on p. XIII).

He was likewise a gifted hymnographer.
